exp.22:18:
God gives two commands. First, to bring to the house of the Lord the best of the first harvest, that is, the firstfruits. The firstfruits are the first portion gathered from the harvest. Second, not to cook a young goat in its mother's milk.

Here God himself speaks, through Moses, to the people of Israel who had just come out of Egypt. These laws stand alongside the rules for the three yearly feasts. The reason for the second command is not explained; some think it opposed a certain pagan custom, but this is not certain. Others see a call to compassion and respect for life.

For today: before I spend my money and my time on my own things, I can first set something aside for God, with gratitude, and treat with tenderness the people around me.
exp.11:18:
For seven days there must be no leaven found in any Israelite house. Whoever eats bread that has been leavened, whether born in Israel or a foreigner living among them, would be "cut off from the congregation," that is, separated from the people. Leavened bread is bread made with yeast, and a stranger born in the country is someone who was born there.

God speaks through Moses just as Israel is about to leave Egypt. The bread without leaven would remind them that they left in haste and that God delivered them. Scholars understand "cut off" in different ways: exclusion from the people or, perhaps, a more severe punishment. The text does not specify. Later, the New Testament uses leaven as an image of sin that spreads (1 Corinthians 5:6-8).

For today: ask God to show you a small habit that gradually draws you away from Him, and decide to remove it from your life, with gratitude for having been set free.
exp.24:21:
God tells Moses that he will meet with him in a very special place: above the lid of the ark, between the two cherubim. From there he will speak to him and give him his commands for the people. The lid of the ark is called the mercy seat. The tablets of the law kept inside are the covenant. The phrase "I will reveal myself" means that he will make himself known.

God himself speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai while giving him instructions for building the tabernacle. He has just freed Israel from Egypt and wants to dwell among his people. The ark would be the center of that meeting, where God would guide his people with his word.

God is not distant; he desires to speak with us. Today we can look for quiet places to pray and read the Bible, with a heart ready to listen and obey what he shows us.
exp.35:12:
He says that Bezalel and the craftsmen made fifty clasps, that is, hooks of gold. With them they joined the two large sets of curtains, which already had blue loops along their edges. So the curtains were hooked together and formed one single tabernacle, the sacred tent. Here "jacinth" refers to a blue or violet-blue color.

It is a narrative passage from Moses. It tells how the people of Israel carried out, step by step, the instructions God gave on the mountain (Exodus 26) to build a place where He would dwell among them. Here the work already completed is described, with great detail and obedience.

For today: God cares about the details and joins together what is separated. We can ask Him for help to do faithfully even the small and hidden tasks, and to value what keeps us united as a community of faith.
exp.1:19:
Reuel asks his daughters where the man who helped them is. He scolds them for leaving him there and asks them to call him so that he may eat with them.

Speaking is Reuel, also called Jethro, priest of Midian. His daughters have just come back earlier than usual, because an Egyptian defended them from some shepherds and helped them with the water. Moses had fled from Egypt, and here he is a stranger without a home. The invitation opens the door to his new life in Midian.

When someone does us a kindness, it is not enough to stay grateful in our hearts. Reuel wanted to respond with concrete hospitality. Today we can do the same: invite to a meal the one who helped us, or the one who is alone or far from home.
exp.11:46:
This verse says that the whole people of Israel had to celebrate the Passover. The word "congregation" refers to the gathered community, and the lamb is what the verse calls the Passover lamb. No one was left out of this celebration.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron, just before the departure from Egypt, and gives them the instructions for the Passover. It was kept in the homes, but it was a celebration of the whole people, remembering how God freed them. The following verses explain that a foreigner could take part if he accepted the sign of the covenant, circumcision.

For today: faith is lived in community. Although each family or person has their own relationship with God, he calls us to remember and give thanks together. Seek to take part in your church and encourage others to join.
exp.19:14:
It says we must not steal. The word "steal" is an old-fashioned term that means taking something that belongs to someone else without permission and in secret. It is a short commandment, but a clear one: what belongs to others is to be respected.

Here God Himself speaks. He says it to the people of Israel, who had just been freed from slavery in Egypt, at Mount Sinai. These commandments taught them how to live as God's people, loving God and caring for others. Some scholars think this command also includes kidnapping people, though this is debated.

Today we can apply it by being honest in everyday life: paying what is fair, not copying other people's work, not using work time for personal matters, and returning what we borrow. In this way we show that we trust God to take care of us.
exp.32:10:
This verse says that God spoke with Moses in a very close and sincere way, face to face, the way a person speaks with a friend. Then Moses would return to the camp, but Joshua, his young assistant, stayed behind in the tabernacle, which here was a tent of meeting set apart from the camp.

The people had just sinned with the golden calf. Moses had pitched the tent far from the camp, and there God met with him in the pillar of cloud. The phrase "face to face" expresses an intimate relationship; it does not mean that Moses saw the whole of God's being, since later God tells him that he cannot see his face.

For today: God wants a close relationship with you. Look for time alone to pray and listen to his Word. And like Joshua, value those quiet moments and stay a little longer in God's presence.
exp.24:10:
God tells Moses that the ark, made of acacia wood (Shittim), must be covered with pure gold, both inside and outside. In addition, it must have a crown of gold running around it, meaning a decorative molding or rim of gold that went around the top edge of the ark.

Here God speaks from Mount Sinai, giving Moses instructions for building the tabernacle and its furnishings. The ark would be the most sacred place, where the tablets of the law would later be kept. God insists on faithfully following the pattern He showed. Scholars often see in the wood and the gold a picture of the human and the divine, though the text itself does not explain this.

For today: God cares about the details of how we come near to Him. We can give Him our best time and heart, not only what shows on the outside, but also what is within.
exp.31:32:
God answers Moses that He will punish every person who sins against Him. To "blot out" means to erase or remove something, as when a written mark is scraped away. "His book" is an image of a record of those who belong to God. Where the source explains its own quoted wording, the reader is simply given the meaning of the verse in plain terms.

Moses speaks with God after the people made a golden calf to worship it. Moses asked that God forgive the people, or else that God blot him out of the book. God does not accept that exchange: each person answers for his or her own sin. Scholars discuss whether this passage speaks of earthly life or of eternal salvation; the Bible does not fully explain it here.

Today we can learn that God takes sin seriously, and that no one is saved by the faith of another. Even so, we can imitate Moses: pray with love for those who have turned away, and ask for mercy on their behalf.
exp.17:23:
It says that Moses listened to the advice of his father-in-law, Jethro, and carried it out completely. "Heard the voice" here means paying attention and obeying, not merely hearing sounds. "Did all that he had said" means that he did not carry out only part of the advice.

Jethro, the priest of Midian, saw that Moses spent the whole day judging the people's disputes and was wearing himself out. He proposed choosing capable men to handle the small cases, so that Moses would keep the serious ones. This verse shows Moses' response: humility to accept correction, even though it came from someone outside Israel.

For today: learn to listen to wise advice and to share responsibilities. No one has to carry everything alone. Asking for help and entrusting tasks to others is not weakness, but good stewardship of the strength God gives us.
exp.2:1:
This verse tells us that the angel of the Lord appeared to Moses in a flame of fire, in the middle of a bush, which is a thorny shrub. Moses saw that the bush was burning, but it was not being consumed.

The narrator tells what happened while Moses was tending the sheep of his father-in-law near Mount Horeb. In the verses that follow, the one who speaks from the bush is the Lord himself. For this reason, many believers see in this "angel" a special manifestation of God; others understand him as a messenger who speaks on God's behalf. God was about to call Moses to a mission.

God often gets our attention in the middle of everyday life. Moses stopped to look carefully, and that opened the door to the conversation. Today we too can pause from our daily work to listen to God.
exp.25:18:
God commands that forty bases of silver be made, which were the bases or pedestals. Each board of the tabernacle rested on two bases, one for each "socket," that is, a tenon or projection on the lower part that fit into the base. Since there were twenty boards on this side, forty bases were needed.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai and gives him detailed instructions for building the tabernacle, the tent where He would dwell in the midst of Israel. The bases gave firmness to the whole structure. Scholars explain the symbolism of the silver in different ways, so it is wise not to claim more than the text says.

For today: God cares even about the foundations and the details no one sees. We can ask Him for help to take care of what is hidden in our lives, such as prayer, honesty, and perseverance, because that is where everything else is held up.
exp.1:20:
Here is the explanation of Exodus 2:21 in plain English.

It says that Moses agreed to stay and live with that man, Reuel (also called Jethro), a priest of Midian. And that man gave him his daughter Zipporah as a wife. Here, "was content" means that he agreed or decided. To dwell means to live or stay.

This is part of the story, told by the narrator. Moses had fled from Egypt after killing an Egyptian. He arrived in Midian, defended the daughters of this priest at the well, and they told their father what he had done. Then their father invited him to eat and to stay. So Moses found a home and family in a foreign land.

For today: God can care for us and give us a place during seasons of flight, waiting, or loneliness. Although Moses felt far from his people, God was preparing him. We can trust that no season is wasted in His hands.
exp.32:22:
God tells Moses that, after his glory has passed by, he will take away his hand and Moses will be able to see his back. But his face will not be seen. "Back" is a way of speaking: Moses will see only a part of God's presence, not all of it. Many understand that this shows God is holy and is above what a person can bear to see.

The Lord speaks with Moses after the sin of the golden calf. Moses has asked to see God's glory (v. 18), and God answers him with mercy: he protects him in the cleft of the rock and allows him to see only what he can endure. Scholars explain in various ways what the "back" means, and we should not claim more than the text says.

For today: we can draw near to God with confidence, but also with humility. We do not understand everything, and yet he cares for us and makes himself known as he knows we need.
exp.18:19:
This verse tells us that God came down to Mount Sinai, to the very top, and from there called Moses. Moses went up. The word "came down" refers to God making himself present in a visible way, and "top" is the peak of the mountain.

The people of Israel were camped at the foot of the mountain, and God was about to give them his law. There was smoke, fire, trembling, and the sound of a trumpet. The narrator describes how God chose Moses as the go-between between himself and the people. Afterward, God asks Moses to warn the people not to come near, because God is holy.

For today: God invites us to draw near to him, but with respect and gratitude. Before we pray or read the Bible, we can pause for a moment and remember who God is, with a humble heart ready to obey.
exp.4:8:
Pharaoh says he wants the work of the Israelites to be made harder and heavier. The phrase about the burden being made heavier means that more work should be laid on them. This way they will be so busy that they will have no time to listen to lying words. With that expression, Pharaoh is referring to what Moses and Aaron were telling them on behalf of God.

Pharaoh, king of Egypt, is speaking to his taskmasters. Moses and Aaron had asked him to let the people go to worship God in the wilderness. He refused, accused them of being idle, and took away the straw for making bricks without lowering the quota required of them.

For today: when life is full of pressure and weariness, it is easy for the voice of God to fade away. Set aside a little time each day, even a brief one, to pray and read his Word. And remember that when the work presses hard, God does not forget you.
exp.13:10:
The Israelites confront Moses with sarcasm and anger: "Was it because there were no graves in Egypt that you brought us out to die in the wilderness?" They ask him why he brought them out of Egypt.

The people speak out of deep fear. They have just left slavery, but now the sea lies before them and Pharaoh's army is behind them. Although they had cried out to God, they quickly blame Moses. Their complaint shows how hard it was for them to trust when they could see no way out.

When fear grips us, it is easy to forget what God has already done and to long for what is familiar, even when it was painful. Today we can pause, remember how God has helped us before, and honestly tell Him our fear, trusting that He can open a way where we cannot see one.
exp.30:9:
It says that God also commanded that special clothing be made for service in the sanctuary: the holy garments for Aaron the priest, and those for his sons. That clothing was so that they could carry out the priesthood. The word for "carry out" means to fulfill or perform that work. The phrase about the cloths of service probably refers to work clothing for the sanctuary, though some understand it in another way.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai. He has just named Bezalel and Oholiab as craftsmen filled with his Spirit to build the tabernacle and everything inside it. This list shows that nothing was done by chance: God cared for every detail of his place of meeting with the people.

For today: God values that we serve him with order, respect, and dedication. Today, our service does not depend on special clothing, but on a prepared heart. Before serving in your church or in your home, ask God to clothe you with humility, love, and sincerity.
exp.15:6:
Moses tells the Israelites that in the morning they will see the glory of the Lord, his power and presence. God has heard their complaints, which in reality are aimed against Him. Moses and Aaron ask, "What are we?", meaning that they are nothing more than servants.

Moses speaks to the people who had just come out of Egypt, now in the wilderness. They were hungry and complaining, even wishing to return to Egypt. Moses makes clear that God hears them and that He is going to provide food for them. Their complaints against the leaders were ending up as complaints against God, who had led them.

For today: when you feel like complaining, remember that God hears you. Instead of grumbling, bring your need to Him in sincere prayer and trust that He cares for you.
exp.4:21:
Moses speaks to God with an honest complaint. He asks why God has allowed the people to suffer more and why God sent him at all. "Afflicts" means to cause suffering or to mistreat someone. "Returned to the LORD" means that he went back to pray to God.

Moses is the one speaking. He had gone to Pharaoh with God's message, but Pharaoh answered by increasing the workload of the Israelites. The foremen of the people blamed Moses and Aaron. Then Moses, confused and hurt, takes his pain directly to God. He does not yet see deliverance, only more suffering.

For today: when things get worse after you obey God, you do not have to pretend that everything is fine. You can bring your questions and your discouragement to him honestly, as Moses did. God did not reject him for asking, and he answered with new promises. Praying sincerely is a way of continuing to trust.
exp.7:0:
God speaks to Moses and tells him to go before Pharaoh. He is to say to him: "Let my people go, that they may serve me." The word "serve" here means worship and obey God, not just work. "Go unto Pharaoh" means "present yourself before Pharaoh."

The Lord, the God of Israel, is speaking. The Israelites had been enslaved in Egypt for many years. Several plagues had already happened, and Pharaoh kept refusing. God gives him another opportunity, with a clear warning. His desire was that his people be free to worship him.

For today: God frees us so that we may serve him with freedom and love. Today we can ask ourselves what things bind us and keep us from worshiping him. We can bring them to him in prayer, trusting that he gives us true freedom.
exp.21:7:
It says that if someone left money or goods in the house of a neighbor for safekeeping, and they were stolen, but the thief is not found, the master of the house must be brought before the judges. They would examine whether he himself had put his hand to what belonged to another. The phrase about putting one's hand to a neighbor's goods means taking the property of another person. The word for goods here refers to possessions.

God gives these laws to Israel through Moses, shortly after the Ten Commandments. They were rules for life in community. When there was no proof, the case was not settled by suspicion but before authorities. In this way both the owner of the things and the one who kept them were protected. Some scholars think there may have been some kind of oath or divine decision involved, but the text does not spell it out.

When we handle what belongs to others, we should be transparent and honest. If something is lost, it is good to face the matter openly, explain clearly, and accept that someone may examine it.
exp.26:15:
This verse describes the entrance to the courtyard of the tabernacle. It was a curtain or screen twenty cubits wide (about nine meters, although the exact measure is debated). It was blue, purple, and bright red, made of fine twined linen, and worked with embroidery. It was held up by four pillars, each with its own base.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai and gives him detailed instructions for building the tabernacle, the place where his presence would dwell with Israel. Before this verse, the curtains along the sides of the courtyard are described. Here the text speaks of the only entrance, which was beautiful and colorful in contrast to the rest of the white enclosure.

For today: God made one entrance, clear and visible. Many Christians see in it a picture of Christ, the way to God. We can draw near to Him with confidence, without seeking other paths.
exp.36:25:
It says that Bezalel covered the incense altar with pure gold: the top of it, and the sides, and the horns, the points that stood out at the corners. He also put a gold molding around it, which is the crown.

The passage is part of the account of building the tabernacle, the tent where Israel worshiped God in the wilderness. The narrator tells how the objects were made just as God had commanded Moses. This altar was used for burning incense, which symbolized prayer and worship.

For today: God deserves our best and not our leftovers. We can set aside a moment of the day, without rush or distraction, to pray with attention and gratitude, treating that time as something precious.
exp.37:29:
This verse tells us what the bronze, or copper, from the offering was used for. With it they made the sockets, the bases that held up the posts at the entrance of the tabernacle. They also made the bronze altar, its grate, and all its vessels. "Vessels" here means the containers and tools of the altar. "Tabernacle of the testimony" refers to the holy tent where the tablets of the law were kept.

The one telling the account is the author of the book, traditionally Moses. He is giving a detailed report of how the materials that the people gave freely for building the sanctuary were used. Everything was counted and recorded in order, like a reckoning of accounts.

For today: God values faithfulness and order in what is given to him. If you handle money, time, or resources for your church or family, do it with transparency and care, knowing that even the small and hidden things, like a base, hold up something important.
exp.34:30:
It says that God filled Bezalel with his Spirit, giving him wisdom, understanding, knowledge, and skill for every kind of artistic work. "Filled" here means completely full. "Knowledge" is the meaning of the word rendered as "science," and "skill" refers to manual skill or ability for creating well-made works.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel, who had already brought freewill offerings for building the tabernacle, the tent where God would dwell among them. Moses explains that God himself chose Bezalel, from the tribe of Judah, and equipped him to lead that work. The verses that follow mention work in gold, silver, bronze, stones, and wood.

For today: our abilities, whether manual, intellectual, or artistic, can be a gift from God. We can ask him to help us use them with excellence and humility, to serve others and honor him.
exp.34:8:
This verse mentions onyx stones and other precious stones that were requested as an offering. They were used for the ephod, a special garment of the priest, and for the breastplate, a piece the high priest wore over his chest. The word "breastplate" is the term used in the King James Version.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel and passes on what God commanded for building the tabernacle, the tent where God would dwell among them. He asks for freewill offerings: cloth, wood, oil, spices, and stones. Then he calls the skilled people to do the work. The exact details of how the stones were used appear in other passages of Exodus.

For today: God does not ask only for what is left over, but invites us to give joyfully from what we have that is valuable. Think about what talent, time, or resource you can offer this week to serve others and honor God.
exp.3:12:
Moses says to God: "Please, Lord, send someone else." The phrase "by the hand of him whom thou wilt send" is an old-fashioned way of putting it. It means: "send whomever you want to send, but not me." It is a polite way of refusing the mission.

Moses is standing before the burning bush. God has just called him to bring Israel out of Egypt. He had already made excuses, and God answered that he himself made the human mouth and would help him to speak. Even so, Moses keeps insisting. That is why God becomes angry, but he does not abandon him: he offers his brother Aaron as support.

For today: sometimes we make excuses when God asks us to do something difficult. He understands our fear, but he reminds us that we do not go alone. Take the step trusting in his help, and accept the support of others.
exp.24:2:
The explanation says that, among the things the people were to bring as an offering to God, the first ones on the list were gold, silver, and brass. The word "take" here means to receive or accept what the people bring. These are valuable materials, and the verse is only the beginning of a longer list.

God speaks to Moses shortly after Israel arrived at Mount Sinai. He asks for an offering to build a sanctuary where He would dwell among them. What matters is that it would be given by whoever was willing, from a willing heart. It was not a forced obligation but a freely given gift.

For today: God looks more at the heart than at the amount. We can give our time, money, or talents with joy and freedom, not out of pressure or habit, but as a response of love to Him.
exp.3:11:
God tells Moses to go, because He Himself will be with his mouth, that is, He will help him speak. He also promises to teach him what to say. "I will be in your mouth" means that God would act through his words. The words "now therefore" indicate that there are no more excuses.

God speaks from the burning bush when He calls Moses to bring Israel out of Egypt. Moses feels inadequate and says that he is "slow of speech and slow of tongue." God reminds him that He made the human mouth. Even so, Moses insists that they send someone else, and God becomes angry, yet He gives him Aaron as a helper.

When God asks you for something that seems greater than your strength, you do not have to be perfect. Place your weakness in His hands, take the step of obedience, and trust that He will give you what you need in the moment.
exp.29:23:
This verse completes the list of ingredients for the holy oil. It calls for five hundred shekels of cassia, a fragrant plant similar to cinnamon, measured by the shekel of the sanctuary, which was the official measure used in worship. It also calls for a hin of olive oil, a liquid measure of about four liters, though the exact calculation is not certain.

God speaks to Moses at Sinai and gives him an exact recipe. With this mixture the tabernacle, its furnishings, and the priests would be anointed, setting them apart as things dedicated to God. Nothing was left to improvisation.

For today: God is interested in the details when we serve him. We can give him our best, not what we have left over, and prepare ourselves with care and reverence to pray, teach, or serve in the church.
exp.31:8:
God tells Moses that He has already seen what this people is like. The phrase "stiff-necked" speaks of the neck, and describes someone stubborn, who will not bow the head or obey, like an animal that resists the yoke. The word "behold" in the verse above is an invitation to notice what God has seen.

The Lord speaks with Moses on Mount Sinai. While Moses was receiving the law, the people made a golden calf and worshiped it, forgetting what God had done in bringing them out of Egypt. God notices that this stubbornness is a pattern among them. Afterward Moses pleads for the people, and this shows that God listens to prayer.

Today we can ask ourselves in what areas of our lives we become stubborn before God. We can ask Him for a heart willing to listen to Him and, like Moses, pray also for others who have strayed.
exp.13:20:
This verse tells how Moses stretched out his hand over the sea, and God made the waters draw back with a strong east wind that blew all night. The bottom was left dry and the water was divided in two. The sea mentioned here is the body of water Israel had in front of them. The word "back" in the verse means the waters pulled away and moved aside.

The narrator describes the most critical moment of the departure from Egypt. Israel was trapped between the sea and Pharaoh's army. God, with the pillar of cloud, had already separated the two camps. Moses acts on God's command, but the text makes clear that it is God who is at work. Exactly where the crossing took place is not known, and scholars debate it.

When you find yourself with no way out, remember that God can open paths you cannot imagine. He often uses simple steps of obedience, and sometimes he does so during the night, before you see the result. Trust and take the next step.
exp.25:29:
It says that Moses was to set up the tabernacle, that is, the sacred tent where God would be present with his people, following exactly the pattern that God had shown him on Mount Sinai. "Pattern" is an old word that means plan or design. "Rear up" means that he would assemble it and stand it up.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai and gives him detailed instructions for building a place where Israel could worship him. The verses before this one describe the boards and the bars covered with gold. This verse closes that part: everything was to be done according to the model received, without changing it to suit each person's taste.

For today: when God shows us something in his Word, it is wise to obey it as it is, without adding to it or taking away from it. We can ask ourselves which area of our life we are arranging "our own way" instead of following the plan God has already given us.
exp.37:17:
The explanation says that the entrance to the courtyard of the tabernacle had a special curtain or covering, embroidered with threads of blue (hyacinth), purple and scarlet, and with fine twined linen, that is, thin thread tightly woven. It was twenty cubits long (about nine meters, although the exact measure is debated) and five cubits high, the same as the other curtains of the courtyard. "Embroidered" means decorated with ornamental needlework. "Hanging" here is the curtain of the gate.

It is part of a account in the book of Exodus, traditionally written by Moses. It describes how the people of Israel built the tabernacle following the instructions God had given them. The white curtains surrounded the courtyard, and this colorful gate was the only entrance. Many see here a sign that people approached God by a way that He had marked out.

For today: God cares about details and wants us to come near to Him with reverence. We can set aside a few minutes of quiet prayer before beginning the day, remembering that He welcomes us.
exp.10:5:
This verse says that, when every firstborn dies, there will be a very great wailing throughout all of Egypt. It will be a grief so strong that nothing like it has ever been seen and nothing like it will ever be seen again.

Moses speaks to Pharaoh on behalf of God. Nine plagues have already come, and Pharaoh still will not let the people of Israel go. This is the warning of the last plague. The text shows that God judges hardness of heart and oppression. At the same time, it distinguishes between Egypt and Israel, and it protects his own people.

For today: This passage reminds us that God takes injustice seriously and that his warnings are real. We can respond with humility, listening to his voice in time and not hardening our hearts. We can also trust that he cares for his people.
exp.35:14:
This verse gives the measurements of each curtain made of goat's hair: thirty cubits long and four cubits wide. The eleven curtains were exactly the same size. A cubit was the distance from the elbow to the tip of the finger; it is usually estimated at about 45 centimeters, though the exact measure is debated.

The passage is part of the account of the building of the tabernacle. The one telling it is the author of the book, traditionally Moses. Bezalel and the craftsmen do the work just as God had commanded it. These curtains formed a tent that covered and protected the tabernacle.

For today: God cares about small details and expects faithful obedience. We can serve him with care in everyday life, without thinking that something is unimportant, because what is done faithfully has value before him.
exp.20:6:
It says that if a man sold his daughter as a maidservant, she did not go free in the sixth year as the menservants did. A "maidservant" was a young woman who remained in the service of a household, and "sell" here is usually understood as an arrangement made out of poverty, often with a view to marriage.

God speaks to Moses at Sinai, within the laws that follow the Ten Commandments. These rules regulated customs that already existed in that time and set limits to protect the weak. The verses that follow show that protection: she could be redeemed, she could not be sold to foreigners, and she was to be treated with the rights of a daughter. Scholars discuss some details of this law.

Today we can learn that God cares for the most vulnerable. If we have power or resources, we should not take advantage of others' need, but instead protect the dignity of those who depend on us.
exp.24:27:
God tells Moses how to make the poles used to carry the table of the tabernacle. They are to be made of shittim wood, which is acacia, and overlaid with gold. They are placed through the gold rings at the corners, so the table can be carried without anyone touching it directly.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai, giving him the design of the tabernacle, the tent where he would meet with Israel while they traveled through the desert. The table would hold the bread of the presence, set before God continually. Since the people moved from camp to camp, everything had to be easy to transport, and carried in an orderly and respectful way.

For today: God cares even about the details of how what belongs to him is carried. We can serve him with order and reverence in the small and little-seen tasks, knowing that he values them.
exp.28:24:
God tells Moses to take from the hands of Aaron and his sons the bread, the cake, and the wafer that had been waved before the Lord, and to burn them on the altar along with the whole burnt offering. A burnt offering is one that is burned up completely. A pleasing aroma is a phrase showing that God receives the offering with favor. An offering made by fire means an offering burned in the fire.

God speaks to Moses giving instructions for setting apart Aaron and his sons as priests. The whole rite of consecration included sacrifices and offerings, and this passage describes one of its steps. The priests placed the offerings in their hands, and then these were burned.

For today: God does not seek only ceremonies, but surrendered hearts. We can ask ourselves what we sincerely offer to God: our time, our work, and our obedience, so that we do everything with gratitude and devotion.
exp.30:6:
This verse is part of a list of what the craftsmen were to make. It mentions the tabernacle, the sacred tent where God met with his people, and the ark of the testimony, the chest that held the tablets of the law. The "covering" is the lid of the ark, called the mercy seat. The "furniture" refers to the utensils and objects used in worship.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai. He explains that he has already chosen Bezalel and Oholiab and has given them the skill to build everything he had commanded. God wanted his dwelling among the people to be made with care and according to his instructions.

For today: God does not despise ordinary skills, such as working with wood, stone, or cloth. When we put them at the service of God and of others, they become an act of worship. Ask yourself what talent you have and how you can use it this week with gratitude.
exp.20:32:
It says that if a person opens a pit or digs a cistern (a well for storing water) and does not cover it, and an ox or a donkey falls into it, there is responsibility.

God speaks to Moses, and Moses gives Israel laws for living in justice after leaving Egypt. After the case of the ox that kills someone, this text moves on to another kind of harm: the one caused by a careless danger. The next verse clarifies that the owner of the pit must pay the owner of the animal and keep the dead animal.

Today it teaches us that we are responsible for the dangers we leave through carelessness. If we open something that can harm others, we must take care of it and repair it. For example, we can fix what is broken at home, at work, or in the church, and so love our neighbor in a practical way.
exp.19:9:
This verse says that the seventh day is a day of rest dedicated to the Lord. No one should work that day: not you, not your children, not your employees, not your animals, nor the foreigner who lives in your house or city. The words "manservant" and "maidservant" refer to those who worked for the family, and "within thy gates" means within your city or home.

God himself speaks to Israel from Mount Sinai, within the Ten Commandments, shortly after freeing them from Egypt. This command reached everyone, including servants and foreigners, and so it protected the most vulnerable from endless labor. The verses that follow connect it to God's rest when he created the world.

For today: set aside time each week to rest, pray, and be with your family, and make sure those who depend on you can rest too. Christians understand in different ways how to apply the Sabbath, but the principle of resting with God remains valuable.
exp.38:0:
It says that the craftsmen of Israel made, with threads of blue (hyacinth), purple, and scarlet, the cloths for service in the sanctuary and the holy garments for Aaron. "Serve" here means to minister in worship, that is, to serve in worship. Everything was done just as the Lord had commanded Moses.

It is part of the account in which the narrator tells how the people built the tabernacle and its furnishings. God had already given the instructions in earlier chapters. Here it is shown that they were carried out. The phrase "just as the Lord had commanded" is repeated several times in this chapter. The exact shades of the dyes are understood in different ways, but the general sense is clear.

God values obedience in the details. Today we can serve Him with faithfulness and care, even in small or little-seen tasks, doing them just as He has taught us in His Word.
exp.13:3:
God says he will harden Pharaoh's heart so that he pursues Israel. In this way God will be honored through what he does to Pharaoh and his army, and the Egyptians will know that he is the Lord. The phrase "and they did so" refers to the Israelites, who obeyed and camped where God had directed them.

God speaks to Moses just after the people left Egypt. He commands them to camp by the sea, in a place that looked like a trap. Pharaoh had already hardened his own heart before this, and the text speaks of both; believers have understood this in different ways. What is clear is that God directs the story toward his purpose.

When God leads us down a path that seems to have no way out, we can obey with confidence. He sees the end and can act even where we see only an obstacle.
exp.3:15:
God tells Moses that Aaron will speak to the people on his behalf. Aaron will be Moses' "mouth," and Moses will be "God" to Aaron, that is, the one who gives him the words he is to say.

Here the Lord speaks. Moses had made excuses, saying that he did not speak well, and God was angry, but still he gave him help. Aaron, his brother, was already coming to meet him and would be glad to see him. Moses would not be "God" in any real sense, but his representative, the one who passes on the divine message.

God does not ask us to be perfect, but to be obedient. When we feel that our ability falls short, he can give us people who walk with us. Accept the help of others with humility, and go forward with confidence.
exp.23:14:
This verse tells that Moses went up Mount Sinai, and that a cloud covered it. Here, "the mount" is the same as Sinai, and the cloud is a visible sign that God was present.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Israel had just made a covenant with God, and Moses was going up to receive instructions from Him. Before leaving, he left the elders waiting and put Aaron and Hur in charge to settle the people's matters. Then the glory of God rested on the mountain for six days, and on the seventh He called Moses.

For today: drawing near to God takes patience. Moses waited in the cloud until God spoke. We can set aside a quiet time to pray and read the Bible, unhurried, trusting that He speaks to us in His own time.
exp.13:16:
God says that he will harden the hearts of the Egyptians so that they pursue Israel into the sea. "I will get me honour" means that God will show his greatness and power through what happens to Pharaoh, his army, his chariots, and his horsemen. The sea is the sea, and the horsemen are the riders on horses.

The Lord speaks to Moses just before the sea is opened. Israel was trapped between Egypt and the water, and the people were afraid. God announces that this moment will reveal who he is. About the hardening of the heart, the Bible says that Pharaoh had already hardened his own heart earlier, and Christians explain in different ways how God's action and human decision come together.

Today: when you feel there is no way out, remember that God can work even in situations that seem lost. Trust him and take the next step of obedience, even when you do not yet see the solution.
exp.11:2:
God tells Moses and Aaron to speak with the whole people of Israel. On the tenth day of that month, each family was to choose a lamb, one for each household. The word "congregation" in the verse refers to the whole community of the people.

The LORD speaks shortly before the last plague on Egypt. God was preparing Israel for their release from slavery. This lamb would be the Passover lamb, and the verse before shows that this month would mark a new beginning for the people. Christians often see in this lamb a sign that points to Christ, though this is a reading made in light of the New Testament.

For today: God made sure that every family took part and had its place. We can ask ourselves how to live out our faith at home, through prayer, thanksgiving, and remembering together what God has done for us.
exp.6:9:
This verse tells how Moses and Aaron went before the king of Egypt and did exactly what God had told them to do. Aaron threw his staff down on the ground, in front of Pharaoh and his officials, and the staff turned into a snake. The word for "officials" in the verse refers to the king's advisers and courtiers, and the word for "became" means that the staff changed into a snake.

God had already told them that Pharaoh would ask for a sign to believe them. Moses and Aaron came in God's name to demand freedom for the people of Israel, who lived as slaves. The sign was not a show trick, but a proof that the one who sent them had real authority. Later, the magicians of Egypt would copy the sign, but Aaron's staff would end up swallowing theirs.

God does not ask his servants to be clever, but faithful. Moses and Aaron did "as the Lord had commanded," without adding or taking away anything. Today we can trust that obeying what God shows us, even when it seems small, is the right path.
exp.39:10:
God tells Moses to anoint the basin with oil, the large bronze vessel filled with water, along with its stand, that is, the base or pedestal on which it rested. To "sanctify" means to set something apart for God's service. In this way, these objects stopped being ordinary and were dedicated to a holy use.

Here God speaks to Moses, giving him instructions for setting up and consecrating the tabernacle, the tent where God would dwell among Israel. Before the priests began to serve, everything had to be set apart. The basin would be used for Aaron and his sons to wash themselves, as seen in the verses that follow.

For today: God cares about the small details when it comes to serving him. We can ask ourselves which everyday things, such as our time, work, or home, we can sincerely dedicate to God.
exp.27:7:
This verse describes the sash of the ephod, a band used to fasten this garment around the priest's body. It was to be made of the same materials and the same craftsmanship as the ephod: gold, blue, purple, scarlet, and fine twined linen. In this way everything looked like one piece, with no parts that clashed.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai and gives him instructions for the sacred garments of Aaron, the high priest. These garments set him apart to serve in the tabernacle and represented the people before God. The colors and materials were costly and beautiful, and they showed that serving God deserves care and reverence.

For today: God is concerned with details and with unity. Strive for your faith and your daily life to be of one piece, that is, for what you believe to show in what you do, even in the small things.
exp.7:3:
This verse says the frogs would not stay in the river. They would come up on the pharaoh, on his people, and on all his servants, that is, his attendants and officials. No one in the palace or in the country would be free from this plague.

The one speaking is Moses, who passes on God's warning to the pharaoh. God was asking him to let the people of Israel go to worship him, and the pharaoh kept refusing again and again. The plague would show that the God of Israel had power over the Nile, something very important to Egypt. Many scholars also see here a blow against the gods of Egypt, though this is understood in different ways.

For today: when God speaks to us and we ignore him, the consequences can reach our whole life. Let us listen to his voice soon and obey with humility, before our hearts grow hard.
exp.30:14:
God says that six days are for work, and he set apart the seventh as a sabbath, a day of rest made holy to the Lord. The phrase "dedicated to God" is replaced here by "made holy to the Lord," and the sentence about the penalty is rewritten to match the wording the reader sees: "he shall surely be put to death" was a very serious penalty for anyone who broke this command within Israel's covenant.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai and asks him to tell the people. The sabbath was the sign of the covenant between God and Israel, a reminder that he had set them apart as his own. It connects to creation, when God rested on the seventh day. Christians understand in different ways how this command applies today.

For today: set aside a regular time to rest and remember that your life depends not only on your work, but on God, who cares for you.
exp.31:22:
Aaron repeats to Moses what the people asked of him: "Make us gods which shall go before us." He says that, as for this Moses, the man who brought us up out of the land of Egypt, we do not know what has become of him, and so they felt left without a guide.

Here Aaron is speaking, trying to explain himself before Moses, who has just come down from Mount Sinai. Aaron blames the people and softens his own part. Note that, according to the account, he himself received the gold and fashioned the calf (in the verses that follow). His explanation reveals a problem: they did not trust God while they waited.

For today: when God seems slow, it is easy to look for quick solutions and point at others as to blame. Instead, we can wait in prayer, remember what God has already done for us, and honestly own our own responsibility.
exp.21:0:
It says that if someone steals an ox or a sheep, and then kills it or sells it, he must pay back much more than he took: five oxen for an ox, and four sheep for a sheep. "Steal" means to take what belongs to another, and "kill" means to slaughter the animal.

God speaks to Moses, and this is part of the laws Israel received after leaving Egypt. In a rural life, an ox or a sheep was the livelihood and the work of a family. Many believe more was paid for the ox because it also served for plowing. This is a common explanation, though the text does not give it.

For today: stealing does not only take things away, it also wounds the trust and the work of others. If we have failed someone, it is not enough to say "I'm sorry"; we should repair the harm with honesty and generosity, as a real sign of repentance.
exp.13:11:
The Israelites confront Moses angrily. They remind him that they had already asked him to leave them alone so they could keep serving the Egyptians. Now they think it was better to be slaves than to die in the wilderness.

The people speak out of fear. They have just left Egypt, but Pharaoh's army is coming up behind them and the Red Sea lies ahead. First they cried out to the LORD, and right away they blamed Moses. The earlier texts do not clearly record that request in Egypt, so their words may be an exaggeration born of the moment.

When fear arrives, it is easy to forget what God has already done and to long for what is familiar, even if it enslaves us. We can instead pause, remember his faithfulness, and wait for his help with confidence.
exp.11:4:
The explanation says the lamb for the Passover had to be perfect, with no flaw or sickness. It had to be a male and one year old. It could be chosen from the sheep or from the goats.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron in Egypt, just before the last plague. They were to pass these instructions on to all of Israel. The lamb would be sacrificed, and its blood would mark the houses so that God's judgment would pass over them. Many Christians see in this a picture of Christ, called "the Lamb of God."

For today: God deserves our best, not what we have left over. We can ask ourselves whether we give him our time, our attention, and our service sincerely, or only what is left at the end of the day.
exp.11:0:
It says that God spoke to Moses and Aaron while they were still in Egypt. "Jehovah" is the name of God, and the "á" is the old way of spelling "a". It is a short verse that opens a new set of instructions.

Here God is speaking, and he addresses the two leaders of the people. Israel was under Egyptian slavery, and several plagues had already fallen. God is about to give them directions for the Passover and for the final plague, which would bring their deliverance. Before acting, God explains to them what they were to do. The text does not say how he spoke to them, only that he did.

God often guides his people with clear words before he acts. Today we can set aside time to listen to his voice in the Bible and to pray, and trust that he shows us the next step, even in difficult situations.
exp.23:12:
Moses got up, along with Joshua, his assistant, and Moses went up the mountain of God. An "assistant" here means a personal servant or aide. "Got up" means that he set out at once to obey.

God had just called Moses to give him the stone tablets with the law. Earlier, the leaders of Israel had eaten in God's presence, after the people accepted the covenant. The one telling the story is the author of the book, traditionally Moses. Joshua appears as a companion, but the text that follows suggests that Moses continued alone toward the summit. This is not stated with complete clarity, so it is understood from the context.

When God calls, obeying means setting out. We also see the value of having companions: Moses did not go up completely alone. Seek out trustworthy people who will walk with you on your journey of faith.
exp.7:10:
Here Moses tells Pharaoh what God will do: the frogs will leave his palace, his houses, his servants, and all the people. They will remain only in the river, which is their normal place.

Moses speaks on behalf of God. Pharaoh had asked him to remove the plague, and Moses lets Pharaoh choose the timing. Pharaoh says "tomorrow," and Moses agrees so that Pharaoh will see that there is no one like the LORD. Afterward, God does what Moses asked.

For today: God is faithful to his word and hears prayer. We can pray with confidence about our problems. It is also wise not to delay a change of heart, as Pharaoh did when he said "tomorrow."
exp.28:20:
This verse says that Moses was to take blood from the altar and anointing oil, and sprinkle them on Aaron, his sons, and the garments of them all. In this way they were "hallowed," that is, set apart for God. The verse's word "sprinkle" means to scatter drops on them.

God speaks to Moses and gives him instructions for consecrating the first priests of Israel. The blood reminded them that drawing near to God requires an offering for sin, and the oil is associated with being set apart for service. Some see in the oil a symbol of the Spirit, but the text does not explain this directly.

For today: serving God does not depend on our merits, but on his provision. Christians see in Christ the fulfillment of this. We can draw near with gratitude and give him our lives and our daily work once more.
exp.16:13:
God tells Moses to write what has happened in a book, so that it will not be forgotten, and to make sure Joshua hears it. God declares that he will completely wipe out the memory of Amalek from under heaven. The word "wipe out" here means to scrape away or erase entirely, and "memory" refers to the remembrance or the name of a people.

The Amalekites attacked Israel in the desert, when the people were tired and vulnerable. Israel won the battle with Joshua at the front and Moses praying, held up by Aaron and Hur. God speaks here as a judge responding to that attack. He asks that it be put in writing so that future generations will remember both the victory and the warning.

For today: write down the times God has helped you. That remembrance will give you confidence when you come to a new weariness or a new battle.
exp.11:36:
The people of Israel left Rameses for Succoth. There were about six hundred thousand men on foot, not counting the children. The phrase "on foot" means simply walking, that is, men who traveled on foot. The Bible does not mention the women here, although they were surely there too.

This is told by the narrator of the book, which tradition attributes to Moses. After centuries of slavery and the plagues, God keeps his promise and sets his people free. Some scholars understand the number literally, and others think it has a different meaning. It is also not known with certainty exactly where these places were.

For today: God keeps what he promises, even when it takes a very long time. If you are waiting for an answer, keep trusting in him and take the next step in faith, even when you cannot see the whole way.
exp.33:14:
It says that Israel was not to make treaties of friendship or peace with the peoples who lived in Canaan. The old wording is explained this way: "go a whoring after their gods" means giving themselves over to worshiping idols, something the Bible compares to marital unfaithfulness. "Do sacrifice unto their gods" means offering animals to their gods. And "eat of his sacrifice" means Israel would be invited to take part in those religious meals.

God speaks to Moses and the people when he renews his covenant after the sin of the golden calf. He presents himself as a God who is "jealous," that is, who desires exclusive loyalty, as in a marriage. The warning aims to protect the people from returning to idolatry, beginning with small concessions such as accepting an invitation.

For today: watch over the small compromises that little by little pull you away from God. You can love and respect everyone, but do not let any friendship, custom, or pressure take the place that only God should have.
exp.27:39:
God tells Moses to make special clothing for the sons of Aaron, the priests. They are to make tunics, sashes (belts or waistbands), and caps, which are headdresses or head coverings; the note in this edition calls them tiaras. The purpose is that the clothing give glory and beauty, that is, dignity and beauty to the holy service.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai while giving him instructions for the tabernacle and the priesthood. Earlier he had already described the clothing of the high priest Aaron. Now he includes his sons, who would serve with him. The clothing set them apart from the people and showed that their work was holy, not common.

For today: serving God deserves respect and care. It is not a matter of fine clothing, but of the attitude of the heart. We can prepare with order, sincerity, and reverence whatever we do for God, whether praying, teaching, singing, or helping others.
exp.33:10:
God asks Moses to obey what he commands him this day. In return, God promises to drive out before Israel six peoples who lived in Canaan: the Amorites, Canaanites, Hittites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites. Driving them out means expelling them so that Israel can dwell in the land.

God, the Lord, is speaking after the people sinned with the golden calf. Moses interceded for them, and God renewed his covenant. This promise is linked to a warning: do not make alliances with these peoples or imitate their idolatry. Obedience would protect Israel's faithfulness.

For today: God keeps what he promises, but he calls us to respond with concrete obedience. Think of an instruction from God that you have put off, and take one simple step today to obey it, trusting that he goes before you.
exp.4:12:
The verse tells us that the taskmasters, meaning the Egyptian overseers who watched over the work, pressed the Israelites without rest. They demanded that the same number of bricks be finished each day, as if the straw were still being given to them. The word "hasted" in the verse means pushing someone hard to hurry, and "daily tasks" refers to the fixed amount of work due each day.

Moses and Aaron had asked Pharaoh for permission for the people to worship God. Pharaoh answered in anger and took away the straw needed to make bricks, but he did not reduce the quota. The taskmasters only passed on that unjust order, and the people were left burdened.

When we face unjust pressure, we can feel exhausted and confused. This passage reminds us that God sees suffering even when we do not yet see his response. We can bring our burden to him honestly, and also help those who are under pressure instead of demanding more from them.
exp.38:34:
It says that among the things brought to Moses were the ark of the testimony, with its staves, and the mercy seat. The ark was a sacred chest that held the tablets of the law. The staves were used to carry it without touching it. The mercy seat is the lid, also called the atonement cover, or the place of mercy.

Here no character speaks; the narrator is making a list. The Israelites finish building the tabernacle, the tent where God dwelt among them, and present it to Moses. It is repeated that everything was done as God had commanded, so that he could inspect it.

For today: God cares about details and values complete obedience. We can ask ourselves what small thing God asked of us that we have left unfinished. Finishing it faithfully, without rushing and with care, is also a way of worshiping him.
exp.20:28:
If an ox already had a reputation for goring, that is, for charging at people with its horns, and its owner had been formally warned but did not keep watch over it or confine it, and the animal kills a man or a woman, the ox must be stoned to death. The owner also deserves to die, because he was negligent.

God speaks to Moses, within the laws that accompany the Ten Commandments, to guide Israel as a people. The previous verse deals with the case of an ox with no history of danger, where the owner goes free. Here everything changes, because the owner knew of the risk. The law shows that human life is valuable and that responsibility grows with knowledge. The following verse allows a ransom to be paid.

If we know that something under our care can harm others, we must act in time: fix the danger, correct a bad habit, or set limits, before we grieve over the consequences.
exp.27:3:
This verse lists the holy garments that were to be made: the breastplate (called the "rational" in the source wording), the ephod (a kind of vest or priestly apron), the robe, the embroidered coat, the mitre (a turban), and the girdle. All of them were for Aaron and his sons, so that they could serve God as priests.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai while giving instructions for worship in the tabernacle. Earlier, He said these garments would be made "for glory and for beauty," and that the work would be done by skilled craftsmen whom He had gifted. The priesthood was not a simple task; it was a calling from God.

For today: God values that we serve Him with order, reverence, and care. We can ask ourselves what we do with diligence for Him, whether in church, at work, or at home, recognizing that both the calling and the abilities come from God.
exp.8:24:
This verse describes the force of the seventh plague. The hail struck everything that was out in the open in Egypt: people, animals, plants, and trees. "Struck" means it hit with great force, and "broke off" means it tore away or snapped the branches and trunks.

Here the narrator is Moses, recounting how God responded to Pharaoh's stubbornness, since Pharaoh kept refusing to let Israel go. Earlier, God had warned of the danger so that people could protect their animals and take shelter. After this, Pharaoh admits for the first time that he has sinned, although the account shows that his repentance did not last.

For today: God gives us warnings and opportunities before the consequences come. If we sense that He is speaking to us, it is wise to respond with humility and not wait until everything collapses. Sincere repentance shows in changes that endure.
exp.35:8:
It says that each curtain of the tabernacle measured twenty-eight cubits in length and four cubits in width, and that all of them were exactly the same. A cubit was the distance from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger, about 45 centimeters, although its exact measurement is debated. So each curtain measured close to 12 meters by 1.8 meters.

This is part of the account of how the tabernacle was built, the tent where God dwelt among Israel. The narrator tells how Bezaleel, Aholiab, and the skilled craftsmen who were wise of heart followed to the letter the instructions God gave to Moses. The identical measurements made it possible to join the curtains into two groups of five.

For today: God cares about details and about work done with care. We can serve him with excellence and obedience even in small tasks that no one will notice, trusting that they all fit into something greater.
exp.13:29:
That day the Lord rescued Israel from the power of the Egyptians. The Israelites saw the bodies of the Egyptian soldiers on the shore of the sea.

This verse is told by the narrator of the book of Exodus, traditionally attributed to Moses. It recounts the end of the pursuit: Pharaoh had gone after the people, but the waters closed over his army. Israel, who had been afraid before, now sees with their own eyes that God kept his promise to deliver them. This leads the people to fear God and to believe.

For today: when you feel trapped by a problem you cannot solve, remember how God has cared for you before. Write down those occasions and thank him; in this way your trust grows.
exp.25:21:
This verse gives one more measurement of the tabernacle: the back wall, on the west side, was to have six boards. "Tabernacle" is the sacred tent, and "west" is the direction toward sunset. The boards were the wooden frames that formed the walls.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai and gives him very detailed instructions for building a place where he would dwell among Israel. After this verse come two more boards for the corners. We do not know every detail of exactly how it was assembled with certainty, and scholars explain it in several ways.

For today: God cares about details and order, and he also cares about being close to his people. We can serve him carefully in small things, knowing that every simple task counts when it is done with obedience and love.
exp.36:28:
This verse tells that Bezalel made the holy anointing oil and the pure incense of fine, fragrant spices. Two words in the source explanation describe these: one means something of good smell, and the other refers to a person who prepares perfumes. The work was done with skill and care, following a special mixture.

It is part of the account of how the tabernacle, the tent where Israel worshiped God in the wilderness, was built. It is not spoken by a character; the narrator, traditionally Moses, reports that what God had commanded was carried out. Just before this, the altar of incense is described, and this oil and this incense served to set apart for God the priests and the sacred objects. Christians often see in the anointing an image of the Holy Spirit, though that is an interpretation.

For today: what is dedicated to God deserves care. You can offer Him your work, your prayer, and your service with care and sincerity, not halfheartedly or out of habit.
exp.39:13:
God tells Moses that, after preparing Aaron, he is to bring Aaron's sons near and put tunics on them. The tunic was a basic linen garment worn by the priests. The sons were thus made ready to serve.

God speaks to Moses as the tabernacle is finished. First Aaron is set apart as high priest, and then his sons. No one became a priest by their own decision: God set them apart, and Moses carried out his instructions step by step. The text adds that their anointing would be a perpetual priesthood for their generations.

For today: draw near to God as He directs, not in your own way. The New Testament says that believers are a holy priesthood (1 Peter 2:5), clothed by grace. Serve God with humility, grateful for having been called.
exp.33:18:
Everything that is the first to be born, whatever "opens the womb," belongs to God. That includes the first male offspring of the herd, whether from a cow or a sheep. The herd here means the animals of the farm, and the firstborn is the first one to be born.

God speaks to Moses, and through him to the people, when he renews his covenant after the sin of the golden calf. He reminds them of the exodus from Egypt, when God spared the firstborn of Israel. For that reason, the first of what comes belongs to him as a sign of gratitude and as a reminder that everything comes from him.

For today: before you spend or share what you receive, whether your time, your money, or your strength, give God the first and the best, with gratitude, not what is left over.
exp.0:6:
The children of Israel, the descendants of Jacob, became very numerous. The words "were fruitful" and "multiplied" repeat the idea of growth. "Waxed exceeding mighty" means grew very strong, and "exceeding" means greatly. "The land was filled with them" indicates that they occupied a large part of the region where they lived in Egypt.

Here the narrator of the book, traditionally attributed to Moses, speaks. From the seventy who came with Jacob, they become a vast people, after the generation of Joseph had died. Many see here an echo of God's promise to Abraham to give him numerous descendants. What follows shows that this growth frightened the new king of Egypt.

For today: God keeps his promises even when years pass and we cannot see how. Trust that he is still working quietly, even in difficult times.
exp.20:10:
It says that if the master does not provide these three things for that woman (food, clothing, and marital rights), she will go free without paying anything.

God speaks to Moses in the laws given to Israel after Sinai. This passage deals with a young woman sold by her father as a servant, usually with the expectation that she would be married. The law protects her: if her master takes her as a wife and then neglects her rights, she regains her freedom. Some see here a limit on abuse in an ancient society, without God approving everything that was practiced in that time.

For today: those who have authority or power over others must care for them with justice. In the family, at work, or in the church, keeping what has been promised and not taking advantage of the weakest is a way of honoring God.
exp.7:15:
God commands Moses to tell Aaron to stretch out his staff and strike the dust of the ground. That dust would become gnats throughout all of Egypt. The Hebrew word can also be translated as mosquitoes or biting insects; scholars are not sure exactly which insect it is. To strike means to hit.

The Lord speaks, and He does so after the plague of the frogs. Pharaoh, feeling relief, hardened his heart and did not keep his word. This third plague comes to Pharaoh without prior warning. Later, the Egyptian magicians fail to imitate it.

For today: when God gives us a breather, it is easy to forget what we promised in the midst of difficulty. We can thank Him for that relief with sincere obedience, and not with a heart that hardens again.
exp.31:34:
The explanation says that God punished the people of Israel with a plague or blow, because they had made the golden calf, and that Aaron was the one who shaped it. The sentence about the word "struck" meaning that they were beaten or punished is removed, since that word does not appear in the verse above. The sentence about the calf being a young bull, made here as an idol, is also removed for the same reason.

The one who narrates is the author of the book, traditionally Moses. While Moses was on the mountain with God, the people grew impatient and asked for a visible god. Aaron made the calf. Earlier, God had said that he would blot out of his book the one who sinned against him, and that he would visit that sin on the appointed day. The text does not explain exactly what the blow consisted of.

For today: impatience can lead us to seek security in things we can see and control. When God seems slow, it is wise to keep trusting him, to pray, and to wait, instead of inventing substitutes. Let us also remember that each person answers for their own decisions, even when others propose them.
exp.14:21:
It says that Moses led Israel from the Red Sea (today called the Sea of Reeds) and into the wilderness of Shur. They traveled three days and found no water. The words "went out" mean that they walked, and "found" means that they came upon something.

The one telling the story is the narrator of the book of Exodus, traditionally credited to Moses. Just before this, the people were singing and dancing because of their deliverance from the Egyptian army. Now joy collides with thirst. Soon they will arrive at Marah, where the water is bitter and the people complain. The text shows that after a great victory came a trial. Some see here a lesson about trusting God.

For today: after a moment of joy or of God's help, difficult days can come. Remember what God has already done for you, and instead of complaining, ask Him with confidence to guide and sustain you.
exp.10:8:
God tells Moses that Pharaoh will not listen to him. But this is neither a surprise nor a failure: God has a purpose, that his wonders, that is, his mighty signs, would be multiplied in Egypt. The word for "listen" here means "obey," and "you" refers to Moses and Aaron.

God is speaking just before the last plague, the death of the firstborn. Moses has just come out angry from Pharaoh's presence. God explains to him that the king's refusal will make his power and his care for Israel more visible. The text that follows says that the LORD hardened Pharaoh's heart, something that has been understood in different ways.

For today: when you hear a "no" or face resistance while doing what is right, do not immediately think you have failed. Remain faithful and trust that God is at work, even in what you do not understand.
exp.31:12:
Moses asks God to remember Abraham, Isaac, and Israel (who is Jacob), whom God calls "thy servants." God had promised them, swearing by himself, that he would multiply their descendants like the stars of heaven and give them the land as an inheritance forever. The words "seed" means descendants, and "inheritance" means the land passed down to them.

Moses speaks after the people made the golden calf while he was on the mountain. God was very angry and spoke of destroying them. Moses pleads for them and relies on God's promise, not on the people's merits. The text says that God "repented" of the harm he had announced; it is understood that God changed his course in response to Moses' prayer.

For today: when you fail or pray for others, rely on God's promises and his faithful character. Pray with confidence, reminding him of what he himself has said in his Word.
exp.17:10:
Jethro says that now he knows, from what he has heard, that the Lord is greater than all gods. The closing phrase, "for in the thing wherein they dealt proudly he was above them," means that God showed his power precisely in the very matter where the Egyptians acted with pride and arrogance against Israel.

Jethro, priest of Midian and father-in-law of Moses, is the speaker. He has just met with Moses and heard how God delivered Israel from Pharaoh. His joy leads him to bless God and to offer sacrifices. Some think Jethro is worshiping the God of Israel at this point; the Bible does not explain in detail what he believed before, so it is best not to say more than the text supports.

For today: when you hear how God has worked in the lives of others, do not stay silent. Rejoice with them, give thanks, and acknowledge God. No human pride, however strong, can stop what He decides to do.
exp.36:13:
This verse says that the gold rings were fixed close to the border, the raised edge that ran around the table. Through those rings the poles were passed, so that the priests could carry the table without touching it.

Here it is not God who speaks, but the narrator, who tells how Bezaleel built the table for the bread of the presence for the tabernacle, following the instructions given to Moses. The people were in the wilderness, so everything had to be movable. The table showed that God wanted to be near his people and to provide for them.

For today: God cares even for the small details, and his service is carried out with order and reverence. We can serve him carefully in everyday life, knowing that our faith must also go with us wherever we go.
exp.8:34:
He says that Pharaoh remained stubborn and did not let the Israelites leave, just as God had announced through Moses. The phrase about his heart being hardened means that it became set and closed, unwilling to obey. The phrase about letting them go means permitting them to leave.

The narrator summarizes what happened after the hail plague. Pharaoh had admitted his sin in the midst of danger, but when the thunder and rain stopped, he refused again. The text speaks of his heart becoming hard and also of his own part in making it worse. Some see here Pharaoh's responsibility, and others add God's action; the book shows both.

Today we might ask ourselves whether we seek God only when there are problems. True repentance does not end when the crisis passes. When God corrects us, it is wise to obey him right away and with humility.
exp.35:26:
This verse says that Bezalel and his helpers made six boards for the back of the tabernacle, the side "westward," that is, the side that faced west. The boards were made of wood, and they stood on silver bases. Earlier the text mentions the north side, which the older wording called "the north side," so I have set out the directions in plain terms here.

Here the one speaking is not a character but the narrator. He tells how the people of Israel carefully carried out the instructions God gave Moses for building the tabernacle, the tent where God would dwell among them. The account repeats details that God had already commanded.

For today: God values faithful obedience, even in small and unremarkable tasks. Doing well what seems simple, with steadiness and love, also honors God.
exp.24:28:
God tells Moses to make the utensils for the table of the tabernacle: dishes, spoons, covers, and bowls, all of fine gold. The "covers" and "bowls" were vessels for the offerings, and the word "pour out" means to pour out a drink offering, such as wine, before God. Scholars are not sure of the exact form of each piece, but the general sense is clear.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai and gives him instructions for building the tabernacle, his dwelling place among Israel. The table would hold the bread of the presence, which was set continually before God. Everything that served in his presence was to be made with care and with the best.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we give God our best and not what is left over. It may be time, attention, or affection in prayer, in service, or in the way we treat others.
exp.3:9:
Moses tells God that he is not a man of easy words. He says he never has been, neither before nor since God began speaking to him. The phrase that reads "never, at no time" is rendered in the verse above as "neither heretofore, nor since," and that is what Moses means: he has never been eloquent at any point in his life. The phrase "slow of speech, and of a slow tongue" means that he speaks slowly and finds it hard to express himself well.

Moses speaks with God at the burning bush. God is sending him to bring the people of Israel out of Egypt, and God has already given him signs so that they will believe him. Even so, Moses offers one more excuse: his difficulty in speaking. We do not know exactly what his problem was; the Bible only tells us what he himself expresses.

Many times we feel poorly equipped for what God asks of us. Instead of hiding behind our limitations, bring them honestly before God and take the first step, trusting that he goes with you.
exp.8:12:
God tells Moses to get up early and present himself before Pharaoh. He must give him a clear message: "Let my people go, that they may serve me." The words "thus says" mean "this is what he says." God presents himself as "the God of the Hebrews."

God speaks after six plagues. Egypt's magicians can no longer compete with Moses, and Pharaoh remains stubborn. Even so, God gives him another chance. What follows shows that he wants Pharaoh to understand that there is no other God like him. It is the same claim from the beginning: freedom to worship.

God invites us to serve him, not to live tied to what enslaves us. Today we can respond promptly, without putting off what he asks of us. If he speaks to your heart, do not harden your hearing; obey today.
exp.35:20:
This verse gives the measurements of each board of the tabernacle: ten cubits long and one and a half cubits wide. A cubit was the distance from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger, roughly 45 centimeters, although scholars do not agree on the exact measure. So each board was about 4.5 meters high and about 70 centimeters wide.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, recounting how Bezalel and the craftsmen built the tabernacle. They did it just as God had commanded Moses. That is why the text repeats the details with such precision: it shows obedience to the instructions received.

For today: God is attentive to details and to faithful obedience. You can offer Him, with care and steadiness, even the small things of your day, such as your work, your family, and your promises, knowing that nothing done for Him is insignificant.
exp.39:2:
God tells Moses to place the ark of the testimony inside the tabernacle, the ark that held the tablets of the law, and to cover it with the veil. The veil was a curtain that separated the Most Holy Place from the rest of the tabernacle. The "testimony" refers to the commandments God gave to his people.
