The LORD speaks, and Moses listens. The parts of the tabernacle had already been made, and now God gives instructions on how and when to set it up, on the first day of the first month. In this way Israel would have a place where God dwelt among them. The order God requires is careful and deliberate.

For today: God deserves reverence and order in our relationship with him. We can set aside time each day, without rushing, to listen to his Word and draw near to him with respect, grateful that Christ opened the way for us.
exp.33:19:
The explanation says that the firstborn son of each family and the firstborn young of the donkey belonged to God. The donkey, an animal that was not offered as a sacrifice, could be bought back, and the price of that release was a lamb. If it was not bought back, its neck was to be broken. The firstborn sons were also bought back. The phrase about not appearing empty means that no one was to come before God with empty hands, without an offering.

God speaks to Moses and to Israel after the golden calf, when he renews the covenant. He reminds them of the departure from Egypt, when God spared the firstborn of Israel. For this reason these offerings served to remind them that they had been redeemed.

For today: remember that everything you have, even your family, is a gift from God. Thank him generously, giving time, affection, and resources to him, and do not come before him with empty hands.
exp.8:0:
God tells Moses to go again before Pharaoh with a clear message. God presents himself as "the Lord God of the Hebrews" and asks that he let his people go. The word "serve" means to worship and obey God. The phrase "go in unto Pharaoh" means "present yourself before Pharaoh."

The Lord speaks, the one who had already sent Moses before. Egypt had already suffered several plagues, and Pharaoh kept refusing. Even so, God gives another opportunity before the next plague, which would affect the animals. God speaks with authority, but also with patience, for he warns before he acts.

For today: when God speaks to us, it is not wise to harden the heart. If we feel he is asking us to change something, to obey, or to let go of something we are holding on to, it is better to respond soon and with humility. His word not only corrects; it also opens a path of freedom and of true worship.
exp.24:3:
This verse continues the list of materials for the sanctuary. It mentions threads and fabrics in various colors: blue, purple, scarlet (a deep red), fine linen (good-quality white cloth), and goats' hair, which was used to make strong fabrics. The blue here is not a flower but a shade of blue or violet.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai. He asks for an offering from the people of Israel, but only from those who are willing to give it freely and wholeheartedly. With these materials the tabernacle would be built, a place where God would dwell among his people. Scholars discuss the exact meaning of each color, so it is wise to be cautious.

For today: God values the willingness of the heart more than the amount given. Today you can offer your time, talents, or resources joyfully, not out of obligation, and even what is simple can serve in God's work.
exp.13:18:
This verse says that the angel of God, who until that moment had been going ahead of the people of Israel, changed position and moved behind them. The pillar of cloud did the same. The sentence about the old wording is removed.

The narrator describes this moment when the Israelites, just come out of Egypt, are trapped between Pharaoh's army and the sea. God had already announced that Pharaoh would pursue them. By standing behind them, the cloud separated the two camps. Some think the "angel of God" is a messenger, while others see in him the very presence of God; the text does not fully clarify this.

For today: when you feel cornered, remember that God can watch over you from behind, in what you cannot see, while He guides you forward. Trust that He protects your path.
exp.10:3:
Moses announces what God said: at midnight God will "go out through the midst of Egypt." It is a way of saying that God himself will pass through the whole land to act in judgment. "Lord" is the name of God, and "midnight" is the middle of the night.

Moses speaks before Pharaoh, just before the tenth plague. Egypt had refused many times to let the people of Israel go. What follows is the announcement of the death of the firstborn. It is a very grave moment, and the Bible presents it as a judgment of God upon a people who oppressed another. Some scholars debate the details of how it happened, but the text emphasizes that it was the work of God.

For today: God takes injustice seriously and has the final word, even if it comes late. This invites us to trust in Him when we see wickedness, and to respond to His voice with humility, without hardening our hearts.
exp.27:40:
God tells Moses to put the sacred garments, already described, on Aaron and his sons. Then they are to be anointed with oil, consecrated, and sanctified, that is, set apart for God. The word "consecrated" means dedicated to a holy use. The purpose is that they would be priests of God.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai as He gives him instructions for the tabernacle. The priests would act as intermediaries between God and the people of Israel. The garments, the anointing, and the consecration showed that this service was holy and was not to be taken lightly. It was God who chose them, not they themselves.

Today we can remember that serving God begins with being set apart by Him, not with our own merits. The New Testament says that believers are a holy priesthood (1 Peter 2:9). This week, offer your work and your relationships to God as a service dedicated to Him.
exp.34:32:
He says that God gave Bezaleel the skill to cut precious stones and set them, to work in wood, and to do all kinds of skilled work.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel while the construction of the tabernacle, the tent where God would dwell among them, is being prepared. He explains that God himself filled Bezaleel with his Spirit, and also Aholiab, to do that work. In this way, craftsmanship is presented as a gift from God to be used in serving him.

For today: your abilities, whether hands-on, technical, or creative, can be a gift from God. Offer them with excellence and humility to serve others and honor him in your work, your church, and your home.
exp.38:39:
This verse is part of a list of the finished pieces of the tabernacle. It mentions the hangings that surrounded the courtyard, with their pillars, their sockets (bases), the hanging for the entrance, the cords and the pins that held everything in place. It also includes the vessels for the service.

The narrator of the book, traditionally associated with Moses, reports that the people have now finished the work and will present it to Moses. God had given these instructions earlier, and here it is confirmed that they were carried out in full detail.

Today we can learn that God values both the great and the small. A pin or a cord seemed like a small thing, yet they held up the whole courtyard. Faithfully do your simple task, even when no one notices it.
exp.9:9:
He says that Pharaoh answers with irony and anger. It is as if he were saying, "May the Lord be with you as much as I will let you go with your little ones!", which means he has no intention of letting them go. Then he warns them: "Look, you have bad intentions." The words "so be it" here sound like mockery, not a blessing. The word for "evil" can be understood as wickedness or ill intent; some interpret it as a threat.

Pharaoh is speaking after the plague of hail. Moses had said that they would all go, with children, elders, and livestock, to hold a feast to the Lord. Pharaoh wants to control the situation and suspects their plans. Shortly afterward he agrees that only the men may go, and he drives them out of his presence.

For today: sometimes someone may seem to give in, but sets conditions that keep us from obeying God completely. We should be faithful without accepting half-measures, and trust God when we are pressured.
exp.36:8:
The explanation says that the two golden cherubim, placed at the ends of the cover of the ark, had their wings stretched upward and with them covered the cover. They faced each other, looking at one another, and their faces leaned toward the cover. The cover is the lid of the ark, also called the mercy seat or the place of forgiveness.

Here the narrator tells how Bezaleel built the ark of the covenant, following the instructions God gave to Moses. It was the place where God promised to meet with his people. The cherubim are spiritual beings that the Bible connects with God's presence and holiness. Their exact appearance is not detailed here.

For today: the cherubim look toward the cover, where atonement for sin was made. We can imitate that gaze: focus our attention on the forgiveness God offers, and draw near to him with reverence and trust.
exp.34:7:
This verse continues the list of offerings for the tabernacle. It asks for oil for the lamps of the sanctuary, and for spices to make the anointing oil and the fragrant incense. The lamp-stand was the light-giving lamp that gave light in the holy place. Anointing was the act of setting something or someone apart for God with a special oil.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel, gathered after the sin of the golden calf. He passes on what God had commanded him and invites them to give willingly to build the place where God would dwell among them. What is asked for is concrete material, and each thing had its use in worship.

For today: God does not despise the simple things we give him gladly. Think about what you have at hand, such as time, a talent, or a resource, and offer it with joy to serve others in his name.
exp.22:1:
It says we should not be swayed by the majority when it wants to do something wrong. Nor should we speak in a dispute by leaning toward the larger side in order to twist justice. The explanation notes that "litigio" means a judgment or lawsuit, and "agravios" means injustices or harms done to someone.

God speaks to Israel through Moses, in the laws given after the Ten Commandments. These rules taught the people how to live justly. The verses around it speak of not spreading rumors, not being a false witness, and treating both the poor and an enemy fairly. Everything aims at honest courts.

For today: when everyone around you holds opinions or acts wrongly, for example by gossiping or mocking someone, do not go along with them just to fit in. Before you voice an opinion, ask yourself what is right before God, and have the courage to say it with respect, even if you stand alone.
exp.39:34:
It says that Moses could not enter the tent where God met with his people. The cloud had settled on it, and the glory of the Lord (his holy and powerful presence) filled it completely. The word "tabernacle" means a tent or dwelling place, and the name of God is the Lord.

The book of Exodus, traditionally attributed to Moses, tells that the people had just finished building the tabernacle following God's instructions. When it was finished, God showed that he was coming to dwell among them. Afterward, the cloud would guide the people: when it lifted, they moved on; when it did not, they waited.

For today: before making plans or serving God, we can pause with reverence before his presence. God is not a tool for our use; he is holy and near. Today you can take a few quiet minutes to ask him to guide you.
exp.31:3:
Aaron received the gold from the people, worked it with a graving tool, and melted it until it formed a calf. Then the people said that this calf was the god who had brought them out of Egypt.

The people were at the foot of Mount Sinai. Moses was taking a long time to come down, and they grew impatient. They asked Aaron for a god who would lead them. Aaron gave in, and then he called the feast a feast to the LORD, so they mixed the worship of the Lord with an image. Scholars debate how they understood the calf: as another god or as a symbol of the LORD. In either case God condemned it.

When God seems silent, it is easy to look for shortcuts and make something visible that gives us a sense of security. Wait on Him, and examine whether anything is taking the place that only God should have.
exp.34:5:
This verse continues the list of materials that the people could bring to build the tabernacle. Here cloth and threads are named: the color "blue" is a bluish-violet hue, "purple" is a reddish-purple dye, "scarlet" is a deep red, "fine linen" is a delicate cloth, and "goats' hair" was used to weave covers.

Moses speaks to the whole congregation of Israel and passes on what God commanded. He asks for an offering, but not out of obligation: it would be brought by "everyone whose heart was willing," that is, whoever had a generous and ready heart. These materials would serve for the place where God would dwell among his people.

For today: God values what we give with joy and willingness. We do not all have the same things, but we can all offer something, whether time, money, talents or service. Ask yourself what you have in your hands and offer it to God with a willing heart.
exp.6:23:
This verse tells that the Egyptians dug wells beside the Nile to get water. The river's water had turned to blood and could not be drunk. The phrase "dug round about" refers to their digging in the nearby ground, looking for water that might seep through clean.

Here no one speaks directly; it is Moses' account of the first plague. God had struck the river because of Pharaoh's hardness of heart, since he would not let the people of Israel go. The magicians copied the sign, and Pharaoh went back to his house without taking it to heart. Meanwhile, the common people bore the consequences.

For today: when God shows us clearly that something is wrong, looking only for temporary remedies, like the wells, is not enough. It is wise to listen, reflect, and turn back to Him with humility, before the heart grows hard.
exp.36:9:
It says that Bezalel made the table of the tabernacle from acacia wood, which in the Hebrew is called shittim, a hardy wood of the desert. It measured two cubits in length, one cubit in breadth, and a cubit and a half in height. A cubit was roughly the distance from the elbow to the tip of the fingers, about 45 centimeters, although the exact measure is debated. So the table was almost a meter long.

This passage is part of the account of building the tabernacle, which follows the instructions God gave to Moses. Earlier the text speaks of the ark and the cherubim; now it describes the table where the bread of the presence was placed. The narrator emphasizes that everything was done just as God had commanded.

For today: God cares even about the details of our worship and obedience. We can serve Him with care and faithfulness in small things, trusting that nothing we do for Him is insignificant.
exp.5:4:
God says that he has heard the crying and the pain of the Israelites, who suffer as slaves under the Egyptians. He also says that he has remembered his covenant, that is, his solemn promise. The word "groaning" speaks of a deep cry of pain, and the phrase about keeping them in bondage means that they are forced to work as servants.

God speaks with Moses after Pharaoh made the burden of the people heavier. Moses is discouraged, and God reminds him who he is and what he promised to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob: to give them the land of Canaan. Then he asks Moses to encourage the people with this hope.

For today: when you feel that no one hears your pain, remember that God does hear and is faithful to what he promises. You can pray honestly, even weeping, and wait with patience, trusting that he has not forgotten you.
exp.27:37:
This verse says that the gold plate with the words "Holiness to the Lord" would be on Aaron's forehead. He would "bear the iniquity of the holy things," that is, he would carry the faults or impurities found in the offerings the people dedicated. In this way God would accept the people.

God himself speaks to Moses on the mountain, giving him instructions for the priesthood and for Aaron's garments. The Israelites were imperfect, even in their worship. For that reason God arranged a priest who would represent them and cover those failures.

For today: many Christians see here a shadow of Christ, our High Priest, who presents us before God. We can draw near to pray without fear, not because we are perfect, but because He represents us. Let us live with gratitude and seek holiness.
exp.37:13:
This verse describes one side of the entrance to the courtyard of the tabernacle. That side had curtains fifteen cubits long, held up by three pillars with their three bases (the bases or stands on which the pillars rested). A cubit measured about 45 centimeters, though its exact length is debated, so these curtains were roughly 7 meters long.

Here the narrator of Exodus is recounting how the tabernacle was built, following the instructions God had given to Moses. The earlier chapters gave the commands, and this passage reports that they were carried out. The curtain surrounded the courtyard and left a single entrance, with hangings on each side of the gate.

For today: God cares about small details, and what is done faithfully in ordinary things has value to Him. Today we can carry out with care and steadiness the tasks that seem unremarkable.
exp.29:30:
God tells Moses to speak to the people and tell them that this special oil belongs to him. It is a holy anointing oil, and it must remain that way throughout all their generations. The words "throughout your generations" simply mean that this command lasts for all the generations to come.

God speaks to Moses at Sinai, giving instructions for the tabernacle. This oil would be used to set apart Aaron, his sons, and the objects used in worship. For that reason it could not be used for ordinary purposes or copied. Some see in it a picture of the Holy Spirit, although the text does not say this directly.

For today: we can ask ourselves which things in our lives belong to God, such as our time, our service, and our worship, and treat them with respect rather than as something ordinary.
exp.32:1:
God promises Moses that he will send an angel before the people to guide them. He also says that he himself will drive out the peoples who lived in Canaan: the Canaanites, Amorites, Hittites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites. Here "drive out" means to expel, and "the angel" is a messenger sent by God.

The Lord speaks, and he does so after the people made the golden calf. God keeps his promise to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, but in the following verse he makes clear that he will not go in their midst, because they are stiff-necked, that is, stubborn. For this reason the people were deeply saddened.

For today: God can keep his promises even when we fail, but our sin has consequences. Let us not be content with his blessings without his presence; let us humbly ask him to go with us.
exp.2:16:
This verse records a promise from God: he will bring Israel out of suffering in Egypt and lead them into the land of six peoples who already lived there: the Canaanites, Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites. That land is described as a place "flowing with milk and honey," meaning fertile and abundant. "Affliction" means oppression and pain.

God speaks to Moses from the burning bush. He gives him the message to carry to the elders of Israel. God says that he has seen how his people have been mistreated and that he has not forgotten it. His promise rests on the covenant he made with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

For today: when you go through a hard season, remember that God sees your pain and is faithful to his promises. Even if the road is long and the answer is slow, you can trust that he is still at work and that he walks with you.
exp.4:2:
Moses and Aaron ask Pharaoh for permission to go three days' journey into the desert and offer sacrifices to the Lord. They say that the God of the Hebrews "has met with us," meaning that he has appeared to them. If they do not obey, they fear that God will strike them with plague (a deadly disease) or with the sword (war or violent death).

Moses and Aaron are speaking after Pharaoh said he did not know the Lord. Now they change their tone and speak more humbly, including the whole people. They ask only for a short leave to worship. Pharaoh, however, takes it as an excuse to stop the people from working. Interpreters explain in different ways whether the warning was meant for Pharaoh, for the Israelites, or for both.

For today: obeying God comes first, even when someone with power opposes it. We can speak with respect and firmness, and set apart time to worship him.
exp.21:29:
God says that the firstborn of cows and sheep must be handled the same way as firstborn sons and the first fruits of the harvest. The newborn animal stays with its mother for seven days, and on the eighth day it is given to God. A firstborn is the first child or the first offspring.

God speaks through Moses to the people of Israel, who have just been freed from Egypt. These are laws for living as God's people. Giving the first of what they had acknowledged that everything comes from him. The seven days probably allowed the young animal to stay with its mother before being offered, although the text does not explain more.

For today: before we spend or make plans, we can set apart the first of our time, money, or energy for God, with gratitude. It is not buying his favor, but recognizing that we receive everything from him.
exp.36:19:
This verse describes the central shaft of the golden lampstand in the tabernacle. Besides the six branches, the shaft had four cups shaped like almond blossoms, each with its knob and its flower. Here "knob" refers to a round ornament, like a button or a handle; the "lampstand" is the stand that held the lamps.

The narrator tells how Bezalel, the craftsman, built the sacred objects following the instructions God had given to Moses. This part repeats in detail what had been commanded earlier, to show that the work was done just as God had asked. Scholars think the almond may have suggested life and awakening, though the Bible does not explain it.

For today: God cares about details and about the beauty of what we make for Him. We can serve Him with care, even in small tasks that no one sees, doing them faithfully and from the heart.
exp.4:16:
Pharaoh answers the Israelite foremen by saying that they are lazy, that they do not want to work. According to him, that is why they ask to go and offer sacrifices to the Lord. The repeated word "lazy" shows his contempt.

Pharaoh, king of Egypt, speaks. Moses and Aaron had asked him to let the people go to worship God in the wilderness. Pharaoh does not recognize the Lord, so he increases their burden: now they must find the straw themselves and still deliver the same quota of bricks. The foremen come to him complaining about the mistreatment.

For today: sometimes those who hold power accuse those who seek God of laziness, or call worship a waste of time. Let us not allow those voices to silence us. Let us seek God steadily, even when it costs us, and trust that he sees our affliction.
exp.22:8:
It says we must not mistreat or oppress the foreigner, the one who lives in a land that is not his own. "Oppress" means to cause suffering, to press down hard on someone or treat them harshly. God reminds the Israelites that they themselves know what it feels like to be a stranger, because they were strangers in Egypt.

It is God who speaks, through Moses, within the laws he gave Israel after bringing them out of Egypt. The verses around it deal with justice: do not lie, do not kill the innocent, do not accept bribes. Within that setting, the way the stranger is treated appears as part of that same justice, since the stranger often had few defenders. Afterward the law moves on to the rest of the land, which also benefited the poor.

Today we can remember our own experiences of feeling out of place, and treat immigrants, or those who arrive new to our community or church, with respect, kindness, and fairness.
exp.21:17:
It says that in Israel a sorceress, that is, a woman who practiced witchcraft or magic to try to know or control hidden things, was not to be allowed to live. "Thou shalt not suffer" is an older way of saying "you shall not let her live." The Hebrew word for this figure is translated in various ways: sorceress, witch, or practitioner of magic arts.

God speaks to Moses and to the people who had just come out of Egypt, within the laws of the covenant at Sinai. These rules protected exclusive loyalty to the LORD, and that is why the verse sits alongside laws about bestiality and idolatry. It was a law for ancient Israel as a nation. Scholars debate how it was applied in practice.

Today, instead of carrying out this penalty, we can take the warning seriously: not seeking security in horoscopes, spiritism, or amulets, but trusting God and his Word, and asking him for direction through prayer.
exp.39:1:
God tells Moses to set up the tabernacle on the first day of the first month. The phrase "shalt thou set up" means that Moses was to command that it be put together and oversee the work. It is called "the tabernacle of the testimony" because it held the tablets of the law, the testimony of the covenant between God and his people.

The LORD speaks and gives the instruction to Moses. The people had already made all the parts, following the plans God had given on the mountain. Now it remained to assemble it. By the book's timeline, this happens about a year after leaving Egypt, although the text here mentions only the first month. God wanted to dwell in the midst of his people.

For today: God does not only want us to prepare good things, but also to put them into motion at the right time. Think of something God has placed on your heart that you have not yet begun. Take one concrete step today, and place God at the center of that beginning.
exp.20:19:
It says that if an owner beats his male servant or his female servant with a rod and the person dies on the spot, the owner must be punished. The phrase "under his hand" is a set phrase that here means the servant dies while still under the owner's control. Here "servant" refers to an enslaved person, and "shall be surely punished" indicates a penalty for his guilt. The text does not say exactly what the punishment was, and some scholars think it could have been the death penalty, though not all agree.

God speaks to Moses and gives laws to the people of Israel after the Ten Commandments. In an ancient society where slavery existed, these rules placed limits on violence and recognized that the life of the servant mattered. The verses that follow are difficult and are interpreted in several ways.

For today: every person's life is valuable to God, whatever their position. Whoever has authority, at work or at home, should use it to care for others and never to harm them.
exp.39:15:
This verse says that Moses did everything the Lord commanded him. The phrase "according to all" means "just as," without changing anything. The repetition, "so did he," emphasizes that he obeyed completely.

Here the narrator of the book is summing up Moses' obedience. God had just given him instructions to set up the tabernacle, to anoint Aaron and his sons, and to set them apart as priests. The account then tells how the tabernacle was erected on the first day of the first month of the second year. This verse marks that everything was done according to God's command.

Today we can learn that obeying God includes the details, not only the big things. Think of an instruction from his Word that you have left half-finished, and take a concrete step today to carry it out faithfully and with trust.
exp.11:21:
Moses gives the Israelites an instruction: they are to take a bunch of hyssop, a small plant with soft branches, and dip it in the blood of the lamb that is kept in a basin, that is, a bowl or dish. With it they will paint the top of the door frame (the lintel) and the two sides (the posts). Afterward, no one is to leave their house until morning.

Moses speaks to the elders of Israel and passes on what God has commanded him. It is the night before the departure from Egypt, when God strikes the Egyptians. The blood on the door was the sign that the house was under God's protection. God would keep his word and pass over.

For today: trust in what God has said, even when it seems simple. The Israelites were saved by obeying in faith. Many Christians see in this an image of Christ, the Lamb of God, and rest in his sacrifice.
exp.16:10:
While Joshua and the army fought below, the outcome of the battle changed depending on what Moses did above. When Moses kept his hand raised, Israel was winning; when he lowered it, Amalek gained the upper hand. "Prevailed" means having the advantage.

This is a story from the book of Exodus. Israel had just left Egypt, and in the desert Amalek attacked them. Moses sent Joshua to fight, and he went up to the hilltop, a small hill, holding God's staff in his hand. Interpreters explain the gesture in different ways: as prayer, as a sign of trust in God, or as a symbol of his authority. The text does not make this clear.

For today: no one carries a long burden alone. Seek out those who will support you in prayer and help, and be the one who holds up another person's weary hands too.
exp.36:11:
This verse describes a detail of the table of the tabernacle. Bezalel made a frame or border (a molding) one handbreadth wide, that is, about four fingers. On top of that border he placed a cornice, an ornament shaped like a finishing crown, made of gold and running all the way around the table.

The narrator of Exodus tells how the instructions God gave Moses for building his sanctuary were carried out. This table held the bread of the presence. It is not known for certain what the molding was exactly for. Some think it kept the objects on the table steady, and others believe it strengthened its structure.

God cares about the details, even those almost no one notices. Today we can serve him with that same dedication in small things: doing a simple task well, keeping a promise, or treating someone kindly, as for the Lord.
exp.27:14:
God commands Moses to make the "breastplate of judgment," a special piece for the high priest. The word "breastplate" in the older wording is not what most versions use today, but the name is the same thing; this is the piece the verse describes. It was to be made with great skill, like the ephod, the other priestly garment. Its materials were gold, blue, purple, scarlet, and fine twined linen.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai, giving him instructions for the tabernacle and the priests' clothing. This piece was fastened with small gold chains and set with precious stones. Later on it is explained that it represented the tribes of Israel, so the priest carried the people over his chest.

For today: God cares about the details and values his people. You can pray knowing that Jesus, our high priest, also carries you in his heart and presents you with love before the Father.
exp.29:10:
This verse is a transition phrase. It says that God spoke to Moses, and with that it introduces a new topic.

The narrator of the book is speaking, presenting God addressing Moses. Before this, God explained how to make the altar of incense. Now the subject changes, and he gives instructions about counting the people and the payment of a half shekel as a ransom. That offering was the same for everyone, and the texts that follow connect it with the protection of the people when they were counted.

For today: God continues to speak to his people through his Word. When you read the Bible, do so with attention and a willingness to obey, even on topics that seem different or hard to understand.
exp.1:5:
She says that Pharaoh's daughter opened the basket, or little ark, and saw the baby crying. She felt compassion and recognized that he was a Hebrew boy. The word "saw" appears in the verse as "saw," and the phrase "had compassion" means that she was moved for him.

The one speaking here is the narrator, and then Pharaoh's daughter. Pharaoh had ordered the Hebrew baby boys to be killed, but she comes upon one who is helpless. The Bible does not explain why she treated him with tenderness; it only says that her heart was moved. Meanwhile, the child's sister watches from a distance, and this prepares the way for the care of her own mother.

For today: when you see someone crying or in need, do not walk past. Compassion may seem small, but God can use it to protect a life and to accomplish great things we cannot yet see.
exp.8:33:
He says that when Pharaoh saw that the rain, the hail and the thunders had stopped, he sinned again. The phrase about continuing in sin means that he kept doing the same thing without changing. The idea of making his heart heavier means that he became harder and more stubborn. His servants did the same.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Moses had just prayed, and God stopped the plague of hail. Earlier, Pharaoh had said, "I have sinned this time" (v. 27), but his repentance lasted only as long as the punishment did. The text also shows that Pharaoh hardened his own heart by choice, although the following passage says that what God had announced was being fulfilled.

For today: let us not confuse relief with conversion. When the difficulty passes, let us not go back to what we were before. Let us ask God for a humble heart that truly changes, not only in times of trouble.
exp.31:14:
Moses turned and came down from the mountain. In his hand he carries the two tablets of the testimony, that is, the commandments God gave him as a sign of his covenant with Israel. They were written on both sides, on the one side and on the other.

Moses had spent forty days with God. There he had interceded for the people, recalling the promises made to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob (Israel), and God did not carry out the punishment he had announced. But down below, the people had already made a golden calf. Moses comes down without knowing everything in detail, carrying God's word toward a camp in sin.

Today we can remember that God speaks to us clearly and keeps seeking us even when we fail. We can pray for others as Moses did, and also take his Word seriously, without letting other things take its place.
exp.27:13:
It says that Moses was to make two small chains of pure gold, twisted together like a thin rope. These chains were to be fastened to the settings, which are the gold bases in which the precious stones are mounted.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai and gives him instructions for the clothing of the high priest Aaron. The stones on the shoulders carried engraved on them the names of the tribes of Israel, as a reminder before God. The chains served to hold those pieces firmly in place. Exactly what they were for within the whole garment, some scholars interpret in different ways.

For today: God cares even for the small, firm details that hold up his people. Just as Aaron carried the names of Israel, we can carry others in prayer, with steadiness and without letting them go.
exp.18:14:
Moses tells the people to be ready for the third day. He also says, "come not at your wives," an old way of saying that they should not have sexual relations during that time.

Moses speaks on God's behalf, just before God reveals Himself on Mount Sinai. Israel had already washed their clothes and was consecrating themselves. In that culture, abstaining from marital intimacy was a sign of setting oneself apart for a time for something holy. It was not because marriage was sinful, but to show respect and undivided attention to God.

Today we can learn to prepare ourselves seriously to meet with God. Before praying, going to church, or reading the Bible, we can set aside a few minutes, turn off distractions, and have an attentive and humble heart.
exp.19:6:
This verse commands that the name of God not be used "in vain," that is, in an empty, careless, or false way. The name "Jehovah" is the name by which God made himself known to Israel. "Will not hold him guiltless" means that God will not overlook or treat as innocent the person who does this.

God himself speaks to Israel from Mount Sinai, shortly after bringing them out of Egypt. This is the third of the Ten Commandments (according to the Protestant numbering). God has just presented himself as the one true and faithful God, and now he asks that his name be treated with respect. Some understand this to include false oaths, and others also include the irreverent or hypocritical use of his name.

For today: think before using God's name in jokes, in promises you will not keep, or in phrases said without thinking. Try to speak of him with sincerity, respect, and gratitude.
exp.18:17:
Mount Sinai was completely covered in smoke, because the Lord came down on it in fire. The smoke rose like the smoke of a furnace, and the whole mountain shook violently.

The smoke rising from the mountain, and the mountain shaking, are described with the same wording the verse uses. The phrase "came down" and the word "fire" are the verse's own words, so no extra definition is needed.

The people of Israel had just left Egypt and were camped at the foot of the mountain. Moses had brought them out of the camp to meet with God. Here the narrator describes how God made himself present to give them his covenant and his law. Scholars do not agree on whether the phenomenon was a volcano or something unique, and the text only says that it was God who came down.

For today: God is holy and deserves reverence. Today you can come to Him with confidence, but without forgetting His greatness. Before you pray, pause and remember who He is.
exp.33:30:
Moses calls to Aaron and to the leaders of the people, and they come near to him. "Rulers of the congregation" means the heads or leaders of the tribes. "Face" refers to the skin of the face. Although they were afraid, they responded to the call, and Moses spoke with them.

The passage tells of Moses coming down from Sinai with the tablets of the law after being with God. His face was shining, and the people were frightened. Moses had not realized it. By calling to them, he breaks the distance and passes on what God had commanded him. The Bible does not explain in detail what that shining was like; it only says it came from having spoken with God.

For today: sometimes fear or distance holds us back from drawing near to God or to others. This verse encourages us to respond when someone calls us with good intentions, and to listen to what God wants to tell us, because being with Him transforms us.
exp.33:27:
This verse tells that Moses spent forty days and forty nights on the mountain with God, without eating bread or drinking water. There he wrote on tablets the words of the covenant, that is, the agreement between God and his people. Those words are the ten commandments, what we today call the Ten Commandments. The name "Lord" is the name of God.

The account is about Moses on Mount Sinai. God had commanded him to write these words, because with them he was making a covenant with Israel. This takes place after the people had sinned with the golden calf, and God renews his covenant with them. Soon after, the face of Moses shines because he had been with God.

For today: Moses set aside undistracted time to be with God. We can set aside a moment each day, unhurried and quiet, to listen to his Word and let it shape our lives.
exp.11:47:
It says that a foreigner who lives among the Israelites and wants to keep the Passover to the Lord may do so, but first all the males in his household must be circumcised. Then he will be treated as one born in the land. Whoever is not circumcised may not eat of the Passover. "Sojourn" means living as a stranger, and "one that is born in the land" refers to a native of the people.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron while Israel prepares to leave Egypt. The Passover was the sign of the people's deliverance. Circumcision was the sign of the covenant with God since Abraham. Thus the foreigner could join in, but by truly entering the covenant. The following text stresses one law for all.

God opens the door to whoever desires to draw near to Him, but drawing near involves sincere commitment. We can welcome with kindness those who seek God and live out our faith with real devotion.
exp.17:19:
It says that Moses must teach the people. He must teach them the ordinances (God's commands) and the laws (the decisions for specific cases). He must also show them the way they are to walk, that is, how to live, and the work they must do, that is, their responsibilities. "Teach them" means teach them.

Jethro, Moses' father-in-law, speaks. He sees that Moses spends the whole day judging the people's disputes and is worn out. He advises him to remain the one who represents the people before God and who teaches the law, and then to share the work with trustworthy men who fear God.

For today: teaching well is stronger than trying to solve everything yourself. If you lead in your family, church, or workplace, train others with clarity and share the burden. In this way you look after your own health and strengthen those around you.
exp.27:36:
The explanation says that the gold plate with the words "Holy to the LORD" was to be fastened with a blue cord. "Blue" is a blue or violet color. The turban is the linen headdress worn by the high priest. The plate went on the front of the turban, in plain sight.

God speaks to Moses and gives him instructions for Aaron's garments, the first high priest. That plate was a reminder that service in the sanctuary belonged to God and that Aaron carried the people's offerings before Him. The next verse says this was so they would be accepted before the LORD.

For today: God cares that our lives belong to Him in a visible way. We can ask ourselves what of Him shows in our words and decisions, and ask Him for help to live each day with that mark: dedicated to God.
exp.11:23:
This verse says that the people of Israel were to keep this instruction as a permanent rule. The word "ordinance" means a law or rule that has been set down. "Observe" means that they were to carry it out and hold on to it. This was not only for them, but also for their children, "for ever", that is, from generation to generation.

Moses speaks to the people, passing on what God had told him, just before the last plague in Egypt. God would deliver them from the death of the firstborn and from slavery. He wanted them to remember that deliverance every year, and the verses that follow show that their children would ask what it meant.

For today: God values the passing down of the memory of his works to the children. We can do this by telling at home, simply, how God has cared for us and forgiven us, so that faith does not stop with us.
exp.25:17:
God tells Moses to make the boards that will form the walls of the tabernacle. On the south side, which the verse calls the "noon" side and the "south," there are to be twenty boards. The "sockets" were pegs or projections that fit into the bases, so the boards stood firm and held together.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai and gives him detailed instructions for building a holy tent. Israel had just left Egypt, and God wanted to dwell in the middle of his people. Scholars do not agree on every detail of the structure, but the care taken with the measurements shows that God values order.

For today: if God was concerned with every board of his house, he is also concerned with the details of your life. Do with care and faithfulness what God has placed in your hands, even when it seems small.
exp.19:2:
This commandment says that Israel was not to have any other gods besides the true God. "Foreign" means strange, or belonging to other peoples. "Before me" can be understood as "in my presence" or "above me"; scholars interpret it in various ways, but the central idea is exclusivity: only the LORD deserves worship.

God himself speaks on Mount Sinai to a people who had just come out of slavery in Egypt. Before giving the command, he presents himself as the God who freed them. His instruction springs from a relationship of deliverance and care, not from authority alone.

Today we can ask ourselves what holds first place in our hearts: money, success, the approval of others. When something rules over us more than God does, it becomes a "foreign god." Let us ask him to order our priorities.
exp.3:10:
God answers Moses with questions: who gave the human being a mouth? Who makes someone mute, deaf, able to see, or blind? The answer is clear: "I, the Lord."

God speaks from the burning bush. He has just called Moses to bring Israel out of Egypt, but Moses excuses himself, saying he is poor at speaking. God does not deny the difficulty; instead he reminds Moses that he has authority over human abilities. This verse is hard, because it says God makes the mute and the deaf, and believers have understood it in different ways. What is certain is that here God affirms his sovereignty and promises to help Moses.

For today: when you feel you are not enough for something God asks of you, bring him your weakness honestly, and trust that his help counts for more than your ability.
exp.38:25:
It says that around the lower edge of the priest's robe there were alternating gold bells and pomegranates, all the way around. The robe is the long blue garment worn under the ephod. Serving in worship is what it means to minister, and everything was made just as the Lord commanded Moses.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, describing how the people finished making the garments of Aaron, the high priest. Exodus 28:33-35 explains that the bells were to sound when he went in and out of the holy place, so that he would not die. The text does not explain the meaning of the pomegranates; some think they speak of fruit or abundance, but that is an interpretation.

Today we can learn that God cares about even the small details when we serve him. Being faithful in obedience in simple things, as the people did, is a real way of worshiping him. Ask yourself: what small task has God asked me to do with care?
exp.15:2:
The explanation says that the people of Israel complained to Moses and Aaron. They would have preferred to have died in Egypt by the hand of the Lord, when they sat beside the pots of meat and ate bread until they were full. The word "Would to God" expresses a wish, "full" means abundance, and "kill with hunger" means to make someone die of hunger.

The whole congregation of Israel is speaking, only about a month and a half after leaving Egypt. They were hungry in the wilderness of Sin and had forgotten how harsh their slavery had been. Their complaint was directed at Moses and Aaron, but at heart it was against God. He responded with compassion, sending them bread from heaven.

When we go through a time of need, it is easy to idealize the past and forget how difficult it was. Instead of grumbling, we can bring our lack to God with sincerity and trust that He provides day by day.
exp.17:22:
It says that if Moses organizes the work as he is advised, and if God approves it, he will be able to endure, or keep standing firm in his labor. Also, the whole people will go back to their place in peace, that is, to their tents or their homes, without waiting for hours for a solution. Here "endure" means to stay on your feet, to hold up without giving way.

The one speaking is Jethro, Moses' father-in-law, a priest of Midian. He saw that Moses spent the whole day judging the people's cases, and that he was wearing himself out, just like the people who were waiting. Jethro proposes sharing the load with capable and honest men, but makes clear that Moses must confirm this with God. Then Moses accepted it.

For today: you do not have to carry everything alone. Ask God for wisdom, entrust tasks to people of integrity, and devote your strength to what matters most. Sharing the load cares for your health and also helps others.
exp.15:33:
This verse says that Aaron placed the jar of manna before the Testimony, that is, before the ark where the tablets of the law were kept. He did it to preserve it, just as God had commanded Moses. The sentence explaining the word "keep" has been rewritten to match the verse: "to be kept" means to be cared for and preserved carefully. The name of God, which the verse does not mention, is left out here.

The people had been eating manna in the desert for some time. God commanded that an omer, a small measure, be kept so that future generations could see with their own eyes how He fed Israel. Moses gives the instruction and Aaron, the priest, carries it out. After this moment, the text mentions that the manna lasted forty years.

For today: God wants us to remember His faithfulness and to tell others about it. We can write down how He has cared for us, so that our children and our community will know it too.
exp.20:21:
The passage describes two men who are fighting and who, without meaning to, strike a pregnant woman. She loses the child, a result the text describes with a word that in the original can mean the baby is born early or that it is lost. If there is no further harm, the one who caused it pays a fine set by the woman's husband and approved by the judges. The text that follows says that if there is a death, the penalty is life for life.

God gives these laws to Moses for the people of Israel, shortly after giving the Ten Commandments. They are rules of justice for everyday life. Interpreters debate whether the text refers to a premature birth or to the loss of the baby, and that uncertainty should be acknowledged honestly.

For today: God cares about protecting the vulnerable and demands accountability when someone causes harm. Take care with your words and actions toward those around you who have the least protection.
exp.31:26:
Moses speaks to the Levites and passes on a harsh command: take the sword, go through the camp from gate to gate, and kill those who had taken part in the idolatry, even if they were brothers, friends, or relatives.

The people had just worshiped a golden calf while Moses was on the mountain. Aaron had let the people run wild, and they were left open to the mockery of their enemies. Moses calls on those who want to stand on God's side, and the Levites respond. It is a very difficult passage; the text presents it as judgment for a serious rebellion against the covenant.

For today: God deserves first place, above the pressure of the group and above family ties. Today we are not asked for violence, but for courageous faithfulness: to humbly decide to belong to Jehovah, even when it costs.
exp.33:13:
This verse says that the people must not worship or bow down before any other god. The word "other" in the verse is rendered here as "another," and the phrase translated as "foreign" or "belonging to someone else" is not carried over into the English reading. God says that his name is "Jealous," meaning that he does not share with anyone the worship that is due to him, just as a faithful husband expects loyalty from his wife.

God himself speaks, through Moses, after Israel worshiped the golden calf. He is going to renew his covenant with them, and he warns that when they enter Canaan they must not make alliances with peoples who worship idols, because those friendships could lead them to abandon God.

For today: ask yourself what things compete with God for first place in your heart, such as money, success, or the opinions of others. Put God first, and watch carefully the influences that pull you away from him.
exp.31:4:
He says that Aaron, seeing how the people reacted to the golden calf, built an altar in front of it. Then he announced aloud: "Tomorrow there will be a feast to the Lord." The explanation notes that "proclaimed" means he announced it publicly. A "feast" here refers to a religious celebration with offerings.

The narrator recounts what happened while Moses was on Mount Sinai, and the people, impatient at his delay, asked for a visible god. Aaron did not use any other name: he called the feast "to the Lord," even though the idol corrupted it. Scholars debate whether Aaron wanted to mix the worship of God with the image or gave in out of fear. The text does not make this clear, but God judged it as corruption.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we are mixing something God does not approve of with our faith, only to please others. To worship sincerely means to obey God as He asks, not as is more comfortable for us.
exp.25:2:
The explanation says the ten curtains of the tabernacle were to be assembled in two groups of five. Each group was sewn or joined together to form one large piece. "The five curtains shall be coupled together one to another" means they were linked to one another, with no separations between them.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai and gives him instructions for building a sanctuary where he could dwell among Israel. These curtains formed the roof and the sides of the tabernacle. The details are very precise because everything had to be done just as God had commanded.

Today we can learn that God values unity. Just as these separate curtains formed a single covering, believers are different from one another, yet God unites us to be his house. Today you can seek to be someone who unites: forgive, listen, and serve to care for unity with your brothers and sisters in the faith.
exp.24:17:
God commands Moses to make two cherubim of solid gold, worked by hammering. He is to place them at the two ends of the cover, which is the lid of the ark. "Hammered" here means the gold was shaped by striking it, not by melting it and pouring it into a mold. The cherubim are angelic beings who serve God.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai and gives him instructions for building the tabernacle, a place where his presence would be near Israel. Inside the ark was the testimony, that is, the tablets of the law. The cover, also called the mercy seat, was the place where God would meet with his people.

For today: God cares about the details and wants to be worshiped with reverence and obedience. We can draw near to him with respect, knowing that he desires to be close to us.
exp.37:3:
He made for the altar a grate of bronze, shaped like a net, and set it under the ledge that ran around the altar, reaching halfway up the altar. Bezalel and the craftsmen made it, according to the account. "Bronze" here is the translation of the metal; the ledge is the rim or shelf around the altar. It is not known with certainty exactly how it was positioned, and scholars explain it in several different ways.

Here the account tells how the tabernacle was built, following the instructions God gave to Moses. The altar was the place where the sacrifices were offered, and the grate was part of its structure and of its carrying, as the next verse shows with the rings and the poles.

For today: God cares even for the details no one sees. We can serve Him faithfully in small things, knowing that nothing done for Him is insignificant.
exp.27:30:
God tells Moses to make the robe of the ephod entirely of blue. The ephod was a sacred garment worn by the high priest, and the robe was worn beneath it. The color blue is not a flower; it refers to a dye of blue or violet-blue, though some scholars think it may have been a deep blue or bluish purple.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai and gives detailed instructions for the clothing of Aaron, the high priest. This clothing set him apart to serve in the sanctuary and to represent the people before God. The verses that follow describe the opening for the head, the pomegranates, and the golden bells on the hem.

God cares about the details of how he is worshiped, because his presence is holy. Today we do not need special garments, since Christ is our high priest. Even so, we can draw near to God with reverence and care, offering him the best of our hearts and of our service.
exp.27:15:
The breastpiece of judgment, a special piece the high priest would wear over his chest, was to be square and doubled, that is, folded in two like a little pouch. It measured a span on each side, about 22 centimeters, which is the length of an open hand. Some older words for this breastpiece are no longer used. The word "doubled" probably indicates that it formed a pocket, although the text gives no further detail.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai and gives him instructions for the garments of Aaron, the high priest. These garments were made for glory and beauty, and they would serve in the worship at the tabernacle. This breastpiece would later hold twelve stones, one for each tribe of Israel.

For today: God cares about the details, and the priest carried the people over his heart. We can imitate him by praying for the people we love by name, carefully bringing them before God.
exp.28:5:
This verse describes one of the final steps in dressing Aaron as high priest. First the mitre is placed on him, which was a kind of turban or cap made of fine cloth. Then, on top of it, the holy crown is set: a plate of pure gold that, according to Exodus 28, had engraved on it the words "Holiness to the Lord."

God speaks to Moses and gives him instructions for consecrating Aaron and his sons as priests. Everything is done in order: washing them, dressing them, and then anointing them with oil. Nothing is left to improvisation, because serving God was something serious and holy.

For today: we can remember that serving God is not a matter of simple custom. God calls us to live set apart for Him, with reverence and sincerity. Today we can ask Him that our thoughts and our decisions, symbolized by the head, belong to Him.
exp.35:3:
It says that all the skilled men who were working on the construction of the sanctuary left their labor and came before Moses. The phrase "each of the work he was doing" indicates that each one came from the specific task he was carrying out.

It is part of the account of the construction of the tabernacle. The narrator tells that the craftsmen, chosen by God and called by Moses, received the offerings of the people. Since the people kept bringing offerings every morning, the workers stopped their work to let Moses know that there was already more than enough.

For today: when you serve God, do it with the trade you have, without looking down on it. And learn from these workers: they had the honesty to say "ya es suficiente," without taking advantage of others' generosity.
exp.17:2:
This verse continues the list of Moses' two sons who came with his wife Zipporah. The first was named Gershom, and Moses gave him that name because he said: "I have been an alien in a strange land." Here "alien" means a foreigner, someone who lives far from their homeland.

The speaker is the narrator of the book, who recalls what Moses said when his son was born in Midian, after he fled from Egypt. Now Jethro, his father-in-law, learns what God has done for Israel and comes to visit him, bringing Moses' family. The name Gershom keeps the memory of those difficult years.

For today: sometimes we feel out of place, far from home, or without direction. God can use those seasons to shape us. Remembering with gratitude what we have lived through helps us trust that He was with us and will continue to guide us.
exp.0:2:
This verse continues the list of the sons of Jacob, also called Israel. Here appear Issachar, Zebulun, and Benjamin, three of the twelve brothers who came to Egypt. The name in the older spelling is simply the same name as Issachar.

The book of Exodus begins with this list to connect its story with Genesis. The narrator is the author of the book, traditionally identified with Moses. Before telling of the slavery and the deliverance, it reminds us that the people of Israel began as a real family, with specific names. God had promised Abraham a great descendance, and this list is the starting point of that promise being fulfilled.

For today: God knows each person by name, even when it seems like an unimportant name in a list. You can rest in the knowledge that your life matters to Him and that He keeps His promises, even in difficult times you do not yet understand.
exp.17:14:
Moses answers his father-in-law that the people come to him because they want to inquire of God. That is, the people come to Moses to learn what God thinks about their problems. The word "unto" is an older way of saying "to," and "inquire" means asking for guidance or an answer.

Here Moses speaks, responding to Jethro, his father-in-law, who saw him sitting from morning until evening, attending to everyone. Jethro asked him why he was doing it alone. Moses explains that he does not see it as a simple job: he serves as a bridge so that the people may know the will of God. Even so, in the next verse Jethro will tell him that this is not good.

For today: serving others with good intentions does not mean doing everything alone. Learn to share responsibilities and to accept advice, so that you and others are better cared for.
exp.20:26:
It says that if a master struck his male servant or his female servant and knocked out a tooth, he had to let that servant go free as compensation for the injury. "Servant" here refers to a person who served another, and the phrase about knocking out a tooth means the tooth was broken out. "Going free" means the person stopped being a servant.

God speaks to Moses, and Moses passes these laws on to Israel after the Ten Commandments. At that time servitude existed in many peoples. This law placed a limit on mistreatment and recognized that the servant was a person of worth, not merely property. Some scholars see here a protection that was very advanced for its time.

For today: no one should use their power to harm someone who depends on them. If you have authority at work, at home, or in the church, treat others with respect, because God cares for them.
exp.24:12:
It says that Moses was to make poles or staves of shittim wood, which is the acacia, a very durable tree of the desert. These staves were to be overlaid with gold. They would serve to carry the ark, a sacred chest described in the preceding verses.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai while giving him instructions for building the tabernacle, the tent where Israel would worship. The ark would hold the tablets of the law. The staves with rings made it possible to carry the ark without touching it, because it was a holy object, and they also made it possible to move it when the people traveled through the desert.

God cares even about the details of how he is served. We can learn to treat what is sacred with respect and care: his Word, prayer, and life in community. We can also serve him with order, without neglecting small things, remembering that simple acts can also honor him.
exp.10:9:
This verse sums up what happened in the nine earlier plagues. Moses and Aaron performed before Pharaoh all the mighty signs that God had commanded them to do. "Wonders" are miracles or extraordinary deeds. Even so, God hardened Pharaoh's heart, and the king would not let the people of Israel leave his country.

The one telling the story is the author of the book, and he closes the section on the plagues before the last one. God had already warned Moses that Pharaoh would not listen, so that his wonders would be displayed in Egypt. Interpreters explain the hardening in different ways: Pharaoh resisted because of his own stubbornness, and God also confirmed that hardness as judgment.

For today: when God speaks to us and we feel resistance inside, we should not wait for bigger signs. It is better to respond quickly with humility and obedience, before the heart grows hard.
exp.27:2:
God tells Moses to speak with all the skilled craftsmen, whom he himself has filled with a spirit of wisdom. Their task will be to make Aaron's clothing, to set him apart so that he can serve God as priest. The words about wise-hearted people and filled-with-spirit wisdom are explained here: "wise-hearted" means people with skill and understanding, and "filled" means full. To "set apart" means to dedicate him to a holy use.

God speaks with Moses on Mount Sinai while giving him instructions for the tabernacle and the priesthood. Aaron and his sons will be priests, and their clothing must give them honor and beauty. It is striking that God attributes the craftsmen's skill to his own Spirit.

For today: every skill, whether manual, intellectual or creative, can be a gift from God. We can use our work with humility and care to serve others and honor God.
exp.38:33:
This verse is part of a list of the parts of the tabernacle that were brought to Moses. It mentions the covering of rams' skins dyed red, the covering of badgers' skins, and the veil of the covering. The word "badgers" is uncertain: some scholars think it was another animal, such as the dolphin or the dugong, or they speak of fine leather.

Moses is the one who receives the work, and the narrator tells how the Israelites finished it just as God had commanded. This list shows that each piece was ready and was checked before the tabernacle was set up.

For today: God pays attention to the details of our obedience. We can serve him faithfully in small things, without looking for shortcuts, trusting that what we do with a sincere heart matters to him.
exp.5:23:
This verse is part of a list of family members. It says that Korah had three sons, Assir, Elkanah, and Abiasaph, and that the families descended from them are called the "Korhites." The word "Korhites" refers to the descendants of Korah, from the tribe of Levi.

Here the narrator of the book, traditionally understood to be Moses, speaks. After God promises to free Israel, he pauses to show the ancestry of Moses and Aaron, from the tribe of Levi. The list shows that they were real people, with families and a history, and not invented figures. Some scholars believe the genealogy is abbreviated, so it does not include every generation.

For today: God knows names and families, not just crowds. You are not a number to Him. Even if your story seems ordinary or hidden, God can use your life in His plans. Thank Him for your family and trust that He sees you.
exp.38:42:
Moses reviewed all the finished work on the tabernacle and its furnishings. He saw that the people had made it just as God had commanded. Then he blessed them. The word "saw" in the verse is the same as the English word, and "blessed them" simply means he blessed them.

This is the closing of the construction of the tabernacle, the tent where God would dwell among Israel. The passage is not a speech but a narrative. Moses inspects the work as the leader of the people. Throughout the passage it is repeated that they did things "as the Lord had commanded." The text does not say here what words Moses used when he blessed them, only that he did.

God values simple and complete obedience, even in the details. Today we might ask ourselves: am I doing my work, my service in the church, or my household tasks faithfully, as for the Lord? Let us also imitate Moses: let us recognize and bless with words those who serve well.
exp.12:15:
The explanation says that the practice of setting apart the firstborn will be like a sign on the hand and a reminder in front of the eyes. The words "it will be" are not quoted here, and "reminder" is the sense of the word translated as a token or memorial in the verse. The phrase "strong hand" speaks of God's power, which freed Israel from Egypt, and needs no separate comment.

Moses speaks to the people shortly after the departure from Egypt. He explains how to answer when their children ask why they sacrifice the firstborn males of the animals and redeem the firstborn sons. Remembering the tenth plague and the deliverance was meant to keep gratitude alive. Some understand the matter of the hand and the eyes as a picture; others take it literally. The text itself does not settle the question here.

For today: look for simple ways to remember what God has done for you, such as a prayer of thanks or a journal, and tell it to your children or to others.
exp.31:16:
Joshua heard the people shouting and thought there was a battle in the camp. The word "shout" describes a loud noise of voices, and "war cry" is a shout of battle. The phrase "said to Moses" is rendered in the verse you are reading as "he said unto Moses."

Joshua speaks with Moses while the two of them are coming down from Mount Sinai. He had gone part of the way up with Moses, and from a distance he could not see what was happening. That is why he took the noise to be war. In fact the people were worshiping a golden calf, and Moses makes this clear in the next verse: it was singing, not fighting.

For today: not every noise means what it seems to mean. We sometimes get things wrong when we judge only by what we hear from far away. Before drawing conclusions, it is wise to draw near, look carefully, and ask God for discernment to understand what is really going on.
exp.0:7:
It says that time passed and a new king came to the throne of Egypt, one who "knew not Joseph." Old wording: where the verse reads "arose up," the meaning is simply "rose to power," and the phrase "in the meantime" shows that time kept moving on. Perhaps he did not know Joseph in a literal sense, or he simply did not care what Joseph had done for Egypt. The Bible does not make this clear, and it can be understood in either way.

The one speaking is the narrator, who sets the scene. Joseph's generation has died, the Israelites have multiplied, and the new king begins to address his people. His speech, which continues in verse 9, shows fear and a desire for control, and from there the oppression begins.

For today: the good deeds of others can be forgotten. Let us be grateful and pass on to our children what God has done, and let us be wary of decisions made out of fear.
exp.19:5:
God says that He shows mercy, that is, a kindness that forgives, to thousands of generations of those who love Him and keep His commandments. The phrase "of them that love me" points to those who answer His love. He contrasts this with the punishment that reaches to the third and fourth generation: God's kindness lasts far longer than His judgment.

God Himself speaks this on Mount Sinai, when He gives the Ten Commandments to Israel, who has just come out of Egypt. He has just forbidden images and declared that He is a jealous God, who wants to be loved by Him alone. This verse shows His heart: He is not only a judge, but also faithful and generous toward those who respond to Him with love.

For today: obeying God is not just following rules, but responding to His love. Today you can choose one concrete act of obedience, such as forgiving or being honest, done out of love for Him and trusting in His goodness.
exp.21:28:
God commands that the first of the harvest and of what is pressed out, such as wine or oil, not be delayed in being given. Here the word for pressed liquid refers to the juice of grapes or olives. He adds: "You shall give me the firstborn of your sons," which means that the eldest son belongs to God.

God speaks to Israel through Moses, among the laws that follow Sinai. These rules teach that everything comes from God and that he deserves the first of it. Later the Law allows the firstborn to be redeemed (Exodus 13:13), so it did not require that he be sacrificed, but that he be acknowledged as belonging to God.

For today: put God first and without delay. Before spending your money or your time, set apart with gratitude what belongs to him, and dedicate to God what is most precious to you, including your family, in prayer.
exp.25:13:
God tells Moses to make two more coverings for the tent: one of rams' skins dyed red, and another of skins of the animal in the verse, placed on top. The word for that animal is translated in different ways; some versions say "fine skins" or "durable leather," and it is not known for certain which animal the Hebrew refers to. These coverings went over the woven curtains.

Here God speaks on Mount Sinai, giving Moses the instructions for building the tabernacle, the place where He would dwell in the midst of Israel. The outer layers were strong and simple, and they protected the beautiful things inside from the rain, the dust, and the desert sun.

For today: God cares for the details of His house, and He also cares for you. Ask Him to be your protection in trials, and value the humble and steady things that sustain what is precious, like the faithful work of each day.
exp.39:24:
It says that Moses lit the lamps of the lampstand inside the tabernacle, in the presence of God. The phrase "before the Lord" means in his presence, in the place where God dwelt among his people. And it repeats that he did it just as God had commanded him.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, recounting how Moses set up the tabernacle, now finished, a year after leaving Egypt. Step by step he places the furnishings: the bread, the lampstand, the golden altar. The statement "as the Lord had commanded" is repeated, which underlines Moses' obedience. Scholars understand the symbolism of the light in various ways, but all note that God gave the instructions.

For today: do what God asks of you faithfully, even in small and repetitive things. Steady obedience is also a form of worship.
exp.34:14:
Here Moses continues listing what the people were to make for the tabernacle: the altar where the incense was burned, its poles for carrying it, the special oil for anointing, the fragrant incense, and the curtain covering the entrance. A curtain or veil is the hanging that covers the entrance, and incense is the fragrant substance burned on the altar.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel after the sin of the golden calf. He repeats the instructions God gave him on the mountain, and invites them to take part with offerings and labor. Each object had a purpose in the worship of God.

For today: God values even the small details when they are done with a willing heart. Incense is often connected in the Bible with prayer (Psalm 141:2). We can set aside time each day to pray, offering God our best attention.
exp.11:39:
This verse says that the children of Israel lived in Egypt for four hundred and thirty years.

The narrator tells us that God had already brought the people out of Egypt. With this detail he wants to show how long that period lasted, and that the departure came at exactly the right moment. It should be said that some older versions and the New Testament (Galatians 3:17) count the time in a different way, which is why scholars discuss how to calculate it. Even so, the text emphasizes that God kept his promise to Abraham.

For today: even when we wait a long time and see no answer, God does not forget his promises. We can trust that he works in his own time, and while we wait, we can remain faithful and thankful.
exp.11:8:
God explains how the Passover lamb must be prepared. It was not to be eaten raw or boiled in water, but roasted directly over the fire. It was roasted whole: the head, the legs, and the organs inside, which the text calls the "entrails" in the King James wording. A "staff" later on is a traveler's walking stick.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron in Egypt, just before the last plague and the departure of Israel. Each family was to put the blood of the lamb on the doorpost and eat in haste. Many understand that roasting it whole shows complete obedience and readiness to leave quickly, though the text does not give all the reasons.

Today we can learn to obey God attentively, without changing or cutting short what He asks. Ask yourself: is there something God has asked of you that you are only doing halfway?
exp.28:9:
God tells Moses to bring the bullock to the entrance of the tabernacle, which is called "of the congregation" here because it housed the tablets of the law. Then Aaron and his sons lay their hands on the animal's head. This gesture is understood as an identification: the animal takes their place.

God speaks to Moses while explaining how to consecrate the priests. Before serving the people, Aaron and his sons had to acknowledge their own need for forgiveness. This bullock was an offering for sin, according to the rest of the passage.

For today: no one serves God on their own merits. Before helping others, we need to come near with humility and recognize our need for God's grace. Many Christians see in this sacrifice a shadow of Christ.
exp.11:12:
The explanation says that the blood of the lamb, placed on the houses of the Israelites, would be a sign. When God saw that blood, he would pass over them and would not let the deadly plague that was coming upon Egypt fall on them. The words "pass over" in this context mean that God would not strike the houses marked with the blood. "Plague of death" means a calamity that causes death. "I will smite" means "I will punish."

God speaks to Moses and Aaron, so that they can tell the people, on the night before leaving Egypt. He was going to judge Egypt, including its gods, and at the same time he was giving Israel a way to be protected. That night became the Passover, which the people would remember every year.

For today: many Christians see in this a picture of Christ, the Lamb of God. We can trust in the protection that God offers, and not in our own merits. Today you can thank him simply for his mercy and live with confidence and gratitude.
exp.15:10:
This verse is very brief: it says that God spoke to Moses. The name "Jehovah" is the name of God, and the spelling of "unto" is an older form of the word. It does not yet bring the message; it only announces that God is about to speak.

The people of Israel were traveling through the desert and complaining because they were hungry. Moses and Aaron told them that the Lord had heard their complaints. Then the glory of the Lord appeared in the cloud, and God spoke. In the next verse he promises to give them meat in the evening and bread in the morning, so that they would know that he is their God.

God listens even to our complaints and does not remain silent. When we are in need, we can come to him with confidence and honesty, but also with a willingness to trust that he will take care of us.
exp.4:14:
The explanation says that the Israelite officers, that is, the Hebrew overseers placed over their own people, went directly before Pharaoh. They complained about the unjust treatment and asked him why he was dealing this way with them, his servants.

Moses and Aaron had just asked permission to go and worship God, and Pharaoh responded by increasing the burden: the people would no longer be given straw, but the quota of bricks would stay the same. The Hebrew officers were the ones who received the beatings for failing to meet it. They speak, caught between the Egyptians and their own people, and they go to the king seeking justice.

For today: when we suffer injustice, we can speak honestly and ask for justice. But let us remember that human authorities can fail. In the end, our hope rests in God, who sees the oppression and acts in his time.
exp.15:28:
It says that God gave the Sabbath to them as a gift, and so on the sixth day he gave them bread for two days. For that reason each person had to stay where he lived and not go out on the seventh day.
