Moses speaks to the people of Israel in the wilderness, after God rebuked some who went out to gather manna on the Sabbath and found nothing. God had already provided what they needed in advance. The rest was not a burden, but something God gave them and cared for through his provision.

For today: Trust that God provides what you need, and set aside regular time to rest without guilt. Resting is a way of saying that your sustenance depends not only on your effort, but also on God's care.
exp.22:14:
God tells Israel to celebrate the Feast of Unleavened Bread. For seven days they must eat bread without yeast, in the month of Abib, because it was in that month that they came out of Egypt. The word "unleavened" means without yeast. To "appear" means to present yourself. And no one should come before God "empty-handed," that is, without bringing an offering.

Here God speaks, through Moses, within the laws given at Sinai. Just before this, he had commanded them to be faithful to him and not to mention other gods. This is the first of three yearly feasts. They were ways of remembering the deliverance from Egypt and of giving thanks to God, who had brought them out and sustained them.

For today: to remember with gratitude what God has done for us. When we gather with other believers or pray, we can come with a thankful heart and a willingness to give, not only to receive.
exp.39:9:
God tells Moses to anoint the altar of the burnt offering and all its utensils with a special oil. To "anoint" means to pour or put oil on something as a sign that it is set apart for God. To "sanctify" means to set it apart for holy use. "Most holy" means it would be of the utmost holiness. The "vessels" here are the utensils or containers of the altar.

God speaks to Moses when the tabernacle is about to be raised, almost at the end of the book. Israel had left Egypt, and God was giving them instructions for living near Him. The altar was the place of the sacrifices, where it was remembered that sin needs forgiveness and that drawing near to God has a prescribed way.

For today: we can place our everyday things, such as our work, our homes, and our time, at God's disposal. Praying over them and using them to serve and bless others is a way of setting them apart for Him.
exp.37:20:
This verse opens the account of everything used in building the tabernacle. It says that a record was made, by Moses' command, and that Ithamar, son of the priest Aaron, was in charge of it. The phrase "as it was counted" means that the materials were tallied and recorded. The word "testimony" refers to the tablets of the law that were kept inside the ark. The Levites would be responsible for the service of the tabernacle.

The narrator of the book, traditionally credited to Moses, closes the description of the work here. He wants to show that everything was done with order and openness. The materials came from the people's offerings, so an accounting of them was given.

For today: if we handle money or resources belonging to the church or to other people, it is wise to do so with clarity and to be accountable for them. Honesty does not get in the way of faith; it honors God and gives others confidence.
exp.35:9:
This verse tells how the curtains of the tabernacle were put together. The ten curtains were joined into two groups of five. First the five were joined to one another, and then the other five. The word "coupled" here means sewn or fastened together, so that each group formed one large piece.

Moses is the one telling the story, describing how the craftsmen did what God had commanded. The skilled workers were people whom God gave talent for this task. The tabernacle was the place where God met with Israel in the wilderness. The verses that follow explain how the two groups would be joined together with loops.

For today: God values detail and teamwork. Even simple tasks, like joining one curtain to another, serve a greater purpose. Do carefully what is yours to do, trusting that God brings everything together for his glory.
exp.7:30:
This verse tells us that God answered Moses' prayer and completely removed the flies that had invaded Egypt. The words that mean "did according to the word of Moses" mean that God did what Moses asked. The "servants" are Pharaoh's officials and employees. The phrase that means "not one remained" means that not even a single fly was left.

The narrator describes the fourth plague. Pharaoh had promised to let the people go if Moses prayed, and Moses warned him not to deceive him again. God kept his word and showed both his power and his mercy. However, the next verse says that Pharaoh hardened his heart again and broke his promise.

For today: God hears our prayers and is faithful, even when people are not. We can pray with confidence. We should also examine whether, after receiving help, we respond to God with gratitude and obedience, or whether we harden our hearts again.
exp.22:16:
Three times a year, it says, all the men of Israel were to appear before God, here called "the Lord God." This was not an optional visit but an appointment set by God.

God speaks to Israel through Moses, after giving them the laws at Sinai. The three festivals were the feast of unleavened bread (which recalled the departure from Egypt), the harvest of the first fruits, and the final harvest. They were times to give thanks, to remember what God had done, and to acknowledge that everything comes from Him.

For today: set aside regular times to come before God with thankfulness, without waiting for free time to appear. Gathering with other believers, praying, and remembering how God has cared for you keeps your heart grateful and steady.
exp.1:24:
This verse says that God looked upon the Israelites and "had respect unto them." The phrase "had respect unto them" is an older way of saying that God took notice of them and paid attention to their situation. It does not mean that God had not known them before, but that now he took them into account in a personal way and took charge of their circumstances. Other translations say that God "took notice of them" or "knew their condition."

The narrator here is the writer of the book of Exodus, traditionally attributed to Moses. The Israelites had spent many years as slaves in Egypt. They had cried out, and the text shows a sequence: God heard, he remembered his covenant, and now he looks and takes notice. It is the prelude to the calling of Moses and to the deliverance.

For today: when you feel that no one sees your pain, remember that God does see and becomes involved. You can bring your cry to him with confidence.
exp.15:19:
Some of the Israelites did not listen to Moses. They kept part of the manna until the next day, even though they had been told not to. Then the manna bred worms, meaning it became full of larvae, and it rotted. Moses was angry with them. The word "but" in the verse is the first word of the sentence, and "left of it" means that they kept a portion.

The people were in the wilderness, and God gave them manna every morning. Moses had instructed them to gather only what was needed for that day. This was a way of teaching them to trust that God would provide food day after day. Here Moses speaks on God's behalf, and his anger shows how serious it was to distrust that provision.

Today we might ask ourselves where we find it hard to trust God and want to secure everything on our own. We can plan wisely, but we can also practice daily prayer, asking and giving thanks for what we need today, without letting fear of tomorrow control us.
exp.29:8:
God commands that nothing other than what he himself has ordered be offered on the altar of incense. "Strange incense" is incense different from that prepared for that place. Neither were burnt offerings to be placed there (an animal burned completely), grain offerings, or drink offerings (liquid, such as wine, poured out as an offering).

The LORD speaks to Moses about the tabernacle. This small altar, located in front of the veil, was used only for burning incense every morning and every evening. The animal sacrifices had their own altar outside. God wanted every element of worship to have its purpose and to remain holy, as the following verse shows.

For today: when we worship God, it is good to do so as he asks in his Word and not as we see fit. We can ask ourselves whether our worship springs from obedience and reverence, or only from our customs and preferences.
exp.19:8:
This verse says that God expects us to work for six days and in that time to do all our tasks. The sense of "work" here is labour or toil. The phrase about doing all your work means that there is enough good time to fulfill our responsibilities.

God himself speaks to the people of Israel from Mount Sinai, when he gives them the Ten Commandments. This verse is part of the commandment about the Sabbath day. Before ordering rest, God honors work: it is not an evil burden, but part of the life he designed. He then explains that the seventh day belongs to him.

For today: work with effort and honesty, but do not let work become your master. If you know there will be a day of rest, you can organize your tasks better and trust that God cares for you more than your own effort.
exp.35:23:
It says that Bezalel and his helpers made forty bases, or foundations, of silver to hold up the twenty boards on the south side of the tabernacle. Each board rested on two bases. In this way they stood firm and upright.

This is part of the account of how the tabernacle was built, following what God commanded Moses on the mountain. The narrator describes the work already finished, with great detail, to show that everything was carried out just as God had directed. The silver bases were made from the silver of the ransom given by the people (Exodus 38:25-27), though some understand this in different ways.

For today: God cares even for what no one sees, such as bases beneath the boards. Serve God faithfully in what is hidden and in what is small, for a steady life rests on foundations well laid.
exp.1:1:
The woman from the house of Levi became pregnant and had a son. When she saw that the child was a goodly child, she kept him hidden for three months. "Bare" means "gave birth," and "hid him" means "kept him hidden."

Here the narrator of the book of Exodus is speaking. The Israelites were living in Egypt, and the pharaoh had ordered that Hebrew baby boys be thrown into the river. That is why this mother hides her baby. His name is not yet given, but later we learn that he is Moses. Hebrews 11:23 says that his parents hid him by faith and were not afraid of the king's decree. Some think that "goodly" suggests something special about him, but the text does not make this clear.

For today: when fear or pressure surrounds you, do with faith what is within your reach to protect what God has entrusted to you, and leave the outcome in his hands.
exp.21:21:
The passage says that widows and fatherless children must not be mistreated. The opening word of the instruction is an old form of a verb that means "to cause suffering" or "to mistreat," and it is a clear command to protect those who have no one to defend them.

God speaks to Israel through Moses, in the laws given after the people left Egypt. In that time, a widow or a fatherless child was left without provision or legal protection. That is why God presents himself as their defender: the next verse says that if they cry out to him, he will hear them. This command sits alongside the one about the foreigner, whom Israel was to treat well because they themselves had been foreigners in Egypt.

Today we can look around us for those who are alone or vulnerable, such as a widow, a child without parents, or a single mother. Helping them with time, companionship, or concrete support, and never taking advantage of their situation, is how we obey this command.
exp.8:3:
It says that God would make a "separation," that is, a clear difference, between the animals of the Israelites and those of the Egyptians. The deadly plague would fall on the livestock of Egypt, but not one animal belonging to the children of Israel would die. "Make a separation" means that God would distinguish between the two.

Moses speaks on God's behalf to Pharaoh. Israel was enslaved in Egypt, and Pharaoh refused to let them go to worship God. This is the fifth plague, and the warning gave Pharaoh an opportunity to reconsider. The following text says it came to pass the next day. Livestock was both food and wealth, so the blow was very serious.

For today: God cares for His own even in the midst of difficult circumstances. We can trust that He sees our need, and also obey Him without delay, because hardening the heart brings consequences.
exp.12:4:
Verse 5 says that when God brings the people into the land of Canaan, they must keep this service in the month of Abib. The names Canaanites, Hittites, Amorites, Hivites, and Jebusites are the peoples who lived there. The phrase about a land flowing with milk and honey is a way of saying it was a good and fertile land. The word "sware" means that God made a solemn promise.

Moses speaks to the people just come out of Egypt. He explains that it is not enough to remember the deliverance on that day; they must also celebrate it every year. This "service" refers to the feast of unleavened bread, which is described in the verses that follow.

For today: do not forget what God has done for you. Set aside regular times to thank him and to remember the promises he has kept, especially when things are going well.
exp.34:21:
It says that both men and women came with willing hearts to give. They brought chains, earrings, rings, bracelets, and every kind of gold jewelry. Each one presented their gold offering to the Lord, that is, to God.

Moses had asked the people for materials to build the tabernacle, the tent where God would dwell among them. The narrator tells that the people responded after leaving Moses's presence. They gave what they had, and the text stresses that no one was forced: their hearts moved them. This happens after the sin of the golden calf, and some see here a restored heart.

Today, God looks not only at how much we give, but at the attitude with which we give. We can ask ourselves what we have on hand, such as time, money, or talents, and offer it with joy, without pressure or comparisons.
exp.1:8:
This verse tells that Pharaoh's daughter asks a woman to take care of the baby and nurse him for her, and promises to pay her for doing so. The words of the verse here read "take this child away" and "nursed it," which in the verse your reader sees mean the same as "take this child away and nurse it" and "nursed it." The woman takes the child and cares for him, and it is not yet said that he is her own son.

The one speaking is Pharaoh's daughter, who has just found the Hebrew baby in the river. The woman is in fact his mother, although the princess does not know it, because the child's sister called her. So the boy whom Pharaoh had condemned is protected and cared for by his own family. How the sister planned this, or how much the princess understood, the Bible does not say.

For today: God can care for what we love by using unexpected circumstances. Trust in Him and act with wisdom and courage, as this family did.
exp.24:15:
God tells Moses that he is to place "the testimony" inside the ark. The word "testimony" here refers to the stone tablets with the Ten Commandments, which are the written proof of the covenant between God and his people. God says that he himself will give them to him.

God is speaking, giving Moses instructions on Mount Sinai. He is designing the ark, a wooden chest covered in gold, for the sanctuary where Israel would worship. The tablets inside the ark were a reminder that God had committed himself to his people and that his word was at the center of their life. What follows, the covering with the cherubim, was to be placed over those tablets.

For today: just as God's law was at the center of the ark, we can give his Word the central place in our lives. That may mean setting aside a fixed time each day to read it and obey it.
exp.17:5:
This verse tells that Jethro sent word to Moses that he was coming to visit him. It says: "I thy father in law Jethro am come unto thee, and thy wife, and her two sons with her." The phrase "father in law" means the father of one's wife. It is understood that the notice was sent by message before he arrived.

Jethro, priest of Midian, is the one speaking. Moses is with the people of Israel in the wilderness, near the mount of God, after the departure from Egypt. Jethro had heard what God had done for Israel and comes to bring Moses back together with his family. It is not said here when or why they had separated, and this is interpreted in different ways.

For today: take care of your family even when you have a great calling. Make time to welcome, listen, and give thanks together for what God has done.
exp.0:11:
The more the Egyptians mistreated the Israelites, the more they multiplied and grew. "But" is the word for "but," and "troubled" here means that the Egyptians felt dread, unease, and dislike toward the children of Israel. The plan to oppress them backfired.

The one telling the story is the author of the book, traditionally identified as Moses. A new pharaoh feared that the Israelites, being so numerous, might side with enemies in a war. So he put heavy labor and taskmasters over them, and forced them to build the storage cities of Pithom and Raamses. But the oppression did not stop the people from growing.

For today: when we go through pressure or injustice, it does not mean that God has forgotten us. He can sustain and strengthen his people even in hard times. We can trust that he is still at work, even when we cannot see how good will come out of it.
exp.0:14:
This verse tells us that the king of Egypt called in the midwives of the Hebrew women to give them an order. Two names are mentioned, Shiphrah and Puah, though there were perhaps more midwives, since the verse speaks of them as "the one" and "the other." Midwives are the women who helped with childbirth.

The one speaking is the pharaoh. The Hebrews were already living under oppression and hard labor, and he wanted to slow their growth. Some scholars debate whether these women were Hebrews or Egyptians, because the Hebrew text can be understood in either way; this cannot be stated with certainty.

For today: when an authority orders something unjust, God calls us to fear Him more than people, as these midwives did. Let us ask for courage to protect life and do what is right, even when it costs us.
exp.20:3:
This verse is about a Hebrew servant who has already served his six years. If his master had given him a wife, and she had borne him sons or daughters, then the wife and her children still belonged to the master, and the servant went out by himself.

God speaks to Moses and gives laws to the people of Israel after the Ten Commandments. These rules regulated servitude for debt, to set limits and protect the Hebrew servant with freedom in the seventh year. This case is hard and painful, for it sets the right to freedom against family ties. The text that follows offers a way out: the servant may choose to stay out of love for his family.

For today: value your family above comfort or personal freedom, and treat with justice and compassion those who depend on you, for God sees every situation.
exp.7:5:
It says that Aaron stretched out his hand over the waters of Egypt, that is, the Nile, the rivers, streams and ponds, and from there the frogs came up and covered the whole land. The word "came up" shows that they were coming out of the water onto the land.

God had commanded Moses to tell Aaron to stretch out his staff. Pharaoh had refused to let Israel go, so this was the second plague. The magicians of Egypt copied the sign, but they only added more frogs. Then Pharaoh asked Moses for help, which shows that only God could take them away.

For today: what we take for granted, like the water of the Nile for Egypt, cannot save us if God does not sustain it. We can ask ourselves what things have taken God's place in our trust, and return to Him with humility, without waiting for the problem to grow.
exp.37:22:
This verse introduces Aholiab, Bezaleel's helper in building the tabernacle. He was from the tribe of Dan. He is described as a skilled craftsman (the verse's "cunning workman"), a designer (the one who draws the patterns), and an embroiderer (the one who sews decorative work). He worked with threads of blue, purple and scarlet, and with fine linen.

The narrator of the book, traditionally understood to be Moses, is giving a report on the work on the tabernacle and the materials used. He mentions Aholiab alongside Bezaleel to acknowledge those whom God had equipped. It is notable that Aholiab came from Dan, a smaller tribe, while Bezaleel was from Judah.

God uses both the well-known and the less noticed. Your talent, whether simple or very visible, can serve God and others. Offer it with humility and work with excellence.
exp.21:5:
If a fire gets out of control, runs into thorns, and burns up grain that has already been piled, standing crops, or someone else's field, the person who started the fire must pay for the damage.

The verse in the King James Version reads: "If fire break out, and catch in thorns, so that the stacks of corn, or the standing corn, or the field, be consumed therewith; he that kindled the fire shall surely make restitution." The explanation's note on the word "stacks" refers to the piles of harvested grain.

God gives these laws to Israel through Moses, shortly after the Ten Commandments. They were rules for daily life in a farming community, where a careless fire could ruin a family's livelihood. The law teaches that saying "I did not mean it" is not enough: whoever causes the harm is responsible for making it right.

For today: take responsibility when your carelessness harms others, whether with money, time, or words. Repair the damage with humility, without excuses.
exp.38:9:
It says that four rows of precious stones were set on the high priest's breastpiece. The first row had three: sardius (a reddish stone), topaz, and carbuncle (a bright stone, perhaps red or green). The old name for the breastpiece is "breastplate of judgment." The exact names of the stones are uncertain, because the Hebrew words have been translated in several different ways.

The narrator describes how the craftsmen of Israel carried out what God had commanded Moses for the tabernacle and Aaron's garments. According to Exodus 28, each stone represented one of the twelve tribes. In this way, the priest carried the whole people on his chest, before God.

For today: God cares for each person as someone valuable and known by name. You can remember that you are not forgotten. And, if you are called to serve others, carry them in your heart, praying for them with love and with perseverance.
exp.38:18:
It says that the craftsmen made two more rings of gold and put them on the two lower corners of the breastplate, on its inner edge, on the side that lay next to the ephod. The "breastplate" is the high priest's breastpiece, with the twelve stones. The "ephod" was a priestly garment worn over the chest and back.

This passage is part of the account of how Aaron's sacred garments were made. The narrator describes, step by step, that the craftsmen followed the instructions God had given to Moses. The rings served to fasten the breastplate to the ephod, so that it would not move or fall.

For today: God cares about small details, and faithfulness is also shown in the simple things. If something seems small in your work, your family, or your service, do it with care and obedience, as for the Lord.
exp.15:14:
The verse tells how the Israelites saw something new on the desert ground and asked one another, "What is it?", because they did not know what it was. Moses explained that it was the bread the Lord had given them to eat. The word "Lord" is God's name, and the phrase "has given you" is rendered by "gave to them" in the verse above. Many understand that the word "manna" comes from that question, though scholars are not entirely sure of its origin.

The people had just left Egypt and were hungry in the desert. They had complained against Moses, and God promised to give them food. That evening the quail arrived, and in the morning this small thing appeared like frost. Here Moses speaks, helping the people understand that it is not chance but a gift from God.

For today: sometimes God cares for us in ways we do not recognize at first. We can ask ourselves each day what simple blessings we have already received, and give thanks to God for them with confidence.
exp.11:50:
God brought the people of Israel out of Egypt on the very day He had appointed. The word "Lord" is the name of God. The phrase "by their armies" means that the people left in organized groups, like companies or divisions, arranged by their tribes and families, not in disorder.

The one telling the story is Moses, or the account traditionally attributed to him. It closes the story of the Passover and the last plague. Earlier, the law was spoken of as applying to everyone, both the native-born and the foreigner who lived among them. The verse emphasizes that the deliverance was the work of God, fulfilling what He had promised after centuries of slavery.

God keeps His promises in His own time, even when we wait a long while. Today you can trust that He is still at work in your life, and while you wait, live with order and obedience, as Israel did.
exp.8:19:
Among the servants of Pharaoh, the explanation says, there was one who took God's warning seriously. The phrase "feared the word of the Lord" means that he respected it and believed it. That is why he made his servants and his cattle hurry into the houses to keep them safe. The verse says that he "made his servants and his cattle flee," which means he got them to hurry to shelter.

God, through Moses, had announced that the next day a terrible hail would fall on Egypt. It was the seventh plague. God gave a chance for protection to anyone willing to listen. Some Egyptians believed and acted; others ignored the warning, as the following verse shows.

For today: when God speaks to us in his Word, it is not enough to hear it; we must obey it in time. Think of a biblical teaching you have put off, and take one concrete step today to put it into practice.
exp.6:6:
This verse says that Moses was eighty years old and Aaron eighty-three when they went to speak with Pharaoh. The narrator gives this detail just as the confrontation with Pharaoh begins, and the ages of the two brothers at that moment are simply given to us.

God had already commanded them to bring Israel out of Egypt, and they obeyed. The ages emphasize that God called men who were already advanced in years. Moses had spent forty years in Midian, according to Acts 7:30, which fits with this detail. Some scholars see in this a sign that the work was God's and not the result of human strength.

For today: it is never too late for God to use you. Perhaps you feel that your age or your past limits you, but God can call you and equip you at any stage of life. Trust and obey, as they did.
exp.32:21:
He says that God will make his glory pass before Moses. While it passes, he will place Moses in a crack in the rock and cover him with his hand until it has finished passing.

God speaks with Moses after the people sinned with the golden calf. Moses asked to see God's glory, but God explains that no one can see his face and still live. So he protects Moses and allows him to see only his back. Some understand this as a way of speaking about God's presence, which is immense and cannot be seen fully.

God knows what we can bear, and he cares for us even when we ask for more than we understand. We can trust him when we do not see everything clearly, because he protects us and guides us with love.
exp.35:27:
This verse says that Bezalel and the craftsmen made two more boards for the corners of the tabernacle, at the back, on the west side. So with the six boards of the back wall, there were eight in all. The silver stands that held each board in place are the ones this explanation calls the "basas."

The passage is part of the account of how the tabernacle was built. It is not a speech: the narrator tells how the people followed, point by point, what God had commanded Moses on the mountain. The details about the corners show that care was taken to make the structure firm and well joined. Scholars do not fully agree on exactly what those corner boards looked like.

For today: God cares about the small details that hold his work together. Do what is given to you faithfully and carefully, even when no one notices; the corners count too.
exp.11:28:
He says this: at midnight, God struck with death every firstborn son in Egypt. No one was spared because of their position: neither Pharaoh's son, who ruled, nor the son of the prisoner in the dungeon. The firstborn of the animals also died.

The book's narrator, whom tradition identifies with Moses, tells of the tenth plague. Pharaoh had refused again and again to let the people of Israel go free. The Israelites had put blood from a lamb on their doors, as God commanded, and for that reason death passed over them. This is where the name "Passover" comes from.

For today: this passage reminds us that God is serious about injustice, but also offers protection to those who trust in Him. Christians see in Jesus the Lamb who covers us. Today you can trust in his provision and not in your own merit.
exp.0:0:
This verse opens the book of Exodus and says that it will name the children of Israel, that is, of Jacob, who came to Egypt. "Came into" means that they arrived to live there. Each one came with his household, that is, with his wife, his children, and his home. It is a list of names.

According to Jewish and Christian tradition, the author is Moses, although the text does not say so here. He connects this book with the story in Genesis, where Jacob and his family went down to Egypt during the famine. The names remind us that the oppressed people who will appear later have their origin in real people and in God's promises.

God knows names, not just crowds. Today we can remember that each person, and each family, matters to Him. This encourages us to pray for our family by name and to value those around us.
exp.22:0:
It says that we should neither accept nor repeat gossip or false news. Nor should we join forces with a wicked person to give a lying testimony, especially in a court of law. Here "admit" means to receive, accept, or spread. "Join" means to unite yourself with others, to make an agreement.

God speaks to Israel through Moses, within the laws that follow the Ten Commandments. These rules teach how to live justly as God's people. Here people are protected from false accusations, and justice is guarded in the courts, where a lie could ruin a life.

For today: before you share a piece of news or a comment about someone, stop and ask whether it is true and whether you know it from a good source. If you are not sure, it is better not to repeat it. And if you are asked to support a lie, even out of group pressure, have the courage to tell the truth.
exp.27:12:
God tells Moses to make "ouches of gold," that is, small settings or frames of gold in which the two stones with the names of the tribes of Israel would be held. A setting is the piece that holds a precious stone in place. In this way the stones would stay firm and well displayed on the ephod, which was the sacred garment of the priest.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai and gives him detailed instructions for the clothing of Aaron, the high priest. The stones on his shoulders would serve as a reminder: Aaron would symbolically carry the whole people before God when he ministered.

For today: God cares for every detail and does not forget his people. We can rest in knowing that he holds us firmly. And just as Aaron carried the names of others, we too can carry the people we love before God in prayer, presenting them to him with care and steadiness.
exp.21:27:
God commands that people not insult (revile) the judges, nor speak evil of, show contempt for, or curse the ruler of the people (the prince, that is, the leader). The Hebrew word translated "judges" can also mean "God," and for that reason some translations read "Thou shalt not revile God." Scholars interpret this in different ways.

God speaks to Israel through Moses, after the Ten Commandments. These are laws for the people's everyday life: justice, care for the poor, and respect. The verses nearby speak of being compassionate toward the needy. Here the order and respect owed to those who lead and judge are protected.

Today we can voice opinions or ask for changes from those in authority without mockery, insults, or hatred. A practical step: pray for your leaders by name and, if you must criticize, do so with respect and with facts.
exp.13:4:
It says that someone told the king of Egypt that the people of Israel had fled. Then Pharaoh and his servants changed their minds, regretted having let them go, and asked themselves how they had allowed their workforce to leave. The phrase "was told" is the same as the verse's "it was told," and "fled" is the same as the verse's "fled"; the phrase "to serve us" refers to working for them as slaves.

The narrator recounts what happened after the plagues, when Pharaoh let Israel go. God had already said that he would harden Pharaoh's heart to display his glory. Even so, the text presents Pharaoh's reaction as his own decision, driven by his pride and his economic interest.

Today we can learn that when we make a right decision, we are sometimes tempted to turn back out of comfort or habit. Let us ask God for firmness so that we do not return to what once enslaved us.
exp.28:35:
It says that during the seven days of the priests' ordination, a young bull was to be offered every day as a sin offering. The altar was also to be cleansed, with atonement made for it, and anointed with oil to set it apart for God. "Atonement" means covering or taking away guilt; "to sanctify" means setting something apart for sacred use.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai, giving him instructions to ordain Aaron and his sons as priests. Before the altar and the priests could serve, they had to be prepared and purified. The process was repeated each day, showing that drawing near to God is a serious matter and that sin must be dealt with.

For today: we approach God with humility, not lightly. Christians believe that Christ made a complete atonement. Because of this we can come with confidence, but also with gratitude, setting aside time each day to acknowledge our failings and return to God.
exp.2:18:
God tells Moses that Pharaoh will not let the people of Israel go easily. The phrase "by a mighty hand" can be understood in two ways: that only a powerful force would compel him, or that God himself would use his mighty hand. The phrase "will not let you go" means "will not let them leave." Translators have debated the exact sense, but both ideas fit with what follows.

God speaks from the burning bush. He is sending Moses to ask the king to free the Hebrews. Before Moses begins, God warns him that there will be resistance. Then he promises that he will stretch out his hand with wonders, and that in the end Pharaoh will let them leave.

For today: when you follow what God asks of you and obstacles appear, it does not mean you got it wrong. God already knew about the difficulty and promised to be with you. Obey with confidence, and do not be discouraged by opposition.
exp.9:15:
Pharaoh called for Moses and Aaron in great haste. He said he had sinned against the Lord your God, and also against you. It is a confession that sounds clear and strong.

The king of Egypt is speaking. A plague of locusts had just destroyed what little was left after the hail, and the land was devastated. Pharaoh becomes frightened and asks for help. Then he begs that they forgive him and pray to take away this plague. However, the account shows that his heart remained hard, so many understand that his repentance arose more from fear of the consequences than from a true change.

For today: asking for forgiveness is not just saying words when we are in trouble. God looks for a humble heart that truly changes, not merely one that wants to escape the pain. Let us ask for forgiveness sincerely and obey.
exp.3:16:
It says that Moses must take the staff in his hand and that he will do the signs with it. "Staff" is a shepherd's rod. "Signs" are miraculous deeds that show God sent him. It is a brief and practical command.

God speaks with Moses in the wilderness of Midian. Moses made excuses because he felt clumsy in speaking, and God promised him help through Aaron. Then he reminds him of the staff he already had in his hand. That common stick had become a sign in Exodus 4:2-5. The power was not in the wood, but in God, who used it.

God often works with what we already have in our hands: a trade, a skill, a simple gift. You do not have to wait to become someone else. Put it at God's disposal today and trust that the power comes from Him.
exp.33:21:
God tells Israel to celebrate two feasts. The "feast of weeks" was held at the beginning of the wheat harvest, and the "feast of ingathering" came "at the year's end," that is, at the close of the farming year. This was when the produce of the fields was gathered in.

The Lord speaks to Moses at Sinai, when he renews his covenant with the people after the sin of the golden calf. These feasts were part of three yearly meetings with God. Later they came to be called Pentecost and the Feast of Tabernacles or of Booths, though here the text only describes their season in the farming year.

For today: God wants us to recognize that the harvest comes from his hand. You can set aside regular time to thank him for what you have received: your work, your food, your family. Do it with a sincere prayer and, if you can, by sharing with someone else.
exp.8:32:
Moses left the city, where Pharaoh was, and spread out his hands toward God in prayer. Then the thunder, the hail, and the rain stopped. "Spread out his hands" was a way of praying. The phrase about praying "to the Lord" simply means praying toward the Lord, and "the Lord" is the name of God.

This happens during the seventh plague on Egypt. Pharaoh had asked Moses to plead with God to stop the storm, and he promised to let Israel go. Moses prayed, and God answered. But what follows shows that Pharaoh did not keep his word: as soon as the danger had passed, he hardened his heart again.

For today: it is easy to seek God when we are in trouble and forget him when everything calms down. May our prayer and our obedience not depend on the storm, but on a sincere trust in God at all times.
exp.31:7:
It says that the people turned aside very quickly from the way that God had commanded them. They made a calf of molten metal, worshipped it, offered sacrifices to it, and called it the god who brought them out of Egypt. The word "quickly" is the one used in the verse itself.

God speaks, and he speaks to Moses, who is on Mount Sinai. Only a few weeks earlier, the people had promised to obey God. While Moses was taking a long time to come down, the people made the calf, and God tells Moses that his people "have turned aside." It is an accusation of betrayal, because they gave to an idol what only God had done.

For today: it is easy to credit our blessings to other things, such as money, success, or our own effort. Today you can thank God for something specific and remember that it was he who sustained you.
exp.27:24:
This verse describes how the breastpiece of the high priest was fastened. The two braided gold chains had their ends fixed in two settings (small gold holders), and from there they were attached to the shoulderpieces of the ephod at the front. The breastpiece is the one called the breastplate in the verse; the ephod was the priestly garment, somewhat like a long apron.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai and gives him detailed instructions for Aaron's clothing. The breastpiece held twelve stones bearing the names of the tribes of Israel. That is why it had to be well secured, close to the priest's chest.

For today: God cares for even the small details when it comes to his people. Just as the breastpiece could not come loose, we can trust that He holds us firmly. Today, pray for someone by name, carrying them in your heart.
exp.24:20:
God tells Moses to place the cover on top of the ark. That cover is the gold lid, also called the mercy seat. Inside the ark he is to put the testimony, which are the tablets of the law that God would give him. Thus the law is kept protected beneath the cover.

God speaks on Mount Sinai while giving instructions for building the tabernacle. Shortly afterward he says that from that cover, between the cherubim, he would speak with Moses. The ark would be the meeting place between God and his people. Some see here an image of mercy covering the law, though the text does not explain this directly.

For today: God wants to be near us and to speak to us. Look for a moment each day to listen carefully to his Word, trusting that his mercy receives you just as you are.
exp.9:3:
God warns Pharaoh through Moses and Aaron: if he keeps refusing to let the people go, he will send locusts over his land the next day. "Borders" in this verse means the boundaries or lands, that is, the whole country. "Refuse" here means that you keep saying no.

Moses and Aaron speak on behalf of the LORD. Egypt had already suffered several plagues, among them the hail, which damaged the crops. God asks Pharaoh how much longer he will resist humbling himself. The warning gives him a new chance to change before the punishment arrives. The verses before this one say that these signs would help future generations know who the LORD is.

For today: God often gives us chances to make things right. If we feel that He is confronting us over a stubborn attitude, it is better to yield humbly today than to wait until the consequences grow.
exp.21:4:
It says that if someone lets his livestock graze in a field or vineyard, or lets his animal loose so that it eats from another person's land, he has to pay for the damage. And he must pay with the best of his own harvest or of his own vineyard. The words about letting animals feed on a field are explained by the verse itself, which speaks of letting a flock or herd go to graze and eat pasture. A beast is a working or breeding animal, such as a cow, a horse, or a donkey.

God gives these laws to Israel through Moses, after the Ten Commandments. They were rules for the people's daily life, and they sought fairness when property was harmed. Some scholars believe that "the best" refers to paying according to the quality of what was lost; others believe it was a generous compensation.

Today: if something you neglected harms another person, respond with honesty and restitution, without excuses and without giving the least you can. Loving your neighbor includes taking responsibility for the harm you have caused.
exp.27:9:
It says that the names of the twelve tribes of Israel were to be engraved on two onyx stones, six names on each. They were to be arranged "according to their birth," that is, in the order in which each son of Jacob was born. The onyx stones are the ones described in the verse, and the stone's color is not explained further here.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai and gives him instructions for the garments of the high priest. These two stones were to be set on the shoulders of the ephod, and Aaron would carry the names before the LORD as a memorial. In this way the priest represented the whole people before God.

For today: God does not forget his people; every name matters. You can pray for your family and your church, naming them one by one, and remember that Jesus, our great high priest, also carries us before the Father (Hebrews 4:14-16).
exp.34:2:
This verse forbids lighting a fire in your homes on the sabbath day. "Habitations" means the places where they lived, and "sabbath" means the day of rest. It was a concrete rule so that no one would work that day, not even in tasks like cooking or warming something.

Moses speaks to all of Israel, just before asking them for offerings to build the tabernacle. He first reminds them of the sabbath, so that they would understand that the work for God did not stand above the rest He commanded. Scholars discuss exactly how this rule was applied, but its central idea is clear: that day was holy.

Today we can set aside a weekly time to truly rest, to put down the rush and the screens, and to devote that space to God, to family, and to gratitude, trusting that He cares for what we do not manage to get done.
exp.34:33:
This verse says that God did not only give Bezalel the skill to work, but also put in his heart the ability to teach others. He did the same with Aholiab, of the tribe of Dan. The word "hath put" means placed or set within him.

Moses is speaking to the people of Israel as the construction of the tabernacle is being prepared, the tent where God would dwell among them. He explains that God himself chose and equipped Bezalel and Aholiab. Thus, the work did not depend only on human talent, but on a gift from God, and it was to be shared with others.

For today: if God has given you a skill, do not keep it only for yourself. Look for someone to whom you can teach what you know, in the church, at work, or in your family.
exp.3:23:
Moses was traveling back toward Egypt, and it says he stopped to spend the night at a place to rest. There the Lord met him, that is, confronted him, and sought to kill him, meaning his life was in serious danger.

The text does not make clear who was in danger, whether Moses or his son. Earlier, God had commanded circumcision as the sign of his covenant with Abraham. Moses was going to be God's messenger before Pharaoh, yet it seems he had not carried out that sign with his son. Zipporah, his wife, circumcises the boy, and the danger passes. Scholars explain this passage in several ways.

For today: God takes obedience seriously, especially from those who serve him. It is not enough to have an important mission; we need to check whether there is something God asked of us that we have left undone.
exp.1:10:
It says that when Moses was already grown, he went out to visit his own people, the Hebrews. There he looked on their burdens, that is, their heavy labor and suffering as slaves. Then he saw an Egyptian striking a Hebrew.

It is the narrator who tells the story. Moses had been raised in the palace as the adopted son of Pharaoh's daughter, but here he identifies with the Hebrews and calls them his brethren. The text does not explain everything he was thinking, but it shows that he could no longer ignore the injustice his people were suffering. What he does next, in the verses that follow, is violent, and interpreters evaluate it in different ways.

For today: do not get used to watching the suffering of others from a distance. Ask God for eyes to see those who suffer and for wisdom to help them with justice and patience.
exp.35:0:
It says that Bezaleel, Aholiab, and all the wise-hearted men began the work of the sanctuary. God himself had given them wisdom and understanding to know how to do everything he had commanded. "Wise-hearted" means skilled and sound in judgment. "Sanctuary" is the holy place where God would meet with his people.

It is part of the account of building the tabernacle in the wilderness, after God gave Moses the instructions. The narrator tells us that the people had already brought their offerings, and now the craftsmen whom God equipped begin to work. Some details of the sequence in these chapters are explained in several ways, but the central idea is clear: God provides and also equips.

For today: what you know how to do can be a gift from God. Offer it with humility to serve others and him, whether it is cooking, teaching, repairing, or caring for others.
exp.14:14:
The explanation says that when the neighboring peoples of Israel hear what God did at the Red Sea, they will be filled with fear. The sentences that explained the old wording are now rewritten to match the verse your reader sees: the word "amazed" here means they will be left shaken and confused. The "mighty men of Moab" are their strong men or their leaders. "Trembling shall take hold upon them" means that trembling will overcome them. "Melt away" means they will lose their courage.

Moses and the Israelites sing this hymn after crossing the Red Sea and seeing the Egyptian army destroyed. They celebrate God's salvation and confidently declare that the nations they will meet on the way to Canaan will feel fear. The text does not say that all of this happened immediately; it is a song of trust that God will guide them to the end.

For today: if God has already sustained you through past trials, you can trust that he will not leave you halfway along the road. Remember his works, and let them strengthen your faith in the face of today's fears.
exp.2:17:
God tells Moses that the elders of Israel will believe him and listen to his voice. Then Moses and the elders are to go before the pharaoh and tell him that the God of the Hebrews "has met with us." They will ask permission to go three days' journey into the wilderness and offer sacrifices to God. "Lord" is the name by which God is known here, and "let us sacrifice" means to offer a gift in worship.

God speaks from the burning bush. He is sending Moses to free his people from slavery. Asking for only three days' journey was a first step. God already knew that the pharaoh would refuse, as the following verses say. Some scholars see in this a modest request; others, the beginning of a complete departure.

For today: when God calls you to a difficult step, he already knows the obstacles and goes before you. Obey with confidence, even when you cannot see the whole road.
exp.22:31:
This verse says that the people of Israel were not to make agreements or treaties with the nations living in Canaan, nor to accept their gods. A treaty is a formal commitment of friendship and mutual support.

God speaks to Israel through Moses, shortly after giving them the law at Sinai. He promises to give them the land little by little. The reason the verse gives is protection: such alliances could lead them to worship idols, and that would be a trap for them.

For today: let us guard against whatever can draw us away from God, such as friendships, business dealings, or habits that push us to put him in second place. We can treat everyone with respect and kindness, but without compromising our faithfulness to Christ.
exp.35:2:
This verse says that the workers received from Moses everything the people had brought as an offering to build the sanctuary. That way they could begin the work. But the people kept bringing voluntary offerings, without fail, every morning. The phrase "to make it withal" means "in order to carry out the work." "Sanctuary" is the holy place where God would dwell among his people.

It is part of the account of building the tabernacle. The narrator tells how Moses handed the offerings to Bezalel, Aholiab and the other craftsmen, to whom God had given skill. The people gave freely, not out of obligation, and that is why they did not stop bringing.

For today: God values what we give with a willing heart. We can offer time, talents or money with joy and steadiness, without anyone pressuring us, to serve his work and others.
exp.24:30:
God tells Moses to make a lampstand, that is, a lamp stand with a base and a central shaft. It was to be made of pure gold and worked by hammering, that is, beaten into shape rather than cast in a mold. Its foot (the base), its shaft (the central stem), its cups, its knops (round ornaments, perhaps like buds) and its flowers were to form one piece with it.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai, giving him instructions for building the tabernacle, the tent where Israel would worship. Earlier He had spoken about the ark and the table of bread; now He moves on to the light that would illuminate the holy place. The details show that God cares that His worship be carried out with care and reverence.

For today: to offer God our best, with dedication and without carelessness. Even the small things we do with love, such as serving or working with honesty, can be a valuable offering to Him.
exp.38:27:
This verse describes part of the priests' clothing: the mitre or turban of fine linen, the goodly bonnets (head coverings) also of fine linen, and the linen breeches of fine twined linen, that is, strong thread made of several strands twisted together. The undergarments that covered the body with modesty are the breeches.

The narrator tells how the craftsmen of Israel finished the garments of Aaron and his sons. Everything was made "as the LORD commanded Moses," a phrase repeated throughout the chapter. God had given precise instructions so that the priests would serve in the tabernacle with order, purity, and reverence.

For today: God values obedience in the details, even in what no one sees. We can serve him with care and faithfulness in small things, without looking for shortcuts, trusting that what he asks has a good purpose.
exp.9:8:
Moses tells Pharaoh that the whole people will go to worship God: the young and the old, the sons and the daughters, and also the sheep and the cattle. The word "feast" in the verse refers to a sacred celebration, a special day set apart to honor God. No one is left behind.

Pharaoh had just offered a half-way exit: he asked who was going to go, thinking of letting only a few leave. Moses speaks in God's name and accepts no cuts. After several plagues, the king's servants were already desperate, but Pharaoh answered in anger and let only the men go.

Today we can learn that faith is not only a matter for a few people in the house. We can look for simple ways to include the whole family in worshiping God, from the youngest children to the grandparents, without letting anything settle for a partial obedience.
exp.9:4:
This verse describes what the locust plague will do. There will be so many that they will cover the ground and the earth will no longer be seen. They will eat what was left after the hail, that is, the plants and crops that survived the previous plague. They will also devour every fruit tree in the field. The phrase "the face of the earth" refers to the surface of the ground.

Moses and Aaron speak to Pharaoh on behalf of God. They warn him of what will come if he keeps refusing to let the Israelites go. God asks him how long he will refuse to humble himself, that is, refuse to acknowledge his authority. It is a warning before the punishment, an opportunity to change course.

For today: when God speaks to us, it is wise to respond quickly. Hardening the heart only brings more losses. Humbling ourselves means recognizing that God knows more than we do and obeying him in time.
exp.28:31:
This verse says that Aaron and his sons, the priests, were to eat the flesh of the ram and the bread that was in the basket. They would do this at the entrance of the tent of meeting, which here is called the tent of testimony in the older wording. The sentence explaining the old spelling is removed, since it refers to wording not found in your verse.

God speaks to Moses and gives him instructions for the ceremony in which Aaron and his sons would be set apart as priests. After the sacrifice was offered, they ate part of it. The verses that follow explain that it was holy and that only they could eat it. Scholars understand this meal as a sign of fellowship with God and of their new service.

Today we can learn that serving God begins with being near Him. Before doing things for God, set aside time to be with Him in prayer, in the Word, and in gratitude for what Christ has done for you.
exp.15:9:
This verse tells us that, while Aaron was speaking to the whole congregation of the children of Israel, they looked toward the wilderness and saw the glory of the Lord appearing in the cloud. "Glory" here refers to a visible sign of God's presence and power.

The Israelites had left Egypt and, in the wilderness, they were complaining because they were hungry. Moses reminded them that these complaints were, at bottom, against God and not against him or Aaron. Aaron passed on Moses' message, and God answered by showing himself. Afterward he promised to give them meat and bread.

When we are in need, it is easy to complain and forget that God sees us. Today we can bring our worries to him sincerely and with trust, instead of grumbling. He listens, and often he reminds us of his presence before giving us the answer.
exp.18:22:
Moses tells God that the people will not be able to come up Mount Sinai, because God himself had already commanded them to set bounds around the mountain and keep it apart as holy.

Moses speaks as the one standing between God and the people. Israel is at the foot of Sinai, and God is about to appear. Moses recalls that the limits were already in place. God, however, insists on repeating the warning, and some think this is because he knew the people's curiosity and the danger of approaching without reverence.

For today: God is loving, but he is also holy, and he deserves reverence. We can draw near to him with thankfulness, but also with humility, never treating him lightly. Today, before you pray or read the Bible, pause for a moment and remember who he is.
exp.5:25:
This verse identifies Aaron and Moses as the men to whom the Lord commanded that the children of Israel be brought out of the land of Egypt. The word "armies" refers to groups in good order, such as companies or divisions. This suggests that the people would leave organized, by tribes and families, and not in disorder.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book. After a moment of discouragement (Moses doubted that he would be listened to), the text pauses the action and presents the family line of Moses and Aaron, of the tribe of Levi. In this way it confirms who they are and where they come from. God did not choose legendary figures, but real people, with family and history.

For today: God often calls ordinary people, with their weaknesses. If He gives you a task, do not depend on feeling capable. Trust the One who calls you, and take the next step with humility and order.
exp.1:2:
She could not hide him any longer. So she made a small basket of reeds, a plant that grows in the water. She covered it with pitch and tar, sticky materials that kept the water out. She put the child inside and left the basket among the tall grasses at the edge of the river.

The narrator tells the story of Israel in Egypt. The pharaoh had ordered that the Hebrew baby boys be killed, and for that reason the mother hid him for three months. When it was no longer possible, she looked for a way out. The text does not say everything she was thinking, but it shows her care and her courage.

Today, when we can no longer protect something precious with our own strength, we can do what is within our reach and entrust the rest to God in prayer.
exp.3:13:
God became angry with Moses because he kept making excuses. He reminds him that his brother Aaron, of the tribe of Levi, speaks well. Besides, Aaron was already on his way to meet him, and he would be glad to see him.

God speaks from the burning bush. Moses had already raised several objections to his calling, and now he asks God to send someone else. God does not withdraw his assignment, but he gives Moses support: Aaron would be his spokesman before the people. Some understand "Levi" as a reference to Aaron belonging to the priestly tribe; others, to his ability to speak. The text does not make this entirely clear.

When God calls us to something and we feel afraid, hiding behind excuses does little good. It is better to trust his promise and accept the help of others that he places in our path.
exp.39:36:
When God's cloud stayed still over the tabernacle, the Israelites also stayed where they were. They did not break camp or continue on their way until the cloud lifted. "Journeyed" means setting out or going on a trip.

This is the end of the book of Exodus. The narrator, traditionally Moses, tells how the tabernacle was now finished and how the glory of the LORD filled it. The cloud showed that God was present and was guiding his people. The Israelites did not decide on their own when to move or when to rest.

For today: sometimes waiting is part of following God, just as much as walking is. Before taking an important step, we can pray, ask for wise counsel, and learn to trust that God knows the right moment, even when waiting is uncomfortable for us.
exp.13:26:
He says that Moses stretched out his hand over the sea, just as God had commanded him. At morning, the water returned to its normal place, to its full strength. The Egyptians were fleeing straight into it, and God brought them down in the midst of the sea. The "sea" here is the water that God had opened; "LORD" is God's name; "overthrew" means that he threw them down or sank them.

The one who narrates is the author of the book, traditionally Moses. Israel had just crossed the sea on dry land, fleeing from slavery in Egypt. Pharaoh's army was chasing them. The Egyptians themselves recognized that God was fighting for Israel, but it was already too late for them. This moment shows how God rescues his people.

Today, when you feel cornered, remember that God can open paths where you cannot see them. Do what he asks of you with obedience, as Moses did, and trust that he takes care of what you cannot resolve.
exp.22:28:
God promises Israel that he will not drive out the peoples of Canaan in a single year. The reason is that the land would become "desolate," meaning empty and without people, and wild animals would multiply and become a danger to the Israelites.

God himself is speaking here, within the laws and promises he gives Israel at Sinai, before they enter the promised land. He had already told them he would send his terror and the hornet ahead of them, an image some understand literally and others as a symbol of fear or of God's power. Here he explains that the conquest will be gradual, so that they can take possession of the land safely.

For today: when God works slowly, it does not mean he has forgotten you. His pace can be a way of caring for you, so that you grow and are ready for what he gives you. Trust his timing.
exp.5:10:
God tells Moses to go again before Pharaoh, the king of Egypt, and to demand that he let the children of Israel go out of his land. "Go in" means that he is to present himself before him. "Speak unto Pharaoh" means that he is to deliver God's message. "Let go" is the same as "let go out" or "set free."

The LORD, the God of Israel, speaks. Moses had just brought a message of hope to the people, but they did not listen, because they were worn down by anguish and hard labor. Even so, God does not change his plan, and he sends Moses again. Afterward, Moses will doubt himself.

For today: when people do not respond or you feel discouraged, it does not mean that God has changed his mind. He still calls us to obey faithfully, trusting that he is the one who keeps his promises, even when we do not see immediate results.
exp.7:19:
God tells Moses to rise up early in the morning and present himself before Pharaoh when Pharaoh goes out "to the water," that is, probably toward the Nile River. There he is to repeat the same message as always: "Let my people go, that they may serve me." The word "serve" here means worship God.

The Lord speaks. This comes after the plague of lice, when the magicians of Egypt recognized the finger of God, but Pharaoh hardened his heart. God gives another opportunity before the plague of flies. Some think Pharaoh went to the river out of a religious custom or because of its importance to Egypt, but the text does not explain it.

For today: when God calls you to obey, do not put it off until later. Moses rose early. Furthermore, recognizing that God acts is not enough; we must respond to him with humility and obedience.
exp.29:1:
God gives Moses the measurements of the altar of incense: one cubit long, one cubit wide (therefore square), and two cubits high. A cubit was about half a meter, so the altar was small. The incense that was burned on it was called burnt incense. The "horns" were projections at the four corners of the top, made from the same piece of acacia wood (Shittim).

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai, giving instructions for the tabernacle, the place where he would meet with Israel. This altar would stand in front of the veil, and incense was burned there every morning and every evening. Many see it as a symbol of prayer, although the text of this verse gives only the measurements.

For today: God cared for every detail of how to come near to Him. We can take our time of prayer seriously and tenderly, setting aside a fixed moment each day to speak with God without rushing.
exp.28:36:
God tells Moses that for seven days he is to make atonement for the altar and sanctify it. Here, "atonement" means cleansing the altar and removing every impurity so that it is set apart for holy use. In this way the altar would be "most holy," that is, completely set apart for God. And whatsoever touches the altar would be holy, meaning set apart for the service of God. Some understand this to refer to the offerings that were permitted upon it.

God speaks to Moses at Sinai while giving him instructions for consecrating Aaron and his sons as priests. Before any sacrifices are offered, the altar itself must be prepared. This shows that approaching God requires reverence and cleanness, and that He sets the way.

For today: God deserves our best and our most sincere. Before serving Him, pray with humility and ask for forgiveness. A clean and willing heart is worth more than any religious activity done without thought.
exp.5:18:
This verse names the two sons of Merari, who was one of the three sons of Levi: Mahali and Mushi. With this, the list of the families of Levi is closed. The phrase "according to their generations" means "according to their family lines" or "according to their branches of the family."

The writer of the book, traditionally attributed to Moses, is the narrator. In the middle of the story of the deliverance from Egypt, he pauses to present the genealogy of Moses and Aaron. In this way he makes clear which family the men whom God chose to lead his people come from. The Levites would later have an important role in serving God.

For today: God knows names and families, not only famous people. If sometimes you feel that your life goes unnoticed, remember that God sees you and can use your story. Serve faithfully where you are.
exp.0:4:
This verse says that the direct descendants of Jacob who came to Egypt numbered seventy persons. The phrase "came out of the loins of Jacob" is an old expression, and it simply means that they were his children and descendants. The word "souls" here means persons. It also makes clear that Joseph was already in Egypt, since he had arrived earlier, sold by his brothers.

The author of the book, traditionally Moses, summarizes how the story of Israel began in Egypt. He lists Jacob's family to show that the people grew from a small household. Some scholars note that other texts, such as Acts 7:14, give seventy-five, and they explain this by differences in the ancient lists. So the exact number is understood in several ways.

For today: God can do great things from small beginnings. If you feel insignificant today, trust that He keeps His promises with patience, even when you do not yet see the result.
exp.15:26:
Verse 27 tells us that, even though Moses had already warned them, some people went out on the seventh day to gather manna. They searched, but found nothing. The word "found" in the verse is the one that appears there, and "gather" refers to collecting the manna from the ground.

The people of Israel were in the desert, and God fed them with manna every day. On the sixth day he gave a double portion so that they could rest on the seventh. Moses explained this to them, but some did not trust that instruction and wanted to check it for themselves. Afterward, God laments their disobedience.

For today: God cares for us, and his instructions are often a sign of his provision, not a burden. We can practice rest and trust that he will supply what we need, rather than worrying endlessly.
exp.3:26:
It says that God spoke to Aaron and told him to go into the wilderness to meet his brother Moses. Aaron obeyed and found him at the mountain of God, which is Horeb or Sinai. There he kissed him, the way relatives greeted each other with affection.

The one speaking is the Lord. Moses was coming from Midian, on his way back to Egypt, with the task of freeing Israel. God had already told him that Aaron would be his spokesman (Exodus 4:14-16). After a moment of tension with his family, this reunion brings him support just when he needed it most.

God does not usually call us to walk alone. Often he prepares someone to walk with us, encourage us, and share the burden. Today we can thank those whom God has placed beside us, and also be willing to be like Aaron: to obey, to go out to meet another, and to give them an embrace of encouragement.
exp.37:25:
It says that every man twenty years old and older, when counted in the census, gave half a shekel of silver, measured by the shekel of the sanctuary, which was the official weight. In total there were 603,550 men.

This is part of the account in the book of Exodus about the offerings for the tabernacle. Moses, or the narrative that records him, notes how much was received and what it was used for. That silver from the census was used to make the bases, that is, the foundations that supported the sanctuary. Everyone gave the same amount, whether they were rich or poor.

For today: God values everyone taking part, not only those who have more. Ask yourself what you can give consistently, whether time, gifts, or money, to support the life of your church.
exp.24:36:
It says that seven small lamps were to be made for the golden lampstand, and that they were to be lit so that they would give light toward the front. The "lamps" are the small vessels holding oil and a wick that sat on the lampstand. "Toward the front" means facing forward, that is, toward the space in front of the lampstand.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai and gives him instructions for building the tabernacle, the tent where God would dwell among his people Israel. The lampstand stood in the holy place and gave light to the area where the priests ministered. Scholars understand that the light from the front shone on the table of bread, although the text gives no further details.

Today we can remember that a lamp is useful when it is lit and well cared for. Jesus said that his followers are the light of the world. We can ask God to help us live in such a way that our faith shines on those who are near us.
exp.23:9:
Moses, Aaron, Nadab, Abihu, and the seventy elders saw the God of Israel. Under his feet there was something like a floor of sapphire stone, of a blue as clear as a cloudless sky. The phrase "paved work" refers to a floor made of stone slabs. The text does not describe God himself, only what was under his feet. Some think it was a vision and others a real experience; the passage does not make this clear.

The narrator tells of this event right after Israel accepted the covenant at Sinai. Moses had sprinkled the blood of the covenant on the people, and his representatives went up the mountain. God did not destroy them, and they ate and drank in his presence, a sign of peace and fellowship.

God is holy and majestic, yet he also draws near to his people through a covenant. Today we can approach him with reverence and confidence, remembering that he receives us by his grace. Today, take a moment to pray with wonder and gratitude.
exp.38:15:
This verse describes how the craftsmen made two settings, small gold bases where the stones are held, and two gold rings. The rings were placed at the two ends of the breastplate, the chest piece of the high priest, which held the twelve stones.

It is part of the account of how Aaron's sacred garments were made, following the instructions God gave to Moses. The narrator shows that each piece was made exactly as the Lord had commanded. The breastplate bore the names of the twelve tribes and was fastened to the ephod with rings and chains.

For today: God pays attention to small details, like a ring or a hook, and nothing done for Him is insignificant. Also, the people were held and presented before God. We can remember that God holds His own with care, and that our faithful service in small things also has value.
exp.29:2:
It says that the altar of incense, made of acacia wood (Shittim wood), was to be covered with pure gold: the top, the four sides, and the horns. In addition, a molding or border of gold was to be placed around it, which the verse calls "a crown of gold round about."

God speaks to Moses on the mountain, giving him instructions for the tabernacle. This altar would stand before the veil, inside the holy place, and sweet incense would be burned there. Many understand that the smoke symbolized the prayer that rises to God, although the text of this verse only describes the piece of furniture.

God cares even about the details of the place where he is worshiped. We can learn to draw near to him with reverence, setting aside times of prayer with respect and sincerity, not in haste or carelessly.
exp.19:23:
God tells Israel to make a simple altar of earth. There they may offer their burnt offerings (offerings completely consumed by fire) and their peace offerings (offerings of fellowship or thanksgiving), using sheep and oxen. God promises that in every place where he causes his name to be remembered, he will come to the people and bless them.

The Lord speaks through Moses, right after the Ten Commandments. He has just forbidden idols of silver and gold. That is why the altar must be humble: worship does not rest on luxury or human works, but on God's presence and goodness. The verses that follow continue with that simplicity.

For today: worship God with sincerity, without pretense and without depending on showy things. Wherever his name is remembered with reverence, he draws near and blesses.
exp.21:3:
It says that if someone steals an ox, a donkey, or a sheep and is found with the animal still alive in his possession, it is not enough to give it back: he must pay double. The stolen goods are called the theft, and "double" means twice the value. "Found with the theft in his hand" means he is caught with the evidence.

God speaks to Moses and gives laws to the people of Israel after freeing them from Egypt. These rules aimed at justice in everyday life, especially in a society where animals were the livelihood of a family. The law required repairing the harm and not only punishing, although some details of how it was applied are understood in different ways.

For today: if we have taken or damaged something that belongs to someone else, it is not enough to say "I'm sorry." God invites us to repair the harm with honesty, returning what is due and, if possible, a little more to heal the relationship.
exp.10:6:
This verse says that while there will be great wailing in Egypt over the death of the firstborn, all will be calm among the Israelites. "Not a dog will move its tongue" is a way of saying that not even a dog will bark or growl at them. The phrase about Dog and tongue belongs to the wording of the verse above, so it stands as written. The verse also says that God will clearly distinguish between one people and the other, so that the difference will be known.

Moses speaks on behalf of God and addresses Pharaoh, just before the last plague. After nine signs, God announces this final judgment. Israel's calm would be a visible sign that God cares for his people and that his word is fulfilled.

For today: when everything around seems confusing or threatening, we can rest in the knowledge that God knows and cares for his own. His care does not always look the same, but we can trust his faithfulness.
exp.38:35:
This verse lists the table of the tabernacle, all its vessels (plates, spoons, pitchers and bowls), and the bread of the presence, which were twelve loaves placed before God each week. The phrase means "set before", that is, presented in his presence.

Moses and the Israelites had finished making all the parts of the tabernacle, and here the complete list is presented so that Moses could review it. The text repeats that everything was done as God had commanded. This list does not tell a story; it shows careful obedience, piece by piece.

For today: God pays attention to the details of our obedience, even in the small and routine. We can serve him faithfully in simple tasks, knowing that he values them, and remember that just as the bread was always set before him, we too live in his presence.
exp.16:15:
Moses says that Amalek raised his hand against the throne of the Lord, and for this reason God will have war with Amalek for many generations. The word "blot out" means to wipe away or remove completely. The Hebrew of the phrase about the hand and the throne is difficult and is understood in several ways. Some believe Moses is swearing or lifting his hand toward the throne of God; others believe that Amalek raised his hand against God.

Israel had just come out of Egypt, tired and without defense. Amalek attacked them in the wilderness, and Joshua fought while Moses prayed with his hands raised. Afterward Moses built an altar and named it "the Lord is my banner." Here Moses is speaking, after the victory that God gave.

For today: God cares for the weak and opposes cruelty. When you face struggles, do not rely only on your own strength; pray and lean on God, and seek also the support of other believers.
exp.34:29:
Moses tells the Israelites to look: God himself chose Bezaleel to lead the work. "Hath called by name" means that he called him by his name, that he chose him. His father Uri is mentioned, along with his grandfather Hur and his tribe, Judah, so that he can be clearly identified.

Moses speaks to the people after many men and women have brought freewill offerings to build the tabernacle, the tent where God would dwell among them. Now he presents the one whom God had appointed to lead the work. Some think Hur is the same man who helped Moses hold up his hands in the battle (Exodus 17), but the text does not say this with certainty.

For today: God calls and equips ordinary people to serve him with their abilities. Ask him in prayer how you can use what you know how to do to bless your church and others, without comparing yourself to anyone.
exp.18:16:
Moses brought the people out of the camp to meet God, as this verse tells us. They stood at the foot of the mountain, at its lower part.

The people of Israel had just left Egypt and had arrived at Mount Sinai. God had told them that He would reveal Himself to them and make a covenant with them.
