Moses, as the mediator, prepared them over three days. With thunder, cloud, smoke, and fire, the scene teaches that God is holy and that we must approach Him with reverence.

Today we too can prepare ourselves to be with God. Before we pray or read the Bible, take a moment in silence, set aside haste, and come with an attentive and humble heart, because He deserves our reverence.
exp.7:24:
Pharaoh calls for Moses and for Aaron and gives them permission to worship their God, but with a condition: that they do it within the land, that is, inside Egypt. Pharaoh's word "Go" carries the sense of "let them go," and the phrase "said to them" simply means he spoke to them.

Pharaoh speaks after the plague of the flies, which left the country in ruins. He is under pressure and wants relief, but he does not want to release the people. He offers a partial concession: to let them worship, but under his control and without leaving his territory. Moses rejects this at once, because God had asked them to go out into the desert.

Many times we want to obey God only halfway, on terms that suit us. God calls for complete obedience, not a comfortable arrangement. Ask yourself today: is there something God has asked of you that you are bargaining over?
exp.31:25:
Moses stands at the entrance of the camp and asks a direct question: "Who is on the Lord's side? Let him come to me." The word for "camp" here is the one already used in the verse. All the Levites, the descendants of Levi, gather around him.

Moses speaks after coming down from the mountain and seeing that the people had made a golden calf, with Aaron at the front. That sin was serious because it broke the covenant just made with God. Moses demands that each person state which side they are on. The verses that follow describe a very harsh judgment, and it is not an easy text to read.

Today we cannot settle for a half-hearted faith. God invites us to decide sincerely whether we truly belong to him, and to show it through obedience and humility in everyday life.
exp.21:16:
It says that if a man had deceived an unmarried young woman who was not betrothed, and her father refused to give her to him as a wife, the man still had to pay money. That sum was the bride-price for a virgin, meaning the amount customarily paid for a virgin bride. The phrase about paying it refers to payment by weight, since at that time there were no coins as there are today.

God speaks to Moses in the laws he gave to Israel after leaving Egypt. These rules aimed to protect the woman and her family in a society where a young woman who had been dishonored could be left without a future. Here the man could not walk away without answering for what he had done. Scholars understand some of the cultural details in different ways.

For today: honestly accept the consequences of your actions and never use another person for your own benefit. If you have caused harm, make an effort to repair what you can.
exp.31:15:
This verse says that the two tablets Moses was carrying down from the mountain were not made by human hands. God himself prepared them and also engraved the writing on them. The word "tables" refers to the stone tablets, and "writing" refers to the commandments God gave to his people, which were carved into the stone.

The narrator describes the moment when Moses comes down from Sinai. Meanwhile, the people have made a golden calf and are worshiping it, though Moses does not yet know this. The text stresses that those tablets came directly from God, to show how serious what Moses was about to see in the camp would be.

For today: God's Word is not just one more human idea, but something that comes from Him. You can read it with respect and obey it with confidence, without changing it to fit your own preferences.
exp.38:40:
It says the Israelites finished making the special clothing for service in the holy place. These were the sacred garments for Aaron the priest and for his sons, so that they could carry out the priestly duties. The word "minister" means to serve, and "holy place" is the set-apart place for worshiping God.

Here the narrator of the book sums up everything that was made for the tabernacle. God had already given Moses the instructions, and now the people carry them out. The list closes by saying they did everything just as the LORD had commanded, and Moses blessed them.

For today: God cares that we serve him with obedience and care, even in small things. We can ask ourselves what simple task God has entrusted to us and do it faithfully, without neglecting the details.
exp.31:6:
God speaks to Moses, who is still on Mount Sinai, and orders him to go down. He tells him that "your people," the ones Moses brought out of Egypt, "have corrupted themselves," that is, they have become morally damaged and have gone to ruin. "Go, get thee down" is a direct command: go down now.

The LORD speaks. Moses had been on the mountain for many days receiving the law, and the people, seeing that he was taking so long, asked for a visible god. Aaron made a golden calf, and everyone held a feast. Notice that God says "your people," as if he were stepping back; Moses will soon answer that they are God's people. Some see a tone of grief here and others a tone of judgment; the text does not make it clear.

For today: we are prone to invent substitutes when God seems silent. If waiting unsettles us, let us return to his Word instead of manufacturing our own assurances.
exp.2:0:
Moses was looking after the flock of his father-in-law Jethro, who was a priest in Midian. One day he led the flock across the far side of the desert and came to Horeb, which is called the mountain of God.

The narrator of the book is traditionally credited as Moses himself. Moses had fled from Egypt and was living in Midian as a shepherd. This simple, everyday scene prepares for the encounter with God in the burning bush. It is called the mountain of God probably because the text is already pointing ahead to what would happen there; its exact location is debated.

God often calls people in the midst of ordinary work and in times that seem like waiting. Moses was not looking for a mission; he was simply faithful in his daily task. Today we too can be faithful in everyday life and stay attentive, for God can speak to us in the places where we least expect it.
exp.14:12:
It says that God, in his mercy, guided the people of Israel, whom he had saved, and with his power led them toward "thy holy habitation," that is, the place where God dwells. The verse's word "guided" means led the way; "strength" means power; and "led" means brought them along.

Moses speaks together with the Israelites in the song they sing after crossing the Red Sea and seeing the Egyptian army fall. They celebrate God's victory and look ahead: if he rescued them, he will also bring them to their destination. Interpreters disagree about the "habitation": it may be the promised land, the mountain of God, or, later, Jerusalem.

For today: God does not only rescue, he also accompanies the journey. If you doubt the future today, remember how he has helped you before and trust that his mercy will keep guiding you.
exp.14:0:
This verse says that Moses and the people of Israel sang a song to God. They say they will sing to the Lord because he showed himself great and powerful by throwing the horse and the one who rode it into the sea. The old-style spelling and the quoted wording that were part of the source text are not used in the verse you are reading, so they are left out here; in the verse above, the phrase "he hath triumphed gloriously" expresses that God showed his great power.

Moses and the Israelites, freshly rescued from Egypt, are the ones speaking. They had just crossed the Red Sea, and the Egyptian army, with its horses and riders, was covered by the waters. It is the first song of praise recorded in the Bible after that deliverance.

For today: when God helps you through a difficulty, do not let it pass in silence. Take a moment to thank him, whether through a prayer, a song, or by telling someone about it. Remembering what God has done strengthens faith.
exp.11:41:
This verse says that night was special, a night of watching kept for the Lord, because on that night He brought His people out of Egypt. "To observe" here means to keep watch, to remember, and to honor. "The children of Israel" are the descendants of Jacob. And "in their generations" means that their children and grandchildren were also to remember it every year.

The author of the book, traditionally Moses, tells of the departure from Egypt after 430 years. Then God gives Moses and Aaron the rules of the Passover. God wants His people never to forget that He redeemed them, and for each generation to tell it to the next.

For today: take time to remember the times God has delivered or helped you. You can write them down, thank Him for them, and tell them to your children or to a friend. Remembering strengthens faith.
exp.35:19:
It says that Bezalel and the craftsmen made the boards, or planks, that formed the walls of the tabernacle. They used acacia wood, which is shittim wood, a tree of the desert. The phrase "standing up" means the boards were raised upright, set firmly on end.

The narrator recounts how the people of Israel built the tabernacle, following the instructions God gave Moses on Mount Sinai. Here the text carefully repeats what was commanded before, to show that everything was done just as God had ordered. These boards held up the coverings and the clasps mentioned earlier.

God is concerned with the details of what we offer him. A firm, upright structure reminds us that our life of faith also needs a solid foundation. Today you might ask yourself: in what part of my life do I need to obey God with more steadiness and care, even when it seems like something small?
exp.39:37:
This verse says that the cloud of the Lord was over the tabernacle during the day, and that at night there was fire in it. All of Israel could see it. This happened throughout all their travels. "Journeys" refers to the stages of the road, and "in the sight of" means "in the view of."

It is the end of the book of Exodus. The narrator, traditionally Moses, summarizes how God guided his people after the tabernacle was finished. When the cloud lifted, they set out; if it did not, they stayed where they were. In this way it is shown that God was present and was directing them.

For today: God does not always show us the whole road, but he does want us to trust his guidance. Before making a decision, pray, seek his Word, and ask for wise counsel. Sometimes it is time to move forward, and other times it is time to wait patiently.
exp.37:30:
This verse closes the list of what was made with the metal from the offering. It mentions the sockets (bases or pedestals) that held up the pillars of the court, the open space surrounding the tabernacle, and those of its gate. It also names the pins, large stakes that kept the curtains and the tent firmly in place.

It is part of an inventory of materials that Moses makes, together with Ithamar and the craftsmen, of what the people gave to build the tabernacle. Each item is counted carefully to show that everything was used honestly and as God had commanded.

For today: God pays attention to small and hidden details, like the sockets and the pins that no one admires. Serve faithfully in what is simple, even when no one notices, because that too sustains the work of God.
exp.13:9:
When Pharaoh was already very close, the Israelites lifted up their eyes and saw that the Egyptians were marching after them. They were terrified and cried out, that is, they shouted for help, to the Lord, who is the name of God. "Lifted up their eyes" means they looked up or off into the distance.

The narrator tells what happened to the people of Israel, who had just left Egypt. They were beside the sea with no way out, and the Egyptian army behind them. Soon after, instead of trusting, they blamed Moses. Their fear was real, but it also showed how hard it was for them to believe God's promise.

When you feel trapped and cannot see a way out, speak to God honestly, even if you are afraid. Crying out to Him is a good first step, and trusting little by little can come afterward.
exp.8:25:
This verse says that the hail fell over all of Egypt, but not in Goshen, the region where the Israelites lived. "Only" in the verse means that the protection applied to that area alone. While the storm destroyed people, animals, crops and trees, that region was kept safe.

Moses is the one telling the story of the plagues. God was showing his power so that Pharaoh would let Israel go. This distinction between Egyptians and Israelites appears in several of the plagues. After the hail, Pharaoh admits his sin and asks for prayer, although the account shows that his heart did not truly change.

For today: God takes care of his people even when there are troubles all around. That does not promise a life without difficulties, but it invites us to trust his care and not to harden our hearts when he speaks to us.
exp.5:26:
This verse says that Moses and Aaron were the men who spoke with Pharaoh, king of Egypt, to ask him to let the people of Israel go out of Egypt. The phrase "spake to Pharaoh" is the verse's wording, and it refers to speaking with the king directly. To "bring out" means to lead the people out or set them free.

Here the narrator of the book of Exodus pauses the story. After giving the list of Israel's families, including the family of Levi, from which Moses and Aaron came, he makes clear who these two men were. God had commanded them to bring the people out in an orderly way, as an organized nation. Then the story goes on with God speaking to Moses again.

For today: God often uses ordinary people, with a particular family and a particular history, to carry out his plans. You can trust that he also calls you to be faithful in the part that is yours to do.
exp.5:3:
God says that He Himself made a covenant, that is, a solemn promise, with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. He promised to give them the land of Canaan, where they lived as strangers and pilgrims, that is, as outsiders without land of their own.

God speaks to Moses. The people of Israel are suffering as slaves in Egypt, and Moses is discouraged. God presents Himself as the LORD and reminds him that He does not forget what He promised the patriarchs. That promise is the basis for bringing Israel out of slavery.

For today: God's promises do not expire, even though they may take a long time to be fulfilled. When you feel that you are only passing through or that nothing changes, remember that God is faithful and remember what He promised. You can wait with patience, pray, and continue to trust in Him.
exp.20:22:
It says that if in a fight someone injures a pregnant woman and a death follows, the one responsible must answer with his own life: "life for life." The word "pay" here does not refer to money but to a fair penalty. Some understand that the death may be that of the mother, others that it also includes the baby; the text does not fully clarify this.

God speaks to Moses to give laws to the people of Israel after freeing them from Egypt. These rules put a limit on revenge: the punishment could not be greater than the harm. They also show that human life has great value and that judges had to make sure justice was done.

Today we can learn to take seriously the value of every life and not to answer harm with more harm than we have received. If someone offends us, let us seek justice calmly, without hatred or exaggeration, and trust in God.
exp.32:7:
This verse describes what the people did each time Moses went to the meeting tent. Everyone would rise and stand at the entrance of their own tent. They watched Moses until he went inside.

The sentence about the word "tabernacle" and the phrase "after" is removed, since those words do not appear in the verse your reader sees.

This happens after the sin of the golden calf. God had been very grieved, and Moses pitched the tent outside the camp. The account is narrated by the author of the book, traditionally Moses. It shows that the people felt respect and kept their distance, while Moses spoke with God on their behalf.

For today: learn to pause and turn your heart toward God, rather than being only a spectator. The people watched Moses, but today we can draw near to God ourselves, through Christ.
exp.26:11:
Here God gives the measurements of the west side of the court, the open space that surrounded the tabernacle. That side was fifty cubits wide (a cubit was roughly half a meter, so about 25 meters). It would have hangings hung from ten pillars, and each pillar stood on a socket that kept it firm.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai and gives him instructions for building a place where He could dwell among Israel. The court marked off a separate space, and to enter it one had to pass through the gate. Scholars agree that all of this taught the holiness of God, though not everyone interprets every detail in the same way.

For today: God cares about details and order. We can approach Him with respect and care, and lay good foundations in our lives, like those sockets that held the pillars steady, through prayer and perseverance.
exp.5:27:
This verse is a short bridge sentence. It says that the Lord spoke to Moses in Egypt. The explanation does not end the thought here; it continues in the next verse, where God says what He spoke to him.

Just before this, the writer paused the account to give the list of Israel's families and to identify who Moses and Aaron were. Now he returns to the story. The narrator wants the reader to remember that these were real men, with family and history, whom God called to speak to Pharaoh. Many scholars see here a way of picking up the thread of the narrative again.

God spoke to Moses in the midst of Egypt, a difficult place. Today God can also speak to you in your present situation, without waiting for everything to be perfect. Take a moment to read His Word and pray, attentive to what He may say to you right where you are.
exp.8:17:
It says that God announces the plague with precision: the next day, at this same hour, a very heavy hail will fall, such as had never been seen in Egypt since it existed as a nation. The phrases of the source wording are rendered here as "at this hour" and "as had never been," and the word for the hail's severity, which in this verse is "grievous," means heavy and intense.

God speaks to Pharaoh through Moses. Egypt had already suffered several plagues, and Pharaoh still refused to let Israel go. God warns him in advance, and the verses that follow show that He gives an opportunity to protect both people and livestock. Some of Pharaoh's servants believed the word and got themselves to safety.

For today: when God warns us through His Word, the wise response is to answer with humility and act in time, not to harden the heart.
exp.20:1:
It says that if someone bought a Hebrew servant, that servant would work for six years, and in the seventh he would go out free, without paying anything.

God speaks to Moses shortly after the Ten Commandments, giving laws for the life of the people of Israel. This law protected the most vulnerable, especially those who, because of debt or poverty, gave themselves to work for another. It was a service with a limit, different from permanent slavery. Some details of this law are understood in different ways, but it clearly put a brake on exploitation.

For today: God cares about the dignity of the one who works. If you have people under your care, treat them with justice, pay them what is due, and do not take advantage of their need. And if you work for someone else, remember that God sees your situation.
exp.26:14:
This verse describes the other side of the entrance to the court of the tabernacle. There were hangings fifteen cubits long there, held up by three pillars, each with its own base. A cubit was an ancient measure, roughly the distance from the elbow to the tip of the fingers; it is estimated at between 45 and 50 centimeters. The bases are the sockets on which the pillars rested.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai and gives him detailed instructions for building the tabernacle, the tent where God would dwell among Israel. The court was the outer courtyard. Its curtains marked a boundary and showed that approaching God required order and reverence. On each side of the entrance there were fifteen cubits of hanging, and in the center was the gate.

For today: God cares even about small details, and He invites us to come near to Him with reverence. We can ask ourselves whether our prayer and our daily life show that care and respect toward Him.
exp.37:12:
The explanation says that the east side of the court of the tabernacle, where people entered, had hangings fifty cubits long. A cubit was roughly half a meter, so that was about 25 meters. The word "east" means the direction where the sun rises.

The narrator describes how the tabernacle was made, the meeting tent that God commanded Moses to build. This part details the court, the open yard that surrounded the tent. The hangings, the pillars and their bases formed a boundary that separated the holy place from the camp. The entrance was on this eastern side, and the verses that follow describe it.

For today: God cares even for the details of how we draw near to him. We can do what belongs to him with order and care, and remember that he himself prepared the way for us to find him.
exp.5:19:
The explanation says that Amram, a descendant of Levi, married Jochebed, his father's sister, that is, a close relative of his father. From them came Aaron and Moses. It also says that Amram lived 137 years. The verse says Amram took Jochebed, his father's sister, as his wife, and she bore him Aaron and Moses.

Here the narrator of Exodus speaks. After Moses doubts himself before God, the text pauses and presents the genealogy of Levi. In this way it shows which family Moses and Aaron came from, the leaders chosen to guide Israel. Some explain "aunt" as the sister of the father; others think it could have been a wider kinship. The text gives no further detail.

For today: God often uses people from ordinary families and with imperfect stories. Trust that He can work in your home and your life, even when they seem small to you.
exp.30:1:
God says to Moses, "See," as if to draw attention, that he has chosen a specific person: Bezaleel. His father Uri is mentioned, along with his grandfather Hur and his tribe, Judah. "Called by name" means that God chose him personally for a task.

The Lord speaks with Moses on Mount Sinai while giving him instructions for building the tabernacle, Israel's place of worship. God not only gives the plans, he also chooses the one who will carry them out. The next verse explains that he filled him with his Spirit and with skill for craftsmanship.

For today: God knows your name and also values your abilities, whether practical, technical, or artistic. You can offer your daily work as a service to God and to others, trusting that he equips you.
exp.5:6:
God says he will take Israel as his people and he will be their God. In this way they will know that the Lord is the one who brings them out from under the burdens of Egypt. The phrase about bringing them out from under the burdens means that he sets them free from the heavy labor that was crushing them. The name of God is rendered in many Bibles today as "the Lord."

God speaks to Moses so that he will repeat it to the people. The Israelites were suffering as slaves in Egypt. God says he heard their groaning and remembered his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Even so, the people did not listen to Moses because of their anguish and the harsh slavery. In other words, pain can make it hard for us to believe a promise.

Today, even when we are tired or discouraged, we can remember that God hears our cry and keeps what he promises. We can speak to him honestly, even when it is hard to believe, and ask him to strengthen our trust in him.
exp.31:19:
Moses takes the golden calf that the people had made and burns it in the fire. Then he grinds it until it is fine powder, scatters it on the water, and makes the Israelites drink it.

Moses comes down from Mount Sinai after receiving the law from God. He finds the people worshiping an idol and, in anger, breaks the tablets. This act shows that the idol has no power at all and that sin must be confronted. Interpreters explain the meaning of drinking the powder in various ways, but all agree that the people had to face the consequences of their sin.

Today we can ask ourselves what things take the place of God in our hearts. Modern idols can be money, fame, or success. We must recognize them honestly, remove them from our lives, and return to God, who forgives those who repent.
exp.13:25:
God tells Moses to stretch out his hand over the sea. Then the waters, which had parted for the people, would come back over the Egyptians, their chariots, and their horsemen.

The Lord, the God of Israel, speaks. The Israelites had just crossed the sea on dry ground, and Pharaoh's army was chasing them. God had already thrown the Egyptians into confusion, and they themselves acknowledged that the Lord was fighting for Israel. This command completes the people's deliverance, which was no longer under threat.

For today: when you feel trapped by a problem you cannot overcome, remember that God can act in ways you do not expect. Keep trusting and obeying one step at a time, and leave in his hands what is not yours to solve.
exp.28:7:
God commands Moses to bring Aaron's sons forward and put the coats on them. The phrase "bring his sons" is explained as meaning "cause them to come near" or "present them." The coats were the basic priestly clothing that identified them for service.

God speaks to Moses at Sinai, giving him the instructions for consecrating Aaron and his sons as priests. First the anointing of Aaron, the high priest, had been described; now his sons are included. The verses that follow say the priesthood would be a lasting arrangement, that is, a permanent rule for Israel. No one became a priest on his own initiative, but by God's calling.

For today: serving God does not depend on our merits, but on his calling and his provision. Receive with humility the place God gives you, and serve it with gratitude and reverence.
exp.22:15:
This verse mentions two more of the year's feasts. The "feast of harvest" marked the firstfruits of the work in the field, that is, the beginning of the harvest. The "feast of ingathering" was held "in the end of the year," at the close of the farming year, when everything that had been sown had already been gathered in. "Labours" here refers to the fruit of the work.

God speaks to Israel through Moses, shortly after giving the Ten Commandments. He teaches them three yearly feasts so that they would remember their deliverance from Egypt and acknowledge that the land and its fruits came from Him. Scholars often connect these feasts with Passover, Pentecost and Tabernacles, although here they are described according to the agricultural cycle.

For today: before thinking about what you have gained, take a moment to thank God for your work and your provision. Give God the first of what you have, not what is left over.
exp.13:22:
It says that the Egyptians pursued the Israelites and went in after them into the midst of the sea. All of them went: the horses, the war chariots, and the horsemen of Pharaoh. The sea mentioned here is the sea that God had opened, and the men on horses are the soldiers who rode them.

The one telling this is Moses, the traditional author of the book. He recounts how God opened the sea to save Israel from slavery. The Egyptians, full of pride and anger, did not stop to think: if the way was safe for Israel, perhaps it would not be safe for them. The verses that follow show that God intervened and threw them into confusion.

For today: sometimes we follow our anger or our pride without stopping to ask whether God is in the path. Before we insist on something, we can pray and ask humbly, "Lord, is this with You?" God cares for His own, and His wisdom is better than our haste.
exp.14:16:
He says that God will bring his people to a place and establish them there, like someone who plants a tree so that it takes root. That place is "the mountain of your inheritance," that is, the land God would give them as their possession. It is also the place where God dwells, the "sanctuary." "Prepared" means made ready, and "established" means made firm and secure.

Moses and the Israelites sing after crossing the Red Sea. They have just been delivered from Egypt. They sing in faith that God will complete his work, and that the nations around them will fear. It is not stated with certainty which mountain is meant: some think of Canaan, of Zion, or of Sinai, and it is interpreted in several ways.

God does not rescue halfway. The one who brought you out of a difficulty also has a purpose for you. Trust that he can make you firm and give you a secure place, and praise him from now on.
exp.33:12:
This verse commands the destruction of the places of worship of the peoples of Canaan. The "altars" were where they offered sacrifices; the "images" were pillars or sacred stones they used in their worship; and the "groves" were the wooden poles or trees of worship to the goddess Asherah (some translators explain it this way, although the term has been understood in several ways).

God speaks to Moses and, through him, to Israel, after the golden calf, when He renews His covenant with them. He warns them not to mix with the peoples of the land, because that closeness would lead them to worship other gods. God presents Himself as jealous: He wants the total loyalty of His people.

Today we do not destroy the belongings of others, but we can remove from our lives whatever competes with God: habits, relationships, or ambitions that pull us away from Him. Ask Him to show you what you should let go of.
exp.13:23:
It says that at dawn, God looked down on the Egyptian army from the pillar of fire and cloud, and threw them into disorder and confusion. The "morning watch" was the last part of the night, just before sunrise, so the rewrite should reflect that without the quoted phrase; I'll render it as the last part of the night before sunrise. "Troubled" means that it caused panic and disorder, so I'll use the verse's word "troubled" directly.

Here the narrator of the book of Exodus speaks, which tradition attributes to Moses. The Israelites were crossing the sea on dry ground, while the Egyptians pursued them into the middle of the sea. The text does not explain in detail how God confused them; what it does show is that God himself intervened to defend his people.

When you feel cornered or without a way out, remember that God sees what you cannot see and acts in his own time. Trust in him, take the step of obedience that is yours to take, and leave in his hands what you cannot resolve.
exp.5:8:
It says that Moses repeated God's promises to the Israelites, but they did not listen to him. The "anguish of spirit" is a very low state of mind, like someone who cannot catch their breath because of discouragement. The "cruel bondage" was the forced and brutal labor they suffered in Egypt.

Moses had carried God's message: he would bring them out from the burdens of Egypt, they would be his people, and they would receive the promised land. Earlier, Pharaoh had made their work heavier (chapter 5). That is why the people were worn out and discouraged. Their lack of attention does not seem like rebellion, but like suffering. Right after this, God sends Moses before Pharaoh again.

For today: when pain or weariness make it hard to believe, we are not alone. God understands our discouragement and keeps carrying out his plan. We can ask him for strength and let other believers encourage us.
exp.3:1:
God asks Moses what he has in his hand, and Moses answers that it is a rod, that is, a shepherd's staff. The question is not asked because God does not know, but to draw Moses' attention to something very ordinary.

Moses has just said that the people will not believe him and will say that God did not appear to him. God answers him with a sign. Moses was a shepherd in Midian, so that rod was part of his daily work.

For today: God often uses the simple things we already have, such as a trade, a skill or an experience. Ask yourself what you have in your hand. If you place it in God's hands, he can use it to serve others, even if today it seems like a small thing.
exp.12:20:
It says that the Lord himself went ahead of the people of Israel. By day he did so in a pillar of cloud, to show them the way, and by night in a pillar of fire, to give them light. The phrase about going "by day and night" means they could travel both day and night. So they could move forward at any hour.

Here the narrator of the book, traditionally attributed to Moses, speaks. Israel had just left Egypt and was camped at Etham, at the edge of the desert. It was an unfamiliar and difficult road. The text shows that God not only brought them out of Egypt but also went with them on the way. How exactly that pillar looked is not explained in detail.

For today: when you cannot see the road clearly, do not despair. God still guides those who trust in him. Ask him for direction, seek his Word, and take the next step with confidence, even if you cannot yet see the whole journey.
exp.31:27:
This verse tells us that the Levites obeyed Moses' command, and that day about three thousand men of the people died.

Moses comes down from the mountain and finds the people worshiping a golden calf, something God had forbidden. Moses calls out to those who are on the Lord's side, and the Levites respond. A severe judgment falls on those who had openly rebelled. It is a hard passage, and not everyone explains it the same way, but it shows how seriously God takes idolatry.

For today: let us honestly ask ourselves what things have taken God's place in our hearts. And we can give thanks that, in Christ, God offers us forgiveness and a way back to Him.
exp.25:10:
God tells Moses to make fifty hooks of bronze. The "hooks" here are the fasteners, and "wire" in this passage refers to bronze. The "loops" are cloth clasps. The hooks go into the clasps to join the curtains, so that the tent becomes one single covering.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai, giving him instructions for building the tabernacle, the place where God would dwell among his people Israel. The curtains of the tent were in two sets, and these hooks joined them together. God took care of every detail of his dwelling.

For today: God can make one thing out of separate pieces. In the church, the family, or the workplace, let us ask him to unite us in love and look for what joins us, without ceasing to value what each one contributes.
exp.4:11:
This verse tells us that the Israelites spread out across all of Egypt to gather stubble, meaning the dry stalks left in the field after the harvest. They used these in place of the straw they had once been given to make the bricks. The phrase "were scattered abroad" means that they dispersed everywhere.

Pharaoh had ordered that the Israelites no longer receive straw, yet they were still required to deliver the same number of bricks. The taskmasters, who were the Egyptian overseers, and the officers passed on that order. Moses had asked permission for the people to worship God, and Pharaoh answered with a heavier burden. The straw was mixed with the clay to give the brick more firmness.

For today: when life becomes heavier without being fair, you are not alone. God sees the suffering of his people. Keep faithfully doing what you can, and seek support in him and in others.
exp.3:30:
The people of Israel believed the message they received. When they heard that the Lord had visited them, meaning that he had remembered them and was coming to help them, and that he had looked upon their affliction, meaning their suffering, they bowed their heads and worshipped him.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Moses and Aaron gathered the elders, and Aaron repeated what God had said and showed the signs. The Israelites were living as slaves in Egypt, so this news restored their hope. Later on, their faith would be tested.

For today: when you are going through a difficult time, remember that God sees your pain and cares for you. Respond to that truth with gratitude and confidence, and take a moment to thank him in prayer.
exp.8:13:
God tells Pharaoh, through Moses, that this time he will send all his plagues upon his heart, that is, with a force that strikes him fully, along with his servants (his officials) and his people. The purpose is that he understand there is no one like God in all the earth. "Plagues" are blows or calamities.

The Lord, the God of the Hebrews, speaks. Several plagues have already come, and Pharaoh still refuses to let the people go. God gives him a new warning before the seventh plague, so that he may know who the Lord truly is.

For today: when we think ourselves stronger than God or ignore his voice, it is wise to stop and humble ourselves. He is unique, and his patience is an opportunity to return to him before the heart grows harder.
exp.37:19:
This verse says that all the pins of the tabernacle and of the courtyard were of brass. The pins were large stakes driven into the ground to hold the curtains and the ropes of the tent. The word "brass" in this version usually refers to bronze or copper, although some scholars translate it in different ways.

Here the narrator of the book, traditionally Moses, is taking an inventory of what was built. Each piece is detailed and the account summarizes how the offerings of the people were used. Everything was done according to what God commanded, under the direction of Bezalel, with the count overseen by Ithamar.

For today: the small things matter too. The pins were almost never seen, yet they kept the place of meeting with God firmly in place. Serve God faithfully in what is simple and hidden, because He values what sustains His work.
exp.27:25:
God tells Moses to make two more rings of gold. They are to be placed on the two lower corners of the breastpiece (the sacred chest piece of the high priest), on its inner edge, the edge that lay against the ephod (a priestly garment shaped like a long apron). These rings would hold the breastpiece fastened at the bottom.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai and gives detailed instructions about the clothing of Aaron, the high priest. The breastpiece held twelve stones with the names of the tribes of Israel. These rings and cords kept it firm, not moving, against Aaron's chest.

For today: God takes care of even the small details so that his people are secure and well supported. We can trust that he sustains us, and we can also serve him with order and care, even in what seems small.
exp.7:26:
Moses says that the people will go out into the wilderness, a distance of three days' journey. There they will offer sacrifices to the Lord their God, in the way he commands them. "We will sacrifice" means offering animals as an act of worship. "As he shall command us" means that God himself will show how it is to be done.

Moses speaks with Pharaoh during the plagues. Pharaoh had offered that they worship inside Egypt, but Moses explains that their sacrifices could offend the Egyptians and provoke violence. For that reason he insists on going away and obeying God's instructions, without settling for a half-measure.

For today: we can worship God according to what he says, not according to what is convenient for us. Sometimes obedience requires separating ourselves from what pulls us away from him, and trusting that he guides every step.
exp.33:4:
This verse tells how God came down in a cloud and stood with Moses there on the top of the mountain. There He declared the name of the Lord, that is, He announced who He is. In this version, the name is given as the Lord, the personal name of God. To declare means to say something out loud.

Moses had gone up Mount Sinai with two new stone tablets, because the first ones had been broken after the people made the golden calf. The narrator tells us that God meets with Moses again and makes Himself known. What He proclaims right away is His character: merciful, patient, faithful, and just.

For today: when you feel far from God or guilty for your mistakes, draw near to Him trusting in His character, not in your own merits. Spend a few minutes reading the following verses in prayer, and thank Him for being patient and compassionate with you.
exp.32:5:
The explanation says that the people of Israel stopped wearing their ornaments as a sign of sorrow and repentance. Where the reader's verse says "ornaments," the explanation's word for them refers to the jewelry and fine clothing a person would dress up with, so the reader can picture those items.

The phrase "by the mount Horeb" is usually understood to mean "from Sinai," since Horeb is another name for the same place, or for its region, although some read it as meaning that from that moment on they went without their ornaments.

God had just said that he would not go up in the midst of the people, because they were stiff-necked, that is, stubborn and rebellious. This happens after the sin of the golden calf. Moses tells what the people did when they heard that hard word: they humbled themselves and took off their ornaments.

For today: when we recognize our wrongdoing, what matters most is a humble heart, not just outward appearances. Today we can stop, set aside whatever distracts us or makes us proud, and come before God with sincerity and confidence in his forgiveness.
exp.39:5:
God tells Moses to place the altar for the burnt offering right in front of the entrance to the tent. A burnt offering was an offering that was burned up completely on the altar. The tent is called the tabernacle of the tent of the congregation, named for the tablets of the law kept inside it.

God speaks and gives Moses instructions for setting up the tabernacle on the first day of the year, almost at the end of the book. Everything was to be done in order. Whoever wanted to draw near to God would first come upon the altar, where the sacrifice was offered, before going any further.

For today: drawing near to God always begins by recognizing that we need forgiveness. Many Christians see in the altar a sign pointing to Christ, who offered himself for us. We can begin our prayer with humility and gratitude, trusting that he welcomes us.
exp.19:7:
This verse tells people to remember the day of rest and set it apart as special.

God speaks to Israel from Mount Sinai, giving the Ten Commandments shortly after bringing them out of Egypt. This is the fourth commandment. It teaches them that their life was not only about work, but also about living in relationship with God. The verses that follow explain that people work six days and rest on the seventh.

For today: set aside regular time to rest from work and hurry, and dedicate it to God, prayer, family, and community. Christians have different ways of understanding how to apply the Sabbath today, but all can value rest as a gift.
exp.17:16:
Verse 17 records that Jethro, Moses' father-in-law, tells him frankly: "The thing that thou doest is not good." The phrase means that what Moses was doing was not the wisest or the most sustainable way to proceed. He is not accusing Moses of wrongdoing, but pointing out a flaw in the way he was working.

Jethro had seen Moses spend the whole day judging the people's matters. Moses explained that the people came to him to seek God's counsel. Jethro, with kindness and good sense, saw that Moses and the people would wear themselves out. He then advised him to share the burden.

For today: even good work can harm us if we try to carry everything alone. Learn to delegate, to ask for help, and to listen to sincere advice from someone who cares about you.
exp.25:15:
This verse gives the measurements of each wooden board of the tabernacle: ten cubits in length and a cubit and a half in width. A cubit was roughly the distance from the elbow to the tip of the fingers, about 45 centimeters, though the exact size is debated. So each board was about 4.5 meters tall and about 70 centimeters wide.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai. He gives detailed instructions for building a holy tent where his presence would dwell among Israel as they traveled through the wilderness. The boards formed the walls of that structure.

For today: God cares even about small details. We can serve him with order and care in simple things, trusting that every task, however minor it may seem, has value when it is done for him.
exp.6:15:
God tells Moses to speak to Pharaoh on His behalf. He reminds Moses that the God of the Hebrews sent him to make the request: "Let my people go, that they may serve me in the wilderness." He adds that, until now, Pharaoh has refused to listen. Here, to listen means to obey, not merely to hear with the ears.

God speaks, and Moses is His messenger. Pharaoh had already refused the request before, and God says that his heart is hardened, that is, stubborn and closed. For this reason Moses must wait for him by the river Nile, where Pharaoh went in the morning. There the first plague will come, the water turned into blood.

For today: God speaks to us with patience and often gives us opportunities. When we sense that He is asking something of us, it is wise to respond promptly with a willing heart, without hardening ourselves or delaying obedience.
exp.28:13:
The explanation says that the flesh of the bullock, its skin, and its dung were not burned on the altar but were burned outside the camp. The word "But" joins this contrast with what came before. The text calls this sacrifice a sin offering, that is, an offering to deal with sin and cleanse.

God speaks to Moses, giving him instructions for setting apart Aaron and his sons as priests. Before they served, their sin needed to be dealt with. Burning outside the camp showed how serious sin is. Hebrews 13:11-12 connects this picture with Jesus, who suffered outside the gate.

For today: let us not take sin lightly. We can draw near to God with confidence because Christ bore our guilt, and that gratitude encourages us to live with humility and obedience.
exp.8:8:
God tells Moses that the ash he will throw toward the sky will become fine dust over all of Egypt. That dust will cause a rash, meaning an irritation of the skin, which will turn into painful sores with pus. This will affect people and animals throughout the country.

The Lord speaks, addressing Moses and Aaron. Pharaoh had just seen that Israel's livestock did not die in the previous plague, and still he hardened his heart. This sixth plague shows that God continues to warn, and that Pharaoh's refusal has consequences that are increasingly personal.

For today: when God shows us something clearly, it is wise to respond promptly. Pharaoh saw an obvious sign and clung to his pride. We can ask God for a humble heart, one that listens and obeys before stubbornness brings us more pain.
exp.20:30:
The explanation says the law about the dangerous ox also applies when the victim is a son or a daughter. "Gored" means struck with the horns, and "judgment" means ruling or sentence. There is no different treatment: the same penalty and the same possibility of ransom apply whether a son or a daughter dies.

God speaks to Moses and Israel in the laws given at Sinai, shortly after the Ten Commandments. These rules taught people to live justly and to value human life. Owners were responsible if they knew of the danger and did not act. Some believe the mention of sons and daughters makes clear that no one could claim the law was softer toward the young.

For today: if you know that something under your care may harm others, such as a vehicle in poor condition or a yard without protection, fix it in time. Loving your neighbor includes preventing harm, not only grieving over it.
exp.20:27:
It says that if an ox gores a man or a woman and the person dies, the ox must be stoned. Its meat could not be eaten. The owner, however, was "quit," meaning free from punishment, as long as he had not been negligent.

God speaks to Moses and gives laws to the people of Israel after freeing them from Egypt. These rules governed daily life and protected everyone, including servants, as the earlier verses show. Here human life is valued above the life of an animal. The following verses clarify that the owner was still responsible if he already knew the ox was dangerous and did not keep it under control.

For today: we are responsible for what is under our care. If we know that something can harm others, such as a behavior, a carelessness, or a tool, we should act in time to protect people.
exp.34:6:
This verse continues the list of materials for building the tabernacle. It mentions rams' skins dyed red, badgers' skins, and shittim wood, which is acacia, a tree of the desert with hard, durable wood. As for the "badgers," it is not known with certainty what animal this is; some think of a sea creature or of a very fine, high-quality leather.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel and passes on what God commanded. He asks for a voluntary offering, from everyone whose heart is willing, to make a place where God would dwell among them. These materials would be used to cover the tent and build its structure.

For today: God values what we give gladly, not out of obligation. All of us can offer something, whether time, talent, or resources, and even simple things, like the wood or the skins, serve in God's work when they are given with a willing heart.
exp.29:17:
God commands Moses to make a basin of bronze, with its stand also of bronze, for washing. It was to be placed between the tent of meeting and the altar, and filled with water.

The Lord speaks to Moses as He gives him instructions for the tabernacle, Israel's place of worship in the wilderness. According to the verses that follow, Aaron and his sons, the priests, were to wash their hands and feet before entering or approaching the altar. In this way it was remembered that God is holy and that He is to be served with reverence.

For today: before you pray or serve God, pause briefly to examine your heart and ask Him for forgiveness. The cleansing God looks for is not only outward, but sincere and humble.
exp.21:30:
God tells the Israelites that they are to be a people set apart for Him. Therefore they were not to eat the meat of an animal that had been torn apart by wild beasts in the field. In place of eating it, they were to throw it to the dogs.

God speaks to Israel through Moses, in the laws He gave after freeing them from Egypt. These rules showed how to live as God's people. Many understand that the prohibition had to do with ritual purity and with not eating meat that was improperly drained of blood or in poor condition, although the text does not give all the reasons.

For today: holiness is lived out in everyday life, even in what seem to be small things, such as what we eat, say, or do. Ask God in what specific habit He is asking you to be more careful, and obey Him with joy.
exp.39:30:
This verse tells us that Moses, Aaron, and Aaron's sons washed their hands and their feet at the bronze basin. That basin stood between the tent of meeting (the tabernacle) and the altar, and it held water for that washing. The priests did this before drawing near to God.

It is part of the closing account of the building of the tabernacle. The narrator, whom tradition identifies with Moses, repeats that everything was done "as the LORD had commanded." God had given precise instructions so that the priests would serve with reverence. The washing showed that approaching God was not a casual matter.

For today: before we pray, read the Bible, or serve others, we can pause for a moment. We can ask God to cleanse our hearts and prepare us. In this way, our life with Him does not become routine, but an encounter made with respect and gratitude.
exp.8:28:
Moses tells Pharaoh that as soon as he leaves the city, he will lift up his hands in prayer to the Lord. Then the thunder will stop and there will be no more hail. The purpose is that Pharaoh may know that the earth belongs to God.

Pharaoh has just admitted that he has sinned and has asked for prayer because the hail was devastating. Moses agrees, but not to win the king's favor. He does it to show that God governs creation. The next verse makes it clear that Moses suspects Pharaoh's repentance is not sincere, and the text then shows that Pharaoh hardened his heart again.

Today we can remember that everything that exists belongs to God, and that truly repenting is more than feeling fear when the consequences arrive. Let us ask for a heart that changes, not only for the problem to stop.
exp.10:7:
The explanation says that Moses announces that Pharaoh's servants will come down to him, bow before him, and ask him to leave with all his people. After that, Moses will go out. When he finishes speaking, he leaves Pharaoh's presence in a great anger. The officials or attendants of the king are the "servants" in this verse, and the words "went out" simply mean "left."

Moses speaks on God's behalf just before the last plague, the death of the firstborn. Pharaoh has refused many warnings. Moses becomes angry because Pharaoh keeps hardening his heart, even after so much suffering. The verses that follow explain that God allowed that hardness in order to display his wonders.

For today: anger at injustice can be valid, but we should bring it to God and trust that he acts in his own time. When someone rejects the truth again and again, we can speak with firmness and then rest in God's justice.
exp.14:24:
Moses asked God for help with a cry of need, and God showed him a tree. When he threw it into the bitter water, the water became sweet. The phrase "when he had cast it" is what the old wording means by "after he put it in," and the words "statute and ordinance" refer to the rules and laws for living. The word "proved" means that God tested them.

The people had just left Egypt and had gone three days without good water. At Marah they found only bitter water and complained against Moses. He is the one who cries out to God, and God answers. The text does not say what kind of tree it was, so it is best not to claim more than what is written. Some see here a test of trust and obedience.

When something bitter discourages you, instead of simply complaining, pray sincerely and ask God for direction. Then stay attentive and willing to obey what he shows you, even when his solution surprises you.
exp.30:0:
This verse is a simple introduction: God speaks to Moses. "Lord" is the name for God used in this translation, and the spelling "Lord" appears in the verse your reader sees. What follows is the message God wants to give him.

Here God speaks, and Moses is on Mount Sinai. God has just given instructions for building the tabernacle, the tent where Israel would worship. Now God makes clear that he will not leave that work to chance: in the verses that follow, he names Bezaleel as the person he himself has equipped to lead the work.

For today: God speaks with purpose and takes an interest in the concrete tasks of his people. If you want to hear him today, set aside time to read his Word with attention. He often guides and equips people to serve him, even in practical, everyday work.
exp.29:26:
This verse continues a list of furnishings of the tabernacle that were to be anointed with a special oil. The table (where the bread of the presence was placed), the lampstand (the golden lamp) with all its utensils, and the altar of perfume (the altar of incense) are mentioned here. "Utensils" means the items or containers used in the service. "Anoint" means to pour or spread oil in order to set something apart for God.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai and gives him instructions for preparing the oil of holy anointing. With it the tabernacle and its furnishings were set apart for the service of God. In this way, everything used in worship was marked as sacred, distinct from what is common.

For today: God values what is dedicated to him with intention. We can ask ourselves which ordinary things in our lives, such as our time, our work, or our home, we can set apart to serve him with reverence and gratitude.
exp.11:26:
This verse says that parents should explain to their children the meaning of the Passover. It is the sacrifice to the Lord, who passed over the houses of the Israelites when he punished the Egyptians, and so spared them. The word "victim" refers to the animal that was sacrificed. "Struck" means that he punished with a deadly blow. Hearing this, the people bowed their heads and worshipped.

Moses speaks to the people before the departure from Egypt, passing on God's instructions. He wants this feast to be repeated in the promised land and for children to ask about its meaning. In this way the story of deliverance would be passed down from generation to generation. The people's reaction shows gratitude and reverence.

Today we can tell our children, friends, or family, in simple words, how God has cared for and helped us. Sharing those stories strengthens faith and awakens gratitude.
exp.15:13:
It says that when the morning dew had evaporated, something fine and round appeared on the surface of the desert, as thin as the frost that covers the ground. The word for "surface" is what the verse calls "the face of the wilderness," and the word for fine and small is the one the verse describes as "a small round thing."

This is the manna, although here it is not yet called that.

The people had just left Egypt and were complaining of hunger. God had promised them meat in the evening and bread in the morning. The quails had already arrived, and now God fulfills the second part. The narrator tells what happened, and the next verse shows that the Israelites did not know what it was.

For today: God often cares for us in ways we do not expect and at first do not understand. Let us learn to trust that He provides, and to receive with gratitude what He gives us each day, without complaining.
exp.39:35:
It says that every time the cloud rose up and moved away from the tabernacle, the people of Israel broke camp and set out. "Journeys" refers to the stages of the trip through the desert, and "went onward" means they set out.

This closes the book of Exodus. The narrator, traditionally identified with Moses, tells how the tabernacle was already finished and how the glory of God filled it. From that moment on, the cloud was the visible sign that God was guiding the people: if it moved, they walked; if it stayed, they rested.

For today: we can learn not to rush ahead or fall behind in our decisions. Before taking an important step, it is wise to pray, seek God's guidance in his Word, and ask for wise counsel, trusting that he knows when to move forward and when to wait.
exp.28:30:
God tells Moses to take the ram of the consecration, that is, the animal used in the ceremony to set apart the priests, and to cook its flesh in a holy place. The Hebrew-era wording here is "seethe," meaning to boil or cook; the verse's own word "seethe" is the same idea, so the instruction is simply to cook the meat. "The holy place" refers to a set-apart site near the tabernacle.

God speaks to Moses and gives him instructions for consecrating Aaron and his sons as priests. After the sacrifice, the meat is eaten as part of the ceremony, together with the bread. It was a sacred meal that marked the beginning of their service. Some scholars see in it a sign of communion with God.

For today: serving God is not only a task, it is also sharing with Him. We can set apart moments to pray, to listen to His Word, and to receive His grace before serving others.
exp.3:29:
Aaron repeated before the people all the words that God had spoken to Moses, and he also performed the miraculous signs in the sight of everyone.

Moses had questioned his own ability to speak, and God gave him his brother Aaron as a spokesman. Here they are before the elders of Israel, who had spent years enslaved in Egypt. Aaron speaks, and the signs confirm that the message comes from God. The next verse shows that the people believed and worshiped.

God often uses several people to carry out his work, each with their own gifts. If you do not feel capable of speaking or leading, remember that God can give you help and companions. And if you are the one who can help another, do so with humility, faithfully passing on what God says.
exp.20:8:
It says that if the master had designated her as a wife for his son, he was to treat her as a daughter, not as a servant. The word "betrothed" means promised in marriage. The phrase "the manner of daughters" refers to the rights and dignified treatment a daughter of the household would receive.

God speaks to Moses and Israel in the laws given after the Ten Commandments. These rules regulated a practice of that time and protected the weaker party, in this case a young woman who depended on others. Some scholars see here a limit on abuse; others stress how much it contrasts with our modern outlook.

For today: God cares for those who have less power. If you have authority in your home, work, or church, treat the people under your care with dignity, justice, and respect, as you would want to be treated yourself.
exp.20:20:
If a master strikes his servant with a rod and the servant does not die right away, but survives a day or two, the master does not receive the punishment named earlier. "Servant" here means a slave, and the phrase "for he is his money" means that the master had bought him and had an interest in him. The phrase "shall be punished" refers to the punishment for death given in the verse before.

God gives these laws to Israel through Moses, after the Ten Commandments. They were rules for an ancient society where slavery existed. They do not approve of mistreatment, since the verse before demands punishment if the servant dies on the spot. Interpreters differ on exactly how to understand this case, but the law limited the violence of masters.

For today: the Bible shows us that God values every human life. Today we should treat those who work for us with respect, justice, and dignity.
exp.2:4:
God tells Moses not to come any closer and to take off his sandals. The old-fashioned phrase that means "do not come near" in the source wording means "do not come any closer," and the word for the footwear there refers to the sandals people wore at that time. The reason is that the ground where Moses is standing is set apart as holy, because God is present there.

The LORD speaks from the bush that burns without being consumed. Moses had approached out of curiosity, but God stops him in order to teach him reverence. Taking off one's shoes was a sign of reverence and humility. Right away God introduces himself as the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and says that he has seen the suffering of his people.

Today we can remember that God is near, but also holy. Before you pray or read the Bible, take a moment of silence to come close with respect, humility, and trust.
exp.39:22:
It says that Moses placed the bread on the table of the tabernacle, one after another and in order, before the presence of God. "The Lord" is the name of God, and "set in order" means that he arranged them carefully, just as he had been instructed. Leviticus 24 speaks of twelve loaves, though the number is not given here.

This is part of the closing account of Exodus. The narrator tells how Moses set up the tabernacle, a year after leaving Egypt. The phrase "as the Lord had commanded" is repeated to show that Moses obeyed every detail of the instructions God had given him.

For today: God values faithful obedience, even in small and little-seen tasks. Today we can do with care and steadiness what God has entrusted to us, whether in the family, at work, or in the church, trusting that He sees and values that service.
exp.25:27:
It says that the middle bar was to run through the boards from one end to the other. A "bar" is a wooden crossbar; the "boards" are the upright frames that formed the walls of the tabernacle; "end" means the far edge. This bar kept the boards joined together and steady. There are different opinions about whether this bar ran the full length of the wall on the inside of the boards or through rings, but the text only says that it went from end to end.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai and gives him exact instructions for building the tabernacle, the tent where he would dwell in the midst of his people. Every detail, even the bars, served to keep the structure firm while Israel traveled through the wilderness.

For today: God cares about the details no one sees, which nonetheless hold up what matters most. We can ask him to help us be steady in small things, such as prayer, and unity in the family or the church, because that is what keeps life firm.
exp.11:22:
God said he would pass through Egypt to punish the Egyptians, but that when he saw the blood of the lamb on the top of the door (the lintel) and on the two sides (the doorposts), he would pass over. He would not allow the destroyer, that is, the one who strikes or destroys, to enter the houses of the Israelites.

Moses speaks to the elders of Israel, repeating what God had commanded him, just before the last plague: the death of the firstborn. The families were to sacrifice the lamb, spread its blood on the door, and stay inside the house until morning. It was a sign of obedience and of trust in God's promise.

For today: God invites us to trust in his provision and not in our own merits. Christians see in the lamb a sign that points to Christ. You can rest today in his protection and obey him with confidence.
exp.35:6:
The explanation says that the people had already brought everything needed to build the tabernacle, and even more than enough. The words "stuff" and "too much" in the verse are the same idea: the materials were metals, cloth, skins, and wood, and there was more than what was required.

The craftsmen leading the work came to Moses to tell him that the people were bringing much more than was needed. Moses gave the order that no one should offer anything more, and so the people stopped bringing offerings. This happens after God gave the instructions for the sanctuary, and the people responded with generosity and willing hearts.

For today: sincere generosity does not seek to show off or to hoard, but to serve God. We can give with joy, trust that God uses what we offer, and also be wise and honest enough to know when enough is enough.
exp.11:17:
From the evening of the fourteenth day of the first month until the evening of the twenty-first day, the people were to eat unleavened bread. Unleavened bread is a flat bread that was not allowed to rise.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron, just before He delivers Israel out of Egypt. He wants the people to remember that hurried departure every year. That is why He asks for seven days of unleavened bread, as a sign that He brought them out and set them apart for Himself.

Today we can gratefully remember what God has done for us. Take a moment this week to recall how He helped or rescued you, and thank Him simply.
exp.38:22:
The explanation says the robe of the ephod had an opening in the middle, through which the head would pass. That opening was like the neck of a light piece of armor, something like a breastplate. Around the opening a reinforced edge was placed, so that the cloth would not tear when the garment was put on and taken off.

The narrator tells how the craftsmen of Israel made the garments of the high priest, following what the LORD had commanded Moses. This robe was made entirely of blue (violet) cloth and was worn under the ephod. Some think the detail of the edging shows the care and quality with which everything was made.

For today: God is concerned with small details and with what holds and protects. We can take care with what we do in private, such as prayer, honesty, and habits, so that nothing "tears" when pressure comes.
exp.8:23:
This verse tells of a hailstorm unlike any seen in Egypt. What was strange was that fire mixed with the hail, and both fell together.

The phrase "since it became a nation" in the verse refers to the time since Egypt had become a nation, that is, since there were people living there.

It is the seventh plague. God had sent Moses to ask Pharaoh to let Israel go, but Pharaoh kept refusing again and again. God works here through Moses, and the plague strikes the fields and whatever was in them. Later it is said that in Goshen, where Israel lived, no hail fell.

For today: God speaks in earnest and is patient, but he expects us to respond. If today you feel God is calling you to change something, do not harden your heart. Obey him with humility and trust that he cares for his own.
exp.20:23:
This verse teaches that the punishment should match the harm caused: no more and no less. It is followed by a list of examples: eye, tooth, hand, foot. The judges who decided the case were the people who settled disputes.

God speaks to Israel through Moses, giving laws for the life of the people. This rule, often called the law of retaliation, put a limit on revenge and aimed at equal justice for everyone. Later Jewish readers often understood it as a payment in money, although scholars debate how it was applied at that time. Jesus mentioned it in Matthew 5:38-39 and called his followers not to repay evil with evil.

Today, when someone hurts you, do not seek to get back at them with more harm. Ask for justice calmly, leave room for forgiveness, and trust that God is the perfect judge.
exp.9:0:
God tells Moses to go back in to Pharaoh. He says that he "hardened" Pharaoh's heart, meaning he made it heavy and stubborn, and also the heart of his servants. In this way God would show his signs among them, that is, his miracles and acts of power.

God speaks to Moses during the plagues of Egypt, before the plague of locusts. Earlier, the text says that Pharaoh himself hardened his heart. For this reason many understand that God confirmed a hardness that already existed. Others place more emphasis on God's action. The purpose is that Israel remember and tell their children who the Lord is.

For today: when we keep insisting on not listening to God, our heart grows harder. Let us ask him for a humble heart, ready to obey. And let us tell the younger ones what God has done in our lives.
exp.36:3:
It says that Bezalel made the poles, or long bars, of acacia wood and covered them with gold. These poles were put through the rings of the ark of the covenant so that it could be carried.

The narrator of the book, traditionally Moses, tells how the ark was built according to the instructions God had given on Mount Sinai. The ark represented God's presence among Israel. The poles made it possible to move the ark without touching it, and they were part of the order and reverence with which holy things were to be handled.

God cares even about the small details of what is done for Him. Today we can serve Him with the same care, even in simple or unnoticed tasks, such as helping, organizing, or carrying burdens for others. What is done in faith and obedience has value before God.
exp.20:17:
This verse describes a fight between two men. One strikes the other with a stone or with his fist, but does not kill him. Even so, the injured man is hurt so badly that he has to stay in bed.

"Strive together" means fight with one another, "neighbor" refers to another person, and "keepeth his bed" means he is left sick or unable to work.

God speaks to Moses, and Moses gives laws to the people of Israel shortly after the Ten Commandments. They are rules for daily life in community. The verses that follow show that the one who caused the harm had to pay the injured man for the time he lost and the cost of his healing. In this way justice was sought without excessive revenge.

For today: when our words or actions hurt someone, it is not enough to say "it wasn't that bad." We should take responsibility, help repair the harm, and seek peace.
exp.13:2:
This verse says that Pharaoh will think the Israelites are lost and have no way out. The phrase "they are entangled in the land" means they are wandering without direction, trapped. The phrase "the wilderness has shut them in" means the desert is like a prison surrounding them.

God speaks to Moses. He has just commanded the people to change their route and camp by the sea, in a place that looks like a trap. God anticipates what Pharaoh will think. Then he explains his purpose: to show his glory and to let the Egyptians know that he is the LORD.

For today: sometimes God leads us along paths that seem like dead ends, and others may think we are lost. Even so, he knows what he is doing. When you cannot see a way out, trust that God can work in the middle of what looks like a mistake.
exp.8:11:
This verse says that God hardened the heart of Pharaoh, and so the king did not listen to Moses and Aaron. "Hardened" means that he made him stubborn or set in his refusal. And "as the Lord had spoken unto Moses" recalls that God had already announced it.

Moses recounts what happened after the plague of boils, which affected even the magicians of Egypt. Earlier, the text notes that Pharaoh himself had hardened his heart (Exodus 8:32). Some understand that God confirmed a stubbornness that Pharaoh had already chosen; others emphasize God's sovereign control. The passage holds both ideas together.

For today: every time we ignore the voice of God, our heart grows harder. Today we can listen with humility and obey promptly, before stubbornness becomes a habit.
exp.2:3:
He says that when God saw that Moses was coming closer to look at the bush that was burning without being consumed, he called him by name from the midst of it: "Moses, Moses." Moses answered, "Here am I." Repeating the name shows closeness and urgency.

Moses was a shepherd in the desert of Midian, far from Egypt. He came near out of curiosity, and then God spoke. The text calls the one who appears the angel of the Lord and then God, and scholars explain this in different ways. God introduces himself in order to send Moses to free his people.

For today: God knows us by name and calls us in the middle of everyday life. We can respond with an attentive and willing heart, saying as Moses did, "Here am I," and listen with respect to whatever He wants to tell us.
exp.16:0:
The explanation says that the whole people of Israel left the wilderness of Sin, moving on in stages, because God had directed it. They came to a place called Rephidim and camped there, but there was no water to drink. The phrase about their journeys simply refers to the stages of their travel, and the phrase about the camp being set up means they pitched their tents.

The narrator of the book tells how Israel traveled after leaving Egypt. It is important to notice that they did not wander off course: they went according to the commandment of the Lord, that is, following God's guidance. Even so, the place to which He led them had no water. The verses that follow show that the people confronted Moses with fear and anger.

For today: obeying God does not always lead us to comfortable places. When we face an urgent need, we can remember His past care and ask Him for help with confidence, instead of complaining in despair.
exp.11:1:
God tells Moses and Aaron that this month will be the first month of the year for Israel. In other words, it marks a new beginning on their calendar. "This month shall be unto you the beginning of months" means that from now on the year will be counted starting from this month.

This takes place in Egypt, just before the last plague and the people's departure. God is about to free Israel from slavery, and He prepares the Passover. That is why He gives them a new calendar: their history as a free people will begin with this act of deliverance. Many understand that this month corresponds to Abib or Nisan, although the text here does not give the name.

For today: God knows how to make a fresh start with those who allow themselves to be rescued. Think about what area of your life needs you to trust Him for a new beginning, and take one concrete step of faith today.
exp.38:28:
This verse describes the sash or belt worn by the priests. It was made of twined linen and threads of blue (hyacinth), purple (purple dye) and deep red (scarlet). It was "of needlework," that is, embroidered with a needle. Everything was made just as the Lord had commanded Moses.

The one telling the story is the author of the book, traditionally Moses. He describes how the people finished the holy garments of Aaron and his sons for service in the tabernacle. The phrase "as the Lord commanded" is repeated many times in this chapter, to show that everything was done with obedience and care.

For today: God values faithfulness even in small things. We can serve Him with diligence and obedience in our everyday lives, even when no one notices, trusting that He sees and that He cares.
exp.19:25:
The explanation says that the Israelites were not to go up to God's altar by steps. This way their nakedness would not be exposed. The word "steps" here means a stairway, and "nakedness" refers to the private parts of the body. In that time clothing was long, and when going up steps it could open or be lifted.

God speaks to Israel through Moses, shortly after giving the Ten Commandments. He is giving simple rules for worship. What is emphasized is reverence and humility, not display. Some think that the aim was also to set Israel apart from certain pagan cults, but the text does not say this clearly.

For today: draw near to God with respect and simplicity, taking care that the way you serve Him does not distract or dishonor. Let your worship point to Him, not to yourself.
exp.1:16:
The explanation says that some shepherds came to the well and drove away the seven daughters of the priest of Midian. Then Moses stood up, helped them, and watered their flock. Some words from the older wording: "drove them away" means the shepherds drove them off or chased them away; "helped them" means Moses came to their defense; "watered their flock" means he gave the animals water to drink.

Here the narrator of the book of Exodus is speaking. Moses had just fled from Egypt because Pharaoh wanted to kill him. He was sitting by a well, alone and as a foreigner. The young women had come to draw water for their father's flock, and other shepherds treated them unjustly. Moses, without anyone asking him to, stepped in on their behalf.

For today: even when we are going through a difficult time, we can help someone who is being treated with injustice. A brave and simple act can be a concrete way of loving our neighbor.
exp.31:24:
Moses comes down from the mountain and sees that the people were out of control, unrestrained, and left without protection. The word used here can be understood in more than one way. The text says that Aaron had left them this way, and that this exposed them to mockery and shame before their enemies.
