Here the narrator speaks, showing what Moses observes. Shortly before, Aaron had tried to justify himself to Moses for making the golden calf. The people, impatient during Moses' absence, had asked for a visible god. This verse sets up Moses' call: "Who is on the Lord's side?"

For today: when a leader gives in to the pressure of the crowd, everyone is left exposed. If you have some responsibility, in the family, the church, or at work, ask God for the courage to be faithful to Him, even when that is not popular.
exp.35:18:
It says that Bezalel and the craftsmen made two more coverings for the tent of the tabernacle: one of rams' skins dyed red, and another on top of it, of skins from an uncertain animal. That word is uncertain: scholars translate it in several ways, such as badgers, dolphins, seals, or simply tough leather. It is not known for certain which animal it was.

The narrator tells how the people of Israel built the tabernacle, following the instructions God gave Moses in the wilderness. These layers protected the beautiful inner curtains from rain, sun, and dust. The account stresses that it was done just as God had commanded.

For today: God cares as much about what is hidden and simple as about what is showy. Do the tasks that nobody applauds faithfully and carefully, as if you were doing them for God.
exp.15:17:
The verse tells how the people measured the manna with an omer, which was a small measure of volume, about two liters, although scholars do not agree on the exact amount. In the end, the one who gathered much had nothing left over, and the one who gathered little had no lack. "They gathered every man according to his eating" means that each one gathered according to what he needed to eat.

The Israelites were traveling through the desert after leaving Egypt, and they were hungry. God gave them manna every morning, and Moses passed on his command: each one should gather what was needed for his family. Then Moses told them not to keep anything until the next day, and some did not obey.

Today we can learn to trust that God gives enough for each day. This invites us to live with gratitude, without hoarding out of fear or envying the one who has more. It also encourages us to share, because what God gives is enough for everyone.
exp.31:31:
Moses asks God to forgive the sin of the people. And if God will not forgive it, he asks God to blot him out of the book that God has written. He offers to share the people's punishment.

Moses speaks after Israel made a golden calf while he was on the mountain. He intercedes like a leader who loves his people. There is debate about what "the book" is: it may refer to the record of the living, or to being with God. It is not certain. God answers that each person answers for their own sin, but does not abandon his plan.

Today, when someone close to you fails, do not judge them from a distance. Pray for that person with compassion, asking God for mercy and offering to help in whatever way you can.
exp.26:4:
God tells Moses that the metal grating, made like a net, is to be placed inside the rim or ledge that ran around the altar, at its lower part. That grating was to reach halfway up the height of the altar. The word "rim" refers to that border or projection around it; its exact placement is not entirely clear and is understood in several ways.

God speaks to Moses at Sinai, giving him instructions to build the altar of burnt offering for the tabernacle. It was the place where the people drew near to God through sacrifice. The grating served to hold up the fire and the coals, and the altar could be carried with poles.

For today: God cares even for the small details when it comes to drawing near to Him. We can give that same care to our life of prayer, setting aside time each day to seek Him with reverence and sincerity.
exp.4:17:
Pharaoh answers the Israelite foremen harshly. He orders them back to work and tells them that no straw will be given to them, yet they must still deliver the same number of bricks. The daily quota of work they were required to meet is what is meant here.

It is Pharaoh who speaks. Moses and Aaron had asked him to let the people go to worship God, and he became angry. He accused the Israelites of being idle and increased their burden. Straw was mixed with the clay to make bricks, so now they would have to gather it themselves. In this way, Pharaoh wanted to smother their hope and their desire to worship.

For today: sometimes, when we try to obey God, things become harder before they get better. That does not mean God has abandoned us. We can keep trusting in Him and ask Him for strength, knowing that the story does not end in that pressure.
exp.3:19:
Moses placed his wife and his sons on a donkey and returned to Egypt. The word for "placed" is simply the verb "put," and the phrase for "turned around" simply means he turned back toward Egypt. He also carried in his hand the rod of God, the shepherd's staff that God had used to show him signs.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. God had already told Moses in Midian to go back to Egypt, because the men who were seeking to kill him had died. His father-in-law Jethro had sent him off in peace. Now Moses obeys and sets out on the road, with his family and with the rod.

For today: when God shows you a step, obeying means setting out, even when you still have doubts. Moses did not have a perfect plan, but he did have the rod of God. Take the step you already understand, and trust that God will guide the rest.
exp.3:17:
Moses goes back to Jethro, his father-in-law, and asks his permission to return to his brothers in Egypt. He says he wants to see whether they are still alive. Jethro answers him, "Go in peace."

Moses had already received his call from God at the burning bush. Even so, he does not leave all at once: first he speaks with Jethro, who had taken him into his home in Midian. Moses gives a simple, familiar reason, and he does not mention everything God had told him. The Bible does not explain why; some think it was prudence or respect. Afterward, God confirms to him that he can now return.

For today: when God calls us to something great, it is still good to act with respect and honesty toward the people who have cared for us, and to ask for their blessing before we set out.
exp.13:27:
It says that the sea closed back over the Egyptians. The water covered the chariots, the horsemen, and all the army of the pharaoh who had gone into the sea chasing Israel. None of them survived.

The narrator of the book tells how God rescued Israel from slavery in Egypt. God had commanded Moses to stretch out his hand, and the sea, which had opened so the people could pass through on dry ground, returned to its place. The pharaoh was pursuing them to bring them back under his control. Scholars debate the exact location of the crossing, but the text presents the event as the work of God.

For today: when you face a situation that seems hopeless, remember that God has delivered his people before. Trust in him, take the step that is yours to take, and leave in his hands what you cannot resolve.
exp.22:2:
This verse says that when someone is being judged, a person should not be favored just because they are poor. The word "countenance" means "to show favoritism toward." Justice must not lean toward anyone because of their condition.

God speaks to Israel through Moses, within the laws for the life of the people. The verses before it ask not to follow the crowd in doing wrong and not to give false testimony. The verses after it ask to help even an enemy. In this way, justice must be impartial: it is not bent by pressure, by pity, or by hatred. Some think that misapplied compassion can also harm the truth.

Today, when you have to give an opinion or decide on a conflict, look for the facts before your sympathies. You can help the needy with generosity without bending the truth in their favor.
exp.24:8:
God tells Moses that the tabernacle and all its furnishings must be made exactly according to the pattern he is going to show him. The word "pattern" here means a plan or model, and the "instruments" refer to the objects and tools used in worship.

God speaks with Moses on Mount Sinai, shortly after bringing Israel out of Egypt. He has just asked that a sanctuary be built so he can dwell among his people. Here he makes clear that it will not be a improvised work: God himself sets out how it must be done. Later on, the book of Hebrews speaks of these things as a shadow or copy of heavenly realities.

For today: when you serve God, do not rely only on your own ideas or preferences. Seek his guidance in the Bible, obey it carefully, and trust that his way is good, even when you do not understand everything at first.
exp.11:15:
The explanation says that the first day and the seventh day of the Feast of Unleavened Bread would be holy days, on which the people gathered to worship God. A holy gathering called by God means a sacred assembly. On those days no work was done, except to prepare the food each person needed.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron, so that they will tell Israel, just before he delivers them from Egypt. He wants the people to always remember that deliverance. The feast included removing leaven from the houses and eating unleavened bread for seven days. Stopping work helped them focus on what God had done for them.

For today: set aside regular time to rest and meet with other believers, and remember with gratitude how God has cared for and rescued you.
exp.12:10:
This verse begins a promise: when God brings the people into the land of the Canaanites, just as he swore to Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and their descendants, and gives it to them, then an instruction will come. The phrase "brought into" the land is explained by the word "entered," and the words "to you and to your fathers" include this generation and its ancestors.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel, who have just left Egypt and are still traveling through the wilderness. He explains how they are to remember God's deliverance. The sentence is left open, and the instruction follows in the next verse: dedicating the firstborn to God as a reminder that he redeemed them.

For today: do not forget what God has already done for you. When you receive a blessing, take a moment to thank him and dedicate something concrete to him, such as your time, your work or your resources. In this way gratitude becomes a habit and not only a feeling.
exp.22:12:
God tells the Israelites to pay close attention and carry out everything he has commanded them. "Be careful" means they should watch themselves and not forget. He also asks them not to mention the names of other gods, that is, neither to call on them nor to name them with honor, and not to let those names come out of their mouths.

God speaks through Moses to the people who have just left Egypt. He has just given laws about justice, the poor, and the weekly rest. This verse closes that section and comes before the yearly festivals. It reminds them that their loyalty must belong to the Lord alone. Some understand it as referring to not using those names in oaths or worship; the text does not spell this out further.

Today we can be careful about what we say and what we repeat. Our words show whom we honor. We can ask ourselves whether what we speak reflects our faithfulness to God and not to things that compete with him.
exp.14:26:
The verse tells us that the people of Israel came to Elim, a place with twelve springs of water and seventy palm trees. There they camped beside the water.

The narrator of the book (tradition attributes it to Moses) recounts what happened after Marah, where the water was bitter and God made it sweet. Israel had come out of the desert tired and thirsty. Elim appears as a place of rest and provision. Some see symbolism in the numbers twelve and seventy, but the text does not explain it, so that is only one possible interpretation.

For today: after trials, God often gives us a breather. Learn to recognize those moments of rest, be thankful for them, and use them to regain strength and keep trusting in Him.
exp.25:36:
God tells Moses to make five pillars of acacia wood for the curtain at the entrance of the tabernacle. The pillars were to be overlaid with gold, and their tops, the decorated upper parts, were also to be gold. Their bases, the sockets, were to be cast in bronze. Bronze, or perhaps copper, is commonly understood as the metal meant here.

God speaks to Moses at Sinai, giving him instructions for building the tabernacle, the place where he would meet with Israel. This curtain marked the entrance, where the people would come near. Many scholars see in the gold and the bronze a sign of what is holy and firm, although the text does not explain their exact meaning.

For today: God cares about the details of how we draw near to Him. We can approach Him with respect and gratitude, remembering that today Christ has opened the way for us. Prepare your heart before you pray, without rushing and with reverence.
exp.21:6:
If someone entrusts money or valuable goods to a neighbor for safekeeping, and they are stolen from that neighbor's house, the thief must pay back double if he is caught. Money is the coins or cash, and valuables are the precious items, and to keep them means to look after them, and stolen means taken without permission.

God gives these laws to Israel through Moses, shortly after the Ten Commandments. They were rules for the people's everyday life, and they aimed to protect property, trust between neighbors, and justice. Paying double was a way to make up for the harm done, not merely to return what was taken.

For today: if someone trusts you with something, whether money, a secret, or a responsibility, look after it honestly, as if it were your own. And if you fail, take responsibility with sincerity, without excuses.
exp.15:16:
The explanation says that the Israelites obeyed Moses' command and went out to gather the manna. Some managed to gather a lot and others a little. Where it says that they gathered, the sense is that they collected it, and "did so" means they did what God had commanded.

The people were in the desert, without food, and God gave them a mysterious food called manna. Moses, the narrator and leader, explains that each household was to take one omer per person, a small measure. The next verse tells that when they measured it, no one had too much or too little.

For today: we can trust that God provides what is necessary for each day, even though our situations are different. Instead of comparing ourselves with others, who have more or less, we can give thanks for what God gives us and share with those who are in need.
exp.0:21:
It says that Pharaoh gave an order to all the Egyptians: they were to throw every newborn Hebrew boy into the Nile River, and leave alive only the girls. The explanation notes that the text does not make clear whether the river is the Nile, though this is the most likely reading.

Here the speaker is Pharaoh, king of Egypt. The Hebrews were growing in number, and he feared their strength. Earlier he had tried to have the Hebrew midwives kill the boys, but they feared God and did not obey. Now, seeing that his plan was failing, he makes the whole people take part in the violence.

For today: the midwives teach us that obeying God is worth more than yielding to unjust power. When an authority or social pressure pushes us to harm others, we can ask God for the courage to protect the life and dignity of the most vulnerable.
exp.14:25:
God tells Israel, and he does so through Moses, that if they listen carefully to his voice, do what is right in his sight, obey his commandments and keep his laws, he will not send upon them the diseases he sent upon the Egyptians. It ends with a declaration: "I am the Lord who heals you." The word for "statutes" refers to rules or laws. "Give ear" means to pay attention.

God speaks to the people, through Moses, in the wilderness after leaving Egypt. At Marah the waters were bitter and the people complained. God made the water sweet and, in that place, tested them and taught them to trust and obey. Interpreters explain in different ways how this promise applies, but here it is addressed to Israel.

For today: when you face a need, remember who God is and listen to him with trust. Begin by reading his Word and obeying one concrete step, without ceasing to seek medical care as well.
exp.24:6:
God asks the people for onyx stones and other stones to be set, that is, mounted into the ephod and the breastplate. The ephod was a special garment of the high priest, and the breastplate (also called the pectoral) was a piece worn over the chest. Some believe the onyx was a stone with bands of color, though it is not known with certainty exactly which stone was meant.

God speaks with Moses on Mount Sinai. He has just freed Israel from Egypt and asks for a voluntary offering to build a sanctuary. The purpose, according to the next verse, is to dwell in the midst of his people.

For today: God invites us to give generously and from the heart, not out of obligation. What we have, whether much or little, can be used so that others come to know his presence. Think about what you can offer him today: time, talent, or resources.
exp.27:8:
God tells Moses to take two onyx stones, which are precious stones with bands of color, and to engrave on them the names of the children of Israel, that is, of the twelve tribes. Some translators think the word "onyx" refers to the onyx stone, although there is no complete certainty about exactly which stone it was.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai, giving him instructions for the garments of Aaron, the high priest. These stones were placed on the shoulder pieces of the ephod, a priestly garment. In this way Aaron would carry the names of the people on his shoulders when he presented himself before God.

For today: God does not forget his people; he carries them engraved and borne upon his heart. You can rest knowing that Christ, our High Priest, intercedes for you with care and love. Today, pray for others, bringing their names before God.
exp.2:7:
God says that he has come down to rescue his people from the power of the Egyptians. He wants to bring them out of Egypt and lead them to a good, spacious land, a land flowing with milk and honey, a way of saying that it is fertile and abundant. Several peoples lived there: the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Amorites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites.

The LORD speaks from the burning bush and addresses Moses. He has just introduced himself as the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. He has seen the suffering of Israel under slavery and has heard their cry. That is why he calls Moses to be his messenger before the pharaoh.

For today: God sees our pain and listens when we cry out to him. We can pray with confidence, even when the answer takes time. And often God acts by calling ordinary people to take part in his help.
exp.16:9:
This verse tells that Joshua obeyed Moses and went out to fight against Amalek. Meanwhile, Moses, Aaron, and Hur went up to the top of the hill, which is a small hill.

The verse's word "fought" shows that Joshua and the chosen men were already in battle.

Israel had just come out of Egypt and was at Rephidim, in the desert, when Amalek attacked them. Moses, as their leader, gives Joshua the task of fighting, and he stays on the hill with the staff of God, a sign that the victory came from God. The verses that follow show that Moses needed help to hold up his hands.

For today: no one does God's work alone. Some fight on the front line, and others hold up through prayer and support. Ask yourself whom you can hold up today with your prayer, and whom you can ask to hold you up.
exp.14:7:
It says that God, with a blast of his nostrils, made the waters of the sea gather together like a heap. The currents stood firm, as in a pile, and the deepest part of the sea became solid in the middle of the waters. "Blast of thy nostrils" is a poetic way of speaking about God's power, as if it were his breath. The word "congealed" means that they became firm and solid.

This is part of the song that Moses and the Israelites sang after crossing the Red Sea, when the Egyptian army that had been chasing them was destroyed. It is a song of praise and gratitude for their deliverance. The language is poetic and deliberately exaggerated to show the greatness of God.

For today: when you face a problem that seems like a sea impossible to cross, remember that God has already shown that he can open paths. You can trust in him and give thanks for what he has already done.
exp.9:24:
Moses answers Pharaoh that not only will their livestock go with them, but Pharaoh himself must also provide animals for the sacrifices. "Burnt offerings" were offerings that were burned whole in honor of God. The phrase "unto the Lord" is simply "to the Lord," the name of God.

Pharaoh had just offered a deal: the people could go and worship, but they had to leave their sheep and cattle behind as a guarantee that they would return. Moses rejects that condition. For him, worship of God is not negotiated or done halfway. As the next verse says, they needed their animals to serve God.

Today we might ask ourselves whether we give God everything or only what suits us. Sometimes the world tells us, "Serve Him, but keep your time, your money, or your decisions out of it." God invites a complete surrender, with trust and without conditions set by others.
exp.24:24:
God tells Moses to make a frame or rim around the table, one hand-breadth wide (about 7 to 10 centimeters). This molding would also include a cornice, that is, a decorative gold edge that runs all the way around the rim.

God speaks with Moses on Mount Sinai and gives him instructions for building the tabernacle, his tent of meeting with Israel. The table was for the bread of the presence. The rim probably helped hold up what was placed on top and gave the table firmness, although the text does not explain its exact purpose.

For today: God cares about the details of what we offer him. We can serve him with care and excellence in small things, such as daily work, prayer, and how we treat others, without thinking that something simple has no value.
exp.15:18:
Moses gives a simple command: no one was to keep manna until the next day. "Let no man leave of it till the morning" means that each person should eat what had been gathered that day and not set aside any leftovers. The explanation of the old measure word has been left out, since it does not appear in the verse your reader sees.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel in the wilderness, after they have left Egypt. God gave them manna each morning, and with this command he was teaching them to trust that he would feed them day after day. The verses that follow tell how some did not obey, kept some anyway, and it filled with worms and rotted.

For today: trusting God does not mean stopping planning, but not living ruled by fear of the future. Today you can do your part honestly and rest in the knowledge that God will also care for tomorrow. Jesus taught something similar when he spoke about daily bread.
exp.1:15:
This verse introduces a family from Midian. The priest of the region had seven daughters, and they came to the well to draw water. They wanted to fill the troughs, which were drinking basins for the animals, so they could water their father's sheep.

The narrator of the book speaks here. Moses had just fled from Egypt out of fear of Pharaoh, and he was sitting by the well. The Bible later names the priest of Midian as Reuel, and later still as Jethro. Some think these are two names for the same person, but this is not known for certain. This moment sets the stage for the encounter that will change Moses' life.

For today: God works in everyday life. An ordinary day of work beside a well became the place of a new beginning. Even when you feel far from home or without direction, keep being faithful in small things.
exp.39:6:
God tells Moses to place the basin, a large bronze vessel, between the tent of meeting and the altar of sacrifice, and then to fill it with water. The priests would use it to wash themselves before they served.

God speaks, and gives Moses the final instructions for setting up the tabernacle, one year after leaving Egypt. Every object had an exact place. This basin stood on the path between the sacrifice and the presence of God, and Exodus 30:17-21 explains that the priests washed their hands and feet there so that they would not die.

For today: drawing near to God in earnest includes cleansing the heart. Before we pray or serve, we can pause, confess what weighs on us, and receive again the forgiveness God offers.
exp.15:5:
Moses and Aaron tell all the children of Israel that, when evening comes, they will know that it was the Lord who brought them out of Egypt. "You will know" means they will understand it with certainty. "In the evening" refers to the arrival of the meat that God would send, as explained later.

The people were in the desert, hungry, and complaining against Moses and Aaron, saying they would rather have stayed in Egypt. God had promised them bread from heaven and wanted to test whether they would walk in his law. Moses and Aaron speak to remind them that their deliverance was not their own doing, but God's. So the people's complaint was really against God.

When we go through scarcity or hardship, it is easy to complain and forget what God has already done for us. Today we can pause, remember with gratitude how God has sustained us before, and bring our need to him in prayer, trusting that he will continue to care for us.
exp.28:40:
This verse commands that the second lamb be offered in the evening, just like the one in the morning, with the same grain offering and the same drink offering of wine. A drink offering is a liquid poured out as an offering. The phrase "for a sweet savour" means that the offering was pleasing to God. An offering made by fire was the one burned on the altar.

God speaks to Moses as he gives instructions for consecrating the priests and the altar. This daily burnt offering was to be continual, at the door of the tabernacle, and there God promised to meet with his people and speak to them. It was a way of keeping the relationship with Him alive each day.

For today: God values consistency. We can set aside a moment at the beginning and at the end of the day to pray, thank him, and give him our lives, without waiting only for special occasions.
exp.38:26:
Here the text tells us that the craftsmen made the tunics for Aaron and his sons, the priests. They were of fine linen, a delicate and light cloth, and they were made "of woven work," that is, woven with care, from one piece of well-worked cloth.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book, who continues to describe how the people of Israel finished the tabernacle and the priestly clothing. Everything was done just as God had commanded Moses. That phrase is repeated several times in this chapter to show that the work was done in obedience and not by human whim.

For today: God notices what is done with care and obedience, even in small details. Today you can do your work, your service in the church, or your household tasks with care, as something you offer to God.
exp.1:9:
When the child had grown, his mother brought him to Pharaoh's daughter, and she adopted him as her son. She gave him the name Moses, explaining that she had drawn him out of the water. It should be known that the name sounds similar to a Hebrew word meaning "to draw out," although some scholars also note that it may have an Egyptian origin.

The narrator tells what happened after Moses' mother, unknown to Pharaoh, raised him as a nurse paid by the princess. Now the boy leaves the Hebrew home and enters the Egyptian palace, where he will grow up with a very different upbringing.

For today: God can care for and prepare his children even in unexpected places. If today you feel out of place, remember that God may be forming you there for something you cannot yet see.
exp.17:20:
It says that Moses was to look among all the people for capable men who respect God, who are honest, and who do not love money or unjust gain. The phrase about men of character is rendered as men of truth, and the word for greed, meaning an excessive desire to gain money, is covered by the phrase hating covetousness. The word for supervisors or overseers is rendered as rulers, meaning those placed in charge. Moses was to set these men over groups of a thousand, a hundred, fifty, and ten people.

Jethro, Moses' father-in-law, is the one speaking. He saw that Moses spent the whole day judging the people's problems and was wearing himself out. He advises him to share the burden, so that Moses would handle the serious cases and others would settle the smaller ones. Then Moses put this into practice.

For today: when you serve or lead in the church, in your family, or at work, do not try to do everything alone. Share responsibilities with people who are upright and trustworthy, because character matters more than talent.
exp.28:41:
This verse says that the burnt offering of every morning and every evening was to be offered always, throughout the generations, at the door of the tabernacle of the congregation. The phrase "continual burnt offering" refers to a burnt offering that was never interrupted. "I will meet with you" means that God promises to meet with his people there.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai and gives him instructions for consecrating Aaron and his sons as priests. The daily offering of two lambs set the rhythm of Israel's worship. God wanted a fixed place and time to meet with his people.

For today: God still desires to meet with us. We can set aside a fixed moment each morning and each evening to pray, read his Word, and give thanks, knowing that he wants to hear us and speak to us.
exp.34:12:
This verse names another piece of the tabernacle: the table, with its staves (the poles used to carry it), all its vessels (dishes and utensils), and the bread set out before God, twelve loaves placed there as a continual offering.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel in the wilderness. He presents the list of what God commanded them to build so that He might dwell among them. This order follows what God had already indicated, and Moses invites everyone to take part with their gifts and their work.

For today: God cares even for the small details of his house, and each person had something to contribute. Ask yourself what you can offer, with humility and joy, in your church or community. A simple service is also valuable to God.
exp.38:11:
The explanation says that in the third row of the high priest's breastpiece were three precious stones: a ligure, an agate, and an amethyst. The ancient names of the stones are hard to identify with certainty, so translations vary. "Row" means a line or rank of stones, and "set" means to fix a stone into its gold frame.

The text is part of the account of how the craftsmen made Aaron's sacred garments, following what God had commanded Moses. The breastpiece had twelve stones, one for each tribe of Israel, and each one bore an engraved name. In this way, the priest represented the whole people before God.

For today: God does not see his people as a faceless crowd. Each person has a place and a name before him. You can pray with confidence, knowing that God knows you and values you personally.
exp.31:10:
Moses stands before God and speaks to Him frankly. He asks why God's anger burns against the people whom He Himself rescued from Egypt with great power. The phrase "before the face of" means "in front of." "Stiff-necked" speaks of a stubborn people. "Wrath" is very strong anger.

Moses speaks after Israel made the golden calf while he was on the mountain. God says He wants to destroy them and offers to make Moses into a great nation. Moses does not accept that honor. He pleads on their behalf and reminds God of His work and His promises to Abraham, Isaac, and Israel.

We can pray sincerely for others, even when they have failed. Let us intercede for them by relying on the character of God and His promises, not on our own merits or theirs.
exp.36:7:
This verse says that Bezalel put one cherub at one end of the cover and the other cherub at the opposite end. The cover is the lid of the ark of the covenant, also called the mercy seat. The end of the cover is the edge or tip. The cherubim were not separate pieces; they were made in one piece with the lid.

The book of Exodus tells how the tabernacle was built, following the instructions God gave Moses on the mountain. Here the narrator describes that everything was done just as God had commanded. The mercy seat was the place where God promised to meet with his people. The cherubim are spiritual beings who serve God; the Bible does not explain all their details here.

For today: God cares about doing things with care and obedience, even in the small details. Today we can serve him with that same faithfulness in our everyday lives.
exp.1:17:
The verse tells that the daughters of the priest of Midian returned to their father, Reuel. He asked them why they had come back so soon that day.

Reuel is the one speaking, the father of the seven sisters. The young women used to take a long time watering the sheep because other shepherds would drive them away from the well. This time Moses defended them and helped them, so they finished sooner. Reuel is surprised by the change. In other passages this same man is called Jethro; scholars explain that double name in several ways.

For today: when someone helps us generously, there are good effects that others notice. Let us be among those who help others without expecting anything in return, and let us thank those who help us.
exp.7:7:
Pharaoh sends for Moses and Aaron. He asks them to pray to the Lord so that he will take the frogs away from him and from his people. In return he promises to let the people of Israel go so that they may offer sacrifice to the Lord. The word "pray" here means "pray," and "said to them" simply reports what he told them.

Pharaoh, the king of Egypt, speaks after the plague of frogs. The Egyptian magicians also made frogs appear, but they could not take them away. That is why Pharaoh turns to Moses. It is the first time he asks for prayer, although his heart is still hard. Later he breaks his promise.

We can seek God not only when we are pressed by a problem. A sincere prayer comes from a desire to obey him, not only from a wish to get out of difficulty. Let us ask for his help and keep what we promise him.
exp.17:24:
Moses chose capable men of good character from all of Israel. He placed them over the people as leaders. Each one was in charge of groups of a thousand, a hundred, fifty, or ten people.

Moses spent the whole day settling the people's disputes and was worn out. Jethro, his father-in-law, saw this and advised him to share the load. Here Moses listens to that advice and puts it into practice. Some scholars think those groups were exact numbers, and others think they were a way of organizing by levels. The text does not fully settle the question.

No one should carry everything alone. If you have responsibilities at home, at church, or at work, look for trustworthy people and share them with others. And if a wise person advises you with care, take the time to listen, as Moses did.
exp.35:33:
It says that Bezalel and his helpers overlaid with gold the boards that formed the walls of the tabernacle. They also made the rings of gold, which were the loops through which the bars passed, and they overlaid the bars themselves with gold. The word "overlaid" means covered with a layer, since the wood was acacia (Sittim). In this way the whole structure shone and stood firm.

Here it is not a character speaking; it is the narrator of the book, describing how the people of Israel built the tabernacle just as God had commanded Moses. The detail is repeated to show that the work was done with obedience and care, without changing anything.

For today: God cares about the details of what we do for Him. We can serve Him with diligence, even in small and little-seen tasks, like bars or rings that almost no one would notice.
exp.7:27:
Pharaoh gives way a little. He says he will let the people go to offer sacrifices to the Lord in the wilderness, but with one condition: they must not go very far away. He also asks Moses to pray for him. The phrase "that ye may sacrifice" means offering animals to God as worship.

Pharaoh speaks in the middle of the plague of flies. Moses had just said they would travel three days into the wilderness, because their sacrifices would offend the Egyptians. Pharaoh accepts only in part: he wants to ease the problem without losing control. Afterward Moses warns him not to deceive again, and prays for him.

Today we can notice that sometimes we seek God only to get out of pain, but we want to obey Him halfway. God invites us to a complete and sincere obedience, not to bargain with Him.
exp.33:2:
What it says: God orders Moses to go up alone to Mount Sinai. No one else may go up with him, and no one may even be seen anywhere on the mountain. The flocks of sheep and the herds of cattle are also not allowed to graze in the grass in front of the mountain. The word "be seen" here means "be seen" or "show themselves," and "graze" means "feed."

Context: The Lord speaks. Moses had broken the first tablets of the law when the people worshiped the golden calf. Now God gives him a new opportunity and renews the covenant. This separation shows the holiness of God, who draws near to his people, but with reverence.

For today: Set aside time alone and in silence to be with God, free from distractions. Turn off your phone, pray, and listen to his Word. He receives us with mercy, but he deserves our respect and full attention.
exp.15:3:
God tells Moses that he will rain bread from heaven for the people. Each person will go out and gather what is needed for that day, and no more. "Gather" here refers to picking up what is given each day, and "test" means to put them to the test. God wants to see whether the people will walk according to his instructions, that is, whether they will live by what he has commanded.

God speaks here in response to the complaints of Israel in the desert. They were hungry and looked back with longing on the food of Egypt, forgetting that there they had been slaves. God does not punish them: he gives them food, but he also teaches them to depend on him each day.

For today: God invites us to trust that he sustains us day by day. When you feel anxious about the future, practice asking him for what you need for today and giving thanks for what he has already given you, without longing for a past that we idealize.
exp.38:2:
They beat the gold into very thin sheets and cut it into fine threads. These gold threads were woven together with colored threads: the "blue" is a violet-blue, the "purple" is a reddish purple, and the "scarlet" is a deep red. Fine linen was also used. "Cunning work" means careful work, done by skilled hands.

The narrator of Exodus describes how the people of Israel made the garments of the priest Aaron, the ephod in particular. It is repeated that everything was made "as the LORD had commanded Moses." The emphasis is not only on beauty, but on obedience to God's instructions for worship in the sanctuary.

For today: God values service done with care and faithfulness, even in small or unseen tasks. We can do our work, at home, in the church, or at our jobs, with diligence and an obedient heart, as for God.
exp.17:11:
He says that Jethro, Moses' father-in-law, offered a burnt offering and sacrifices to God. Then Aaron and all the elders of Israel came to eat bread with him "before God." A "burnt offering" was an offering burned up completely. "Eat bread" means to share a meal.

Jethro had heard what God did in freeing Israel from Egypt, and he had visited Moses in the wilderness. After praising the LORD, he presents offerings. The meal together suggests fellowship and thankfulness. It is not known for certain whether Jethro worshiped the God of Israel before, and scholars interpret this in different ways.

For today: when God helps you with something, don't stop at relief. Give thanks, and do it in the company of other believers. Sharing a meal and remembering what God has done strengthens everyone's faith.
exp.22:25:
It says that if Israel obeys God, the women in their land will not lose their children before birth, and none will be barren. It also promises that God will give them a full life: "the number of your days I will fulfil" means that they will live a long life, not dying before their time. The word "miscarry" here refers to losing the pregnancy.

God speaks, through Moses, to the people of Israel shortly after Sinai. He promises them blessings if they reject the idols of Canaan and serve only the LORD. It was a promise within the covenant with Israel and their land. Not everyone understands it as a personal guarantee for every believer, since the Bible also shows cases of suffering and of waiting.

For today: we can trust that our life is in God's hands, and seek to be faithful to Him with sincerity. And when we suffer losses, we do not need to conclude that God has rejected us; He remains near and comforts.
exp.11:5:
God commands that the lamb be kept apart, or set aside, until the fourteenth day of the month. On that day, the whole people of Israel shall kill it in the evening. The phrase "in the evening" can be understood in more than one way: the time of evening, or the stretch of time between sunset and full darkness.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron in Egypt, just before the last plague. He gives them instructions for the first Passover. All the people take part together, as one community, and the lamb without blemish must be cared for a few days beforehand.

For today: God values careful preparation and thoughtful devotion, not what is done in a rush. This week, set aside a quiet time to pray and thank him calmly, and if you can, do it together with your family or your church.
exp.3:14:
God tells Moses that he will speak with Aaron and put the words in his mouth, that is, he will tell him what to say. God promises to be with the mouth of both of them and to teach them what they must do. The old form of "a" was written with an accent, and "hayáis de hacer" means "have to do."

God speaks from the burning bush. Moses made excuses for not going to Egypt, saying that he did not know how to speak well and asking that God send someone else. God was angry, but he did not leave him alone: he gave him his brother Aaron as a helper and spokesman. Even so, God makes it clear that the true help comes from Him.

For today: when you feel that you are not prepared for something God asks of you, do not stay in your excuses. Take the step, ask for his help, and accept the support of other people whom he places in your path.
exp.23:5:
This verse tells us that Moses divided the blood of the animals that had been sacrificed into two parts. He put half of it in basins, which were deep bowls, and sprinkled or poured the other half on the altar.

Here the narrator is speaking, and the central figure is Moses. God had just given his law on Mount Sinai, and the people were about to enter into a covenant with him. The blood on the altar, and afterward on the people, was the solemn sign of that commitment. Scholars agree that the blood represented life and a sacred bond, though they explain the details in somewhat different ways.

For today: God relates to us through a serious commitment, not something casual. Today we can take our response to him seriously, promising to obey him with humility and trusting in his grace to carry it out.
exp.25:5:
God commands Moses to make fifty clasps of gold. The "clasps" were hooks or fasteners used to join the curtains, catching onto the loops (small rings) of blue cloth that were already along the edges. In this way the curtains were fastened together and formed one single tabernacle.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai, giving him detailed instructions to build a sanctuary where his presence would dwell in the midst of Israel. Before this, the curtains were made in two sets; the gold clasps turned them into a single unit. Some see in this a symbol of unity, but the text does not explain it directly.

Today we can remember that God values the joining of what is separate. Just as the gold joined the curtains, love and humility unite us as a church. Ask yourself: what can I do this week to draw near to a brother or sister and strengthen that bond?
exp.5:16:
This verse names the two sons of Gershon, the eldest son of Levi: Libni and Shimei (written here as "Shimi"). From them came two families within the tribe of Levi. The phrase "according to their families" means that each son became the head of a family group.

The one telling the story is the author of the book, which tradition attributes to Moses. Just as Moses receives his calling and God promises to free Israel, the account pauses to give a genealogy. It reaches back to Levi because Moses and Aaron came from that tribe. In this way it shows that they are real people with a known family history.

For today: God pays attention to names and to families, not only to the great moments. If sometimes you feel your life is ordinary, remember that God knows you and can use you in his plan, even when no one else notices.
exp.15:12:
This verse tells how, when evening came, many quails arrived and covered the whole camp. In the morning, there was a layer of dew all around the camp.

The people of Israel were traveling through the desert and complaining because they were hungry. God told Moses that he had heard those complaints and that he would give them meat in the evening and bread in the morning. This verse shows the fulfillment of that promise. God wanted them to know that he was their God and that he was caring for them.

For today: God remains faithful even when we complain. We can bring our needs to him honestly, trusting that he knows what we need and provides in his own time. It is also good to stop and thank him for what he has already given us.
exp.35:28:
It says that the boards at the corners of the tabernacle were joined both at the bottom and at the top, by means of a fitting. That word is old and unclear; it probably refers to a ring or fitting that held them together. The translators are not completely sure of its exact meaning. The same was done at both corners.

Exodus 36 is the narrator's account of how Bezalel, Aholiab, and the craftsmen built the tabernacle, following the instructions God gave to Moses. Here the western side is described, the back, where the corners had to stand firm. Everything was done just as God had commanded.

For today: God cares even about the details that almost no one sees. We can do our work and serve faithfully and carefully, even when no one notices, because we do it for Him.
exp.27:26:
This verse gives instructions for making two more rings of gold. They would be placed at the lower part of the ephod, on the two sides of the front, near where it joins the belt. The ephod was a special garment of the priest, and the belt was the woven sash that fastened it. These rings would hold the breastpiece (the chest piece) in place with a blue cord.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai and gives him the design of the garments of Aaron, the high priest. Every detail had a practical purpose: the breastpiece was not to come loose from the ephod. In this way, the names of the tribes of Israel rested over Aaron's heart when he entered before God.

God sees to it that nothing belonging to him is left loose or slack. Just as the breastpiece was held firmly in place, we can trust that God holds his people securely. Today, pray for others with steady faithfulness, carrying them in your heart.
exp.35:34:
It says that Bezalel and the craftsmen made the veil of the tabernacle with threads of colors: a dark blue or violet (the word for it is "blue"), purple, and scarlet (a deep red), together with fine twined linen, that is, fine linen of twisted threads. In addition, they decorated it with cherubims, figures of heavenly beings, embroidered with great detail.

The narrator tells how the people of Israel carried out the instructions that God gave to Moses to build the tabernacle. This veil separated the holy place from the most holy place, where the ark was. The cherubim remind us of God's holiness and that access to Him was not something ordinary. The New Testament connects this veil with the work of Christ (Hebrews 10:19-20).

Today we can learn that God deserves our best and that it is worth obeying Him carefully, even in small things. We can also be thankful that, through Jesus, we can now approach God with confidence.
exp.4:15:
They say that the Hebrew workers are no longer given straw, which had been mixed with the clay to make bricks, yet they are still required to produce the same number. That is why they are beaten. The word "servants" here refers to slaves or workers under authority, and the phrase "is in the wrong" means that someone is accused of a failure. The foremen point out that the blame is truly unjust.

The speakers are the Israelite foremen, who present themselves before Pharaoh. Moses and Aaron had asked him to let the people go, and Pharaoh answered by increasing the burden. Now the foremen, beaten for not meeting the quota, bring their complaint to Pharaoh. He does not listen to them and accuses them of being lazy.

For today: when you do what is right and things get worse, do not immediately assume that God has abandoned you. Bring your complaint honestly to God, keep trusting in Him, and seek help from others, because He works even in difficult times.
exp.0:18:
The midwives answer Pharaoh with an explanation: they say the Hebrew women are "lively," meaning strong and vigorous, and that they give birth before the midwife arrives. Here the midwives speak before the king, who had ordered them to kill the Hebrew baby boys. They feared God and did not obey. Many scholars see in their answer an excuse meant to protect themselves and save the babies. Others think it may be only part of the truth. The text does not make this clear, but it does show that God honored them.

For today: when an authority asks us to do something that goes against life or against God, we can ask for wisdom to act with courage, respect, and compassion, putting God first.
exp.4:10:
It says that the Israelites were to go out and gather their own straw wherever they could find it, yet still not produce fewer bricks. The straw was mixed with the clay to make them. "Quota" is the daily amount of work demanded. "Find" is the word for what they were to do with the straw.

Here Pharaoh is speaking, and his overseers repeat his words to the people. Moses and Aaron had just asked him to let Israel go to worship God. Pharaoh answered with a heavier load, so that the people would have no time to think about those "lying words," as he called them. It was a form of oppression and control.

For today: when someone demands more from you with fewer resources, do not immediately blame yourself. Ask God for wisdom and patience, and look for support from others. God sees injustice, even when he does not resolve it right away.
exp.31:23:
Aaron is telling Moses what he did. He says he asked the people for the gold they had, and they handed it over to him. He threw it into the fire, and out of it, he says, came a calf.

Aaron is speaking, and Moses has confronted him about the golden calf that the people worshiped. Aaron tries to make excuses: he blames the people and presents the result as something almost accidental. But earlier in the account, he himself shaped the idol with a tool (v. 4). His explanation does not match what he actually did.

For today: when we fail, it is tempting to blame others or to soften the truth. God invites us to acknowledge our mistakes honestly, ask for forgiveness, and return to Him, who is merciful.
exp.22:19:
God himself promises to send an Angel ahead of the people. His task is to watch over them along the journey and to bring them to the land that God has already made ready for them. Here, "to keep" means to protect, and "to bring in" means to lead them into a place.

God is speaking to Israel through Moses, after giving them laws at Sinai. The verses that follow call for obeying this Angel's voice, because God's name is in him. Some think he is a messenger sent with God's authority; others see in him an appearance of God himself. The Bible does not make this entirely clear, and Christians have understood it in different ways.

For today: God not only shows the way, he also cares for it and prepares it. We can move forward with confidence, but while listening and obeying his voice, especially in difficult decisions. Today you can set aside a few minutes to pray and read his Word before you decide.
exp.11:6:
It says that the people were to take some of the blood of the lamb and put it on the two side posts, that is, the sides of the door, and on the upper post, which is the top part. This was done in the houses where they were going to eat the lamb.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron in Egypt, just before the tenth plague, the death of the firstborn. The blood on the door was the sign that God gave to each Israelite family; later the text says that, upon seeing it, he would pass over that house without destroying it (v. 13). In this way God asked for concrete trust and obedience.

For today: God invites us to trust in what he has provided, not in our own means. Many Christians see in this lamb a sign that points to Christ. Today you can thank him for his care and obey him in something simple that he has asked of you.
exp.6:4:
God says that the Egyptians are going to recognize who he is when he acts with power against Egypt and brings the people of Israel out from there. "I will stretch out my hand" is a way of speaking that means intervening with force. "Lord" is the personal name of God.

Here God speaks to Moses and Aaron, before the plagues. He explains to them what is coming: Pharaoh will resist, but God will carry out his plan. The Egyptians worshiped many gods, and these events would show that the God of Israel is the true one. God speaks to them this way so that they will not lose heart when Pharaoh rejects them. The sentence about hardening Pharaoh's heart is understood in different ways, and scholars discuss it.

For today: when something seems closed off or harder than expected, remember that God does not lose control. We can obey with confidence, even if we do not see the result soon, because he keeps what he promises.
exp.20:15:
The verse says that whoever steals a person and sells them, or is found still holding them in their possession, must be put to death. Stealing a person here means kidnapping them.

God speaks through Moses, after giving the Ten Commandments, and gives civil laws for the people of Israel, who had just been freed from slavery in Egypt. This verse stands alongside other serious offenses against life and family. It shows that the freedom and dignity of every person are sacred. Some understand it as referring to the slave trade; the text does not clarify this further.

Today it reminds us that no person is a thing to be used or bought. We can respect the dignity of others, reject all exploitation, such as human trafficking, and support those who defend the vulnerable.
exp.39:27:
This verse tells that Moses hung the curtain that covered the entrance of the tabernacle, that is, of the sacred tent. The hanging at the door was the cloth that was hung at the entrance, to separate the holy space from the rest of the camp.

The narrator describes how Moses finishes setting up the tabernacle, a year after Israel left Egypt. Each step is told carefully, and it is repeatedly said that he did it as the LORD had commanded. The purpose is to show that everything was done according to God's instructions, and that the way into his presence had an order.

For today: God cares even for small details, like a curtain at a door. We can learn to obey him also in the simple things and in what no one sees, trusting that drawing near to him is something precious and worthy of reverence.
exp.30:10:
This verse ends the list of things God asked to be made for his place of worship. It mentions the anointing oil, which was used to set apart something or someone for God, and the fragrant perfume, that is, the sweet-smelling incense that was burned in the sanctuary. God says they are to do it "according to all that I have commanded thee," that is, just as He directed.

God is speaking, giving instructions to Moses on Mount Sinai. He has just named Bezaleel and Aholiab to build the tabernacle and everything it would hold. This list closes that task. Right after this, God speaks about the Sabbath as a sign that He sanctifies his people.

For today: God cares that we obey him carefully, even in small things. You might ask yourself in what area of your life you are doing things your own way, and ask him for help to do them as he teaches in his Word.
exp.35:31:
It says that Bezalel and his helpers made five bars of wood for each side of the tabernacle, and another five for the back, the western side. The bars held the boards in place so the tent would stand firm. "Tabernacle" means God's holy tent, and the wood is acacia wood.

Here the narrator tells how the people of Israel built the tabernacle in the wilderness, following what God had shown Moses. This chapter repeats the earlier instructions in great detail, to show that everything was done just as God had asked.

For today: God cares even about details that seem small, like simple bars. What we do faithfully in hidden places, without anyone noticing, also helps hold up God's work. Let us do with care what is ours to do.
exp.20:0:
It says God gives Moses a list of regulations or "judgments" for the people to know. The word "judgments" here means fair decisions, that is, rules for settling specific cases. "You shall set before them" means Moses had to put them before the people and explain them to them clearly.

God has just given the Ten Commandments on Mount Sinai (chapter 20). Now he continues speaking with Moses and gives laws for the daily life of Israel. He begins with the situation of servants, protecting the most vulnerable. This is the start of what is often called "the Book of the Covenant." Scholars debate how to apply these ancient laws today, but their concern for justice is clear.

For today: God is interested in everyday life, not only in the spiritual. Today we can ask ourselves whether we treat with justice and respect those who depend on us, such as employees, family members, or neighbors.
exp.39:23:
Moses placed the lampstand, that is, the gold lampstand with its lamps, inside the tabernacle. He set it across from the table of the bread, on the south side.

Here the narrator of the book describes how Moses set up the tabernacle, the place where God dwelt among Israel. Each object was placed exactly as God had commanded. The lampstand gave light in the holy place, and the table and the lampstand stood facing each other. There are different interpretations of its symbolic meaning, but the text stresses above all obedience.

For today: God cares about faithfulness in small things. We can obey Him in the simple details of each day, neither removing nor changing what He asked, trusting that His command is good.
exp.13:0:
This verse says that God spoke to Moses to give him an instruction. "The Lord" is the name of God, and the phrase is an introduction: what matters comes in what God says next.

Moses and the people of Israel had just left Egypt. God was leading the people, and he gives Moses specific instructions about where to camp. The verses that follow show that this direction seemed strange, but God had a purpose, which becomes clear later in the account at the sea.

For today: God does not leave his people without direction. Before we act, it is worth stopping to listen to his voice in prayer and in the Bible. Sometimes his way seems to make no sense, but we can trust that he knows what he is doing.
exp.31:5:
The verse tells that the next day the people got up early and offered burnt offerings, which were animals burned completely on the altar, and also peace offerings, which were offerings of fellowship where the meat was shared as food. Then the people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play, a phrase that here suggests unrestrained revelry.

The narrator describes what happened while Moses was on the mountain. Aaron had made the golden calf and announced a feast to the LORD. They mixed the name of the true God with an image that He had forbidden. For this reason, in what follows, God says that the people had corrupted themselves.

For today: religious sincerity is not enough if we worship in our own way. It is worth asking ourselves whether we worship God as He has revealed Himself, and not as is convenient for us.
exp.11:11:
God says that night he will pass through the whole land of Egypt and take the life of every firstborn, both of people and of animals. He also says he will bring judgment on the gods of Egypt. The word "smite" means to strike down, and "beast" refers to the animals. At the end he declares, "I am the Lord," as his signature and his authority.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron before the last plague. Israel was close to leaving slavery. The Egyptians worshiped many gods, and this judgment showed that none of them could compete with the God of Israel. The Israelites would be protected by the blood of the lamb on their doorposts, as the following verses show.

For today: we can trust that God is just and also protects those who take refuge in him. If anything in your life holds the place that belongs only to God, today is a good day to put him back in first place.
exp.28:23:
God tells Moses to place the portions of the ram and the bread he has just mentioned into the hands of Aaron and his sons. Then Moses must wave them, that is, move them back and forth, before the Lord. The phrase describing this gesture of presenting the offering to God is part of the original wording, and it reflects the same act.

God speaks with Moses on Mount Sinai, giving him instructions for consecrating the priests. With their hands full, Aaron and his sons symbolically received their service as a charge from God. Scholars explain the exact movement of the gesture in several ways, but all agree that it signified handing the offering over to God.

For today: serving God begins with hands ready to receive what He gives and to offer it back to Him. Today you can present to Him your time, your talents, and your work, saying simply: "Lord, this is yours."
exp.20:11:
It says that if someone strikes another person and that person dies, the attacker must also be put to death. The verse speaks of a killing caused by a blow.

God speaks to Moses, and Moses passes it on to the people of Israel, shortly after the Ten Commandments. These are laws for life in community. They declare that human life is very valuable. The verses that follow distinguish planned murder from accidental death, for which there was a place of refuge. Scholars discuss how this law was applied in practice.

Today it reminds us that every life is sacred and that our actions have serious consequences. We can take care in how we treat others, control anger, and seek peace, treating each person as someone valuable before God.
exp.11:27:
This verse says that the people of Israel went away to their homes and carried out exactly what God had commanded. The phrase "went away" here means that they withdrew to do what had been ordered, not that they were already leaving Egypt. The phrase "did as the Lord had commanded" means that they did it precisely, without changing anything.

Moses had just explained how to keep the Passover: sacrifice a lamb, mark the doorposts with its blood, and then teach the children the meaning of the rite. The people bowed down and worshiped. Then they obeyed what God had said through Moses and Aaron, just before the night of judgment on Egypt.

For today: simple obedience shows trust in God. We do not always understand everything, but we can faithfully do what He has said, and so teach by example those who watch us.
exp.25:23:
This section describes the boards at the corners, at the back of the tabernacle. They were to be joined together at the bottom and also at the top, into one ring. Scholars do not agree on exactly how the joining worked, though the ring or loop is commonly understood as the means of connection. What is clear is that the corners were to be firm and well secured.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai. He gives precise instructions for building a portable sanctuary, where He would dwell among Israel. Every detail of the construction mattered so that the place would be stable and fitting for its sacred use.

For today: a sturdy house needs well-joined corners. The same is true of the family and the church. Let us ask God for help to care for what holds us together: forgiveness, patience, and steady service, even in small things.
exp.13:5:
This verse says that Pharaoh prepared his war chariot, that is, he had it hitched to the horses, and he took his people with him, meaning his soldiers.

Here the speaker is the narrator of the book. Pharaoh regretted having let Israel go, because he was losing his enslaved labor. The text says that God hardened his heart, and it also says that Pharaoh himself turned against the people. Some see here God's action together with the king's decision.

For today: when pride or self-interest moves us, we can end up running against what God is doing. It is wise to stop, pray, and ask for a humble heart before acting in haste.
exp.34:34:
It says that God filled Bezalel and Oholiab with wisdom of heart, that is, with skill and good judgment. "Filled completely" is the sense of the wording used for them. Engraving is skilled craftwork. Fine embroidery is what the verse calls embroidery, and the blue thread was the blue of the verse's "blue," the reddish-purple was the "purple," and the intense red was the "scarlet." With this ability they could weave, embroider, and design all kinds of work.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel in the wilderness. He tells them that God chose these two men to build the tabernacle, the tent where God would be worshiped. Earlier he had asked them for offerings, and now he shows that the skills for the work also came from God. In this way, manual and creative work was joined to the service of God.

Today we can see our abilities, whether artistic, technical, or practical, as a gift from God. Use them with care and gratitude to serve others and to honor Him.
exp.22:3:
This verse says that if you come across the ox or donkey of someone who hates you, and the animal has wandered off, you must return it to them. An "enemy" is a person who holds a grudge against you or with whom you are in conflict. "Astray" means lost, having wandered off the path. A donkey is what the verse calls an ass.

God speaks to Israel through Moses, within the laws given at Sinai. Before and after this, the laws deal with impartial justice in legal matters and with helping those who suffer. Here, justice does not stay in the courts: it reaches into everyday life and extends even to someone you dislike. Animals were the livelihood of a family, so helping carried a real cost.

For today: if you have the chance to do someone concrete good with whom you are estranged, do it without expecting anything in return. For example, return something of theirs that was lost, or let them know about something they need to know.
exp.32:0:
God tells Moses to get moving and leave that place, together with the people he brought out of Egypt. They are to go to the land that God promised with an oath to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. "Seed" means descendants, that is, their children and their children's children. "Sware" means that God pledged his word.

The Lord speaks. This happens after the people made the golden calf (Exodus 32). Even so, God keeps his promise to give them the land. But, as the next verse shows, he announces that he will not go up among them, and this greatly saddens Moses and the people.

For today: God is faithful to what he promises, even when we fail. Yet his promise should not lead us to carelessness, but to seek his presence more than his blessings. Today you can ask him for forgiveness and desire him more than any of his gifts.
exp.24:4:
God asks, among the materials for the sanctuary, for ram skins dyed red, skins of badgers, and acacia wood. The acacia is a tree of the desert. The Hebrew word translated as "badgers" is uncertain: some think of badgers, others of seals or dolphins, or of a fine and durable leather. These skins would serve to cover the tent.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai, shortly after freeing Israel from Egypt. He asks the people for a voluntary offering to build the tabernacle, a place where his presence would be close to them as they walked through the desert.

Today, this list reminds us that God uses ordinary, simple things when we give them wholeheartedly. You do not need to have something extraordinary. Think of a skill, a block of time, or a resource you have, and offer it with joy to serve others and honor God.
exp.20:18:
It says that if the injured man recovers and is able to get up and walk outside with his staff, the one who struck him is free of punishment. Even so, he must pay him for the time he lost by being unable to work, and cover the costs of his healing.

God gives these laws to Israel through Moses, shortly after the Ten Commandments. They were rules for life in community, and they aimed to make justice fair in proportion to the harm and to keep the injured person from being left abandoned. Here the passage speaks of a fight in which no one died.

For today: if our actions or words cause harm to someone, it is not enough to say "it's over." We can take responsibility, help repair what was lost, and stand by that person until they recover.
exp.26:1:
God tells Moses that the altar must have horns at its four corners, that is, projections shaped like horns that were part of the same piece of wood. Then the whole altar, with its horns, was to be covered with bronze, which here means brass or copper. The wood itself is acacia.

God speaks with Moses on Mount Sinai and gives him instructions for building the tabernacle, the tent where the people would worship. This altar was for sacrifices. The horns were part of the place where the blood was offered. The Bible does not explain every detail, but it indicates that atonement was made there (Exodus 29:12).

For today: approaching God calls for reverence and cannot be done our own way. Today Christians believe that Christ opened the way for us, so we can draw near with gratitude and respect.
exp.24:35:
This verse says that the knobs (the round ornaments of the lampstand) and the branches formed a single piece with the lampstand. Everything was to be of pure gold, worked by hammering, not assembled from parts joined together. The phrase about being hammered out means gold beaten and shaped by hand.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai and gives him instructions for building the tabernacle, his dwelling among Israel. The lampstand with seven lamps would give light to the holy place. Its beauty and its unity showed the care with which God was to be honored.

For today: Just as the lampstand was one piece, our life of faith should not be divided. Let us ask God to shape us, even through hard "blows," so that we live with integrity, with what we believe and what we do joined together.
exp.5:5:
God tells Moses to encourage the people with a promise. He first says who he is, the faithful God, and then promises three things: to bring them out from the burdens of Egypt, to deliver them from their slavery, and to redeem them. To redeem means to rescue someone by paying a price or by acting on their behalf. The mention of a stretched out arm speaks of power in action, and great judgments are acts of justice against Egypt.

God speaks to Moses after Pharaoh made the Israelites' work harder. The people were discouraged. God reminds them that he heard their groaning and that he had not forgotten the covenant he made with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

For today: when you feel exhausted or see no way out, remember that God hears and keeps what he promises. Speak to him honestly and wait with confidence, even when the answer takes a long time.
exp.33:32:
This verse says that Moses, when he finished speaking with the people, covered his face with a veil. The word "face" means the front of the head, and "veil" is a cloth that covers. Moses had already passed on to them what God commanded him.

Moses was coming down from Mount Sinai after being with God, and his face was shining. First he spoke with the leaders and then with all Israel. The verses that follow explain that he removed the veil when he went in to speak with God, and put it on when he spoke with the people. Paul, in 2 Corinthians 3, comments on this veil, though interpreters explain it in several ways.

For today: God transforms us when we spend time with Him. Look for daily moments of prayer and Bible reading, and let that closeness shape your character and your words.
exp.27:4:
This verse names the materials that skilled workers would use to make the sacred clothing of the priests: gold, blue-violet (a dark blue or violet thread), purple, scarlet (a deep red), and fine linen, meaning finely woven and well-twisted linen thread. The phrase "they shall take" means that the workers would receive these materials for their work.

God speaks to Moses at Sinai. He asks him to gather the wise-hearted people, those to whom God himself gave skill, to make the garments of Aaron and his sons. Those garments set them apart to serve as priests. Many understand that the costly and beautiful materials expressed the dignity and holiness of worship, although the Bible here does not explain the meaning of each color.

Today we can remember that God values the abilities he has given us and wants us to use them to serve him with excellence, whether in cooking, sewing, teaching, or building.
exp.29:13:
This verse says that every man who was counted in the census, from twenty years old and upward, was to give an offering to God. That offering was the half shekel mentioned earlier. The phrase "pass among those who are numbered" means that he was registered in the census, and the word "offering" here refers to a contribution given to God.

God is speaking to Moses while giving him instructions for the tabernacle. When the people were counted, each one gave a ransom for his life, so that a plague would not come upon them. Everyone gave the same amount, and that money went toward the work of the tabernacle.

For today: God values each person equally, regardless of their money or position. We can give with gratitude, knowing that our lives depend on his mercy, and simply support the work of our church.
exp.5:22:
This verse says that Aaron married Elisheba, daughter of Amminadab and sister of Naashon. She bore him four sons: Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar. The phrase "took her to wife" means that he married her, and the word "bore" means that she gave birth to them.

Here the narrator pauses the story of Israel's deliverance to give a list of families. It shows which family line Moses and Aaron came from, the leaders whom God chose. From these sons of Aaron the priests would come. Naashon appears later as the leader of the tribe of Judah, so this family also had ties to Judah.

God works through real families, with concrete names and histories. Value your family and pray for it, since God can use your home to serve others, even when today it seems like something very ordinary.
exp.9:16:
Pharaoh asks Moses and Aaron to forgive his sin, just this once. He also asks them to pray to the Lord, "your God," so that he may take away from him "this death," that is, the plague of locusts that is destroying everything.

He speaks as the king of Egypt. The locusts had eaten what the hail left, and the land was left with nothing green. Desperate, he calls for Moses and admits his sin. However, he says "your God," not "my God," and the story shows that his heart remains hard. His words sound like repentance, but they are aimed at relief.

Today: true repentance does not only want the suffering to end, but seeks God and changes the heart. Before asking God to remove a difficulty, we can ask ourselves whether we are willing to obey him.
exp.29:32:
This verse says that no one was to make a perfume or ointment like the holy anointing oil, nor put it on a stranger, that is, someone who was not a priest or part of the service of the sanctuary. Whoever did so would be "cut off from his people," a phrase that can mean being excluded from the community or suffering a severe penalty; scholars understand it in several ways.

God speaks to Moses and gives him instructions for the tabernacle. This oil was used to consecrate the sacred objects and the priests. By forbidding its imitation, God protected what He had set apart as holy, so that the people would not treat it as something common.

For today: God deserves to be treated with reverence. We can ask ourselves whether in our lives we take care of what is sacred, such as prayer, the Bible, and worship, or whether we take them lightly. Without copying or using God for our own purposes, let us learn to approach Him with respect and gratitude.
exp.21:15:
If a man persuades a young woman who is single and not engaged, and sleeps with her, he must pay the bride price and marry her. The explanation says that "entice" here means to persuade or seduce. A young woman who is a virgin is the one meant. To pay the bride price means giving the father the marriage payment, a compensation that gave the young woman security.

God speaks to Moses and gives civil laws to the people of Israel after the Ten Commandments. In that society, a woman who lost her virginity before marriage was left very vulnerable and had few prospects of getting married. The law held the man responsible. The next verse makes clear that the father could refuse the wedding, and even so the man was still required to pay.

Today we learn that actions have consequences and that we must answer for the harm we cause others. No one should take advantage of another person's trust or vulnerability. If we have hurt someone, God calls us to take responsibility for it with honesty and respect.
exp.24:34:
This verse describes a detail of the golden lampstand of the tabernacle. There would be a knop, a round or knot-shaped ornament, under each pair of branches, at the point where the branches came out of the central stem. There were three pairs, one for each pair of branches, and they added up to six branches. The candlestick is what we would today call a lampstand or standing lamp.

God gives these instructions to Moses on Mount Sinai, as he explains how to build the tabernacle, the place where Israel would worship. The lampstand was to stand in the holy place and was to be made of one piece of gold, hammered into shape.
