Scholars do not fully agree on the exact meaning of each ornament; many see images of a tree that bears fruit and flowers.

For today: God cares about details and about the beauty of what is made for Him. We can serve Him with care and diligence in the small things, without looking for shortcuts, trusting that He values what we do with a sincere heart.
exp.0:1:
This verse begins the list of the sons of Jacob, also called Israel, who came to Egypt. Here the first four appear: Reuben, Simeon, Levi, and Judah. They are the sons of Leah, and the book names them first, following the order in which they were born.

The one who tells the story is the author of the book, traditionally attributed to Moses. At the start of Exodus, he recalls the origin of the people: a family of seventy persons that became very numerous. The names connect this story with Genesis and with the promises made to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

For today: God knows people by their names, and does not treat them as a faceless crowd. Today you can remember that God knows you personally, and you can also value those around you by learning their names and their stories, because each one matters before Him.
exp.22:4:
This verse says that if you see the donkey of someone who hates you lying on the ground, crushed under the weight of its load, you must not leave it there abandoned. The phrase "hateth" means to hate, and "forbear" means to hold back or refrain. The command is clear: you must help lift it up, even though the owner is your enemy.

God speaks to Israel through Moses, in the laws that followed the covenant at Sinai. These rules taught people to live with justice and compassion within the community. Earlier, the law commanded returning the lost animal of an enemy, and afterward it speaks of fair judgments. In this way, kindness toward an enemy is joined with justice for everyone.

For today: when someone you have conflict with needs concrete help, give it to them without waiting for reconciliation. It can be a simple favor, such as offering support in an emergency. Doing good does not depend on whether we like the other person.
exp.36:16:
This explains Exodus 37:17. It says that Bezalel made the lampstand of pure gold, hammered into shape. The whole piece was one solid piece: the base, the central shaft, the bowls shaped like almond blossoms, the round ornaments (perhaps knobs or calyxes), and the flowers. "Hammered" means the gold was shaped by beating it, not by pouring it into a mold.

Context: This is a narrative passage from the book of Exodus, not a speech. It describes how the tabernacle was built, following the instructions God gave to Moses. The lampstand gave light in the holy place. Some see in it a symbol of God's light or of life, though the text does not explain this here.

For today: God cared about every detail of that lampstand, and this reminds us that it is worth serving him with care and dedication, even in small tasks that no one applauds.
exp.7:2:
This verse announces that the Nile will be filled with frogs. They will come out of the water and get into every place: the house of Pharaoh, his bedroom and even his bed, the houses of his servants and those of his people. They will also reach the ovens, where bread was baked, and the kneading troughs, which were containers used to knead the flour.

God speaks through Moses and orders him to warn Pharaoh. Israel was enslaved in Egypt, and God asked for their freedom so that they could serve him. Before sending this plague, God gives a clear warning. The frogs touch what the Egyptians considered safe: the river, their food, and their rest. Some scholars think this challenged Egyptian gods linked to the river, though this is interpreted in different ways.

For today: God speaks to us with patience before correcting us. If we feel that He is asking us to change something, let us obey in time, without hardening our hearts.
exp.31:17:
Here Moses answers Joshua, who thought he heard a battle in the camp. Moses tells him that the sound is neither like shouts of victory nor like cries of defeat. The shouting of victory is a loud uproar, and the cries of defeat are the wails of the beaten. What Moses hears is singing, and later it becomes clear that it was a festival.

Moses and Joshua were coming down from Mount Sinai, where Moses had received the tablets of the law. Without realizing it, the people had made a golden calf and were celebrating it with songs and dancing. Moses distinguishes the sound and understands that something is wrong, though he does not yet see it.

For today: not all cheerful noise is good. Let us ask God for discernment to see beyond what looks like a celebration, and to examine honestly what or whom we are giving our hearts to.
exp.5:11:
In this verse, Moses answers God with an objection. He says that if the people of Israel themselves do not listen to him, then Pharaoh will listen even less. He adds that he is "uncircumcised in lips," an old expression that probably means he did not feel able to speak well. Some think of stammering or simple awkwardness in speech; the text does not make this clear.

Moses speaks before God. Earlier, the people, weighed down by harsh slavery, did not pay attention to the promise of deliverance (Exodus 6:9). Now God orders him to go to Pharaoh, and Moses hesitates out of fear and from feeling inadequate. God does not dismiss him: he keeps calling him and accompanies him with Aaron.

For today: when you feel too unqualified for what God asks of you, tell him honestly, as Moses did. God can use your weaknesses, and he gives you help to obey.
exp.28:18:
This verse says that Moses must take the second ram, and that Aaron and his sons must lay their hands on the head of the animal. It is the second ram of the ceremony; the first had already been burned completely. Laying on the hands was a gesture that joined the priests with the animal that was going to be offered.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai and explains how to set apart Aaron and his sons for priestly service. This second ram is used in the ceremony of consecration. Scholars explain the exact meaning of laying on the hands in various ways, but it is usually understood as identification and surrender.

Today we can remember that serving God begins with surrender, not with pride. Before doing anything for Him, we can come before Him with humility, recognizing that we depend on His provision and His grace.
exp.39:29:
He set the laver between the tent of meeting and the altar, a large bronze basin for water, in an exact place. Then he put water in it for washing. The "testimony" was the tablets of the law kept inside.

Here the narrator of the book describes how Moses set up the tabernacle, following every command of God. The priests were to wash their hands and feet before entering or approaching the altar. It was a sign that drawing near to a holy God calls for cleanness and reverence.

For today: before praying or reading the Bible, take a moment to ask God to cleanse your heart. You can confess what weighs on you and come near with sincerity, trusting in his forgiveness.
exp.4:19:
This verse says that the Israelite foremen, as they came out from speaking with Pharaoh, ran into Moses and Aaron, who were waiting for them in plain view.

The foremen were Israelites placed in charge of the workers. Pharaoh had just ordered them to keep producing the same number of bricks, but without giving them straw. They asked for relief and were turned down. They come out distressed and, on seeing Moses and Aaron, pour out their anger on them, as we will see in the next verse. Moses had brought the promise of deliverance, but at first everything got worse.

For today: when obedience to God first brings more hardship, it does not mean that He has made a mistake. We can do as Moses did, who took his complaint directly to God in prayer, instead of remaining trapped in blame.
exp.8:18:
God, through Moses, tells Pharaoh to send for his livestock and everything he has in the field. Whoever is left outside, whether person or animal, will die under the hail.

The Lord speaks through Moses during the plagues of Egypt. Pharaoh kept refusing to let the people of Israel go. Even so, God gives a warning before the punishment, and this shows his patience. The next verse tells how some of Pharaoh's servants believed and got themselves to safety, while others paid no attention.

Today, when God warns us through his Word, the wise response is to answer with humility and act in time. Listening without obeying does not protect us. Let us ask God for an attentive heart so that we take seriously what he says.
exp.21:1:
If a thief is caught breaking into a house (that is, breaking through the wall or the entrance to get in and steal), and the owner strikes him and he dies, the owner is not guilty of murder. "Caught" means found in the act, and "will not be held guilty" means that he carries no guilt for bloodshed.

God gives these laws to Israel through Moses, after the Ten Commandments, to order the life of the people. It is understood that the event happens at night, when the owner cannot see well or call for help, and fears for his family. The following verse makes clear that the case is different in daylight. Scholars agree that the law distinguishes between defense in danger and unnecessary violence.

Today, this text reminds us that God values both life and justice. Before reacting in anger, let us try to act with prudence, seeking to protect rather than to take revenge.
exp.6:11:
The explanation says that Pharaoh's magicians each threw down their staffs, and the staffs became snakes. But Aaron's staff swallowed up their staffs. The word about the swallowing means that it ate them or gulped them down. The magicians were men who practiced magic arts.

Moses and Aaron had gone to Pharaoh by God's command to ask for the release of Israel. Aaron cast down his staff as a sign, and Pharaoh called his wise men to imitate it. It is not made clear how they did it: some think of tricks, others of hidden power. What is clear is that God's power was greater. Even so, Pharaoh did not want to listen.

For today: sometimes evil seems to imitate what belongs to God and confuses us. Trust that God's truth is greater. And remember that seeing signs is not enough; a heart willing to listen is also needed.
exp.12:8:
It says that the festival of unleavened bread will be for Israel like a sign on the hand and a reminder before the eyes. So the law of the Lord will always be on their lips, because God brought them out of Egypt with a strong hand. The phrase "will be for you" is the sense here; "memorial" means reminder.

Moses speaks to the people just freed, before they enter Canaan. He explains how to remember the Passover and the unleavened bread, and how to tell it to their children. Many understand the "sign on the hand" as a figure of speech; some Jews later practiced it literally with phylacteries. Interpreters do not fully agree.

For today: build simple habits that remind you of what God has done for you, such as reading the Bible, praying at the start of the day, or telling your children how he helped you. In this way your words will speak of his faithfulness.
exp.21:19:
It says that anyone who offers sacrifices to other gods, and not only to the Lord, was to be put to death. The word "sacrifice" here means the act of offering a sacrifice, and "shall be utterly destroyed" means "shall be put to death." The Hebrew word behind "shall be utterly destroyed" can be connected with the idea of being set apart for destruction (herem), although scholars explain this in different ways.

God speaks to Israel through Moses, in the laws given after the exodus from Egypt. Israel was a newly formed nation, with a covenant with the Lord as its only King. Worshiping other gods was seen as betrayal of that covenant, not merely as a religious mistake. The laws nearby also protect the foreigner, the widow, and the orphan.

Today we do not use this law to punish anyone. But we can still ask ourselves: what in my life holds the place that belongs only to God? Give it to Him, with humility and gratitude.
exp.27:28:
This verse says that Aaron, the high priest, would carry the names of the tribes of Israel on a breast piece. The explanation calls it the "breastplate of judgment," and the verse above gives that name in English. He would wear it over his heart each time he entered the sanctuary, as a constant reminder before God.

God gives these instructions to Moses on Mount Sinai, while explaining how the priests' garments were to be made. The breastplate had twelve stones with the names of the tribes. Aaron represented the people before God, and so he carried all of them with him, forgetting none of them.

For today: Christians see in this a foreshadowing of Jesus, who intercedes for us (Hebrews 7:25). You can rest knowing that God keeps you in mind. And you can imitate that care by bringing your family, your church, and your friends before God in prayer, "upon your heart."
exp.23:0:
God speaks to Moses and invites him to come up the mountain together with Aaron, his sons Nadab and Abihu, and seventy elders of Israel. He tells them they must worship from a distance, and that worshiping means bowing down in reverence before the Lord.

God has just given the people the Ten Commandments and several laws. Now he prepares the ceremony in which Israel will confirm its covenant with him. There is a clear order: only Moses comes closer, the leaders worship at a distance, and the people wait below. This shows God's holiness and that he sets the terms for how we approach him.

For today: when we pray or worship, let us do it with respect and gratitude. Today we can draw near to God with confidence through Christ, yet without losing reverence. Before praying, pause and acknowledge who he is.
exp.18:7:
The explanation says that all the people of Israel answered together, with one voice: "We will do everything the Lord has spoken." Then Moses brought that answer back to God.

God had just rescued Israel from Egypt, and at Mount Sinai he offered them the chance to be his special people, a kingdom of priests. Moses gathered the elders and explained everything to them. The people responded with enthusiasm. Later in the story, they did not always keep that promise, which reminds us that wanting to obey is not enough without God's help.

Before promising something to God, think honestly and humbly. You can say to him: "I want to obey you, but I need your help." Choose one concrete step of obedience today and ask him for strength to carry it out.
exp.16:5:
God tells Moses that He will stand before him there, on the rock at Horeb. Moses is to strike the rock, and water will come out of it so that the people may drink. Moses obeys, and he does it in the sight of the elders of Israel, who serve as witnesses.

God speaks here in response to Moses' cry. The people, thirsty at Rephidim, were complaining and nearly stoned him. God does not rebuke him harshly but gives him a concrete solution. The elders witness the miracle to confirm that the water comes from God. Afterward, the place was called Massah and Meribah, names that recall the people's distrust.

For today: when you feel exhausted or see no way out, bring your sincere need to God, as Moses did. He can provide in unexpected ways, and He invites us to obey step by step, trusting that He is present with us.
exp.26:16:
This verse describes how the pillars surrounding the court of the tabernacle were to be decorated. They were "filleted with silver," meaning they had rings or rods of silver that joined them together or wrapped around them. The capitals were the top part of each pillar, and they were also made of silver. The sockets were the bases on which the pillars stood, and they were made of metal, which probably refers to bronze or copper.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai and gives him exact instructions for building a place where he would dwell among Israel. The court was the outer courtyard, the first space one passed through to approach God. Nothing was left to chance.

Today we can learn that God values order and care in what we offer him. Serving him with dedication, even in small details, is a way of honoring him.
exp.8:10:
This verse says that the magicians of Egypt could no longer stand before Moses, because they too were covered with painful sores, just like all the Egyptians. The boils here are a rash of the skin, and the sores are swellings or inflamed wounds. We do not know for certain exactly what disease it was.

The one who tells the story is the author of the book, who recounts the sixth plague. Earlier, the magicians had imitated some of the signs and had tried to compete with Moses. Now they cannot even stand in front of him. The account shows that the God of Israel has power over the false powers of Egypt.

For today: no human power, neither fame nor prestige, can hold its ground before God. We can trust that He is greater than anything that seems impossible for us to overcome. It is also an invitation not to harden our hearts when God speaks to us.
exp.18:2:
Moses went up the mountain to meet with God, and from there the Lord called to him. He was asked to carry a message to the house of Jacob, that is, to the descendants of Jacob, the people of Israel. The explanation of the verse's wording has been removed here, since the reader's version does not use those words.

God is speaking, and Moses is the messenger. Israel has just arrived in the wilderness of Sinai, three months after leaving Egypt. God is about to remind them how he rescued them and to propose a covenant with them. Before giving the law, he first reminds them of what he has already done for them.

For today: God speaks to us first and calls us to listen to him. Before asking anything of us, he reminds us of his faithfulness. We can set aside a quiet moment each day to listen to his voice in the Bible and remember what he has done for us.
exp.16:7:
This verse tells that the people of Amalek came out to attack Israel at a place called Rephidim. "Fought" means there was a real battle. Rephidim is the same place where they had just complained about the lack of water.

The narrator of the book of Exodus tells what happened just after God gave water from the rock. Israel had doubted and asked: "Is the LORD among us, or not?" Right after that, an enemy arrives. The Amalekites were a desert people, and the text does not explain all their reasons here. Later, Moses prays and Joshua fights.

For today: after doubting God, new trials sometimes come. Remember how God has helped you before, pray and act with responsibility, trusting that He is with you.
exp.12:3:
Moses tells the people that the departure from Egypt takes place "this day," in the month Abib. The source's comment that "ye come out" means "you go out" is not needed for the reader, since the verse uses "came ye out," so that sentence is deleted. Abib is explained as the time when the grain began to ripen, and later this month came to be called Nisan.

Moses speaks to the people before they cross the sea. He wants them to fix in memory the exact date of their deliverance. For this reason he gives them instructions to remember it every year with the feast of unleavened bread and the dedication of the firstborn. God did not only rescue them; he wanted his children to also know the story.

For today: put a date and place to what God has done in your life. Write down his answers and tell them to your family. Remembering with gratitude strengthens faith when difficult days come.
exp.15:30:
The explanation says that the Israelites named this food that God gave them in the desert "Manna." It was white, similar to coriander seed, and had a sweet taste, like wafers made with honey. The word "manna" is usually understood to mean "What is this?", although some explain its origin in other ways.

The one who tells this is the narrator of the book, traditionally Moses. Israel had just left Egypt and had no food. God gave it every morning, and on the sixth day He gave double so that the Sabbath would be a day of rest. Afterward Moses commands that some be kept so that future generations could see how God sustained them.

For today: God takes care of us day by day, and sometimes with sweet surprises. Practice gratitude: before eating, or at the start of the day, thank God for something specific He has given you. And rest, trusting that He provides.
exp.24:23:
God tells Moses that the table made of acacia wood (Shittim) must be covered with pure gold. In addition, it must have a gold molding running around it, that is, a decorative edge or rim that goes around the top edge of the table and probably kept things from falling off.

God speaks with Moses on Mount Sinai and gives him instructions for building the tabernacle, a place where he would dwell among Israel. This table was part of the furnishings of the holy place, and on it the bread of the presence was set. Some see in it a sign of God's provision, although the text here only gives the measurements and materials.

For today: God cares about the details and deserves our best. We can offer him with care what we do, even the simple things, such as work, home, or service, knowing that he values our dedication.
exp.34:11:
This verse lists the furnishings that were to be made for the tabernacle: the ark of the covenant, the poles for carrying it, the lid of the ark (also called the mercy seat), and the veil, the curtain that separated the holy place from the most holy place. The poles were the long wooden bars used to carry it.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel in the wilderness, after the episode of the golden calf. He passes on what God commanded and invites them to take part, especially those who were skilled and willing, people with wise hearts. The ark symbolized God's presence among them, and the veil marked his holiness.

Today we might ask ourselves: what skill or ability do I have that I can offer to God and to my community? Serving with what we know how to do, with a willing heart, is also a way of worship.
exp.28:4:
He says that Moses was to take the sacred garments and dress Aaron with them, one by one: the coat, the robe of the ephod, the ephod itself, the breastplate, and the girdle. The "ephod" was a special priestly garment, something like a long apron. The "breastplate" is the chest piece, worn over the heart. The "girdle" was the sash that held everything in place.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai and gives him instructions for setting apart Aaron and his sons as priests. First comes the washing with water, then the garments, and after that the anointing with oil. Aaron did not dress himself: it was God who prepared him for service.

For today: we cannot draw near to God on the strength of our own merits. He himself prepares us and covers us. Christians see in this a picture of being clothed with Christ; that is why we can serve with humility and gratitude.
exp.14:10:
This verse asks who among the gods can be compared to the Lord. It says God is glorious in holiness, meaning he is majestic and completely pure. The praise he deserves is full of awe and reverence, and he is the one who does wonders, carrying out extraordinary works.

Moses speaks together with the Israelites in the song they sing after crossing the Red Sea. The Egyptian army, which pursued them full of pride, sank into the waters. The question does not seek an answer; it affirms that no other god is equal to him. Some scholars think that "gods" refers to the deities of the neighboring peoples.

Today, when you face something that seems impossible, remember what God has already done. Praise him sincerely and trust that he is still powerful and faithful.
exp.32:20:
God tells Moses that there is a place near Him, and that there he will be able to stand on a rock. "By me" means "beside me" or "near me." The rock is a large stone, a firm and safe place.

The Lord speaks with Moses after the people made the golden calf. Moses has asked to see God's glory, but God makes clear that no man can see His face and live. So He prepares a place where Moses can be safe and come to know His goodness. Some understand this as a sign of God's care for Moses; the text does not explain more.

God knows how much we can bear, and He cares for us as He draws near. You can ask Him to show you more of Himself, trusting that He will give you a firm and safe place to stand.
exp.33:9:
God answers Moses' prayer and promises to make a covenant with Israel. He says he will do wonders never seen in any nation, and that all the people will see his work. A "covenant" is a solemn agreement or promise. The word "terrible" here means that it causes awe and reverence, not that it is something bad.

God is the one speaking. Israel had sinned with the golden calf, and Moses had just asked him to continue with them, even though they were a stiff-necked people, meaning stubborn and rebellious. God renews his covenant with them, and right away he asks them to remain faithful to him and not to mix in with the customs of the peoples of Canaan.

For today: God remains faithful even when we fail. You can come to him with humility, as Moses did, ask for forgiveness, and trust that he is at work. His grace is not an excuse to neglect obedience, but a reason to live grateful and faithful.
exp.23:10:
God did not punish the leaders of Israel who went up the mountain. The people who are called "nobles" here were the leaders or important people among the nation, and the verse says God did not strike them down or destroy them. They saw God, and afterward they ate and drank in his presence.

Israel had just agreed to the covenant with God at Sinai. Moses, Aaron, Nadab, Abihu, and seventy elders went up as representatives of the people. What they saw is described with great care: the text only mentions the pavement under his feet, like sapphire. Eating and drinking was a sign of peace and fellowship, as in a meal that seals a covenant.

Today we can draw near to God with reverence, yet without fear of being rejected. He invites us to his table by grace. Take a moment this week to thank him for his nearness.
exp.3:0:
Moses answers God with an objection: he thinks the people of Israel will not believe him or listen to his voice. They will say that the Lord has not appeared to him.

Moses speaks with God on Mount Horeb, beside the burning bush. God has just sent him to bring Israel out of Egypt. Moses feels afraid and doubts his own ability. God does not rebuke him right away but gives him a sign with his staff, which turns into a serpent. Later in the text, Moses is still shown to struggle with insecurity.

For today: when God asks something of you and you feel that no one will believe you, do not stay in your excuses. Tell God your fear honestly, and look at what you already have in your hand: what God has already given you to begin obeying.
exp.25:24:
This verse sums up how many boards there were on the back side of the tabernacle: eight in all. Each board rested on two bases, which were silver footings or pedestals. That is why there were sixteen sockets in total, two under each board.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai and gives him exact instructions for building his portable sanctuary, where he would dwell among Israel. This passage describes the western side, including the corner boards. Some details, such as the exact way the corners were joined, are understood in different ways.

For today: God cares even about the details of what we offer him. We can serve him with order and care, trusting that every small task done faithfully has value before him.
exp.2:6:
God tells Moses that He has carefully seen the suffering of His people in Egypt. He has also heard their cries of pain caused by their taskmasters, the overseers who forced them to work hard. He says that He knows their sorrows: He understands well what they feel.

The LORD speaks from the bush that was burning without being consumed. Moses has just covered his face out of fear. God presents Himself as the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and explains to him why He is calling him: Israel is enslaved, and He is going to act to deliver them, using Moses.

For today: when you feel that no one sees your pain, remember that God is not indifferent. You can speak to Him honestly, trusting that He hears you and knows you. And sometimes He uses us to help others who are suffering.
exp.20:16:
He who curses his father or his mother, that is, who insults them, despises them, or speaks of them with contempt, was to be put to death. Cursing here is not merely saying a vulgar word; it means treating with complete contempt those who are to be honored.

God gave these laws to Israel through Moses, after the Ten Commandments, to form an orderly people. The family was the foundation of society, and seriously dishonoring one's parents was an attack on that foundation. This was a civil law for ancient Israel, and scholars debate how it was applied in practice.

Today we can take seriously the honor owed to our parents: speaking of them with respect, even when there are disagreements, and caring for them patiently in their old age. Jesus himself recalled this command (Mark 7:10).
exp.37:18:
This verse describes the four pillars at the entrance of the courtyard of the tabernacle. They stood on bases of metal (bronze, according to other translations), and their capitals, which were the top part of each pillar, and their fillets, or decorative rings, were of silver. The overlaying was a covering of silver over those tops.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, following the report of the materials used in the sanctuary. Everything offered and how it was used is recorded, under the direction of Moses and with Ithamar, son of Aaron, in charge of the accounts. It is an orderly and faithful record of the work.

For today: God values work done with order, honesty, and care. If you manage money or resources, whether for the church, your job, or your family, strive to be transparent and keep good accounts. Serving God is also expressed in attention to detail.
exp.15:32:
Moses tells Aaron to take a pot, put an omer full of manna in it (a small measure, about two liters, though scholars calculate its size in different ways), and set it before the Lord. In this way it would be kept for future generations.

Moses speaks to Aaron, the high priest, while Israel travels through the desert. God had fed the people with manna every day. Now he wants a visible reminder of that care, so that children and grandchildren would know that God sustained them when they left Egypt. Afterward, Aaron placed it before the Testimony, that is, near the ark.

For today: make a reminder of what God has done for you. You can write in a notebook the times he helped you, and share them with your family, so that your faith and theirs may be strengthened.
exp.38:1:
Here the text says that Bezalel and the craftsmen made the ephod, a sacred garment for the priest. They made it with gold thread and with threads of several colors: violet (a dark blue or purple-blue), purple, and scarlet (an intense red), along with fine twined linen, that is, fine linen made of braided threads.

This is part of the account of how Aaron's garments were made. The narrator repeats that everything was done "just as the LORD had commanded Moses." The details of materials and colors show the care with which the plan given at Sinai was obeyed. Scholars differ on the exact meaning of each color, so it is best not to claim more than the text says.

For today: God values faithful obedience, even in small and laborious things. Doing your work well, with care and for God, is also a form of worship.
exp.33:7:
This verse tells us that Moses, when he heard how God described his own character, responded at once. "Hastened" means he did it without delay. "Bowed" means he bent his whole body low, as a sign of reverence and worship.

God had just passed before Moses and proclaimed his name: merciful, patient, full of goodness and truth, yet also just. This takes place after the sin of the golden calf, when Moses went up Mount Sinai again. After falling down before God, Moses asks him to go with the people and forgive them, even though they are stiff-necked, that is, stubborn.

For today: when we think about what God is like, his goodness and his justice, the most natural response is humility. Before asking for anything, we can take a moment to worship him and give thanks for his mercy.
exp.28:29:
It says that the priest who takes Aaron's place, one of his sons, will wear the holy garments for seven days. This would happen when he enters the tabernacle of the congregation (the tent where God met with his people) to serve in the sanctuary, the holy place.

God speaks to Moses and gives him instructions on how to consecrate Aaron and his sons. The garments would pass from father to son, and each new priest would be set apart through a week of ceremonies. In this way, service to God was not taken lightly or improvised.

For today: God values preparation and reverence in service. Before taking on a responsibility in the church or in life, take time to pray, learn, and ask God to set you apart to serve with a sincere heart.
exp.12:6:
This verse commands that for seven days the people eat only bread made without yeast. Throughout the whole territory there must be nothing leavened to be seen, meaning dough made with yeast, nor yeast itself. "Territory" can be understood as the land or borders where they live, and "leavened" refers to bread made with yeast.

Moses speaks to the people who have just come out of Egypt. He gives them instructions for the Feast of Unleavened Bread, which they would remember each year as the deliverance God gave them. He also looks ahead to when they would live in the promised land. The verses that follow say that parents were to explain the meaning of this feast to their children.

For today: God invites us to remember his works and to teach them to others. You can build a simple habit, such as telling your family how God has helped you, so that gratitude passes from one generation to the next.
exp.23:6:
Moses takes the book of the covenant, which is the writing containing the words and laws that God had just given, and reads it aloud to the people. They answer that they will do everything the Lord has said and will be obedient. The phrase "in the audience of the people" means in front of everyone, in the hearing of all the people.

Moses is the one who speaks and serves as the mediator between God and Israel. God had just given them the Ten Commandments and other laws (Exodus 20–23). Before sealing the covenant with sacrifices and blood, Moses reads everything to the people so that they know what they are committing themselves to. Afterward, the people failed several times, so their promise was sincere but weak.

Before we commit ourselves to God, it is good to listen and to get to know his Word with attention. Reading it regularly helps us obey with understanding. And since our strength is small, we can ask him for help to keep what we promise.
exp.15:25:
It says that the people were to gather the manna for six days, but that on the seventh day, the sabbath, there would be no manna in the field. The word for "shall find" is rendered in the verse as "there shall be none," and "gather" means picking up what God gave each morning.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel in the wilderness. God gave them manna every day, and on the sixth day He gave a double portion so that they could rest on the seventh. Moses explains this so that they would trust in God's provision and keep the day of rest. Even so, some went out to look for manna on that day and found nothing.

For today: God cares for us and invites us to trust Him, not only in our work. We can set aside regular time to rest, pray, and be with God and family, believing that He will supply what we need.
exp.33:17:
This verse commands keeping the Feast of Unleavened Bread. Seven days the people were to eat bread made without yeast, in the month of Abib (spring, later called Nisan), because it was in that month that they came out of Egypt. Bread made without yeast is the meaning of the unleavened bread the verse names, and here the eating of bread with leaven is forbidden.

God speaks to Moses in the passage where he renews the covenant after the sin of the golden calf. Earlier he had warned against making alliances with the peoples of Canaan and against idolatry. This feast appears as a way of keeping alive the memory of the deliverance and of exclusive faithfulness to God.

For today: set aside moments to remember with gratitude what God has done for you. Write down, or tell your family, a time when he sustained you, so that remembrance nourishes your faithfulness.
exp.37:9:
It says the south side of the tabernacle courtyard had twenty pillars, each set on a base of bronze. The capitals (the top part of each pillar) and their bands (the rods or rings that joined the pillars and held the curtains) were of silver. The bronze here is the metal used for the bases.

The narrator, in the book of Exodus, describes how the courtyard was built just as God had commanded Moses. It is a detailed account of obedience. The bronze mirrors of the women who served at the entrance were used for other pieces, and the text goes on with the measurements of each side.

For today: God cares about the details of our obedience, even the small and unremarkable ones. Serve faithfully in the simple things, for God values what is done with a willing heart.
exp.36:26:
This verse says that Bezaleel made two rings of gold for the incense altar. He placed them under the gold crown, at two opposite corners, one on each side. They served as places to put poles through so the altar could be carried. The other words quoted in the explanation are simply the wording of the source, so I have translated them into the verse's language: "made it" and "carried" are the ideas they express.

The passage belongs to the account of building the tabernacle, which Moses had received by God's command. The narrator describes in detail how what had been commanded was carried out. The altar of perfume stood in the holy place, and the people traveled through the desert, so everything had to be movable with reverence, without being touched directly.

For today: God cares about the details of what we offer to him. Just as the altar was made to travel with the people on their journey, our prayer and worship should not stay in one place or one moment, but go with us wherever we go.
exp.9:10:
Pharaoh rejects Moses' proposal. He says that only the men may go to serve the Lord, because that is what they asked for. Then they are driven out of his presence.

Moses was asking permission for the whole people to leave: children, the elderly, sons, daughters, and livestock, since they had a festival to hold for the Lord. Pharaoh accepts only in part, but he keeps the families behind as if they were a guarantee that the men would return. Some understand that he suspected an escape; the text does not fully explain this. His refusal leads afterward to the plague of locusts.

God wants to be worshiped with the whole family and with everything we have, not halfway. Today we can ask ourselves whether we set limits on our commitment, or whether we include our children in the faith through example and affection.
exp.35:5:
Moses gave orders to announce throughout the camp that no one, neither man nor woman, should keep bringing offerings for the sanctuary. The word "proclaim" in the verse means to announce out loud so that everyone hears about it.

The workmen in charge of the project, that is, those responsible for building the tabernacle, had told Moses that there was already more material than was needed. Moses, who led the people on behalf of God, gave the command so that no more would be gathered in excess. The people had responded with great generosity.

Today we can learn that giving with joy is beautiful, but it is also good to do it with order and wisdom. If you serve in your church, listen to those who lead the work and help with what is truly needed. And if there is abundance, thank God.
exp.11:43:
This verse says that a servant bought with money could eat the Passover, but only after being circumcised. The phrase about a servant bought with money refers to a slave who belonged to the household. The word for "but" in the sense of "however" is simply "but," and the old form for "when you have" is simply "when."

God speaks to Moses and Aaron, giving the rules of the Passover, the night when he brought Israel out of Egypt. The nearby verses exclude the foreigner and the hired worker, who were not part of the household. The servant of the house could take part if he entered the covenant through circumcision. The Bible does not explain here all the details of how this was lived out in each family.

For today: communion with God is not something casual, but an invitation that calls for commitment. We can ask ourselves whether we take part in the things of God with a heart truly given over to Him, and also help others feel welcome in their faith.
exp.11:14:
God commands the people to eat unleavened bread for seven days. From the first day they must remove all the yeast from their houses. Bread made with yeast, that is, with fermented dough, is what the verse refers to when it speaks of leavened bread. Whoever eats it during those days will be cut off from Israel, an expression that can mean being separated from the people; it is not known with certainty whether it refers to expulsion, to a greater punishment, or to both.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron, just before the last plague and the departure from Egypt. He wants Israel to remember forever that they were rescued. The unleavened bread recalls the hurried departure, and the feast unites the people in gratitude.

Today we can ask ourselves what things we should remove from our lives in order to live grateful to God. Perhaps a habit, an attitude, or a custom that keeps us away from Him. Let us do it with joy, remembering that God rescued us.
exp.8:14:
God speaks to Pharaoh through Moses. He says that he could have stretched out his hand to strike Pharaoh and his people with a deadly disease and cut them off from the earth. Some of the words here are old: "smite" means to strike or punish, and "pestilence" is a disease that kills many people. Some translations render this verse as something God could have done, not as something he was already doing.

Moses brings Pharaoh God's message, which asks him to let his people, Israel, go so they may serve him. Pharaoh has refused again and again, and the plagues come. God wants Pharaoh to acknowledge that there is no one like him. The verses that follow show that, instead of destroying him, God has kept him standing in order to make his power known.

For today: God's patience is not weakness. If God gives you time, do not harden your heart; use it to turn back to him with humility.
exp.37:15:
It says that all the hangings that surrounded the courtyard of the tabernacle were made of twined linen, that is, strands of fine linen woven together so that the cloth would be strong and well made. These hangings formed a fence around the place of worship.

This is part of the description of how the tabernacle was built, the tent where God dwelt among Israel. The narrator tells us that Moses and the craftsmen followed the instructions given earlier. This passage summarizes the measurements and materials of the courtyard, and shows that the work was done just as God had asked. Some think the white linen may speak of purity, but the text here does not explain this.

For today: approaching God with respect and care. Just as Israel paid attention to the details of its worship, we can take care of our life of prayer and obedience, without treating God lightly.
exp.6:19:
Here we are told that Moses and Aaron obeyed God to the letter. Aaron lifted up the rod and struck the water of the Nile River, in the sight of the king and of his servants. Then all the water was turned to blood.

The phrase "his servants" here means the officials and attendants of Pharaoh.

God had commanded this sign to show his power before Egypt. Pharaoh refused to let the people of Israel go free from slavery. The Nile was vital to Egypt, and some believe it was revered, though scholars explain this in different ways. This was the first of the ten plagues.

For today: obeying God is worthwhile even when others will not believe or respond well. Moses and Aaron did what God asked, without expecting Pharaoh to change. Our task is to be faithful, and we leave the results in God's hands.
exp.5:9:
This verse is a transition phrase. It says that God spoke to Moses again. "Lord" is the name of God in this translation, and the word "unto" is an older way of saying "to." It does not yet bring the message; it only announces that God is going to speak once more.

Moses had just brought the people the promise of freedom, but the Israelites did not listen to him because of their discouragement and the hard work they were suffering. Then God speaks again to Moses and orders him to go before Pharaoh. Although the people do not respond, God does not change his plan or leave Moses alone.

For today: when people do not listen to you, or you feel discouraged, do not stay silent before God. Hear him again in his Word and in prayer. He can give you new strength and direction, even when everything seems closed.
exp.28:28:
The sacred clothing that Aaron wore was not his alone. It would pass to his sons after him, and they would wear it when they were anointed and consecrated as priests. "Anointed" means that oil was poured on them to set them apart for God. "Consecrated" means set apart for his service.

God speaks to Moses on the mountain, giving him instructions for the ordination of Aaron and his sons. The priesthood was meant to continue from one generation to the next. The clothing showed that the office was holy and that it did not belong to one person alone, but was handed down in an orderly way.

For today: what God entrusts to us, such as faith, teaching, or service, is not only for us. We can think about who comes after us and prepare them with patience, so that they will continue to serve God with reverence and faithfulness.
exp.15:0:
The verse tells us that the whole nation of Israel left Elim and came to the wilderness of Sin, which lies between Elim and Sinai. It was the fifteenth day of the second month since they had left Egypt. "Congregation" means the community gathered together, and "journeying" means that they set out on the road.

Here the narrator of the book, traditionally attributed to Moses, marks the time and the place: only a month after leaving Egypt, the people are already in a dry desert. Elim had been a place with water and palm trees. What follows shows that, as food ran short, they began to complain.

For today: when circumstances change and scarcity arrives, it is easy to forget what God has already done. Remembering his past faithfulness helps us trust him and pray instead of grumbling.
exp.20:35:
It says that if an ox had a known habit of goring with its horns, having done so "for some time past" (that is, for a long while), and its owner did not watch it or keep it penned in, the owner had to pay "ox for ox." That means he gave a live ox to replace the one that died. The dead animal then became the property of the responsible owner.

Known here means well established, something everyone already knew about the animal.

God speaks through Moses to the people of Israel, after giving them the Ten Commandments. These are civil laws meant for living justly. Here a distinction is made between an unforeseen accident, which was shared between both parties, and negligence, which was paid for in full.

For today: if we know that something under our care can harm others, such as a habit, a vehicle, or a tool, we should act in time. And if through carelessness we cause harm, we should make amends honestly.
exp.38:20:
This verse says they tied the breastplate, the high priest's chest piece, to the ephod, which was a kind of sacred vest. They did it with a blue cord, passing it through the rings of both pieces. In this way the breastplate stayed firmly above the girdle, the belt of the ephod, and did not come loose.

It is part of the description of how the craftsmen of Israel finished Aaron's garments. The narrator repeats that everything was done as the Lord had commanded Moses. The phrase points to careful obedience, even in the small details.

For today: God values faithfulness in what is small and hidden. A cord and some rings seem like little things, yet they held something important. We can serve God with steady devotion in simple tasks, knowing that he sees and is pleased with our obedience.
exp.15:1:
This verse tells us that the whole people of Israel complained loudly against Moses and Aaron while they were in the wilderness.

The people had only just left Egypt, about six weeks earlier, and they arrived in the wilderness of Sin. There, the food they had brought ran out. Hungry and afraid, they forgot what God had done for them and remembered Egypt as a place of plenty. Although they complained against their leaders, deep down they doubted God, who was guiding them. He answered by sending them bread from heaven.

When something is missing from our lives, it is easy to complain and forget what God has already done. Today we can turn complaint into prayer: telling God our need honestly and remembering how he has helped us before.
exp.35:17:
This verse tells that Bezalel and the craftsmen made fifty clasps of brass. With them they joined the loops of the two great curtains of the tabernacle, so that the whole tent would be one piece. The clasps are hooks or fasteners. The word for the material here is brass, according to the Hebrew, though in other passages about the curtains gold is mentioned; translations vary.

Here the narrator of the book describes how the people of Israel carried out, point by point, the instructions God gave Moses on the mountain. What had already been commanded in Exodus 26 is repeated here as finished work, done in obedience.

For today: God cares about the small details that hold everything together. Just as simple hooks made one tent, our everyday acts of forgiveness, service, and patience help keep the family and the church united.
exp.3:20:
God tells Moses that, when he arrives in Egypt, he should perform before Pharaoh all the mighty signs that God has placed in his hand. But God warns him that he will harden Pharaoh's heart, and for that reason the king will not let the people go.

The Hebrew word here is a plain verb meaning "to make hard," so the translation above follows the verse's own sense. Put simply, the words used for the signs are "wonders" in the verse above, meaning signs or miracles.

Jehovah speaks with Moses while he is still in Midian, as he is already on the way with his family. God is preparing him for what is coming: strong resistance. The text says that God hardens the heart, and later it also says that Pharaoh hardened his own. Scholars explain this in several ways, but all of them see that God remains in control.

For today: if God calls you to a task, do not expect everything to be easy. Obey faithfully, and trust that God is at work even when others respond negatively.
exp.36:20:
This verse describes the golden lampstand of the tabernacle. It had six branches, and under each pair of branches there was a rounded ornament. The Hebrew word most likely refers to a rounded decoration, like a knob or a bulb, not to the fruit. The "branches" are the arms of the lampstand, and "of the same" means that everything was one piece.

The account tells how Bezalel and his helpers built the tabernacle, following the instructions God gave to Moses. Here the design is repeated in detail, to show that the work was done just as God commanded it. Scholars do not fully agree on the meaning of the almond, knop and flower ornaments.

For today: God cares about what we do with faithfulness, even in small things. Serve God with care and joy in your daily tasks, even when no one notices them.
exp.7:11:
This verse tells us that Moses and Aaron withdrew from the presence of Pharaoh. Then Moses cried out to God, that is, he prayed earnestly, about the matter of the frogs that God had sent upon Egypt.

Pharaoh had asked that the plague be removed, and Moses had let him choose the time. He had made a specific promise before the king, so now he needed God to answer. Moses knew that the power was not his own, and that is why he prayed.

For today: when you face a problem that is bigger than you, do as Moses did and bring it to God in sincere prayer. Do not depend only on your own strength or your own words. God hears those who trust in Him.
exp.25:26:
The verse speaks of the wooden bars that held the boards of the tabernacle together. They were crossbars that kept the structure firm and aligned. Five bars were to be placed on each side, and five on the back side, toward the west. This older translation reads somewhat confusingly, but the idea is that the whole structure was well secured.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai and gives him detailed instructions for building a place where he would dwell among Israel. Nothing was left to chance: God wanted an orderly, firm dwelling, made as he had directed.

For today: our spiritual life also needs things that give firmness, such as constant prayer, the Word, and the community of faith. They are simple, unremarkable habits, but they help keep us united to God.
exp.28:44:
God promises to live in the middle of the people of Israel and to be their God. The word "dwell" means that he will stay with them, like someone who lives in a house with his family. It is not a passing visit, but a constant and close presence.

God is speaking, giving instructions to Moses on Mount Sinai. He has just explained how the tabernacle, the altar, and the priests will be set apart. All that order has a purpose: that a holy God might be near a people who had just been freed from Egypt. The next verse confirms it: he brought them out in order to dwell with them.

For today: God still desires closeness with us. Christians believe that, through Christ, his presence now remains with his people through the Spirit. Today you can set aside a moment to speak with him, remembering that he is not far away.
exp.28:32:
It says that Aaron and his sons were to eat the meat of the ram and the bread with which atonement had been made, that is, with which their sin was covered. The phrase "to fill their hands" is an old expression that means to fill them, that is, to officially install them in their office as priests. "Stranger" here means someone who was not from the priestly family. Only the priests could eat this, because it was holy, set apart for God.

God speaks to Moses and gives him instructions for the ceremony of consecrating the first priests of Israel. Eating together what was offered was part of receiving their service before God. Some see in this a sign of communion with God; the text itself stresses above all the holiness of the act.

For today: God draws us near to himself by his grace, not by our own merit. We can live thankful and treat with reverence what he has set apart, such as his Word, prayer, and fellowship with other believers.
exp.17:18:
Jethro, Moses' father-in-law, asks him to listen, and promises to give him counsel. He tells him that God will be with him. His advice is that Moses represent the people before God and bring to him the matters or cases that arise. The word "matters" here means issues or problems, and "bring" means present or carry.

The speaker is Jethro, priest of Midian. He had watched Moses spend the whole day judging the people's disputes, from morning until evening. He warned him that this work was too heavy and that he would wear himself out along with the people. Then he proposes sharing the burden with other trustworthy leaders.

For today: do not carry everything alone. Bring your worries to God in prayer and accept the wise counsel of others. Asking for help is not weakness, but humility and good care for the life God has given you.
exp.9:23:
Pharaoh calls Moses and gives him permission to go and worship the Lord. He sets one condition: the Israelites may take their children, but they must leave their sheep and cattle behind. "Serve" here means worship. "Called for" means that he sent for Moses.

Pharaoh speaks after three days of thick darkness over Egypt, while Israel had light. He is already frightened, and that is why he gives a little ground. But he holds back the livestock, perhaps to make sure they would come back or to have some kind of guarantee. The text does not fully explain this. Moses will refuse the offer, because they need the animals for the sacrifices.

For today: sometimes we are offered a half-hearted obedience, "serve God, but leave something behind." God deserves what we are and what we have. Ask yourself what part of your life you are tempted to leave out of your devotion to Him.
exp.27:31:
It says the robe of the ephod, the blue garment the high priest would wear, had to have an opening in the center at the top, through which the head would pass. That edge had to be woven with care, like the neck of a "coselete," which was an ancient piece of armor made of strong cloth or leather. The purpose was that the cloth would not tear when it was put on and taken off.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai and gives him detailed instructions about Aaron's garments. These clothes set the priest apart for his service and showed that drawing near to God was something serious and orderly.

For today: God cares even about the details that sustain our service. Take care of what keeps your life and your faith firm, such as constant prayer and the Word, so that they do not tear apart in the midst of trials.
exp.16:1:
Here the people argue sharply with Moses because they are thirsty and demand water from him.

Israel had just been freed from Egypt and had seen great miracles. Now they are at Rephidim, without water. The need is real, but the complaint turns against Moses and, at its root, against God, who had led them to that place. Moses speaks as a leader who knows the problem is one of trust.

For today: when need comes, we can bring our burden to God honestly, as Moses did when he cried out to Him, instead of pouring out distrust and anger on those around us.
exp.24:14:
God tells them that the poles for carrying the ark were to stay always inserted in the rings of the ark, never to be pulled out. "They shall be in" means "they shall remain," and "they shall not be taken from it" means they would never be removed. In this way the ark could be carried without anyone needing to touch it.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai while giving him the instructions for building the tabernacle. The ark would hold the testimony, that is, the tablets of the law, and it represented God's presence with his people. It was to be ready to move whenever Israel walked through the wilderness. Many understand that this also protected its holiness, since it prevented the ark from being handled carelessly.

For today: be always ready to follow God. We can live with an attitude of availability, attentive to his guidance, ready to go wherever he leads us, and treating what is his with reverence.
exp.24:22:
God gives Moses instructions to make a table of acacia wood. The old word for it is "Sittim," which I'll leave aside here; the verse you see says "shittim wood." It was two cubits long, one cubit wide, and a cubit and a half high. A cubit was roughly half a meter, so the table was close to one meter long, half a meter wide, and about 75 centimeters high.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai while explaining how to build the tabernacle, the place where He would dwell among Israel. Earlier He spoke about the ark, where He would meet with His people. Now He moves on to the furnishings of the holy place. Later it is said that the bread of the presence would be placed on this table.

For today: God cares about details and order in our worship. We can serve Him with care and dedication, even in small and everyday things, trusting that He wants to be close to us.
exp.38:30:
It also repeats that they did it just as the Lord commanded Moses.

The text is a narrative. It describes the clothing of Aaron, the high priest, and it comes near the end of the building of the tabernacle. The plate bore the words "Holy to the Lord," and it sat on the forehead, in plain view of everyone. The phrase "as the Lord had commanded" appears many times in this chapter.

For today: God also pays attention to the small details of our obedience. We can ask ourselves what simple thing God is asking of us today, and do it faithfully and wholeheartedly, as a way of saying that we belong to him.
exp.1:22:
This verse tells us that after a long time, the king of Egypt died. But the Israelites were still enslaved. They "sighed," that is, they groaned in pain, and they "cried out," meaning they called for help at the top of their voices. That cry "came up to God," like a complaint that rises all the way to heaven.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Moses is living far away, in Midian, with his wife and his son, and he feels like a foreigner. Meanwhile, in Egypt, the people are suffering. Many think that the change of king would give them hope, but the verse does not say that the oppression ended. The cry shows that they needed help that Egypt would not give them.

For today: when the pain does not go away, you do not have to pretend to be strong. You can bring God your sighs and your cry, even when you do not know how to pray. He hears, and the verse that follows confirms it.
exp.37:10:
The explanation says that the north side of the tabernacle courtyard had hangings one hundred cubits long, that is, about 45 meters (a cubit was about 45 centimeters). There were twenty pillars, each set on a base of bronze. The pillar tops are the upper parts of the pillars, and the hooks and bands that joined the pillars were rods or rings that linked them; all of these were of silver.

The book of Exodus tells how the tabernacle was built, following the instructions God gave to Moses. Here the narrator describes the courtyard, the enclosure surrounding the tent, with the same design as the south side. It marked off a space set apart for worshiping God.

For today: God cares about the details of what is offered to him. We can serve him with order, care, and joy, even in small and little-seen tasks.
exp.32:14:
What it says: Moses speaks to God with great frankness. "Your presence" is a way of speaking of God's personal presence. Moses says that if God himself does not go with them, he would rather not leave that place. The phrase "this people" simply means "these people."

Context: Moses speaks after Israel made the golden calf. God had said he would send an angel, but that he himself would not go up in the midst of the people. Moses is not content with the promise of a land without God's company. He asks that God's presence accompany them, and God answers that it will.

For today: before taking a path, a project, or a major change, we can first ask for the presence of God, not only that things turn out well. His company is worth more than any goal. Today, before deciding something, pray: "Lord, if you do not go with me, I do not want to go."
exp.18:15:
It says that at dawn on the third day, thunder began to be heard and lightning was seen. A thick cloud covered the mountain, and a very loud sound of a trumpet was heard, which is a horn or ram's horn. All the people who were in the camp, that is, in the encampment, trembled with fear.

The people of Israel had been out of Egypt for about three months and were standing before Mount Sinai. God had asked them to prepare themselves: to wash their clothes and set themselves apart for Him. Here the narrator describes the moment when God reveals Himself to make His covenant with them. The details show His holiness and His greatness.

For today: God deserves to be approached with reverence. Before you pray or read the Bible, take a moment to pause, set aside the rush, and remember who He is.
exp.29:27:
It says the holy anointing oil would also be used on the altar of burnt offering, which was where the sacrifices were burned. It includes all its vessels, the laver (the large bronze basin where the priests washed themselves) and its foot, which is the base on which it rested. Thus every object of the tabernacle was set apart for God.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai and gives him instructions for preparing the anointing oil. To anoint something meant to set it apart for sacred use. With this oil the furnishings were consecrated, and then the priests. In this way God teaches that his presence deserves reverence and order.

For today: God cares as much about the great things as about the small details. We can ask ourselves what part of our life, even the everyday, we can dedicate to him with a grateful and reverent heart.
exp.1:21:
This verse tells that Moses and Zipporah (today the name is written Zipporah, or Séfora) had a son. Moses named him Gershom, and explained the name by saying: "I have been a stranger in a strange land." The name sounds like a Hebrew expression meaning something close to that.

Moses had fled from Egypt and was now living in Midian, with the family of Jethro. The one speaking is Moses, and with his son's name he shows that, although he already had a home and a family, he still felt like a foreigner, far from his people. The verses that follow show that God had not forgotten Israel.

For today: if you feel out of place or in a season that is not what you expected, remember that God sees you. Your waiting may be part of what He is preparing.
exp.20:33:
It says that if someone leaves a pit open and another person's animal falls in and dies, the owner of the pit must pay the value of the animal to its owner. "Making it good" means making up for the loss or repairing the harm. And the dead animal becomes the property of the one who paid, since he has already bought it with his money.

God speaks to Moses at Sinai, and these are laws that He gives to Israel shortly after the Ten Commandments. They deal with everyday situations, such as animals and accidents. They show that God cares about justice and about protecting the property of our neighbor. Responsibility falls on the one who could have prevented the harm and did not.

For today: if something I own or handle could hurt others, I must take care of it in advance. If I cause harm through carelessness, I must make right honestly and without excuses what my neighbor has lost.
exp.31:1:
Aaron asks the Israelites to bring him the golden earrings, that is, the rings or earrings that their wives, sons, and daughters were wearing. With that gold he is going to make something, and the following text shows that it will be a calf. The sentence explaining the old wording is removed, as the reader's verse uses "break off" directly.

Moses had been on Mount Sinai with God for a long time, and the people grew impatient. They asked Aaron for a visible god to lead them. Instead of correcting them, Aaron asked for the gold. We do not know everything he was thinking, but the account shows that he gave in to the pressure of the people.

For today: when waiting becomes long, it is easy to look for shortcuts and visible things that give us a sense of security. Let us learn to wait on God, and not to give in to the pressure of others when that pulls us away from Him.
exp.31:13:
The explanation says that God "repented" of the punishment he had announced against Israel. The word does not mean that God admitted a mistake, but that he changed course and did not carry out the judgment he had announced. The word translated here as "evil" means disaster or destruction, not wickedness.

Israel had just made the golden calf and worshiped it. God said he would destroy them, but Moses interceded. He reminded God of his reputation among the Egyptians and of his promises to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Some understand that God truly responded to the prayer; others understand that he shows his compassion in a way that is like human feeling. In both cases, the prayer matters.

Today we can pray with confidence for others, even when they fail. God listens, and his mercy is greater than we can imagine.
exp.26:0:
God commands Moses to build an altar of shittim wood, which is the acacia, a tree of the desert. It was to be five cubits long and five cubits wide, meaning square, and three cubits high. A cubit was the distance from the elbow to the tip of the fingers, about half a meter, although its exact measure is debated. So the altar was roughly two and a half meters on each side.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai, giving him instructions for the tabernacle, the tent where Israel would worship. This altar, where the sacrifices were presented, stood in the courtyard. The verses that follow describe it as covered with metal, with horns and utensils.

For today: God cared about every detail of how to draw near to Him, which reminds us that worship is not something casual. Today we can approach Him with reverence and gratitude, and Christians see in Christ the sacrifice that opens the way for us.
exp.2:9:
In this verse God says to Moses: "Come now, and I will send you to Pharaoh, to bring my people, the children of Israel, out of Egypt."

God speaks to Moses from the burning bush, on the mountain, while Moses was tending sheep in the wilderness. God has just said that he heard the cry of his people in slavery and saw their suffering. Now he calls Moses to take part in their deliverance. Moses answers with doubts, but God promises him: "I will be with you."

For today: God often hears the pain of people and, many times, invites others to help. If you feel that God is giving you a task, even when you feel small, remember that his presence matters more than your ability.
exp.11:25:
This verse imagines a future moment: the children of the Israelites will ask what the Passover ceremony means. The source term for a ceremony or practice that is repeated is not something the reader sees in the King James wording, so the comment about it is removed. The explanation of the old phrasing is also removed, since the verse your reader sees uses "say unto you" instead.

God speaks through Moses, before the departure from Egypt. He wants the Passover to be not merely a custom, but a teaching that is passed from parents to children. The children's question opens the door to telling how God delivered them. Afterward, the people bow down and worship, and they obey what they were commanded.

Today, we can make use of our children's questions about our faith. Instead of giving quick answers, let us simply tell what God has done for us, so that faith is passed on with affection and not merely out of habit.
exp.6:12:
What it says: Pharaoh grew stubborn. Even though he saw that Aaron's staff swallowed the staffs of his magicians, he would not listen to Moses and Aaron. "He hardened" means that his heart became firm and closed, unwilling to give in. "As the Lord had said" means that God had already warned that this would happen.

Context: The narrator tells what happened when Moses and Aaron came before Pharaoh to ask that he let the people of Israel go. God gave them a sign, but the Egyptian magicians imitated something similar. Throughout the account, Pharaoh's hardness is spoken of; interpreters explain in different ways how his own obstinacy and God's action come together.

For today: When God shows us something clearly, we can respond with humility or with pride. Let us ask him for a soft heart, ready to listen and obey, before stubbornness closes our ears.
exp.22:6:
This verse urges us to stay away from every lie, especially when it is used to harm others. God commands that the innocent and righteous not be put to death, that is, those who have done nothing wrong. And he warns that he will not declare the wicked to be innocent. Here, "justify" means to leave someone without blame.

God speaks to Israel through Moses, after the Ten Commandments. These laws describe how to live justly as a people, especially in judgment. Before this, he asks them to help even an enemy and not to pervert the rights of the poor. Afterward, he forbids bribery and the mistreatment of the foreigner.

Today we can be careful with our words: we should not repeat gossip or accusations without proof. If we doubt something said about another person, it is better to stay silent or seek the truth, because a lie can ruin a life.
exp.12:7:
It says that during the Feast of Unleavened Bread, each father was to explain to his son the meaning of what they were doing. The sentences about the source-language words are removed, since the reader's verse does not contain them. The reason was to remember what God did when He brought the people out of Egypt. Leaven is the fermented dough that makes bread rise.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel, newly freed from slavery, and passes on God's instructions. He wants this feast to be not merely a ritual but a living teaching. The verses that follow compare it to a sign on the hand and a reminder before the eyes, so that the law of God may be in their mouth. Some understand this figuratively and others literally.

Today we can speak naturally with our children, or with others younger than us, about what God has done in our lives. A simple testimony, shared within the family, helps faith pass from one generation to the next.
exp.38:31:
This verse says that all the work on the tabernacle was finished, the tabernacle being called the "tent of the congregation" (the tent where God met with his people, where the tablets of the law were kept). The Israelites did everything just as God had commanded Moses.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, traditionally understood to be Moses. After describing each piece, the text repeats that it was done "as the Lord had commanded." Then the people present the finished work to Moses so he can review it.

For today: obedience to God is lived out in the details. We can ask ourselves what specific thing God is asking of us at home, at work, or in church, and carry it out carefully until it is finished, without leaving it half done.
exp.8:21:
God commands Moses to stretch out his hand toward heaven. Then hail would fall on all of Egypt: on people, on the animals, and on every plant of the field.

God speaks, and gives the command to Moses. This is the seventh plague. Pharaoh had refused again and again to let Israel go. God had warned of the hail beforehand, and some Egyptians who believed that word brought their servants and livestock to safety. Others ignored it.

For today: when God warns us through his Word, it is wise to take it seriously and obey in time. Listening with humility protects us, and ignoring the warning can cost us dearly.
exp.24:29:
God commands Moses to set on the table the "bread of the presence," that is, bread that was presented or displayed before God. It was to be there "continually," that is, always, without ever being missing. The word "presence" here does not mean a proposal or suggestion, but something placed before Him.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai while giving him instructions for building the tabernacle, the tent where God would dwell among Israel. The table, with its plates and gold bowls, was part of that place of worship. Later, Leviticus 24 explains that there were twelve loaves, although this verse does not give that detail.

God desires a constant relationship with His people, not just occasional visits. We can set aside a moment each day to be with Him, to pray and to read His Word, knowing that God always receives us and invites us into His presence.
exp.33:15:
This verse warns that if the Israelites took wives from the peoples of Canaan for their sons, those women would lead them to worship other gods. Here the word "whoring" is used in a spiritual sense: giving to other gods the loyalty that belongs to God alone. The phrase "go after" means "following" or "going behind."

God speaks to Moses after the sin of the golden calf, when he renews his covenant with Israel. He is "jealous" because he wants a faithful people. The warning aims to protect the people from alliances that would pull them away from him. The text focuses on the danger of idolatry, not on the origin of the people.

For today: think about which relationships, partners, or close influences might cool your faith. Value those who bring you closer to God, and if you have ties that are different, keep your loyalty to him firm, with love and without contempt.
exp.36:18:
This verse describes the ornaments on each branch of the golden lampstand of the tabernacle. Each branch had three cups shaped like almond blossoms, and each cup had a knop and a flower. The word "knop" probably refers to a round ornament, like a bud or small knob; its exact shape is not known for certain. The lampstand was a stand that held the lamps. The six branches all had the same design.

Here the narrator tells how Bezaleel made the lampstand, following the instructions God gave Moses for the tabernacle. It was the lamp that lit the holy place. God asked that it be made of pure gold, beaten into shape by hammering, with everything carefully done.

For today: God cares about details and about the beauty of what is offered to Him. We can serve Him with care in small things, whether at work, at home, or in the church, knowing that nothing done for Him is insignificant.
exp.9:1:
God tells Moses that He allowed the signs in Egypt so that the people would tell them to their children and grandchildren. The word "signs" refers to the miracles and punishments. "Tell" means to count or relate. The final purpose is that they would know that the Lord is the Lord.

God speaks to Moses before the eighth plague, the plague of locusts. He says that He hardened Pharaoh's heart, that is, He made it harder and more stubborn. The Bible also says that Pharaoh himself hardened his heart, and interpreters explain this in different ways. God wants Israel to remember His work of deliverance and pass it on.

For today: tell your children, nephews, nieces, or friends how God has helped you. You can write down or share with your family those memories of His faithfulness, so that faith may pass from one generation to the next.
exp.29:9:
This verse speaks of the altar of incense. Once a year, Aaron was to put the blood of the sin offering on its horns (the four corners that stuck out) to cleanse it from sin. Making atonement means covering over or cleansing sin, and restoring the relationship with God. Throughout your generations means across every generation. And it is most holy to the Lord means that this altar was set apart for God alone.

God speaks to Moses at Sinai while giving him instructions for the tabernacle. He had already explained how incense would be burned each day. Now he adds that this place also needed a yearly cleansing, because the people and their priests were sinners and God is holy. Christian scholars often see a sign here pointing to Christ, though the text itself does not say so.

For today: come near to God with humility and gratitude. We do not approach Him on the basis of our merits, but through a cleansing that He Himself provides.
