exp.28:42:
It says that God will meet with the children of Israel in a special place, the tabernacle, and will make himself known to them. "I will testify of myself" means that God himself will bear witness to who he is, that is, he will show himself. The place will be "sanctified," that is, set apart as holy, by the presence of his glory, not by human effort.

God speaks to Moses at Sinai. He has just explained the daily burnt offering, one lamb in the morning and another in the evening, which was offered at the door of the tabernacle. God wants to dwell among his people, and the instructions prepare for that meeting. The verses that follow say that he will also set apart the priests and dwell among them.

For today: God desires to be close to us. We can set aside a fixed moment each day to pray and to listen to him, trusting that his presence, and not our merits, makes that encounter holy.
exp.27:0:
God tells Moses to bring near, that is, to call to his side, his brother Aaron and Aaron's sons: Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar and Ithamar. He sets them apart from among the people so that they will be his priests, the ones who serve him on his behalf.

God speaks from Mount Sinai while giving instructions for the tabernacle, his dwelling place among the people. Before describing the clothing and the service, he makes clear who will be the priests. The text shows that it is God who chooses, not they who choose themselves. Later, Nadab and Abihu died for offering a fire that God had not commanded (Leviticus 10).

For today: serving God is a calling, not a privilege one takes for oneself. We can ask ourselves with humility, "Why has God brought me near?" And we can serve with reverence, doing things as he teaches and not in our own way.
exp.26:5:
God tells Moses to make poles for the altar of burnt offering. They are to be of acacia wood, called shittim wood, a strong wood from the desert. These poles are to be overlaid with bronze, which in this passage is bronze according to the Hebrew text, although the Reina-Valera 1909 says "metal."

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai while giving him instructions for building the tabernacle. The altar had to be portable, because the people were on the move through the desert. The poles passed through rings and made it possible to carry the altar without touching it directly.

For today: God cares about the details of how he is served, and also about the journey. His presence and his work do not stay fixed in one place, but accompany his people. We can ask ourselves whether we are willing to follow God when he asks us to move, and to carefully do what he entrusts to us.
exp.34:1:
The passage says that God gave six days for work, but the seventh is holy, a Sabbath of rest set apart for the Lord. "Shall be holy to you" means it is set apart for God. The reference to "unto the Lord" is "for the Lord." The penalty was severe: whoever worked on that day "shall be put to death."

Moses speaks to all of Israel gathered together, after the sin of the golden calf and the renewal of the covenant. Before asking for the offerings to build the tabernacle, he reminds them of the Sabbath. This makes it clear that even sacred work is not placed above the rest that God commanded. The harsh penalty was part of the law given to Israel as a nation.

For today: set aside a regular time to rest and be with God, without guilt and without hurry. Trusting that God provides while you rest is a real way of worshiping him.
exp.35:10:
This verse tells how Bezaleel and the craftsmen made loops, which are small eyelets or fastening loops of cloth, in blue-violet color. They placed them on the edge of the first curtain, where it would join with the other. They did the same on the edge of the second curtain.

It is part of the account of building the tabernacle, the tent where God dwelt among Israel. The narrator describes how the people carried out exactly what God had commanded Moses. These loops, together with the gold clasps, served to join the curtains and form one single tabernacle.

For today: God notices the small details that hold the large things together. Although no one sees them, the loops kept the tabernacle united. In the same way, your faithfulness in simple, hidden tasks can help keep your family or your church united.
exp.29:31:
The explanation says that the holy anointing oil was not to be poured on the body of an ordinary person. Nor was anyone allowed to make another oil like it, using the same recipe. "Flesh of man" means an ordinary person, not the priests set apart for God. "Holy" means set apart for God. That is why the people were to treat it with respect, as something sacred.

God speaks to Moses while giving him instructions for the tabernacle. This oil would be used to set apart Aaron, his sons, and the objects of worship. By forbidding anyone to copy it or use it for other purposes, God protected the seriousness of the sacred service and kept what was consecrated from becoming ordinary.

For today: we can learn to treat with reverence what belongs to God, such as prayer, his Word, and worship. We should not handle what is holy carelessly or for our own benefit. Let us guard our hearts and our words when we speak of God.
exp.14:22:
It says that the people of Israel came to a place called Marah and could not drink its water because it was bitter. That is why the place received that name. "Marah" means "bitterness" in Hebrew.

The one telling the story is Moses, the traditional author of the book. The Israelites had just been freed from Egypt and had sung songs of praise by the sea. Then they walked for three days through the desert without water. At last they found water, but it could not be drunk. After this the people grumbled, and God answered by showing how to make the water sweet.

For today: after a great victory, surprising trials can come. When we arrive at a "Marah" in life, we do not have to complain as our first reaction. We can cry out to God, as Moses did, and trust that He knows how to care for us even in what is bitter.
exp.8:26:
Pharaoh summons Moses and Aaron and says: "I have sinned this time." He acknowledges that the Lord is righteous and that he and his people are wicked, meaning evil, living without regard for God. The word "sent" here simply means that he gave orders for them to be sought out.

Pharaoh speaks out of fear because of the hail, the seventh plague. He admits his wrong, but right away he asks Moses to pray so that the plague will stop. Later he hardens his heart again (v. 34-35). For this reason many think his repentance was more fear than a true change, although the text does not let us see his heart completely.

For today: it is not enough to say "I was wrong" when the consequences arrive. Sincere repentance changes a life. Ask God to give you a humble heart, one that recognizes its failings and obeys even when the difficulty passes.
exp.39:4:
It says that Moses was to place the golden altar, where the incense was burned, directly in front of the ark of the testimony, which held the tablets of the law. He was also to put the curtain at the entrance of the tabernacle, the sacred tent.

God speaks to Moses near the end of Exodus, when the tabernacle was already finished. He gives him the exact order for setting it up and consecrating it. Each object had its place, and everything prepared the space where God would dwell among his people.

For today: in the Bible, incense is associated with prayer (Psalm 141:2). Just as the altar stood before the ark, our prayer places us in God's presence. You might set aside a fixed moment each day to pray calmly, without hurry.
exp.28:43:
God says that He Himself will make holy, that is, set apart for His use, the tabernacle, which was the tent where He was worshiped, and also the altar. He will also set apart Aaron and his sons so that they serve as His priests. The words "of the congregation" remind us that the tables of the law were kept there, a sign of the covenant.

God speaks to Moses at Sinai while giving him instructions for Israel's worship. The verses before and after explain the purpose: God wants to meet with His people, show His glory, and dwell among them, because He brought them out of Egypt.

For today: holiness begins with God, not with our effort. He sets us apart to be close to Him and to serve Him. We can draw near with humility and gratitude, and dedicate to Him in concrete ways our day, our work, and our family.
exp.15:15:
Here Moses explains how to gather the manna. The word "gather" in this verse is the one used throughout the passage. Each person was to collect what they could eat, and the measure was figured at one omer per head, that is, per person. An omer was a small measure of volume, about two liters, although scholars do not agree on the exact amount. Each head of a household took enough for everyone who lived in his tent.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel in the wilderness, shortly after leaving Egypt. They were hungry and complaining. God gave them a food they did not recognize, and Moses tells them how to gather it, as instruction from the Lord.

For today: God knows what we truly need. We can learn to trust his daily provision, not to hoard out of fear, and to share so that no one is left without what is necessary.
exp.9:28:
Moses accepts Pharaoh's words: "Thou hast spoken well." By this he confirms that he will no longer come before him. "Face" means presence; that is, they will no longer see each other face to face.

Moses had gone many times to ask that the people of Israel be allowed to leave Egypt. After the plague of darkness, Pharaoh, with a hardened heart, drove him away and threatened him with death. Moses answers calmly and firmly. Here the time of negotiations ends, and the last plague comes (ch. 11).

For today: when we have spoken with truth and love, and the door still stays shut, we can withdraw without resentment. We do not have to force hearts. God continues to work, and we rest in Him.
exp.11:49:
This verse says that all the people of Israel obeyed the instructions God had given them through Moses and Aaron about the Passover. Nobody did things their own way; they did exactly what they had been commanded.

The narrator of the book tells how Israel acted on the night before leaving Egypt. God had given clear rules for the Passover, including for the foreigner who wished to join them, under the same law for everyone. When the account ends, the text says that on that very same day God brought them out of Egypt as a people in good order, company by company.

For today: simple obedience to what God has already told us opens the way to seeing his work. Today you can choose one specific thing you know God is asking of you, such as forgiving someone or being honest, and do it without delay.
exp.27:19:
This verse describes the fourth row of precious stones on the high priest's breastpiece: a beryl, an onyx, and a jasper. Each was to be set in gold, meaning fixed in place and surrounded by a gold frame made to fit it. The exact identities of these stones are uncertain, and scholars do not always agree on which minerals they were.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai and gives instructions for Aaron's garments. This breastpiece, which carried twelve stones, one for each tribe of Israel, held the people before God. In this way, the priest presented them before God each time he ministered.

For today: God does not see his people as a faceless mass. Each stone had its own name, carefully engraved. You can rest knowing that God knows you by your name and that Christ, our great High Priest, carries you close to his heart. You can also value those around you.
exp.33:22:
It says that three times a year all the men of Israel were to present themselves before God. The phrase "will be seen" means they would appear before him at his sanctuary. The word "Lord" here refers to God as the Master and owner of all things. The three occasions were the feast of unleavened bread, the feast of weeks, and the feast of harvest.

God speaks through Moses when he renews his covenant with Israel after the sin of the golden calf. Before this command, God reminds them of the weekly rest and the feasts. Then he promises to protect their land while they go up to worship. It was a way of reminding them that God was their first priority and their protector.

For today: set aside regular times to stop and seek God with your family or your church. Trust that he takes care of what you leave behind while you give him first place.
exp.1:23:
This verse says that God heard the cry and pain of the people of Israel, who were suffering as slaves in Egypt. "Groaning" is a deep lament. The verse's word "remembered" does not mean that God had forgotten them, but that he decided to act in line with what he had promised. The "covenant" is the solemn promise God made to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

Here the narrator of the book, traditionally attributed to Moses, is speaking. After the death of the king of Egypt, the oppression continued, and the people cried out. The text shows that God responds because he is faithful to his word, and so it prepares the way for Moses' calling and for the deliverance.

For today: when you feel that your pain goes unnoticed, remember that God hears and is faithful to his promises. You can pray honestly, even with just a sigh, and wait with confidence, even when his answer takes time.
exp.5:1:
God speaks to Moses again and says to him, "I am the Lord." It is a solemn declaration of who He is. The word "again" shows that He keeps speaking, and the verse's "said unto him" is simply "told him." The name Lord is God's personal name, which many connect with the name He gives in Exodus 3:14.

Moses was discouraged. He had gone before Pharaoh, but the people suffered more labor and complained. God answers by reminding him who sends him and that He will keep His promise. Here He does not begin to be the Lord; rather, He makes Himself known in a fuller way. Scholars explain in several ways what is meant by the verse's wording about being made known.

For today: when things go the wrong way and you feel tired, remember who God is. Your trust rests on His faithful character, not on how well circumstances are going.
exp.35:7:
This verse tells that the most skilled craftsmen, described as wise-hearted, built the tabernacle, the sacred tent where God dwelt among his people. They used ten curtains of finely twisted linen, with threads of blue, purple, and scarlet. The curtains bore embroidered figures of cherubim, spiritual beings who serve God.

Here the narrator of the book, traditionally attributed to Moses, speaks. Just before, the people had given so much material that Moses asked them to stop bringing offerings. Now the account of the construction begins, carried out according to the instructions God had given.

For today: God uses the abilities he has given us, whether great or simple, for his work. Offer what you know how to do with generosity and excellence, without comparing yourself to anyone.
exp.1:12:
Moisés sale otra vez al día siguiente y ve a dos hebreos peleando entre sí. Le habla al que estaba golpeando al otro y le pregunta por qué le pega a su compañero, a alguien de su mismo pueblo. "Strove together" significa que discutían o peleaban, y "wrong" aquí quiere decir el daño o la agresión.

Habla Moisés, que ya era adulto y se identificaba con su pueblo. El día anterior había matado a un egipcio que maltrataba a un hebreo. Ahora intenta frenar un conflicto entre hermanos, pero su intervención sale mal: el hombre rechaza su autoridad y eso lo lleva a huir.

Para hoy: corregir a otros pide humildad y sabiduría. Antes de intervenir en un conflicto, conviene orar, escuchar y actuar con paciencia, no con impulso, buscando la paz y no imponerse.
exp.32:12:
Moses humbly asks God: "If you truly look on me with favor, teach me your way so that I may know you well." The phrase "I pray thee" is rewritten here as "I ask you," and "this nation" is simply "this nation" as in the verse. Moses also reminds God that this people belongs to Him.

Moses speaks here after the sin of the golden calf. God had told him to lead the people, but had not said who would go with him. Moses does not want to move forward alone; he desires to know God's ways and His companionship. God answers that His presence will go with him and will give him rest.

Today we can pray as Moses did: asking God not only for help, but for a deeper knowledge of Him. Before making decisions or taking on responsibilities, we can seek His guidance and His presence, and remember that the people we care for belong to Him.
exp.35:22:
He says that Bezalel and the craftsmen made twenty boards for the south side of the tabernacle. The words "south" and "south" mean the same thing: the south. Each board was about five meters tall (ten cubits) and about seventy centimeters wide (a cubit and a half), although the exact length of the cubit is calculated only approximately.

The narrator tells how the tabernacle was built, the tent where God would dwell among Israel in the wilderness. These instructions had been given by God to Moses, and now it is told that the people carried them out with care, without changing the details.

God cares about small things done in obedience. Perhaps your work seems like just one board hidden in a large structure, but it has value. Do faithfully what is yours to do today, and trust that God brings everything together for his purpose.
exp.19:22:
God says that they should not make gods of silver or of gold. The phrase "with me" can be understood as "alongside me" or "to be compared with me." Some believe it refers to idols placed next to God, and others to any image that represents him. In both cases, the idea is clear: no one should make a god.

God speaks to Moses after giving the Ten Commandments. The people were afraid and stayed at a distance. God reminds them that he spoke to them from heaven. They did not need a visible image, because they had already heard his voice.

Today we can ask ourselves what thing has taken God's place in our hearts: money, success, or what others will say. Let us trust God as he has revealed himself, listen to his Word, and give him first place.
exp.17:4:
Jethro, Moses' father-in-law, traveled out into the wilderness to meet him. He brought Moses' wife and the two sons of the couple. Moses had his camp near the mount of God, which is usually associated with Sinai or Horeb, although its exact location is not known with certainty.

The narrator tells us that Israel had already left Egypt. The previous verses recall the names of the sons: Gershom and Eliezer. Those names speak of Moses' difficult years and of how God helped him and delivered him from Pharaoh. Jethro comes to gather the family and to hear what God had done.

For today: take advantage of family reunions to give thanks to God together. Tell simply how He has helped you, and also listen to how He has been at work in the lives of others.
exp.31:11:
Moses asks God not to destroy Israel. He asks what the Egyptians will say: that God brought them out with bad intent, to kill them in the mountains and wipe them off the face of the earth. He begs God to turn from his burning anger and change his mind about the punishment.

Moses speaks after the people made the golden calf and worshiped it. God had said he wanted to consume them and make a great nation from Moses. Moses intercedes for the people, appealing to the honor of God's name and to his promises to Abraham, Isaac, and Israel. When the text says God "relented," Christians understand this in different ways: as human language describing God's compassion, or as his real response to prayer. Both views recognize his mercy.

Today we can pray boldly for others, even for those who have failed, trusting in the character and promises of God.
exp.28:17:
He says that the priest was to burn the whole ram on the altar. This is called a burnt offering, an offering that was consumed completely by the fire. "Sweet savour" is a pleasant aroma, a way of saying that God received it with favor.

God speaks to Moses and gives him instructions for consecrating Aaron and his sons as priests. This ram was part of that ceremony. Because all of it was burned, it expressed total devotion to God. Christians often see here a shadow of Christ's self-giving, although the text itself does not say so.

For today: God values a heart that gives itself completely, not halfway. Today you can ask yourself what area of your life you still keep for yourself, and place it in his hands with sincerity.
exp.28:37:
This verse commands that two lambs of one year old be offered on the altar every day. Later it is made clear that one was offered in the morning and the other at the close of the day.

God speaks to Moses and gives him instructions on how to consecrate Aaron and his sons as priests and how to prepare the altar. After the seven days of consecration, this daily offering began. It was a sign that the people were drawing near to God in a constant way. Christians often see in this an image of Christ, although the text itself does not say so.

Today we do not offer lambs, but we can learn from the steadiness. Setting aside a moment of prayer at the beginning of the day and another at its end is a simple way to keep our relationship with God.
exp.9:5:
It says the plague of locusts will fill the houses of Pharaoh, of his servants, and of all the Egyptians. It will be so great that neither Pharaoh's fathers nor his grandfathers ever saw anything like it. "They shall fill" is the sense of the phrase here. Then Moses turned and went out from Pharaoh's presence.

Moses speaks on God's behalf. Pharaoh refused to let the people of Israel leave, even after several plagues, including the hail. This is the warning before the eighth plague. Moses withdraws without waiting for an answer, and then Pharaoh's servants ask him to give in.

For today: God gives us opportunities to correct our course before the consequences grow. If we sense that God is speaking to us about something, it is better to respond with humility and obedience, rather than hardening our hearts and waiting for everything to get worse.
exp.38:23:
It says that on the lower edge of the priest's robe they made pomegranates from colored threads: blue, purple, scarlet, and fine twined linen. The reference to a blue robe worn beneath the ephod, the sacred vest of the high priest, is part of the same description.

The passage is part of the account of how Israel built the tabernacle and Aaron's garments. The narrator repeats that everything was done just as the LORD commanded Moses. The details follow the instructions given earlier in Exodus 28. Commentators do not agree on the exact meaning of the pomegranates; some think they speak of fruit and blessing, but the Bible does not explain this clearly.

For today: God cares about obedience and about details done with care. Faithfully doing even the small things of our work and service can be a way of worshiping him.
exp.4:22:
Moses speaks to God with great frankness. He says that since he went to Pharaoh to speak in the Lord's name, Pharaoh has made things worse for the people, and that God still has not rescued them. "Afflicted" means made to suffer or mistreated. "Delivered" means rescued or set free.

Moses and Aaron had asked Pharaoh to let Israel go. He responded by increasing the workload of the slaves. The Israelite foremen blamed Moses, and he, confused and hurt, brings his complaint to God. This shows that faith does not always understand God's timing.

For today: when things get worse after you obey God, do not keep silent or turn away. You can honestly tell God your pain and your doubts, as Moses did. God listens, and in the chapters that follow he continues to work.
exp.33:6:
This verse describes what God is like. He keeps his mercy for thousands of generations and forgives three things: wrongdoing (doing what is crooked), rebellion (deliberately defying God), and sin (missing the mark). But he does not leave unpunished the guilty person who does not repent. It also says that the consequences of a parent's wrongdoing reach their children, grandchildren, and great-grandchildren.

God himself speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai, passing before him and proclaiming his name. This happens after the people made the golden calf. Moses pleads for them, and God shows him that he is just and at the same time very compassionate.

For today: trust that God truly forgives when we come to him with sincerity. And recognize that our choices affect our family, so seek today to leave a good example for those who come after you.
exp.34:31:
This verse continues describing the talents God gave to Bezalel. "Devise curious works" means to design or come up with creative works using skill and imagination. Bezalel also knew how to work in gold, in silver, and in brass, materials important for building the tabernacle.

Moses speaks to the Israelites as they gather what is needed to build the tabernacle, the place of worship. He explains that God himself chose Bezalel, of the tribe of Judah, and filled him with his Spirit to do this work with excellence. In this way, craftsmanship appears as a gift from God.

For today: your abilities, whether manual, creative, or technical, can be a gift from God. Offer them with dedication in your work, your church, or your family, to serve others and honor God.
exp.14:11:
It says that God stretched out his "right hand," that is, his right arm, a symbol of power and action. As a result, the earth swallowed them. It refers to the Egyptians who were pursuing Israel. Although they died in the sea, the text speaks of the earth swallowing them, and it is not certain why it uses that image; some understand it as a poetic way of speaking of death or of the grave.

Moses speaks to the Israelites, in a song of praise just after crossing the Red Sea. They have just been delivered from Pharaoh's army. The song celebrates that no one compares with the LORD and that he led his people with mercy.

For today: when you face something that seems impossible, remember that God has already shown his power to save. Take a moment to thank him for how he has helped you before, and trust that he continues to care for you.
exp.32:6:
This verse tells how Moses took a tent and pitched it outside the camp, far away from the people. He called it "the tabernacle of the congregation," which here was a tent for meeting with God, not the great sanctuary that was built later. Anyone who sought the Lord went out to that tent.

It is the narrator who speaks. Israel had just made the golden calf, and God said he would not go up in the midst of them because they were a stiff-necked people, that is, stubborn. By pitching the tent outside, the distance that sin had created is shown. Even so, God still allowed people to seek him.

Today, when sin pulls us away from God, he still opens a way back. Find a quiet time and place to pray sincerely, and draw near to him with humility.
exp.21:11:
It says that if an animal that someone was looking after was stolen, the one caring for it must pay the owner for the loss. The word translated here as "restitution" means making good the damage or paying back what was lost. The word for "stolen" in the verse means taken by theft.

God gives these laws to Israel through Moses, after the Ten Commandments, to guide the people's daily life. Here the text distinguishes cases: if the animal died or disappeared without any fault on the caretaker's part, an oath before God was enough. But if it was stolen, the caretaker was expected to pay, since it was understood that he should have watched it more carefully. Some scholars see it this way; the text does not explain more.

For today: when someone entrusts us with something of theirs, money, work, or a responsibility, we should care for it diligently. And if we fail, the honest thing is to accept the loss and repair the damage, without excuses.
exp.20:12:
This verse speaks of someone who kills another person without having planned it. "He did not lay a trap" means that he set no ambush and had no hidden intention to kill. The phrase "God delivered him into his hand" suggests that it happened unexpectedly, like an accident. God says that he will appoint a place to which that person can flee for protection.

God speaks to Moses, within the laws he gave Israel after freeing them from Egypt. The previous verse says that whoever strikes another person and kills him must be put to death. This verse makes a distinction: a planned murder is not the same as a death without intent. Later, the Law speaks of cities of refuge for these cases.

For today: before judging someone, let us try to understand the circumstances and the intention. True justice seeks the truth, and it is also merciful toward those who have done wrong without evil intent.
exp.15:8:
Moses asks Aaron to tell the whole people of Israel: "Come near before the Lord, for he has heard your complaints." The word "murmurings" in the verse refers to complaints spoken quietly or with resentment. "Congregation" means the community gathered together. The name "Lord" is the name of God.

The Israelites had just left Egypt, and in the wilderness they were complaining about having no food. Moses and Aaron remind them that their complaints were, at bottom, not against them but against God. Even so, God does not abandon them: he prepares to give them meat and bread, and he shows them his glory.

When we are tired or afraid, we can draw near to God instead of turning away in complaint. He listens to us, even when trusting him is hard. We can honestly bring him what we feel and ask him to help us believe in his care.
exp.22:7:
The explanation says that we should not accept gifts or bribes. The word "gift" here means a present given to influence a decision. And "blinds those who see" means that even a person who understands well what is right can lose clear sight when they receive something in return. Thus the "righteous words," that is, the right causes or reasons, end up twisted.

God speaks to Israel through Moses, after giving the Ten Commandments, in laws for the life of the people. Before and after this verse, He takes care of the poor, the innocent, and the stranger. Bribery punishes above all the weak, who have nothing with which to pay to be heard.

For today: if you have some responsibility over others, as in a job, in the church, or in the family, do not let favors, gifts, or friendships lead you to decide wrongly. Ask God for an upright heart and treat everyone with the same justice.
exp.26:17:
This verse gives the measurements of the court, the open courtyard that surrounded the tabernacle. It was one hundred cubits long and fifty cubits wide (a cubit is roughly half a meter, so about 50 by 25 meters). The hangings were of fine twined linen, that is, finely woven linen threads, and five cubits high. The sockets were the bases on which the posts rested, made of metal, probably bronze.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai and gives him detailed instructions for building a place where he can dwell among his people. The court marked off a separate and orderly space, with a single entrance, for drawing near to God.

Today, this detail reminds us that approaching God is not a careless matter. We can set aside a quiet moment each day to pray and read the Bible, with reverence and gratitude, knowing that He welcomes us.
exp.12:16:
When Pharaoh finally let the people go, God did not lead them by the shorter route, the one that passed through the land of the Philistines. God thought that, on seeing a war, they might become frightened, change their minds, and go back to Egypt.

The one telling the story is the author of the book, traditionally Moses. He has just recounted the last plague and the command to remember the deliverance. Now he explains why the route was a detour: God knew how fragile the people were, having only just come out of slavery, and did not put them to the test beyond what they could still bear.

God sometimes leads us along longer paths, and this is not out of carelessness. He may be caring for our faith while we grow. If your path today seems slow or indirect, trust that God sees what you cannot yet see.
exp.34:27:
This verse lists other things the people brought for the tabernacle: fragrant spices and oil. The oil was used for the lamps of the holy place, and the spices and oil were also used for the anointing oil and for the sweet incense. The lamps are the light the oil kept burning, and the anointing is the act of setting apart people and objects for God.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel in the wilderness, and the narrator goes on describing what each one contributed. God had asked for freewill offerings to build the tabernacle, and the people responded with what they had. The whole passage stresses that everyone took part, men and women, leaders and ordinary people.

For today: God values what we give him with a willing heart, whether great or small. Ask yourself what you have on hand, time, a talent, or money, and put it gladly at the service of God and of others.
exp.2:8:
God says that the cry, that is, the weeping and the plea for help of the Israelites, has already reached him. He also states that he has seen the oppression, that is, the harsh and unjust treatment with which the Egyptians mistreat them. Oppression means the abuse of power over someone weaker.

The Lord speaks from the burning bush, addressing Moses. Israel had for years been a people enslaved in Egypt. God repeats that he sees, hears, and knows their suffering, and for that reason he is going to deliver them. Right away he calls Moses to be the one sent, and Moses responds with doubts about himself.

For today: when you feel that no one sees your pain, you can cry out to God with confidence, because he listens and cares. And if you see others suffering injustice, ask him to also use you to help them, even when you feel small.
exp.5:13:
This verse begins a list of the families of Israel. It says that these are the "heads," or leaders, of their ancestors' households. It starts with Reuben, the oldest son of Jacob (Israel), and names his four sons: Hanoch, Pallu, Hezron, and Carmi. "Firstborn" means the first child born.

Moses has just said that even his own people will not listen to him, and that speaking is hard for him as well. God answers by giving him and Aaron the task of bringing Israel out of Egypt. Then the text pauses and presents the genealogy, to show who Moses and Aaron were and which family they belonged to. The list goes on to the tribe of Levi, the tribe they came from.

God works with real people, with names and families. If you feel small or unable today, remember that God knows you and calls you with your own story. He does not depend on your eloquence, but on his faithfulness.
exp.15:24:
Moses told the Israelites to eat that day the manna they had kept from the day before. The word "sabbath" means "rest." Moses explains that this day was set apart as a day of rest for the Lord, so they would not find manna in the field.

Moses speaks to the people in the wilderness, shortly after leaving Egypt. God gave them manna every morning. On the sixth day they gathered twice as much, and what was kept did not spoil, as it did on other days. In this way God was teaching them to trust in his provision and to rest one day each week.

For today: God cares for us also when we rest. We can set aside time to stop, give thanks, and trust that he sustains our needs, without living enslaved to work or anxiety.
exp.33:16:
This verse forbids making idols of molten metal, which were poured into a mold to give them shape. Images made of gold, silver, or other metal are what this refers to. God says that his people must not make gods like these to worship them.

God speaks to Moses and to Israel as he renews his covenant, after the sin of the golden calf. Before this command, he warns them not to mix with the peoples of Canaan or with their gods, so that they would not turn away from him. Afterward he mentions feasts and offerings that would keep them remembering their rescue from Egypt.

Today almost no one casts idols, but we can still give something the place of God: money, success, or the approval of others. Ask yourself what takes away your peace when you lose it, and put God first again.
exp.19:4:
God says that we should not bow down before images or give them honor, because He is Jehovah, a strong and jealous God. "Jealous" means that He wants our complete loyalty, as in a marriage. "Visiting the iniquity" means that He brings the consequences of sin upon several generations of those who reject it. "Them that hate me" refers to those who turn away from Him.

God Himself speaks, on Mount Sinai, within the Ten Commandments. He had just freed Israel from Egypt and wanted to form a faithful people. The next verse shows that his mercy reaches to thousands, far more than the punishment. Some understand that the consequences of sin are reflected in families; others emphasize that God judges each person (Ezekiel 18).

Today we can ask ourselves what things take God's place in our hearts, such as money or fame, and decide to put Him first.
exp.18:1:
This verse tells that the people of Israel departed from Rephidim, came to the desert of Sinai, and pitched their tents there in front of the mountain. The words "departed" and "camped" describe the people settling down and stopping in that place and setting up their camp.

The narrator is the author of the book, traditionally understood to be Moses. About three months have passed since they left Egypt. The account shows their arrival at the place where God will speak with his people. Right after this, God calls Moses from the mountain to remind the people that he rescued them and brought them to himself.

For today: sometimes God leads us to places of pause, like a desert, not to punish us, but so that we will listen to him with attention. If today you are in a quiet or difficult season, ask yourself what God may be saying to you, and set aside time to pray and read his Word.
exp.7:14:
When Pharaoh saw that the plague of frogs was over and he had relief, he became stubborn again. "Hardened his heart" means that he grew stiff and more obstinate. "Respite" means relief or a break from trouble. For that reason he did not listen to Moses and Aaron, just as the Lord had said he would.

This is part of the account of the plagues of Egypt. Moses was asking Pharaoh to let the people of Israel go. Pharaoh had promised to do so if the frogs went away, but when he saw the relief, he changed his mind. The text tells what happened, and other passages say that Pharaoh hardened his own heart and also that God hardened it; scholars explain this in different ways.

For today: let us not wait until a problem passes to forget about God. When we receive relief, it is a good time to give thanks and to keep what we promised.
exp.20:9:
This verse says that if a man takes another wife, he may not take away from the first one the basic things: her food, her clothing, and her conjugal right, that is, her right to marital intimacy and to be treated as a wife.

God speaks to Moses, and this is part of the laws given to Israel after leaving Egypt. It concerns a woman who was given as a servant and later taken as a wife. In that society she was very vulnerable, and the law sets limits on the man to protect her. It does not in itself approve of polygamy; it regulates a custom of the time. If he did not comply, she was free to leave without paying anything.

For today: whoever has more power in a relationship must care for the other person with justice and respect. In marriage, this includes provision, affection, and faithfulness, without neglecting or abusing.
exp.34:28:
This verse says that all the Israelites, both men and women, whose hearts were willing, brought an offering for all the work that God had commanded through Moses. "Willing" means they gave gladly, not out of obligation. "The Lord" is the name of God. "Made" means "done" in this verse.

The one telling the story is the author of the book, traditionally understood to be Moses. Israel was in the wilderness, and God had asked for the tabernacle to be built, his place of meeting with the people. Before this, the offerings of the leaders are mentioned, and afterward Moses presents Bezaleel, to whom God gave skill for the work.

For today: God values what we give with joy, whether money, time, or talent. Ask yourself what you can offer him this week with a willing heart, without pressure or comparison with others.
exp.32:9:
It says that when the people saw the cloudy pillar stand at the entrance of the tabernacle, they all stood up, each one at the door of his own tent, and worshipped. Here "tabernacle" means the tent of meeting, and the word for "rose up" simply means "stood up."

The passage describes what happened after the sin of the golden calf. Moses would set up a tent outside the camp to meet with God. When the cloud came down, the people understood that God was speaking with Moses. Although the people did not go in, they responded with respect and worship from where they stood.

For today: you do not need to be in a special place to worship God. We can stop in the middle of everyday life, at our own "door," and acknowledge his presence with gratitude and reverence. A simple moment of prayer at home or at work counts too.
exp.32:16:
Here God answers Moses that he will indeed do what he asked: go with the people on the journey. He gives two reasons: Moses has found grace, that is, favor, in his sight, and God knows him by name, which expresses a close and personal relationship. The word "Lord" is the name of God, and the old wording "said unto" is simply an older way of saying "said to."

Moses speaks with God after the people made the golden calf and sinned gravely. Moses insists that, without God's presence, it is not worth going on. He sees that presence as what sets Israel apart from the other peoples. God hears his plea and grants what he asks.

For today: you can approach God with confidence, even when you feel weak or have failed. Ask him for his company before anything else, and remember that he knows you personally, not as just one more person in the crowd.
exp.39:17:
This verse describes how Moses set up the tabernacle, the sacred tent where God would dwell among his people. First he set the bases, which were the silver foundations on which the boards stood. Then he placed the boards, which formed the walls, put in the bars that held them together, and raised the pillars, which supported the curtains of the entrance and of the veil.

The narrator tells us that, a year after leaving Egypt, Israel completed the work. Everything was done "as the LORD had commanded Moses." The account stresses this obedience to show that God guided every detail and that Moses followed him faithfully.

For today: obedience to God is lived out in small things, one step at a time. Today you can faithfully do what He has placed in your hands, even when it seems like a detail of no importance.
exp.34:4:
Moses asks for an offering for God. The word translated here as "take" means "gather" or "set apart." A word meaning generous, someone who gives gladly and of their own free will, is also used here. No one was forced: only those who wanted to give brought their offering. The first materials are named here: gold, silver, and bronze (the metal likely refers to bronze or copper).

Moses speaks to the whole congregation of Israel and repeats what God commanded. Earlier he had reminded them to keep the Sabbath. Now he moves on to the building of the tabernacle, the tent where God would dwell among his people. That work needed materials, and God invited the people to take part with their possessions.

For today: God values a willing heart more than the amount given. We can ask ourselves what we have to offer, whether time, money, or talents, and give it with joy, not under pressure, to support God's work in our community.
exp.38:13:
This verse says that the twelve stones of the high priest's breastpiece bore the names of the sons of Israel, one for each tribe. The breastpiece is a piece of rich cloth that the priest wore over his chest. The engraved letters on the stones were cut with great precision, like the lettering on a seal used for signing.

Here the narrator tells how the craftsmen made Aaron's sacred garments, just as God had commanded Moses. These garments enabled the priest to serve in the tabernacle. The names on his chest showed that he represented the whole people before God. Scholars do not fully agree on exactly which stones were which.

For today: God does not see his people as a faceless crowd, but with personal names. You can trust that He knows you and carries you close to his heart. Christians see in Jesus the high priest who intercedes for us.
exp.27:42:
The explanation says that the linen undergarments, that is, the underclothing that covered from the waist to the thighs, were to be worn whenever Aaron and his sons entered the tent of meeting or came near the altar. This way they would not bear iniquity (carry guilt) and die.

God speaks to Moses at Sinai, giving him instructions for clothing the priests. These garments covered nakedness and showed that approaching a holy God calls for reverence, order, and purity. Some think they also guarded against any carelessness in the sacred service.

For today: we can draw near to God with reverence and sincerity, not lightly. Christ opens the way for us and clothes us with his righteousness, yet we still pray and serve with a humble heart, taking care in how we live before him.
exp.26:12:
It says the courtyard of the tabernacle measured fifty cubits in width on the east side, where the sun rose. A cubit was roughly half a meter, so it would be about 25 meters. The courtyard was the open enclosure surrounding the tent, and the east side was the side facing the sunrise.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai and gives him the exact measurements for building the tabernacle, his dwelling among the people of Israel. The courtyard measured one hundred by fifty cubits. Here the side of the entrance is described, the side facing east. The verses that follow explain how that side was divided, with the gate in the middle.

For today: God cares about order and care, and he also shows us that approaching him has a clear way. We can draw near with reverence and without haste, thankful that today, through Christ, we have free access to his presence.
exp.13:7:
God let Pharaoh become stubborn once again, and because of this he went out to pursue Israel. The explanation points out two old-fashioned expressions: "hardened" means he made Pharaoh stubborn and set in his decision, and "pursued after" means he went chasing them. It also clarifies that the Israelites did not leave secretly or in hiding, but openly, under the visible power of God.

The one telling the story is the author of the book, traditionally Moses. Israel had just left Egypt after the plagues. Pharaoh regretted letting them go and gathered his army. The text says God hardened his heart, and elsewhere it also says Pharaoh himself hardened his own heart. Christians explain this in several ways, but all of them see that God is in control.

For today: when you feel that a problem is chasing you, remember that God brought you out with power and will not leave you halfway. Call on Him with confidence.
exp.29:0:
God commands Moses to build a special altar for burning incense. The wood described here is acacia, a tree of the desert, strong and firm.

Here God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai as He gives him the instructions for the tabernacle, the tent where the people of Israel would worship. This altar was to stand in the holy place, in front of the veil. Many believers see in the smoke of the incense a picture of prayer, as mentioned in Psalm 141:2 and Revelation 5:8.

For today: God wants us to draw near to Him with reverence and consistency. Set a fixed time each day to pray, like someone offering something pleasing before Him.
exp.14:23:
The people of Israel complained out loud against Moses because they had no water to drink. The verse says they "murmured," which means they complained with anger and discontent. They asked, "What shall we drink?"

The people speaking had just been freed from Egypt. They had been walking through the wilderness for three days without water, and when they reached Marah, the water was bitter and could not be drunk. Their complaint was understandable, but it showed that they had already forgotten how God had recently saved them. Moses, by contrast, cried out to God, and God showed him how to make the water sweet.

When we face an urgent need, we can choose between complaining or bringing the problem to God in prayer. He hears us and knows how to help us, even in the wildernesses of life.
exp.18:9:
God tells Moses to go to the people and consecrate them for two days, today and tomorrow. Consecrating here means setting themselves apart and getting ready to meet with God. He also asks them to wash their clothes. The instructions to wash and to prepare speak of a personal and visible kind of preparation.

The LORD speaks with Moses on Mount Sinai. The people have just said, "All that the LORD has spoken we will do." Now God is getting ready to come down on the third day and speak to them. Washing clothing was an outward act that showed respect and a desire to draw near to a holy God. Interpreters see it as a symbol of inner cleansing.

For today: before you pray, read the Bible, or gather with others, take a few minutes to prepare yourself. Turn off distractions, acknowledge your failings, and ask God for a clean and attentive heart.
exp.29:20:
It says that Aaron and his sons, the priests, were to wash their hands and their feet with water before serving God. If they did not, they would die. This command was to hold forever, for them and their descendants. "Seed" means offspring, and "a statute forever" means a rule that stays in force from generation to generation.

God speaks to Moses while giving him the instructions for the tabernacle, the tent where Israel worshiped. Before this verse, the bronze basin is described, which stood between the tent and the altar. The washing taught that approaching a holy God was not something to be done casually. Afterward, God continues with other instructions, such as the holy anointing oil and the incense.

For today: before praying, serving, or reading the Bible, pause for a moment and ask God for a clean and sincere heart. It is about coming near with reverence, knowing that he is holy and good.
exp.9:26:
It says that the Lord hardened Pharaoh's heart, and so the king refused to let the people of Israel leave. "Hardened" means that he made him firm and stubborn in his decision. "Would not let them go" shows that Pharaoh kept rejecting God's command.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Moses had just said that all the livestock had to go with them, because they needed it to worship God. Pharaoh had offered a partial way out, but not a complete one. The texts of Exodus say that Pharaoh also hardened his own heart, and that God also hardened it; scholars explain that relationship in different ways.

For today: each time we sense God speaking and answer "no," our heart becomes harder to change. Today we can obey promptly, even when it costs us, and ask God for a soft and willing heart.
exp.31:30:
Moses returns to God and speaks to him with candor. He acknowledges that the people committed a great sin: they made gods of gold for themselves. He does not try to excuse the people; he calls what they did sin.

Moses speaks after Israel made the golden calf while he was on Mount Sinai. He had already confronted the people, and now he goes up to intercede for them. His prayer shows the heart of a leader who loves his people, even though they have failed badly.

For today: when someone close to you fails, or when you fail, there is no need to deny the sin or harden your heart. You can name it for what it is and still come before God with humility, asking for mercy for yourself and for others.
exp.5:15:
This verse gives the names of Levi's three sons: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari. It says that the families of the tribe of Levi came from them. It also tells us that Levi lived 137 years. "Lineages" means the families that come down from one same person.

Here the one telling the story is the author of the book, traditionally Moses, and he does so just before God sends Moses and Aaron to the pharaoh. The list begins with Reuben and Simeon and reaches Levi, because Moses and Aaron came from this tribe. In this way it shows which family the men God would use to free his people came from.

For today: God cares about the names and the stories of families. Remember that He can use ordinary people, with a particular history and a particular origin, to carry out his plans. Trust that your life matters to him too.
exp.24:32:
This verse describes how the branches of the lampstand were to be decorated. Each branch would have three bowls shaped like almond blossoms, and on each one there would be a knob (probably a round ornament, like a bud or a button) and a flower. The lampstand is the stand that held the lamps, and the phrase "hammered work" means work shaped by beating the gold. There were six branches in all.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai. He gives him instructions for building the tabernacle, the tent where God would meet with Israel. The lampstand would light the holy place. The detail of the almonds and the flowers speaks to us of beauty and life, although the Bible does not explain their exact meaning, and interpreters understand them in various ways.

For today: God cares about details and about the beauty of what is made for him. We can serve him with dedication and care in small things as well as large ones, working gladly even when no one notices.
exp.8:29:
Moses tells Pharaoh that he does not believe he or his servants truly fear God yet. The word "fear" here means to acknowledge God with reverence and to obey him. The word "yet" shows that, although Pharaoh promises to change, Moses sees that his heart is still the same.

Moses speaks after Pharaoh, under the plague of hail, admitted that he had sinned and asked for prayer. Moses agrees to pray, but he knows that Pharaoh says those words out of fear of the moment. The verses that follow show that, once the punishment stopped, Pharaoh hardened himself again.

For today: true repentance is more than feeling afraid when troubles come. We can ask ourselves whether, when the difficulty passes, we still obey God sincerely. Let us ask him for a heart that respects him in good times and in bad.
exp.8:20:
It says that, when God gave His warning about the hail, some Egyptians did not take it seriously. "Did not take it to heart" means that he gave it no importance and did not decide to obey. For that reason he left his servants (his workers or attendants) and his livestock (animals) outside, in the field, exposed to danger.

This is part of the plagues of Egypt. Moses had warned, on behalf of the Lord, that a very severe hail would come. God was giving the opportunity to protect oneself, and some of Pharaoh's servants believed and brought their people and animals to safety. Others, as is seen here, ignored the warning. The warning also showed God's patience.

For today: when God speaks to us through His Word, it is not enough to hear it; we must keep it in our hearts and act. Today you could choose a teaching from the Bible that you already know and put it into practice this week.
exp.32:15:
Moses asks God how it will be known that he and the people have found grace, that is, favor, in God's sight. He answers his own question: it will be known if God goes with them. That presence will set them apart, meaning distinct and set aside for God, from all the other peoples on the earth.

Moses speaks with God after the sin of the golden calf. God had said He would send an angel, but that He would not go in their midst Himself. Moses does not want to move forward toward the promised land without God's presence. So he presses the request, and God agrees to his plea.

For today: before seeking success, plans, or blessings, ask God to let His presence accompany you. What makes a believer different is not having more things, but living each day close to God, in prayer and obedience.
exp.9:21:
It says that Moses stretched out his hand toward heaven, just as God had commanded him, and a thick darkness covered all of Egypt for three days. The text before this verse describes the darkness as so heavy that it could almost be felt, which is why the word "thick" is used here.

This is the ninth plague. Pharaoh was still refusing to let Israel go, and God acted through Moses. The Egyptians placed great importance on their gods of the sky, so this sign showed that the LORD rules even over light and darkness. Meanwhile, according to the text, the Israelites still had light in their homes.

For today: even when there are dark and confusing times, God remains in control and cares for his people. We can trust that he guides our path, and ask him for light and direction when we cannot see the next step.
exp.37:14:
This verse describes the entrance side of the courtyard around the tabernacle. On each side of the gate there were hangings fifteen cubits long, supported by three pillars and three bases (the bases or stands into which the pillars were set). A cubit was roughly the distance from the elbow to the tip of the finger, about 45 centimeters, though the exact measure is debated.

Here the author of the book, traditionally Moses, summarizes how the courtyard was built according to the instructions God had given. The fifteen cubits on each side, added to the width of the gate, completed the fifty cubits of the eastern side. The courtyard marked out a separate and orderly space for approaching God.

For today: God attended even to the small details of his dwelling, and that invites us to serve him with care and faithfulness in ordinary things, knowing that nothing done for him is insignificant.
exp.10:2:
This verse says that God caused the Egyptians to look kindly upon the people of Israel. Moses was also highly respected in Egypt, both by Pharaoh's servants and by ordinary people.

The phrase "gave the people favour" means that God gave them goodwill or sympathy in the eyes of others. "A great man" refers to Moses as someone important and esteemed.

This is a note from the narrator in the middle of God's instructions to Moses. Before the last plague, God is preparing his people to leave Egypt. The Israelites would ask their neighbors for objects of silver and gold. This favor shows that God was working even in the hearts of the Egyptians, and that the respect shown toward Moses had grown after the earlier plagues.

For today: God can open doors and soften hearts when things seem impossible. Trust that he cares for you, and strive to live with integrity, because an honest life also earns respect.
exp.3:21:
God tells Moses to speak to Pharaoh in his name. The message is that Israel is his son, his firstborn. With that name, God shows that Israel belongs to him and that he has a close relationship with them, like a father with a beloved son.

The LORD speaks to Moses just as he is returning to Egypt. God had already told him that Pharaoh would resist. So here he gives him the central argument: Pharaoh is holding back the son of God. What follows in the text is a warning: if Pharaoh does not let him go, he will lose his own firstborn.

For today: if we belong to God, our identity does not depend on those who pressure or dominate us. We can rest in the knowledge that he knows us, cares for us, and is faithful to his own, even when the situation seems difficult.
exp.3:4:
The explanation of this verse says what the sign of the staff is for. God tells Moses that when the people see this miracle, they will believe that the Lord, the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, has truly appeared to him.

The Lord speaks to Moses at Mount Horeb, beside the burning bush. Moses was afraid that the Israelites would not believe him. So God gives him signs: the staff that becomes a snake and then becomes a staff again. In this way Moses could show that his mission came from God.

For today: God knows that we sometimes doubt, and He gives us help to trust. When He asks you to do something difficult, do not stay with your fears. Remember how God has been faithful before, and take the step with confidence in Him.
exp.29:29:
God tells Moses that he must anoint Aaron and his sons with oil. "Anoint" means to pour oil over someone as a sign that God sets them apart. "Consecrate" means to dedicate someone fully to God, so that they may be his priest and serve him.

God speaks, giving Moses instructions in the wilderness about the tabernacle. Earlier he had commanded that the altar and its utensils be anointed, and now that same holy oil is used on the people. In this way Israel understood that serving God was not an ordinary thing: it had to be done by his calling and in his way. Afterward God warns that this oil was holy and must not be used for anything else.

Today we can remember that serving God begins with being set apart for him, not with our talent. The New Testament says that believers are a holy priesthood (1 Peter 2:5). We can begin each day by offering to God our work, our family, and our decisions.
exp.1:7:
This verse tells that Pharaoh's daughter said to the child's sister, "Go." Then the young woman ran to call the baby's mother.

Pharaoh's daughter had just found the Hebrew baby in the river and felt compassion for him. The child's sister, who had been watching him from a distance, came near with a wise proposal: to find a Hebrew nurse. Pharaoh's daughter agreed. Here the text does not give the sister's name; in later passages she is known as Miriam, though this chapter does not mention it.

For today: God often works in the midst of difficult situations through simple and brave actions. When you see an opportunity to help, speak with respect and act with prudence. God can use your small initiative to care for someone.
exp.31:33:
Moses is told to go on and lead the people toward the promised land. God promises that his angel will go before him. But God also warns that when the day of reckoning comes, the moment when God steps in to call people to account, he will punish the sin of the people. The explanation of that phrase is dropped here, since the reader's verse does not use the old wording, and the second word is simply rendered as punish.

God speaks in answer to Moses. The people had just made and worshiped the golden calf. Moses had interceded and even offered to be erased from God's book in their place. God does not accept that exchange, but he does not abandon his plan either: the journey continues, though the sin will have consequences. The following verse says that God struck the people.

For today: God is merciful and faithful to his promises, but he is also just. We can trust that he guides us, and at the same time we must take sin seriously, ask for forgiveness, and not use grace as an excuse to keep doing the same thing.
exp.37:4:
It says that Bezaleel and his helpers made four rings of cast metal, one at each corner of the bronze grate of the altar. Those rings were used to pass the poles through, the poles by which the altar was carried. The "ends" are the corners or extremities, and the "cast" metal means it was melted and poured into a mold.

Here the narrator tells how the tabernacle was built, following the instructions God gave to Moses. The altar of burnt offerings had to be portable, because the people were moving through the desert. That is why rings and poles were planned, so that it could be moved without anyone touching it directly.

God cares even about the small details of what we offer him. Today we can serve him with order and care in ordinary things: preparing a class, attending to someone, doing everyday tasks well. And we can remember that his presence goes with us wherever we go.
exp.22:22:
God promises that his Angel will go ahead of the people of Israel and bring them into the land where several nations live: the Amorites, the Hittites, the Perizzites, the Canaanites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites. God says that he himself will cause them to be destroyed.

God speaks to Israel through Moses, after giving them the laws at Sinai. He warns them that they are traveling toward Canaan and that they must obey the Angel, in whom God's name dwells. Some think he is a special messenger of God; others see in him God himself present. The Bible does not fully explain this. The promise depends on obedience, and the next verse forbids following the gods of those peoples.

For today: trust that God goes before you in what you do not know, but listen to his voice and obey him every day, without keeping loyalties that compete with him.
exp.25:7:
This verse gives the measurements of each curtain made of goat hair: thirty cubits long and four cubits wide, and the eleven curtains all the same. A cubit was the distance from the elbow to the tip of the fingers, roughly 45 centimeters, though its exact measure is debated. So each curtain was about 13 meters long by 1.8 meters wide.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai and gives him detailed instructions for building the tabernacle, the tent where God would dwell among Israel. These curtains formed a covering over the inner curtains. That they were all the same size helped them fit together well.

For today: God cares about details and order. We can serve him with care and faithfulness in small things, knowing that what is simple also forms part of something greater.
exp.27:23:
This verse says that Moses was to put the two chains of gold into the two rings that were at the two upper corners of the breastplate. The breastplate is a piece of cloth that the high priest wore over his chest. The chains were small cords of twisted gold. They held the breastplate in place and joined it to the ephod, another priestly garment.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai and gives him detailed instructions about the clothing of Aaron, the high priest. This clothing was to be beautiful and well made. The breastplate carried twelve stones with the names of the tribes of Israel.

For today: God cares about details and about every part of what we do for Him. Just as the breastplate was held firmly over the priest's heart, we can remember that God carefully sustains His people, and that our service deserves to be done with care and faithfulness.
exp.1:3:
This verse says that a sister of the child stood at a certain distance, watching to see what would happen to him. The phrase "stood afar off" in the verse above matches the sense of the original wording: she kept her distance from the river's edge.

The text is narrative, with no one speaking. It tells how a Hebrew mother protected her son when Pharaoh had ordered that the baby boys be killed. After placing the basket in the river, the sister keeps watch. The text does not give her name here; later, the Bible mentions Miriam as Moses' sister, and many understand that this is her, although this passage does not say so.

For today: when we have done what we can and the outcome does not depend on us, we can remain near with love, praying and attentive, trusting that God cares for what matters most to us.
exp.0:10:
They put slave drivers over the Israelites, whom the explanation calls "tax collectors" in the old wording, to make them suffer under heavy labor. In this way the Egyptians forced them to build for Pharaoh "supply cities," that is, storage cities where provisions were kept. The text names Pithom and Raamses.

The new king of Egypt speaks out of fear in the verse before this one. He saw that Israel was growing very large and thought they might join forces with enemies in a war. Out of fear, he decided to oppress them. Scholars debate the exact date and location of those cities, so it is wise not to claim more than the text says.

For today: fear can lead us to treat others badly. Ask God that when you feel afraid, you do not pass that fear onto others, but seek justice and compassion instead. He sees the oppressed and does not forget them.
exp.6:20:
This verse describes the result of the first plague. The fish in the Nile died, the water spoiled and smelled bad, so the Egyptians could not drink it. There was blood throughout all of Egypt. "Spoiled" means that it rotted and gave off a foul smell. "Egyptians" are the people who lived in Egypt.

God had commanded Moses and Aaron to strike the river with the staff in front of Pharaoh. They wanted Pharaoh to let the people of Israel go free from slavery. The Nile was vital to Egypt, and some scholars think the Egyptians revered it. That is why this sign touched something very important to them. Experts do not always agree on how to understand the word "blood" here.

God takes injustice seriously and hears the oppressed. Today we can trust that he sees what people suffer and acts in his own time. We can pray for those who suffer injustice.
exp.7:6:
This verse says that the magicians of Egypt, called "enchanters," did the same as Aaron: by their arts they brought more frogs up onto the land. The word "enchantments" refers to magical practices. The verse does not explain how they accomplished this; some think of tricks, and others of a deceptive spiritual power.

God had commanded Moses and Aaron to produce the plague of frogs before Pharaoh. The magicians imitated the sign, but they only added more frogs. Notice that they could not take them away. For this reason Pharaoh ends up asking Moses to pray to the LORD.

For today: not everything that seems powerful comes from God or brings a solution. Imitations can impress, but they do not solve the underlying problem. Let us seek God in prayer, for only he can give true relief.
exp.28:21:
This verse says that Moses was to take the best parts of the ram: the fat, the fatty tail, the fat that covers the inner organs, the fatty membrane over the liver, the two kidneys with their fat, and the right thigh. It was the "ram of consecration," that is, the animal used to set apart the priests for God.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai and gives him instructions for ordaining Aaron and his sons as priests. Earlier, blood was put on their right ear, thumb, and big toe, and oil was put on them. These parts were then presented to God. Many understand that the fat represented what was best and most valuable, though the text does not explain this in detail.

For today: God deserves our best, not our leftovers. We can give Him the best of our time, attention, and affection, and remember that Christ gave Himself completely so that we would be set apart for God.
exp.34:9:
It says that every skilled person among the people who is able should come forward and do everything the Lord has commanded. "Wise of heart" does not refer to academic study, but to someone with practical skill and a willing disposition. "Lord" is the name of God, and the verse's wording is the plain English you see above.

Moses speaks to the whole community of Israel, gathered after the sin of the golden calf. He passes on God's instructions for building the tabernacle, their meeting place with the people. First he asked for voluntary offerings (materials), and now he calls on those who have talent to work with them.

For today: God values ordinary skills, such as sewing, building, cooking, teaching or organizing. Ask yourself what you know how to do and offer it with joy to serve in your church or community.
exp.8:15:
God tells Pharaoh that he has been raised up, or set in his place, to show his power in him, so that his name may be made known throughout all the earth. Where the wording is unclear, the sense is that God is the one who placed Pharaoh where he stood, for God's own purpose.

God speaks through Moses to Pharaoh, in the midst of the plagues on Egypt. Pharaoh resisted letting the people of Israel go. Some understand that God allowed or sustained his rule for this purpose; others stress that Pharaoh hardened his own heart. Both ideas appear in the account.

For today: God is greater than any human power that seems impossible to overcome. We can trust that he acts with purpose, even when we see injustice. And he invites us to respond to him with humility, rather than harden our hearts as Pharaoh did.
exp.9:6:
Pharaoh's servants, his officials and advisers, ask him how long Moses will be a snare to them. They urge him to let the Hebrew men go so that they may serve the Lord their God, and they point out that Egypt is already ruined. The phrase "knowest thou not yet" amounts to asking: "Don't you see it yet?"

Moses had just announced the plague of locusts. The earlier plagues had already struck the land, and the hail had destroyed the crops. The advisers see the disaster, though they do not say that they believe in the Lord. Pharaoh listens to them and calls Moses back, but, as what follows shows, he is still bargaining and does not yield completely.

For today: sometimes we see clearly the damage that foolishness causes, and yet we are slow to obey. Let us not wait until we have lost everything before we listen to God. Surrendering to Him in time saves us much pain.
exp.15:22:
Moses repeats what God commanded: tomorrow would be the Sabbath, a holy day of rest to the Lord. So the people were to bake and boil today whatever they needed, and keep whatever was left over for tomorrow.

Moses speaks, passing on the word of the Lord. The leaders of the people were surprised to see that on the sixth day they gathered twice as much manna, and they asked him what was happening. Moses explains that God was teaching Israel to rest and to trust that He would provide. Even before the law at Sinai, this lesson was being given to them.

Today we can prepare in advance what is needed so that we can set apart a day of rest, trusting that God cares for us even when we pause our work.
exp.37:0:
It says that Bezalel, the craftsman of the work, built the altar of burnt offering, where sacrifices were burned. He made it of shittim wood, which is acacia, a tree of the desert. It measured five cubits on each side, that is, it was square, and three cubits high. A cubit was roughly half a meter, so the altar measured about two and a half meters on each side and a meter and a half high.

This passage is part of the account of how the tabernacle, the tent where God dwelt among Israel, was built. The narrator tells that it was made just as God had commanded Moses (Exodus 27). The altar stood at the entrance, because no one drew near to God without a sacrifice.

For today: God cares about the details of how we come near to him. Christians see in this altar a sign of Christ, who offered himself for us. We can approach God with gratitude, trusting in that sacrifice and not in our own merits.
exp.3:24:
Zipporah, Moses' wife, takes a very sharp stone knife and cuts off the foreskin of her son. Then she throws it at the feet of the one she is addressing and says: "You are a bloody husband to me." A flint is a hard stone with a sharp edge; the foreskin is the skin removed in circumcision.

Moses was on his way to Egypt by God's command. At a lodging place, the Lord sought to kill him, and the text does not clearly explain why. Many think it was because Moses had not circumcised his son, the sign of the covenant with Abraham. It is not clear to whom "his feet" refers, nor what "bloody husband" means exactly; it is interpreted in several ways. When the circumcision was carried out, God let him go.

For today: one cannot serve God with half-hearted obedience. If He points out something left undone, it is wise to attend to it with humility and without delay.
exp.31:20:
Moses asks his brother Aaron what the people did to him that he has brought such a great sin upon them. The word "á" is the old way of writing "a", and "traído sobre él" means that Aaron was responsible for the people falling into that sin.

Moses has just come down from Mount Sinai. There God had given him the tablets of the law, but in the camp the people had made a golden calf to worship it. Moses broke the tablets in anger and destroyed the idol. Now he confronts Aaron, who had been left in charge while he was away.

For today: whoever has some responsibility over others, in the family, the church or the workplace, should remember that their decisions influence those around them. When we fail, it is good to acknowledge it honestly, without blaming others.
exp.20:34:
If one man's ox injures another's ox so that it dies, and there is no clear fault, the two owners sell the living ox, split the money equally between them, and also divide the dead ox between them.

God speaks through Moses to Israel, in the laws that accompany the Ten Commandments. These were rules for daily life in community. This case deals with an accident without clear negligence. The law seeks to share the loss fairly, to avoid lawsuits and resentment. The next verse changes the case: if the owner knew his ox was dangerous and did not restrain it, he must pay in full.

For today: when harm happens without evident blame, look for a fair, shared solution with your neighbor rather than fighting. And if you knew of the risk, accept your responsibility.
exp.9:25:
Moses tells Pharaoh that all the livestock will go with the people, without leaving behind even a single hoof (the "hoof" here is the hoof of the animals). He explains that they will take from those animals what is needed to worship the Lord, and that they do not yet know which ones or how many God will require, until they arrive at the place of worship.

Moses speaks with Pharaoh during the plague of darkness. Pharaoh offers a half-way solution: that they may go, but leaving the livestock behind, which was his wealth and also a way of making sure they would return. Moses does not negotiate, because worshiping God required animals for the sacrifices.

For today: serving God is not about giving him what we have left over while keeping the best for ourselves. We can ask ourselves what "livestock" we are leaving behind, whether it is time, money or talents, and offer it to him with trust, even though we cannot yet see the whole road ahead.
exp.7:9:
Pharaoh asks that the frogs be removed "to morrow," and Moses agrees: "Be it according to thy word." He does this so that Pharaoh will know that there is none like the Lord our God. The phrase "according to thy word" simply means that Moses will do what Pharaoh asked, and "know" here means that Pharaoh will come to recognize and understand the truth.

Pharaoh is desperate because of the plague of frogs, and he asks Moses to pray. Moses lets Pharaoh choose the time for the prayer, as a sign of trust. In this way, when the frogs disappear on exactly that day, it will be clear that it was no coincidence. Some wonder why Pharaoh did not ask for "today"; the text does not explain this.

We can speak with confidence about God, without fear that he will fail us. When we pray, we want others to see that God is real and faithful, and not that we ourselves are powerful.
exp.28:11:
