God tells Moses to take some of the blood of the bullock and put it with his finger upon the horns of the altar. After that he is to pour out the rest of the blood beside the bottom of the altar. The "horns" were the four projecting corners of the altar, and "bullock" is a young bull.

God speaks to Moses to instruct him about the consecration of Aaron and his sons as priests. This bullock was an offering for sin (atonement). The blood represented a life given up, and placing it on the altar showed that sin had to be covered before the priests could serve. Christians often see here a shadow of Christ.

For today: I do not come to God trusting in my own purity. I can draw near with humility and gratitude, because Jesus has already given his life for me.
exp.35:24:
It says that Bezalel and the craftsmen made twenty boards for the north side of the tabernacle. The word for the north side is "north" in the verse you are reading, and so the north side was made the same as the south side, also with twenty boards. These boards rested on bases of silver.

The passage is a narrative. Moses had received God's instructions on the mountain for building the sanctuary, and here it is told how the people carried them out with exactness. The measurements and details are repeated because the text stresses that everything was done just as God had commanded.

For today: God values faithful obedience in small and repetitive things. Some tasks seem routine, but when they are done with steadiness and for God, they have value. Do your simple work well today, as a service to Him.
exp.6:21:
The explanation says that the magicians of Egypt, called "enchanters," managed to imitate the sign of turning water into blood by their arts. That is why Pharaoh kept his stubbornness and paid no attention to Moses and Aaron. "Hardened" means that he became stubborn and closed-minded. "As the Lord had said" means that God had already warned that this would happen.

Moses and Aaron had just obeyed God and struck the Nile River, which turned to blood. The text is narrative, not a speech. God wanted to show his power and ask for the freedom of Israel. How the magicians managed to copy it is not explained; some think of tricks, and others of deceptive spiritual power.

For today: an impressive sign does not always convince a stubborn heart. Ask God for a humble heart, one that listens to his voice and does not look for excuses to stay on its own path.
exp.2:2:
Moses sees a bush that is burning but is not consumed, and he decides to go closer to look. He says, "I will now turn aside, and see this great sight, why the bush is not burnt." The "great sight" is this strange scene, and he wants to know why the bush is not burnt.

Moses was tending the flock of Jethro, his father-in-law, in the desert, near Mount Horeb. There the Angel of the LORD appeared to him in the midst of the fire. Moses speaks to himself, moved by curiosity. Then God calls him by name, and so begins his call to bring Israel out of Egypt.

God often calls us when we stop to look with attention. Moses could have continued on his way, but he drew near. Today, in the middle of routine, we can pause to listen to God in his Word and in prayer, with a heart ready to obey.
exp.0:5:
This verse says that Joseph died, and also all his brothers and all the people of that time. Those who had come to Egypt with Jacob were no longer alive. The word "generation" refers to the people who live more or less in the same time.

Here the narrator of the book, traditionally attributed to Moses, speaks. He wants to mark a change of era: those who knew Joseph and the protection he brought are gone. Then comes the growth of the people and a new king who did not know Joseph. In this way the beginning of slavery in Egypt is prepared.

For today: no generation lasts forever, and faith is not inherited on its own. If today we have people who teach us to trust God, we should thank them and learn from them. And we should pass on that faith, both in words and by example, to those who come after us.
exp.31:21:
Aaron answers Moses by asking him not to be angry with him. He tells Moses that Moses already knows the people, that they are "set on mischief," meaning they tend to do wrong and are easily carried away by it. The words "my lord" are a respectful way of addressing Moses.

Moses had come down from Mount Sinai and found that the people were worshiping a golden calf. He asks Aaron what the people did to him that he would lead them into such a great sin. Aaron does not admit his guilt; he blames the people and then says the calf "came out" of the fire, as if he had no part in it. The Bible does not say that Aaron lied about what the people asked for, but we do see that he avoids taking responsibility.

When we fail, it is tempting to make excuses by pointing to others or to circumstances. God invites us to be honest, to acknowledge our own part, and to ask for forgiveness.
exp.18:8:
God tells Moses that he will come to him in a thick cloud, that is, a dense and dark cloud. This way the people will be able to hear when God speaks with Moses, and for that reason they will believe him always. At the end, Moses brings the people's answer back to God. The word "told" here means "passed on" or "reported," not "accused."

God speaks to Moses shortly before giving him the law on Mount Sinai. The people had just promised to obey everything God said. God wants them to hear his voice themselves, so that Moses' authority does not rest only on his word, but on something the people can recognize as coming from God.

God draws near to us so that we will trust him, not because of what others tell us, but because we truly know him. Today we can set aside a moment to read his Word and pray sincerely, without relying only on what others say about him.
exp.32:19:
God tells Moses that he cannot see his face, because no man could see it and still live. The word "face" here refers to the full presence of God, without any filter. The phrase "and live" means that the person would remain alive.

God, or the LORD, is speaking with Moses. Moses had just asked, "Show me your glory." This happens after the people made the golden calf and God forgave them. God does not refuse him altogether: he promises to show him his goodness and to proclaim his name. Then he hides him in a cleft of the rock to protect him. Some understand "face" as an expression of closeness, and others as the complete glory; the text shows that Moses would see only a part.

For today: God is holy and is greater than we can grasp. Approach him with reverence and trust, knowing that his mercy covers you and that he makes himself known in the way that is best for you.
exp.38:38:
This verse is part of a list of the pieces of the tabernacle that were already finished. It mentions the bronze altar, with its grate, its poles for carrying it, and all its utensils. It also mentions the basin, or laver, where the priests washed, together with its stand.

Moses is the one who carries the account, and the people of Israel bring before him everything that was made. The text repeats that each thing was made as God had commanded. On the altar the sacrifices were offered, and the basin served for the cleansing of the priests before they ministered.

For today: God cares about obedience in the details. Before we draw near to Him, forgiveness and cleansing are needed. We can approach with confidence because of Christ, and also with a sincere heart ready to obey Him.
exp.14:9:
God says he blew with his wind and the sea closed back over the Egyptian army. The soldiers sank like lead, meaning a very heavy metal, into violent waters. The sea covered them. They went under and sank. The words are poetic: the wind recalls the breath of God.

Moses speaks together with the people of Israel, who sing after crossing the Red Sea. Pharaoh had pursued them in order to subdue them again, and the verse before shows his pride: he said he would pursue, overtake, and seize them. The song celebrates that God delivered them and defeated the enemy. It is poetry, so it uses strong images.

For today: when something seems bigger than you, remember that God is stronger. You can entrust your fears to him, give thanks for what he has already done, and not depend on your own pride or your own strength.
exp.36:10:
He says that Bezaleel covered the table with pure gold and put a gold border around it. The word for that border refers to a molding or raised rim that goes around the table. The phrase meaning "covered it" and the phrase meaning "made for it" are also used in the original wording of this verse. The wood of Sittim is acacia wood.

Here the narrator of the book of Exodus speaks, telling how the furnishings of the tabernacle were made, following the instructions given to Moses. This table was the table of the bread of the presence, which stood in the holy place. The gold border probably served to keep whatever was set on top from sliding off, though the text does not explain it.

God cares about details, even the ones almost no one notices. We can offer our daily work with care and faithfulness, even when no one sees it, because we do it for Him.
exp.33:20:
God tells Israel to work six days, but to rest on the seventh. That rest included even plowing time (preparing the ground for sowing) and harvest, the most urgent tasks in the fields. Not even in those seasons of pressure could they work.

God himself speaks, through Moses, when he renews his covenant with Israel after the sin of the golden calf. Before and after this verse he mentions the firstborn and the yearly feasts. In this way he reminds them that time, the land, and the harvest belong to him.

For today: set aside a regular time to rest and to be with God, even when you have much left to do. Resting is a way of trusting that he sustains your life, and not only your effort.
exp.36:14:
It says that Bezaleel made the poles or staves from acacia wood and overlaid them with gold. These staves were slipped through the rings of the table so it could be carried without being touched.

The passage is part of the account of building the tabernacle. It is a narrative text, not a speech. Moses had received instructions from God, and here it is told that the work was done just as it had been commanded. The table held the bread of the presence. The staves show that the tabernacle was a sanctuary that could be moved as Israel traveled through the wilderness.

God cares about details, even ones that seem small, and he is served faithfully in the simple things. Today we can ask what small task, done with care and obedience, we can offer to God at home, at work, or in the church.
exp.6:24:
God struck the Nile River and turned its waters to blood, and the text says that seven full days passed after that. "Struck" means that God hit it or affected it with his power. The phrase "were fulfilled" means that this period came to an end. So the punishment was not a brief moment, but an entire week.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Moses and Aaron had announced this first plague so that Pharaoh would let Israel go. The verse before says that Pharaoh went home without taking to heart what had happened. The Egyptians had to dig wells to get water. Many understand that this verse closes the first plague and prepares the next one.

For today: God sometimes gives us time to reflect. Do not harden your heart or ignore the warnings. If you sense that something in your life calls you to change, listen soon, pray, and take a step of obedience.
exp.35:11:
It says that Bezaleel and the craftsmen made fifty loops along the edge of each of the two large curtains of the tabernacle. The loops are small rings of cloth, and here they were a violet-blue color. They were placed facing each other, so that later they could be fastened together with the gold clasps.

This is part of the account of the building of the tabernacle, the tent where God would dwell among Israel. The narrator tells how the people did everything just as God had commanded Moses (chapters 25–31). The repetition of the details shows careful obedience. Scholars do not agree on the symbolic meaning of each element, so it is best not to claim too much.

For today: God cares about the small things and about doing them well. Something as simple as loops joined together made the tabernacle one whole. We can serve faithfully in what is unseen, and take care of what unites the community.
exp.28:14:
God tells Moses to take one of the two rams used in the ordination ceremony. Aaron and his sons must place their hands on the head of the animal. The phrase "take one of the rams" is the sense of the words quoted above, meaning "take one of the rams."

God speaks to Moses and gives him instructions for setting apart Aaron and his sons as priests. Before this, the bull was offered as a sin offering. Now comes the first ram, which is burned whole on the altar. Placing the hands is usually understood as a way of identifying oneself with the animal being offered, although scholars explain it in several ways.

Before serving God, we need to recognize that we depend on his forgiveness and his provision. Today you can begin your day with a simple prayer, giving God your work and your heart, and trusting that Christ has already made the complete sacrifice for you.
exp.24:26:
It says the gold rings were to be fixed right by the molding, or rim, of the table. Through those rings the poles would pass, so the table could be carried. Here "over against" means "next to" or "close to." The "places for the poles" are the spots where the poles went in.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai and gives him instructions for the tabernacle, the tent where Israel would worship in the wilderness. The table would hold the bread of the presence. Since the people moved from one place to another, everything had to be portable without anyone touching the holy objects directly.

For today: God cares even about the details of how we serve him. We can ask him to help us do the small, unremarkable tasks with care and faithfulness, knowing that they matter to him.
exp.27:38:
God tells Moses to have a coat of fine linen embroidered for Aaron, to make a mitre (a turban or cap) also of fine linen, and a girdle or sash of "needlework," that is, woven with fine embroidery and worked with great care.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai, giving him instructions for the tabernacle and for the clothing of the high priest. Earlier he had already described the plate of gold on Aaron's forehead. These garments were not mere decoration: they showed that Aaron was serving God in something holy, and the text says they were for glory and beauty.

Today we can learn that God cares about the service we give him, and that it deserves our best rather than what is left over. Think of one thing you do for God, such as prayer, helping in your church, or serving someone, and do it this week with care and from the heart.
exp.11:32:
The text says the Egyptians pressed the Israelites and hurried to send them out of their land. The words "urged" and "in haste" are the ones that express this pressure and urgency. They were afraid, and so they said, "We be all dead men," meaning, "we are all going to die."

This happens after the tenth plague, the death of the firstborn. The pharaoh had called Moses and Aaron at night and allowed them to leave. Now the Egyptian people, struck by grief and terror, also want them gone quickly. What they had earlier refused to accept, they now demand with urgency.

For today: God can change hearts and even the hardest circumstances at the moment He decides. If you face a situation that seems closed, keep trusting and obeying, because God is faithful to His promises.
exp.26:7:
God tells Moses that the bronze altar must be made of boards and be hollow inside, that is, like a box with nothing filling it. "Thou shalt make it" is a direct command. The mountain refers to Mount Sinai, where God showed him the design. Some believe the altar was filled with earth or stones when it was used, but the text does not make this clear.

God speaks, and Moses receives instructions for building the tabernacle, the place where Israel would worship while traveling through the wilderness. God does not leave the design to human imagination. What is built must correspond to the pattern He showed. This sentence sums up the obedience expected of Moses.

Today, we can learn that serving God does not mean doing it our own way, but listening to His Word and obeying it carefully, even in the details that seem small.
exp.16:12:
It says that Joshua defeated Amalek and his people in battle. The word for "defeated" means beaten or overcome. The phrase "with the edge of the sword" is an older way of describing fighting with a sword. Amalek was an enemy people who attacked Israel in the desert.

The account is told by the narrator of Exodus, traditionally Moses. Israel had just come out of Egypt and was attacked at Rephidim. While Joshua fought, Moses kept his hands raised, and Aaron and Hur held them up. The victory came through the effort of everyone. Afterward God commanded that it be written down as a memorial, and Moses built an altar called "Jehovah-nissi," which is usually understood to mean "the Lord is my banner."

For today: we do not fight alone. Carry out your responsibilities faithfully, but pray and lean on God. Let others support you when you are tired, and support those who need it.
exp.34:17:
It says that the people were also to bring the pins of the tabernacle and the pins of the court, together with their cords. The pins were long stakes driven into the ground, and the cords held the curtains and the tent so that they would not move in the wind. The court was the open area that surrounded the tabernacle.

Moses speaks to the whole congregation of Israel and repeats what God had commanded for building his sanctuary. This list includes even the smallest details, and all of them were necessary so that the tabernacle would stay firm while the people traveled through the desert.

For today: God values small and hidden services, not only the ones that are seen. There are simple tasks, such as helping, tidying up, praying, or accompanying others, that sustain God's work. Do your part faithfully, even when no one notices it.
exp.28:2:
God commands that the breads, the cakes, and the wafers made without yeast are to be placed together in one basket. Then they are brought before God, along with the young bull and the two rams. The sentence about the small basket and "to offer" is dropped because those words are not in the verse your reader sees; the verse itself says "one basket" and "bring them in the basket."

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai. He gives instructions for consecrating Aaron and his sons as priests of Israel. The breads without yeast and the animals without defect were part of that ceremony. Many understand that the absence of yeast spoke of purity and complete devotion, although the text does not explain this in detail here.

Today we can learn that serving God begins with bringing Him the best we have, with a sincere heart. Think of one concrete thing, such as your time, your work, or your talents, and give it to Him today with gratitude and without holding anything back.
exp.28:15:
He says that Moses was to kill the ram, take its blood, and splash it on all sides of the altar. The word translated "sprinkle" means to scatter or splatter. This ram was the first of two and was offered whole as a burnt offering, meaning it was burned up entirely.

God speaks to Moses at Sinai. He gives instructions for setting apart Aaron and his sons as priests. Before this, they placed their hands on the head of the animal, a gesture that many understand as identifying themselves with the offering. The blood represented life given up, and the altar was the place where God received the offering.

For today: God takes sin and total surrender seriously. Christians believe that Christ offered his life for us. We can respond by giving God everything, not just a part, with gratitude and sincerity.
exp.14:4:
This verse describes what happened to the Egyptian soldiers in the sea. The deep waters covered them completely, and they sank to the bottom like a stone. The phrase "the depths" refers to the deepest parts of the sea. "Red Sea" is the traditional name for the sea that Israel crossed, although some scholars debate exactly where it took place.

Moses and the Israelites sing this hymn after crossing the sea and seeing that Pharaoh's army has been destroyed. They had been slaves in Egypt, and now they celebrate that God has rescued them. The song presents the Lord as the one who fights for his people.

For today: when you feel that something is chasing you and there seems to be no way out, remember that God has delivered his people before. You can bring your fear to him in prayer and then give thanks for his help, as Israel did.
exp.24:19:
God describes how the two golden cherubim must be placed above the ark. They will have their wings spread upward, covering the lid of the ark, which is also called the mercy seat. Their faces will be turned toward one another, looking down toward that lid.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai, giving him instructions to build the tabernacle, his sanctuary among the people. Later he says that from that place, between the cherubim, he would speak with Moses. The cherubim are spiritual beings who serve God; the Bible does not give a single detailed description of their appearance.

For today: God wanted to be close to his people and to communicate with them. We can approach him with reverence and attention, setting aside a moment each day to listen to him in his Word, with humility and respect.
exp.9:17:
This verse says that Moses left the presence of the king of Egypt and prayed to God, asking Him to remove the plague. "And he went out from Pharaoh" means that he went away from where the king was. "The Lord" is the name of God, and "intreated" means that he prayed to Him.

Pharaoh had just admitted that he had sinned and begged Moses and Aaron to pray for forgiveness on his behalf. The land was covered with locusts that devoured everything. Moses did not argue or reproach him; he went straight to God. But what follows shows that Pharaoh's repentance was not deep, because his heart hardened again.

Today we can learn from Moses to pray even for those who have treated us badly or are not sincere. It also reminds us that saying "I was wrong" is not enough; God seeks a real change of heart.
exp.10:0:
God tells Moses that one more plague will come upon Pharaoh and Egypt, the last one. After it, Pharaoh will let the Israelites go. The words "he shall surely thrust you out hence altogether" mean that he will send them away completely, even driving them out. The word "plague" here means a strong blow or punishment.

The Lord speaks, and gives these words to Moses after nine plagues in which Pharaoh hardened his heart again and again. God announces that the end is near. The verses that follow show that the people leave with favor among the Egyptians. This final plague is the death of the firstborn, which is explained in the next chapter.

For today: although difficult situations sometimes seem never to change, God knows when the time of deliverance will come. We can keep trusting and obeying with patience, knowing that he fulfills what he promises.
exp.9:20:
God tells Moses to stretch out his hand toward heaven, so that darkness will fall over the land of Egypt, a darkness so thick that it can be felt, that is, touched or sensed. "Jehovah" is the name of God, and "Red Sea" is the sea that the Israelites crossed.

God speaks now, sending the ninth plague. Pharaoh remains stubborn: after seeing the locusts disappear, he again refused to let Israel go. The Egyptians worshiped the sun, so this darkness confronted their gods. It is not known with certainty how it happened; the text only says it was dense and supernatural.

For today: when the heart becomes hard, life grows dark even when there is light all around. Today we can ask God for a heart willing to listen and to obey quickly, without waiting for things to get worse.
exp.17:21:
This verse says that the appointed judges will help Moses settle the people's problems at all times. They themselves will resolve the small matters, and the serious cases will be brought to Moses. In this way his load will be lighter, because others will carry it with him.

The one speaking is Jethro, Moses' father-in-law. He had seen that Moses spent the whole day judging the people's cases and was wearing himself out. Jethro advised him to share the work among honest men who feared God. Moses listened to the advice and put it into practice.

For today: you do not have to carry everything by yourself. Whether in the family, the church, or the workplace, entrust tasks to honest and capable people. Sharing responsibility protects your health and also helps others grow and serve.
exp.24:16:
God tells Moses to make a lid of pure gold for the ark. The "cover" is the lid of the ark, which is later called the mercy seat. A cubit was roughly half a meter, so it measured about 1.10 meters long by 70 centimeters wide. It was the same size as the ark.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai while giving him the instructions for the tabernacle. Inside the ark would go the tablets of the testimony, that is, the law. Over them this lid would be placed, and then the cherubim. Many understand that there God would meet with his people; the text says so later on.

God wanted a place where his people could draw near to him with forgiveness and not only with judgment. Today we can approach God with confidence, knowing that his mercy covers our failings.
exp.17:17:
Here Jethro tells Moses that he will wear himself out completely, and the people waiting for their turn with him as well. "Wear away" means to lose your strength, and "this thing" refers to the task, the matter at hand. In other words, the burden of attending to everyone is too great for one person.

Jethro, Moses' father-in-law, speaks. He had visited the camp and saw that Moses spent the whole day settling the people's disputes. With affection but also with frankness, he says, "Thou art not able to perform it thyself alone." Then he offers a plan, which the following verses lay out: teach the law and share the work.

For today: you do not have to carry everything by yourself. Recognizing your limits is not a lack of faith but wisdom. Accept help, share responsibilities, and listen to the advice of sensible people who care for you.
exp.12:9:
This verse says that the people of Israel were to observe this ceremony every year, at the appointed time. The word "ordinance" refers to a ceremony or practice with set steps, and "keep" means they were to carry it out faithfully.

Moses speaks to the people just freed from Egypt. The ordinance refers to the Feast of Unleavened Bread and the Passover, which are explained in the verses before. God wanted each generation to remember their deliverance and to tell it to their children. Repeating the feast every year helped them not to forget what God had done.

For today: memory needs habits. We can set aside regular moments, such as a Sunday, a family meal, or a devotional time, to remember and to tell others what God has done for us.
exp.34:23:
This verse says that whoever was willing to give silver or bronze brought it as an offering to the Lord. And whoever had acacia wood brought it for all the work of the service, that is, for building the tabernacle.

The people of Israel were in the wilderness, and Moses had passed on God's command to build a sanctuary where He would dwell among them. Moses invited them to give willingly. The text repeats that each person brought what they had, and not everyone gave the same amount.

For today: God does not ask for what we do not have, but for us to joyfully use what is already in our hands. Think about what you have, whether time, a talent, or money, and offer it wholeheartedly to serve God and your community.
exp.31:0:
This verse tells how the people of Israel saw that Moses was taking a long time to come down from Mount Sinai. So they gathered around Aaron and asked him to make them gods to lead them. They said they did not know what had happened to Moses. The people are the ones speaking, and they address Aaron, Moses' brother, who had been left in charge. They recognize Moses as the one who brought them out, but they do not mention God.

The Israelites had been freed from Egypt shortly before. Moses was on the mountain with God, receiving his law. As many days passed, the people grew impatient and afraid.

For today: when God seems slow, it is easy to look for quick solutions that appear or feel secure. We can instead wait patiently, remain faithful, and trust that God is still present, even when we do not yet see him acting.
exp.30:17:
He says that when God finished speaking with Moses on Mount Sinai, he gave him two tables of the covenant, that is, two stone tablets that served as a record of the agreement. They were written by the finger of God, a way of saying that the work came directly from Him.

God had spent forty days instructing Moses about the tabernacle, the priests, and the Sabbath. These tablets put the covenant with Israel, the people He had rescued from Egypt, into writing. It is almost always understood that they contained the Ten Commandments, although this verse does not list them. Soon after, the people would sin with the golden calf.

For today: God wanted to leave His word in writing so that it would not be forgotten or distorted. Set aside time each week to read the Bible calmly, as one who receives something valuable from God's hands, and ask Him for help to put it into practice.
exp.25:1:
This verse gives the measurements of each curtain of the tabernacle: twenty-eight cubits long and four cubits wide. A cubit was the approximate distance from the elbow to the tip of the fingers, about 45 to 50 centimeters, so each curtain measured close to 13 meters by 2 meters. All of them were to be exactly the same.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai and gives him instructions for building the tabernacle, a holy tent where God would dwell among Israel while they journeyed through the wilderness. The curtains, joined in two sets of five, would form the inner covering of that tent.

For today: God cares about order and care in small things. We can serve Him faithfully and diligently in our everyday lives, knowing that every piece, even the simplest, matters when it is made for Him.
exp.27:34:
This verse speaks of the robe of the priest Aaron, which had little golden bells around its hem. "Upon Aaron" refers to that robe. The phrase "to minister" means serving in his office. The sound of the bells "shall be heard" as Aaron went into the holy place and as he came out, "that he die not."

God gives these instructions to Moses on Mount Sinai, as he describes the holy garments of the priests. Coming before the Lord was something very serious, and it had to be done with reverence and as God had directed. Scholars do not fully agree on the exact purpose of the sound: some think it showed that the priest was still alive and was serving in an orderly way; others think it announced his presence before God.

For today: approach God with reverence and gratitude, not with carelessness. Before you pray or read the Bible, pause briefly and remember who God is.
exp.7:20:
God warns Pharaoh that, if he does not let his people go, He will send swarms of flies upon him, his servants, his people, and into his houses. The houses of the Egyptians will be full of swarms of flies, and the ground where they stand as well.

The LORD speaks through Moses. This is the fourth plague. The magicians had already recognized the finger of God in an earlier plague, but Pharaoh hardened his heart. God first gives a warning, and then promises to set a difference between Goshen, where Israel lived, and the rest of Egypt. The Hebrew text does not make clear with certainty what kind of insect it was; some think of flies, others of various insects.

For today: God speaks to us patiently before He corrects us. If you sense that He is calling you to change something, do not harden your heart; respond with humility today.
exp.9:7:
This verse tells that Moses and Aaron were called back before Pharaoh. He says to them, "Go, serve the Lord your God," but then immediately asks, "But who exactly is going to go?"

Pharaoh's servants, frightened by the plagues, had urged him to let the people go, because Egypt was being ruined. Pharaoh seems to give in, but he sets conditions. In the verses that follow, Moses answers that everyone will go, and Pharaoh becomes angry. His apparent permission was a negotiation, not a sincere obedience.

For today: sometimes we want to obey God only in part, or on our own terms. God invites us to serve him with our whole heart and with our whole family. Today you can ask yourself: is there some area of my life that I am leaving out?
exp.26:2:
God gives Moses instructions about the utensils of the altar. The pots were for collecting the ashes; the shovels, for removing them; the basins, for catching the blood; the hooks, for handling the flesh; and the firepans, for carrying the coals. Everything was to be made of metal, which at that time was usually bronze or copper (the translations vary).

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai while showing him how to build the tabernacle, the tent of meeting where Israel met with him. The altar was the place of the sacrifices, and even the simplest objects were to be made as God had directed. Their exact use is explained in other passages.

For today: God also cares about small and unremarkable service. Today you can offer him your daily work, such as cleaning, tidying, or helping quietly, doing it with care and from the heart, as for him.
exp.4:5:
This verse says that on the same day Moses and Aaron spoke with him, Pharaoh gave an order. He addressed it to the taskmasters, who were the overseers who watched over the workers, and to the officers, who were the Israelite foremen placed under them. The word "commanded" here means "gave orders."

Pharaoh is the one speaking. Moses and Aaron had asked him to let the people go to worship God in the wilderness. Instead of listening, Pharaoh took this as an excuse from lazy people and decided to increase the burden. His response was immediate and harsh.

For today: sometimes, when we try to obey God, things get worse at first. That does not mean God has abandoned us. Let us keep trusting Him, even when the world's response is rejection.
exp.2:20:
God promises that His people, Israel, will find favor before the Egyptians. "Favor in the sight of" means that the Egyptians will look on them kindly and treat them with goodness. "When ye go" means "when they leave." So they will not go out "empty," that is, with their hands holding nothing, after so many years of slavery.

God speaks to Moses from the burning bush, when He sends him to bring Israel out of Egypt. Earlier He had told him that Pharaoh would not give in easily, but that He would act with power. This promise shows that God cares not only for the freedom of His people, but also for their provision for the journey.

For today: when God calls you to take a difficult step, trust that He will also care for whatever you need. Obey and take the step, and do not let the fear of being left without resources defeat you.
exp.8:5:
The explanation says that the next day God did what he had announced: a plague killed the livestock of Egypt, but not a single animal belonging to the Israelites died. "Livestock" refers to farm animals such as horses, donkeys, camels, cows and sheep. "Children of Israel" is the Hebrew people.

This is the fifth plague. Through Moses, God had warned Pharaoh in advance and even named the day. His purpose was that Pharaoh would let the people go. The difference between the Egyptians and the Israelites showed that this was no coincidence. Even so, Pharaoh saw the fact and hardened his heart.

For today: God keeps his word, and he also cares for his own in ways we sometimes do not understand. Trust him, and when you see his work clearly, do not harden your heart; respond to him with obedience.
exp.20:24:
If someone causes another person a burn, a wound, or a bruise, the punishment must match that injury. A "wound" is an injury that breaks the skin, and a "bruise" is a dark mark left by a blow. This is the continuation of the rule of "eye for eye."

God speaks to Moses and gives laws to the people of Israel after freeing them from Egypt. This rule worked as a limit for judges: justice had to be proportionate, without exaggerated revenge. The verses that follow show that even a mistreated servant was to receive justice and freedom. Some scholars think it was applied through compensation and not always literally; the text does not fully make this clear.

For today: when someone wounds you, seek justice without revenge. Respond with moderation, forgive, and do not repay evil with evil.
exp.18:13:
This verse tells that Moses came down from the mountain and went to where the people were. There he sanctified them, that is, set them apart and prepared them for a special meeting with God. As part of that preparation, the people washed their clothes.

God had told Moses that in three days he would appear to the people on Mount Sinai. Moses acts as a mediator: he passes on what God commands. Washing clothes was an outward sign of cleanness and reverence before a holy God. The Bible does not give more details of the rite here.

For today: before prayer, before reading the Bible, or before gathering with others, take a moment to calm your heart. Ask God to cleanse you inwardly, and approach him with reverence and gratitude, not with haste or out of mere habit.
exp.20:14:
It says that whoever strikes his father or his mother must be put to death. The word "smiteth" means to strike or hurt violently. "Shall be surely put to death" was the penalty the law set for that act.

God speaks through Moses to the people of Israel, newly come out of Egypt, in the laws given at Sinai. These rules shaped the life of a new nation. In that world, the family held society together, and attacking one's parents was an attack on the most basic authority of the household. Some scholars think this refers to a serious, deliberate blow rather than an accident, but the text does not spell this out.

For today: we do not live under that civil law, but the principle of honoring one's parents still stands. We can respect them with kind words, patience, and care, and seek help if there is violence at home.
exp.12:18:
Moses took with him the bones of Joseph. Before he died, Joseph had made the Israelites swear an oath that when God came to their aid and rescued them, they would carry his bones up out of Egypt with them. To swear an oath means to bind them to a promise made under oath.

The narrator tells this in the middle of the departure from Egypt. Centuries earlier, Joseph had spoken these words at the end of his life (Genesis 50:24-25). Now the people carry out the promise. This shows that Joseph believed God would fulfill what he had promised to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and that Israel remembered his word.

For today: keeping what we promise, even when a long time passes, is a way of honoring God and others. We can also live with the same hope as Joseph, trusting that God is faithful even when we do not see the fulfillment right away.
exp.22:26:
He says that God himself will go before Israel. The enemies' "turning their backs" was an expression meaning that they would be seen fleeing, showing their backs, defeated.

God speaks to Israel through Moses, in the laws given at Sinai, shortly after leaving Egypt. It is part of a promise: if the people served the LORD alone, He would bless them and bring them into the promised land. The verses that follow explain that the conquest would be gradual, not all at once.

For today: when you face a challenge that frightens you, remember that God goes before you. Obeying Him and trusting Him does not remove the difficulties, but it gives you the assurance that you do not advance alone.
exp.37:8:
This verse tells how Bezaleel and his helpers built the court, the open area that surrounded the tabernacle. On the south side, they hung curtains that were one hundred cubits long. A cubit was about half a meter, so the curtains measured roughly 45 to 50 meters. They were made of fine twined linen, that is, thin thread that was finely twisted together.

The narrator of the book, traditionally Moses, describes how the instructions God had given for His sanctuary were carried out. The court marked a boundary: it separated the holy space from the camp and showed that approaching God involves order and reverence.

Today we can learn that God cares about details and reverence. We can come to Him with confidence, but also with an attentive heart, carefully obeying what He asks of us.
exp.3:22:
God tells Moses what he must say to Pharaoh. Israel is his son, and he asks that Pharaoh let him go so that he may serve him, that is, worship him. The firstborn is the eldest son, the one who holds the most important place. Since Pharaoh refused to obey, God announces that he will take the life of Pharaoh's firstborn son.

The LORD speaks to Moses before he returns to Egypt. God had already warned him that Pharaoh would harden his heart. This message is a serious warning: God defends his people and calls Pharaoh to obey. Later on, the story is fulfilled in the last plague.

For today: God speaks to us with clarity and hopes that we will answer him with obedience. It is not wise to harden the heart. If today he points something out to you, answer him with humility and trust.
exp.11:3:
If a household was too small to eat the whole lamb, it was to invite its nearest neighbour to share it. The amount was worked out according to the number of people and how much each one could eat.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron and tells them to speak to the whole congregation of Israel before the departure from Egypt. He was preparing the first Passover. The instruction aimed to ensure that nothing of the lamb would be wasted and that no household would be left without taking part.

For today: do not celebrate or enjoy only what God has given you. Think of a neighbour, a brother or sister in the church, or someone who is alone, and invite them to your table. Sharing generously reflects the heart of God.
exp.11:30:
He called for Moses and Aaron in the middle of the night. He ordered them to leave among his people, together with all the Israelites, and to go and serve the Lord, just as they had asked.

Pharaoh speaks, broken by the death of the firstborn, the tenth plague. For months he had refused to let Israel go, but now the grief of all Egypt forces him to give way. Moses had asked to leave in order to worship God in the wilderness, and now Pharaoh repeats those very words.

For today: God keeps what he promises, even when it seems that no one can stop those who oppress us. We can trust that he is faithful and keep obeying him with patience, even when the answer is slow in coming.
exp.25:20:
Here the text speaks of the "basas," which are bases or pedestals. Each wooden board on the north side of the tabernacle rested on two silver bases, and there were forty in total. In this way the boards stood firm and upright.

God gives these instructions to Moses on Mount Sinai. He wants the people to build a portable sanctuary where He can dwell among them. Later, Exodus 38 tells how the silver for the bases came from the money each Israelite gave as a ransom. Some see in this a sign that worship is supported by redemption.

For today: God is concerned even with what almost no one sees. Think about what holds up your life of faith. Take care of your foundations, such as prayer, the Word, and community, because your steadiness depends on them.
exp.7:8:
Moses says to Pharaoh, "Glory over me," which means something like "You have the honor; you choose." He lets Pharaoh choose the time when Moses will pray for the frogs to be removed from him, from his houses, from his servants and from his people, so that they remain only in the river.

Pharaoh had just asked Moses and Aaron to pray to take away the frogs, and he promised to let the people go. Moses speaks with respect, but with confidence. By letting Pharaoh choose the hour, it will be clear that the plague ends by the power of God and not by chance. Pharaoh answers, "Tomorrow."

For today: we can trust that God acts in his own time and in a clear way. We also learn to pray with humility and sincerity, even for those who have wronged us, and to keep what we promise without delay.
exp.12:14:
It says that Pharaoh became stubborn and would not let the people of Israel go. Because of this, God caused every firstborn in Egypt to die, both of people and of animals. For this reason the Israelite offers to God every first male of his animals, and sets apart his firstborn sons by paying a price. To redeem is to pay a price to take back something that belongs to God.

Moses speaks to the people shortly after the departure from Egypt. He explains to them how to answer when their children ask why they do this. The rite serves to remember the tenth plague and the deliverance. The details of how it was practiced over time are explained in other passages.

Today we can teach our children, in simple terms, what God has done for us. Remembering his help and thanking him through concrete acts, such as giving the first of our time or resources, keeps our faith alive.
exp.15:23:
This verse says that the people kept some of the manna until the next morning, just as Moses had commanded. This time it did not spoil: it did not go bad, and no worms were in it.

The Israelites were traveling through the wilderness, and God fed them with manna every day. On the other days, what they saved filled with worms and smelled bad. But before the Sabbath, Moses told them, on God's behalf, to gather double and keep what was left over. In this way they could rest on that day. The people obeyed, and God took care of the food they had saved.

Today we can learn to trust that God provides, and to obey him when he asks us to rest. Planning ahead helps us set aside time for rest, without worrying too much.
exp.6:8:
God tells Moses what to do if Pharaoh asks them for a sign. The word "responds" stands in for the verse's wording, and a "miracle" is a sign that shows God sent them. Aaron was to take his staff, throw it down in front of Pharaoh, and the staff would become a serpent, that is, a snake.

The Lord speaks to Moses and Aaron, who were already elderly, eighty and eighty-three years old. God prepares them in advance, since he knows Pharaoh will hesitate. The sign was meant to show that their message came from God. The passage that follows tells how the magicians of Egypt did something similar, and scholars explain in several ways how they managed it.

For today: God does not ask us to obey blindly, but prepares us for what is coming. We can take the step he asks of us, even when others doubt or resist, trusting that he sustains his work.
exp.28:10:
He says that Moses was to sacrifice the young bull (a young ox) in the presence of God, right at the entrance of the tabernacle. "Before the Lord" means that the act was done as if before God's own eyes. "Tabernacle of the congregation" was the sacred tent where the ark with the tablets of the law was kept.

God speaks to Moses and gives him instructions for consecrating Aaron and his sons as priests. Before serving, they placed their hands on the animal, and the blood was used at the altar. This showed that they needed to be cleansed from sin before drawing near to God.

For today: approaching God requires humility and sincerity. Christians believe that Jesus made the final sacrifice for us, so we can come to God with confidence, grateful and ready to live for him.
exp.26:8:
God tells Moses to make the courtyard of the tabernacle, the open enclosure that surrounded the sacred tent. The south side, which the text calls the south side, would have hangings of finely twined linen, that is, fine linen woven from interlaced threads, one hundred cubits long on that side. A cubit measured about half a meter, so the length would have been around fifty meters.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai, giving him detailed instructions to build a place where he would dwell among Israel. Shortly before, the altar is described, and it is recalled that everything had to be made according to the pattern shown on the mountain. The hangings marked out a separate and orderly space for drawing near to God.

For today: God cares about the details and desires that we approach him with reverence and order. We can set aside a quiet moment each day to pray, putting distractions aside.
exp.17:26:
It says that Moses let his father-in-law, Jethro, go, and that Jethro returned to his own land. "Let go" here means he sent him off with respect, not that he drove him away. "Went his way" is an old way of saying he left.

The narrator is the author of the book, who describes how Jethro's visit ends. He had come to the camp and saw Moses worn out, judging the people alone. He advised him to share the work with capable men, and Moses did so. This verse closes the scene. Jethro was a priest of Midian and was not part of Israel. That is why he takes his leave and goes back home. The text says nothing more about his return.

For today: Moses listened to wise advice, put it into practice, and sent off with gratitude the one who helped him. Learn to receive help, to share responsibilities, and to thank those who guide you.
exp.19:21:
God tells Moses to remind the people of something they have already lived through: they themselves heard God's voice speaking "from heaven." The name "Jehovah" is God's name, and the phrase "you have seen" means "you have seen." God does not speak to them as people who had only heard rumors, but as witnesses.

This takes place right after the giving of the Ten Commandments. The people were afraid and stayed back, and Moses drew near to the thick darkness where God was. Now God speaks through Moses to remind them of what they witnessed. Right away He forbids them to make idols and gives them instructions for worshiping Him. What they experienced is the foundation for what follows.

Today we can remember the times God has shown Himself faithful in our lives, in His Word, and in what we have seen of His care. That remembrance helps us obey Him with confidence and not look for support in things that cannot save.
exp.39:28:
He put the altar of burnt offering at the entrance of the tabernacle, the tent where God met with his people. There he offered the burnt offering, an animal burned completely for God, and the grain offering. Everything was done just as the Lord had commanded.

Here the narrator of the book describes how Moses finishes setting up the tabernacle, in the first year after leaving Egypt. The altar stood at the entrance, so no one could approach God without first passing through the sacrifice. This underlines that God himself marks the way to draw near to him.

For today: draw near to God with obedience and humility, not on your own terms. Today you can ask yourself: is there something God has already asked of me in his Word that I am still putting off?
exp.38:36:
This verse is part of the list of the pieces of the tabernacle that the craftsmen presented to Moses. It mentions the pure gold lampstand, with its lamps (the small lights set on each branch), all its utensils, and the oil to keep the light burning. The word "vessels" here means utensils or tools, not cups.

The one who tells the account is the author of the book, traditionally understood to be Moses. After finishing the work, the people showed each object just as God had commanded. The list stresses obedience in the details. There are several interpretations of the symbolic meaning of the light, but the text only emphasizes that it was made and ready.

For today: just as the lampstand needed constant oil to give light, our life of faith needs daily care. Find a short moment each day to pray and read the Bible, and let God be the one who fills and guides you.
exp.39:33:
Dice que, cuando Moisés terminó de armar todo el tabernáculo, una nube lo cubrió y la presencia de Dios, llamada "the glory of the Lord", lo llenó por completo.

Es el final del libro de Éxodo. El narrador cuenta que Moisés hizo todo tal como Dios lo había mandado. Después de la obra, Dios mismo responde y viene a habitar entre Israel. Tanto la nube como la gloria muestran que Dios estaba realmente presente y que guiaría al pueblo.

Para hoy: Dios se acerca a quienes lo buscan con obediencia y reverencia. Antes de pedirle grandes cosas, podemos preparar el corazón, hacer lo que él ya nos mostró y desear su presencia más que sus beneficios.
exp.30:3:
This verse says that God gave Bezalel the ability to "devise cunning works", that is, to think up and plan artistic works with creativity. He also gave him the skill to work in gold, in silver, and in brass (here the word for "brass" most likely refers to bronze).

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai while giving him instructions for building the tabernacle, the tent where the people would worship. God himself chooses Bezalel, from the tribe of Judah, and gives him the skill for this work. Then he adds Aholiab as an assistant. The text shows that God cares even about the details of the work.

For today: talents and trades, whether manual, artistic, or technical, can be gifts from God. We can offer our work with excellence and gratitude, serving others and honoring God.
exp.19:1:
It says God presents himself to his people with his name, and reminds them what he did for them: he brought them out of Egypt, here called the house of bondage, that is, a place where they were enslaved. The word bondage here means slavery, a state of having no freedom.

God himself is speaking, just before giving the Ten Commandments on Mount Sinai. Before asking for obedience, God begins by reminding them of his love and his deliverance. The Israelites had just been set free, so the relationship begins with grace, not with demands. Then comes the first commandment: no other gods.

For today: before we think about what God asks of us, we can remember what he has already done for us. Today, take a moment to thank him for a specific situation in your life where you felt his help or deliverance, and let that gratitude move your obedience.
exp.38:14:
They made chains for the breastplate, thin ropes of pure gold woven like braids or cords, to fasten at its ends. The breastplate is the high priest's piece of cloth set with twelve precious stones. The chains held it in place, attaching it to the other parts of his garment.

Here the account tells how Bezalel and the other workers carried out everything God had commanded Moses for the tabernacle and the sacred clothing. The stones bore the names of the twelve tribes, so the priest carried all the people on his chest before God.

For today: God cares for even the smallest details, and he cares for you too. Just as the chains kept the names of Israel secure, you can trust that God holds you up. Do your work faithfully, even when it seems small.
exp.28:26:
God tells Moses to set apart two parts of the ram used in the ordination of the priests: the breast and the shoulder (the front leg or foreleg). The word "waved" means it was presented by being moved back and forth before God, as if handing it over to Him. "Sanctified" means set apart for sacred use.

God speaks to Moses at Sinai while giving him the instructions for consecrating Aaron and his sons as priests. These portions, first offered to God, would then become food for the priests, as the next verse says. In this way God cared for those who served Him.

For today: what we have first we present to God with gratitude, and He often cares for those who serve. We can support generously those who are devoted to ministry in our church.
exp.1:0:
This verse says that a man from the family of Levi married a woman who was also from the tribe of Levi. The word "man" means a man, and "went" and "took to wife" simply mean that he got married. The names of the couple are not yet mentioned here.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book of Exodus. After telling how the people of Israel were oppressed in Egypt, he begins the story of an ordinary family. Later, the Bible says they were Amram and Jochebed (Exodus 6:20), and from them Moses would be born. Some scholars note that "daughter of Levi" may mean a descendant of that tribe.

For today: God often begins great things with simple and faithful families. Your home, though it may seem small or unimportant, can be a place where God works. Trust Him and be faithful in everyday life.
exp.39:16:
The explanation says that the tabernacle, the holy tent where God would dwell among his people, was raised up on the first day of the first month of the second year. That is, almost a year after Israel left Egypt. "Was reared up" means it was set up and stood on its feet. The word "was" appears in the verse, so the sentence about the old spelling is deleted.

The narrator of the book, traditionally understood to be Moses, tells that what God had commanded was fulfilled. For months the people had prepared each piece according to the pattern received on the mountain. This verse marks the moment when everything is ready. Later, the cloud of God's glory will fill the place.

For today: God values patient and complete obedience. Moses did not do things his own way or halfway. Today we can ask ourselves what small step of obedience God is asking of us, and take it with steadiness, trusting that He will take care of the rest.
exp.11:44:
This verse says that two kinds of people could not eat the Passover lamb: the foreigner and the hired servant. A "foreigner" was someone passing through, living among the people for a time. A "hired servant" was a worker brought in for pay, who was not part of the family.

God himself speaks to Moses and Aaron and gives them the rules of the Passover. The feast remembered Israel's deliverance from Egypt. Taking part in it was a sign of belonging to the people of the covenant. For that reason, whoever was not joined to the family or to the community through the covenant did not eat. A bought slave, however, could eat, if he was circumcised, since he entered the household and the covenant.

For today: God's table is a place of belonging, not of mere convenience. We can ask ourselves whether we draw near to God only for what we receive, or as members of his family, with a sincere commitment.
exp.29:3:
God tells Moses to make two golden rings for the altar of incense. They are to go under the golden crown, at two corners, one on each side. Through these rings the poles, which are long wooden bars, would be placed so the altar could be carried without anyone touching it directly. The phrase "corners" here is understood to mean the two sides of the altar.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai, giving him instructions for the tabernacle, the tent of worship the people used in the wilderness. The altar of incense stood in front of the veil, near the ark. Because the people moved from place to place, the altar had to be portable, carried with order and respect.

God cares about the details of how he is worshiped. Today we can draw near to him with reverence and order, knowing that our prayer, like incense, is precious to him. Take a quiet moment of prayer today, without rushing.
exp.9:22:
It says that the darkness in Egypt was so thick that no one could see another person, and people stayed in their place for three days. By contrast, the Israelites had light in their homes. The explanation of the word "neighbor" and "dwellings" has been left out, since those words do not appear in the verse you are reading.

This is the account of the ninth plague. God told Moses to stretch out his hand, and a darkness came that could almost be felt. Egypt worshiped sun gods, so this plague showed that the LORD rules over light and darkness. The Bible does not explain how it happened, and some see it as a miracle that goes beyond natural laws. Afterward, Pharaoh again negotiated with Moses.

For today: God cares for his own even when everything around seems dark. In difficult days, seek his light in prayer and in his Word, and trust that he does not forget you.
exp.34:10:
This verse is part of a list of what was to be built for the tabernacle, the sacred tent where God dwelt among his people. It mentions the tent, its covering, the clasps, the boards, the bars, the pillars, and the sockets (the bases where the pillars rested).

Moses speaks to the people of Israel in the wilderness. He repeats what God commanded and invites them to take part, bringing offerings and using their skills. Earlier, he said that everyone who was skilled, every person with a gift for the work, should come and labor.

For today: God values even the small details, like a clasp or a base. Your service, though it may seem hardly visible, matters. Offer your skill to God with joy, knowing that it supports something greater.
exp.14:6:
This verse says that God, with his great power, brought down those who rose up against him. "Overthrown" means to bring down or make fall. "Wrath" is his righteous anger. "Stubble" refers to the dry remains of leaves or straw, which the fire consumes instantly.

Moses and the Israelites sing after crossing the Red Sea. The Egyptian army was pursuing them, and God saved them from slavery. The song celebrates that the power that delivered them was God's and not their own. What seemed an invincible enemy fell with ease.

For today: when you face something that seems bigger than you, remember that God is still stronger. Trust in him, and when he helps you, give him thanks out loud, as they did.
exp.25:0:
God tells Moses to make the tabernacle with ten curtains of fine twined linen, woven or dyed in blue (a deep blue, almost violet), purple, and scarlet (an intense red). He also asks that cherubim, angelic beings, be worked into them with fine and careful craftsmanship. "Delicate work" speaks of an art done with great care.

God speaks on Mount Sinai, shortly after freeing Israel from Egypt. He wants a holy tent in which to dwell among his people. The details are very precise because everything had to be done as He directed. Scholars see in the cherubim a sign of God's presence and holiness, though not all explain each symbol in the same way.

Today we can learn that God values excellence and reverence. Let us serve Him with care and from the heart, not carelessly, whether in church, at work, or at home.
exp.24:18:
It says that Moses was to put one cherub at each end of the gold cover, one on one side and the other on the opposite side. The cherubim were not made separately and attached: they were made from the same piece as the cover, forming a single work. The cover is the lid of the ark, also called the mercy seat. A cubit measures roughly half a meter.

God himself speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai. He gives him instructions for building the tabernacle, a place where his presence would dwell among Israel. The ark would hold the tablets of the law, and above the cover God would meet with Moses. The cherubim are beings who attend God's presence; their exact appearance is not described here.

God cares about the details of how we draw near to him, and he wants us to approach him with reverence. Today we can set aside a few minutes of prayer to come before him with respect and gratitude, knowing that he receives us with mercy.
exp.15:20:
They went out every morning to gather the manna, and each person gathered what they needed to eat. When the sun grew hot, the manna that was left on the ground melted away. The words "melted away" translate the source's wording, and the phrase "as soon as" means "as soon as the sun grew hot."

The narrator tells how God fed his people in the desert. Moses had commanded them not to keep manna until the next day, but some disobeyed, and the manna became full of worms. God was teaching them to trust his daily provision, one day at a time.

For today: we can practice trusting God for each day's needs, without letting anxiety about tomorrow take over our lives. Ask God today for what is necessary, and give thanks for what he has already given you, working diligently and without hoarding out of fear.
exp.38:6:
It says that Bezalel and the craftsmen set the two onyx stones on the shoulder pieces of the ephod, which was a sacred garment of the priest. It calls them "stones for a memorial," that is, stones to bring to mind. On them were engraved the names of the children of Israel. And everything was made just as the Lord had commanded Moses.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, and tells how the tabernacle was finished. Aaron, the high priest, would carry those stones on his shoulders when he came before God. In this way he represented the people. Some see here an image of bearing the people before the Lord, although the text itself speaks only of a memorial.

For today: you can carry in prayer the people you love, mentioning their names before God. Also, notice the careful obedience of those who did the work: God cares about the small things.
exp.18:4:
God tells Israel that, if they listen to his voice and keep his covenant, they will be his peculiar treasure among all peoples. "If ye will obey my voice indeed" is the verse's own phrasing, so the idea of listening closely and obeying is found in the words the reader sees. "Peculiar treasure" speaks of something very valuable and cherished, like a jewel kept with care. God adds that all the earth belongs to him.

The Lord speaks through Moses at Mount Sinai, shortly after bringing Israel out of Egypt. First he reminds them of what he has done for them: he carried them as on eagles' wings. Then he offers them a covenant relationship. His love came first; obedience is the response. Moreover, God does not choose them because he belongs only to them, but so that they may serve as a kingdom of priests among the nations.

Today we can remember that obedience springs from gratitude, not from fear. Ask yourself: what has God done for me, and how can I respond to him today by listening to him carefully?
exp.19:11:
It says we should honor our father and our mother. "Honor" means treating them with respect, worth, and consideration. The word "á" is an old way of writing "a," so that part needs no separate explanation. The promise is that in this way our days will be "prolonged," that is, that we will have a long and stable life in the land that God gave to his people.

God himself speaks to Israel at Mount Sinai, after bringing them out of Egypt. This is the fifth of the Ten Commandments. It comes right after the commandment about the Sabbath rest and before those that speak about how we treat our neighbor. In this way, it joins love for God with love for others, beginning with the family. Some see here a promise for the whole nation, not a personal guarantee.

Today, honoring your parents can be something simple: calling them, listening to them with patience, and thanking them, even when they do not agree with you or have failed.
exp.12:5:
For seven days the people were to eat bread without yeast. The phrase "eat unleavened bread" is the old wording here, and it refers to the same thing: bread made without yeast, so it does not rise or ferment. The seventh day would be a feast to the Lord, a time set apart for God.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel, who have just come out of Egypt. He gives them instructions to remember their deliverance every year, even after they are living in the promised land. The bread without yeast would bring that departure to mind, and parents were to tell their children about it.

For today: take time to remember what God has done for you and share it with your family. You can set aside a fixed moment, such as a meal or a prayer, to give thanks and pass on your faith to the younger generation.
exp.35:4:
The craftsmen went to tell Moses that the people were bringing far more than what was needed to build the sanctuary that God had commanded. The quoted words in the source are not in this verse, so I will not use them; the verse itself speaks of "the service of the work," which is the task or labor that had to be done.

This happens in the wilderness, while Israel is building the tabernacle, the tent where God would dwell among them. The skilled men who were directing the work saw more and more voluntary offerings arriving each morning. That is why they speak to Moses, and he orders that the donations be stopped. It is rare to see a people so generous that they must be asked to stop.

For today: God rejoices when we give willingly and not out of obligation. Ask yourself what you can offer freely, whether time, talent, or money, and do it without expecting applause. And if you lead something, be honest and open: say clearly when there is already enough.
exp.22:23:
God commands Israel three things: not to bow down before the gods of Canaan, not to serve them, and not to imitate their religious customs. Instead, they were to overthrow their images and break their statues (the pillars or sacred stones they used in worship). The word "break" here means to smash, and "utterly" means completely.

God himself speaks, through Moses, in the laws given at Sinai shortly after bringing Israel out of Egypt. He promises that his Angel will lead them toward the land of Canaan. The command aims to protect the people's loyalty, because idolatry and the practices of those nations could turn them away from God. Then he tells them that serving the LORD would bring blessing.

For today: ask yourself what things compete with God in your heart, such as money, fame, or bad habits. With God's help, set aside one concrete thing this week, so that he may take first place.
exp.39:20:
It says that Moses brought the ark into the tabernacle and hung up the veil, which was the curtain that separated the holy place from the most holy place. In this way the ark was covered and set apart from sight. The word "testimony" refers to the tablets of the law that were inside the ark. The phrase "as the Lord had commanded" is the one that is repeated throughout the chapter.

This takes place when the tabernacle is set up for the first time, one year after leaving Egypt. The narrator tells us that Moses did each step just as God had indicated. Everything is prepared so that God's presence may dwell among his people.

For today: God values faithful obedience, even in small details. Today we can ask ourselves what simple thing God has asked of us, and do it with care and from the heart, without leaving it half done.
exp.11:35:
This verse tells us that God caused the Egyptians to look favorably on the Israelites. Because of this, they gave them what they asked for: silver, gold, and clothing. The word that describes how they handed these things over means that they gave them those items, and the action in the verse is described as the Israelites taking those riches away from Egypt. Some translators use "lend" and others use "give"; the Hebrew verb can be understood in either way.

The narrator tells of the end of slavery in Egypt, right after the last plague. The Israelites leave in haste, following Moses' instruction. This also fulfills what God had promised earlier to Abraham and to Moses: that his people would go out with possessions (Genesis 15:14; Exodus 3:21-22).

For today: God cares for those who trust in Him, even in impossible situations. When you feel there is no way out, remember that He can open paths and provide what is needed. Trust and take the next step.
exp.3:3:
God told Moses to stretch out his hand and grab the snake by the tail. Moses obeyed, and the creature became a rod in his hand. The word "became" in the verse is the same as "turned into" or "turned back into" here, so a rod is what Moses held. A snake is what the text calls the creature. Grabbing it by the tail was a risky thing to do, since a snake is normally taken by the head.

God speaks with Moses at the burning bush. Moses fears that the people will not believe that God sent him. So God gives him signs to support his message. This miracle shows that God has control over what Moses fears, and that the rod changes by God's power, not by Moses' power.

For today: God sometimes asks us to take a step of trust before we see the result. If He calls you to something that frightens you, obey one step at a time, remembering that His power supports what He entrusts to you.
exp.28:1:
God tells Moses what else must be prepared for the ceremony of the priests. Besides the bull and the rams, three kinds of bread must be made: unleavened loaves, cakes mixed with oil, and wafers (thin flat cakes) spread with oil. Everything is made with wheaten flour, that is, the finest and purest flour.

God speaks to Moses in the wilderness, near Sinai, while He sets out how Aaron and his sons will be set apart to serve Him as priests. Unleavened bread is usually understood as a symbol of purity or of a hurried departure from Egypt, though scholars explain it in several ways. The oil is connected with consecration.

For today: serving God deserves the best, not what is left over. We can give Him our time and our heart with sincerity and devotion.
exp.28:25:
Exodus 29:26 says that Moses was to take the breast of the ram used in Aaron's consecration and wave it, that is, lift it up and move it back and forth, as an offering before God. "Sacrificed" is the word for the ram being put to death as an offering. Afterward, that part would be Moses' portion, for him to eat.

God speaks to Moses at Sinai, giving him instructions for consecrating Aaron and his sons as priests. This ceremony showed that priestly service was a holy calling. First the offering was presented to God, and then a part of it was shared. Scholars agree that the waving symbolized giving something to God, although the details of the gesture are explained in various ways.

For today: God invites us to first place in his hands what we have, and to receive with gratitude what he gives back to us. We can pray this way: "Lord, this is yours; use it as you wish."
exp.11:7:
That night, the night of the Passover, each family was to eat the lamb roasted over the fire, together with unleavened bread and bitter herbs. "Roasted over the fire" means cooked directly over the coals, not boiled. Unleavened bread means bread that was not allowed to rise, made quickly.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron, and they pass the instructions on to the people, just before the last plague on Egypt. Each family was to put the lamb's blood on the posts of their door. The meal was eaten in a hurry, ready to leave. Many understand the bitter herbs as a reminder of the harsh slavery, though the text does not explain this here.

For today: take a moment of grateful remembrance of what God has done for you. Pause, remember both the hardships and his deliverance, and give him thanks simply.
exp.26:6:
This verse says that the poles were passed through the rings of the altar, and that they stayed on both sides when the altar had to be carried. In this way the altar was lifted without anyone touching it directly. The phrase about being carried means being moved from place to place.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai and gives him instructions for building the tabernacle, a tent of worship that the people could carry from one place to another during their journey through the desert. The altar of the burnt offering had to be portable.

For today: our faith should not stay in one place. God walks with us, so we can bring prayer, gratitude, and devotion to Him at every stage of life, whether at home, at work, or in times of change.
exp.35:25:
This verse describes the silver bases on which the boards of the tabernacle stood. Each board had two tenons, which were pegs or projections that fit into the bases. That is why two bases were used for each board. Here the text speaks of forty bases for twenty boards on one side.

It is part of the account of building the tabernacle. Moses had received instructions from God, and Bezalel and his helpers carried them out with care. The text repeats what God commanded, to show that everything was done just as He directed. The silver for the bases came from the people's offerings.

For today: God attends to the details no one sees, like hidden bases that held everything up. We can serve faithfully in what is small and quiet, trusting that God values that steady obedience.
exp.18:10:
God asks the people to be "ready", that is, prepared, because in three days He is going to come down on Mount Sinai. He will do it "in the sight of all the people", that is, in a way that is visible to everyone. It would not be a secret meeting, but a public event.

The Lord speaks to Moses shortly after Israel arrived at Sinai following their departure from Egypt. God wants the people to hear when He speaks with Moses, so that they will trust his leadership. For this reason He commands that they be made holy and wash their clothes. Afterward He sets limits around the mountain, showing that God is holy and must be treated with reverence.

For today: before praying, reading the Bible, or going to church, take a few minutes to quiet your heart. God does not ask you to be perfect, but He does ask that you approach Him with respect, humility, and attention.
exp.22:9:
This verse says that the people were to sow their land for six years in a row and gather in its harvest. It is the start of an instruction about the work and the rest of the land.

God speaks to Israel through Moses, within the laws He gave them after freeing them from Egypt. Shortly before, He commanded justice through the judges and compassion for the foreigner. This verse prepares the command for the seventh year, when the land would rest and the poor could eat from what it produced on its own.

For today: working hard is good, but we should not live only to produce. We can set aside regular time to rest, trust that God provides, and share part of what we have with those in need.
exp.35:29:
He says that on the back side of the tabernacle, the side facing west, there were eight boards in total. Each board rested on two "basas," which were bases or supports of silver with openings where the boards fit. That is why there were sixteen silver sockets, two under each board.

Here the writer of Exodus tells how the craftsmen, led by Bezalel, built the tabernacle according to the instructions God gave Moses. It is a account of obedience: what God had commanded is repeated in detail, because the people wanted to do everything just as He asked. The text does not explain the meaning of each piece.

For today: God cares about the details, and our obedience in small and unremarkable things also has value. Today you can faithfully carry out a simple task, as if it were a service to God.
exp.4:13:
It says that the Israelite foremen, who were chosen from among their own people to lead the work, were beaten. The Egyptian overseers, appointed by Pharaoh, demanded the same quantity of bricks as before, even though they no longer gave them straw.
