Moses had asked Pharaoh to let the people go. Pharaoh became angry and ordered the Israelites to gather their own straw and keep up the same level of production. The Egyptian overseers speak here on Pharaoh's orders, and the Hebrew foremen pay the price for the pressure on the whole people.

For today: when doing what is right first brings more hardship, this does not mean that God has withdrawn. We can keep trusting Him, and also care for those who carry the unjust burden of others.
exp.1:13:
A Hebrew man, whom Moses had rebuked for fighting another Hebrew, answers him in anger. He asks who appointed Moses as ruler and judge over them. He also shows that he knows about the Egyptian who was killed. Moses becomes afraid and realizes that his secret is already known. "Known" here means that what he did has become public.

It is one of the Hebrews who were quarreling. Moses had already killed an Egyptian who was mistreating a Hebrew, and he had hidden the body. The next day he tried to make peace between two brothers of his people, but he was rejected. Soon after, Pharaoh heard about it, and Moses fled to Midian.

For today: wanting to do justice is not enough if we do it our own way and without direction from God. Before correcting others or acting, it is wise to pray, wait, and seek wisdom. God can use even our mistakes to shape us.
exp.0:19:
God dealt well with the midwives, that is, he blessed them for what they did. Meanwhile, the Hebrew people kept growing in number and became very mighty. The words "dealt well" mean that he showed them favor, and "multiplied" means that they grew strong in number.

The narrator tells what happened after Pharaoh called the midwives to account for not killing the Hebrew boys. They gave him an excuse about the Hebrew women. Some think it was a partial truth and others that it was a deception; the text does not make it clear. What does stand out is that they feared God more than Pharaoh, and for that reason God blessed them.

For today: when we face a choice between pleasing powerful people and doing what is right before God, we can ask him for courage and wisdom. He sees our faithfulness, even when no one else notices it.
exp.35:30:
This verse tells how Bezalel and his helpers made the bars of acacia wood. There were five bars for the boards on one side of the tabernacle. The bars held the boards together and kept them firm, like a skeleton that supports the whole structure.

The one telling the story is the writer of Exodus, who describes how the people of Israel built the tabernacle, the tent where God would dwell among them. Everything was made following the instructions God gave Moses on the mountain. The account repeats the details to show careful obedience.

For today: God also notices what is not seen much, like these bars that held everything up. We can serve Him faithfully in small and hidden tasks, trusting that they have value before Him.
exp.2:19:
God says that he himself will act with power against Egypt. "I will stretch out my hand" is a way of speaking about his strength in action. The verse says he will strike Egypt with all his wonders, and at the end of all that, Pharaoh will let the people go.

God speaks to Moses from the burning bush. He has just told him that the king of Egypt will not give way easily, but only under a strong hand. With these words, God shows him the path ahead: there will be resistance, but also a deliverance that will come from him and not from Moses's own strength.

For today: when a task seems bigger than you, remember that God does not ask you to do everything with your own strength. Obey the step that is yours to take, trust that he is at work, and do not lose heart if there is opposition at the start.
exp.21:12:
If someone was looking after their neighbor's animal and a wild beast tore it apart, the caretaker was to bring the remains as proof. In this way he was free from having to pay. The phrase about bringing evidence has been rewritten here to say the same thing in plain words: he was to bring the remains as proof. The word "torn" in the verse above is the key idea.

Context: God speaks to Israel through Moses, right after the Ten Commandments. These are laws for the people's daily life. They aim at justice in cases of loss, when someone was caring for property that belonged to another. A distinction is made between carelessness or theft, which had to be paid for, and a misfortune that was not under the caretaker's control, which was not charged.

For today: When something is entrusted to us, whether money, a job, or a task, let us be honest and open. If something goes wrong without fault on our part, let us show the truth clearly. And if we are the ones who judge, let us do it with justice and compassion.
exp.13:15:
God tells Moses to lift up his rod, stretch out his hand over the sea, and divide it. In this way the Israelites will be able to cross through the middle of the sea, walking on dry ground. The phrase "the sea" in the old wording is the same word as "the sea" in the verse above, and "dry ground" here means ground without water or mud.

God is speaking. The Israelites are trapped between the sea and Pharaoh's army, which is chasing them, and the people are very afraid. Moses had cried out, and God answers him with a command: move forward. The rod was the tool Moses had already used, but the power to open the sea comes from God, not from the rod.

When God asks us to take a step, sometimes the way is not yet visible. We can obey with confidence in what He has already shown us, and leave in His hands what we cannot resolve ourselves.
exp.39:21:
He says that Moses placed the table inside the tabernacle, on the north side, on the outer part of the veil. "Northward" simply means toward the north. "Tabernacle" here refers to the sacred tent. "Testimony" recalls the tablets of the law that God had given to his people. The veil separated the holy place from the most holy place, where the ark was.

The narrator tells how Moses raised and arranged the tabernacle, a year after the departure from Egypt. He did it step by step, just as the LORD had commanded. After setting the ark, the table for the bread followed. Everything was placed in order, exactly as God had directed.

For today: God cares about the details of our obedience. Doing things as He asks, even when they seem small, is a way of worshiping Him. Today we can ask ourselves what simple act of obedience we have left undone.
exp.8:30:
This verse tells which crops the hail destroyed. The flax and the barley were damaged because the barley already had its ears and the flax was already in stalk, that is, with its stem formed and firm, so it broke easily.

The one telling the story is the writer of Exodus, and he explains the damage done by the seventh plague in Egypt. Moses had just told Pharaoh that God would stop the storm, though he knew Pharaoh did not yet truly respect him. The next verse makes clear that the wheat and the rye, which ripen later, were not harmed. The agricultural details show that the plague was precise and real.

For today: God pays attention to details and to timing, and he also invites us not to harden our hearts. When God speaks to us, let us respond with humility and not wait for disaster before we listen.
exp.22:24:
God says that his people must serve him alone. If they do, he will bless their bread and their water, that is, their daily food and drink, and he will take sickness away from among them. The words "but" and "shall serve" are rendered in the verse above as "and ye shall serve" and "shall bless," so no further comment is needed on them here.

God speaks to Israel through Moses, in the laws he gives them after leaving Egypt and before entering Canaan. He warns them not to adopt the gods of the peoples of that land. The promise joins faithfulness to God with his daily care. It is a promise given to Israel as a nation, within the covenant with God.

For today: put God first each day, starting with the simplest things, such as thanking him for your food. Trust that he cares for you, even when he does not always explain how or when he heals or provides.
exp.21:9:
This verse presents a case: someone entrusts a neighbor with an animal to look after, such as a donkey, an ox, or a sheep. The animal dies, is badly injured, or is taken away while no one sees it. The sentence is left open, and the resolution comes in the following verse.

God speaks to Israel through Moses, shortly after giving the Ten Commandments. These laws taught how to settle disputes fairly in a society of farmers and shepherds, where entrusting animals to another person was common. When there were no witnesses, people relied on an oath made before God.

For today: when someone entrusts us with something of theirs, whether money, a job, or a secret, we look after it as if it were our own. And if something goes wrong, we answer honestly, even when no one has seen us.
exp.36:22:
This verse tells that Bezalel made the seven lamps of the lampstand, along with its snuffers and its snuffdishes, all of pure gold. The "lamps" were the small lamp cups where the oil and the flame burned. The "snuffers" were tongs used to trim the wick and remove what had burned. The "snuffdishes" were small trays used to catch the residue.

The passage is a narrative, not a speech. It describes how the lampstand of the tabernacle was built, following the instructions God gave to Moses. It goes into such small detail because the place of worship had to be made exactly as God had directed.

For today: God cares about the small details that serve his work. Even the simplest tools were made with the best materials. We can offer him, with excellence and faithfulness, the everyday things, such as our work, our service, and our prayer, without thinking that anything is too small for him.
exp.12:0:
This verse is only an introduction. It says that God spoke to Moses to give him an instruction. "The Lord" is the name of God in the Old Testament, and "saying" announces what comes right after.

God speaks to Moses just after the departure from Egypt and the last plague, in which the firstborn of the Egyptians died. Now God asks that the firstborn of Israel, of people and of animals, be set apart to him. It was a way of remembering that he had redeemed and protected them.

For today: before acting, it is worth listening to God. Set aside a few minutes each day to read the Bible and pray, and remember with gratitude what God has done for you.
exp.11:42:
God tells Moses and Aaron the rules for keeping the Passover. The first is that no outsider may eat of it. The word for the rule itself means a standing command or decree.

The Lord speaks, and he does so just after the departure from Egypt. The Passover was a reminder that God rescued Israel. The verses that follow explain that whoever was circumcised and entered the covenant could take part. So the rule was not meant to shut anyone out, but to ensure that the meal was shared with those who belonged to the covenant.

For today: value moments of communion with God and with his people, such as the Lord's Supper. Take part with reverence and with a prepared heart. And remember that God has always invited people to come near to him.
exp.39:18:
It says that Moses spread the tent (the curtains of goat-hair cloth) over the framework of the tabernacle, and on top of it he put the covering, an outer layer to give protection. The covering is an extra layer of cover. The final phrase repeats that everything was done just as God had commanded.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, telling how Moses set up the tabernacle a year after leaving Egypt. God had given detailed instructions, and now the people carry them out step by step. This place would be where God would dwell among Israel. Scholars explain in different ways how the layers were arranged, but the text emphasizes obedience.

For today: God values faithful obedience, even in small and unremarkable details. Today you might ask yourself what simple task God has entrusted to you, and do it with care and trust, even if no one notices.
exp.3:8:
God says to Moses that he will give him a third sign, in case the people do not believe the first two. Moses was to take water from the Nile and pour it out on dry ground, and that water would turn into blood.

God speaks with Moses at the burning bush. He sends him to free Israel from Egypt, but Moses fears that no one will believe him. For this reason God gives him signs to support his message. Afterward, Moses makes an excuse, saying that he is slow of speech. God answers him that he made the human mouth. Some see in this sign a foreshadowing of the plagues, although the text does not say this directly.

For today: when God calls you to something and you feel insecure, remember that he does not ask you to do it with your own strength. He walks with you and gives you what you need to obey.
exp.35:21:
Each board of the tabernacle had two tenons, which were pegs or projections on the lower part. They were set "one beside the other," that is, lined up in a row and fitted closely together. Each peg fit into a silver base. All the boards were made alike, with the same measure and the same shape.

Here the narrator tells how Bezaleel and the craftsmen built the tabernacle, following what God had shown Moses on the mountain. This passage faithfully repeats the instructions given earlier. The tabernacle was the place where God dwelt among Israel. Some technical details of the assembly are not entirely clear to scholars.

For today: God cares about details and faithfulness in small things. Do with care and steadiness what you have been entrusted with, even when no one sees it.
exp.33:26:
God tells Moses to write down the words he has just given him. "Jehovah" is the name of God, and "covenant" means a solemn agreement, a promise between God and his people. God says that this covenant is based on these words, and he makes it with Moses and with all of Israel.

God speaks on Mount Sinai. Israel had just broken the covenant with the golden calf, and Moses had gone up again to renew it. The earlier instructions about the Passover and the first fruits were part of that renewal. Then Moses writes for forty days. As for the "ten words" in the following text, many understand them to be the Ten Commandments.

For today: God wanted his Word to be written down so that it would not be forgotten. Set aside a few minutes each day to read the Bible and write down something God shows you, so you can remember it and put it into practice.
exp.35:13:
It says that Bezalel and the craftsmen made eleven curtains of goats' hair. They served as a tent or covering that went over the tabernacle, that is, over the fine linen curtains that formed the dwelling place of God. "Goats' hair" was a strong cloth, made from the hair of the animal.

Here the narrator of the book of Exodus speaks. He tells how the people of Israel built the tabernacle, following point by point the instructions that God had given to Moses on the mountain. These chapters repeat what had already been commanded, to show complete obedience. The details about the symbolism of this covering are not explained here, and interpreters see them in different ways.

For today: God cares even for small details, and obedience is also lived out in the simple and everyday. Let us faithfully do what He asks of us, even when it seems hardly visible.
exp.27:22:
It says that Moses was to make two rings of gold and put them on the two upper ends of the breastplate. The breastplate was a square piece that the high priest wore over his chest. It had twelve stones with the names of the tribes of Israel. The rings were used to hold the small gold chains that fastened it to the ephod, the priestly garment.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai and gives him detailed instructions for Aaron's garments. These garments were used for worship in the tabernacle. The rings and chains made sure the breastplate stayed firmly on the priest's chest, with the names of the people close to his heart.

God cares even for small details so that his people are secure and present before him. Today we can pray with confidence, knowing that Christ, our high priest, carries us close to his heart and holds us steady.
exp.18:5:
God tells Israel that they will be "a kingdom of priests, and a holy nation." A priest is someone who draws near to God and represents God before others. "A holy nation" means a nation set apart for God. The words "to the children of Israel" are God's instruction to Moses to repeat this message to the people.

God speaks from Mount Sinai, shortly after freeing Israel from Egypt. He reminds them how he carried them "on eagles' wings" and offers them a covenant: if they obey, they will be his special treasure. Some understand that Israel would serve as a bridge between God and the other nations, although the text does not explain this in detail.

God first rescues and then asks for obedience. Today we can live with that same order: giving thanks for what God has already done for us and letting that gratitude shape our daily conduct, at home, at work, and with our neighbors.
exp.15:21:
On the sixth day, that is Friday, the people gathered twice as much manna: two omers for each person. An omer was a small measure of grain or dry food, about two liters, though estimates vary. The rulers of the congregation were the leaders of the people, and they went to tell Moses what had happened.

This is part of the account of the manna in the wilderness. God had taught them to gather only what they needed each day. Some had disobeyed by keeping food for the next day, and it had spoiled. Now, on the sixth day, there was twice as much, and the leaders did not know what it meant. Moses explains to them that God was preparing the day of rest.

For today: God takes care of us and also wants us to rest. We can plan our responsibilities ahead of time so that we can rest peacefully, trusting that He provides.
exp.11:20:
Moses gathers the leaders of Israel's families and gives them a clear command. Where the text says "Sacad," it means that they are to go to the flock and choose lambs, one for each family. Then they must kill the Passover, that is, the lamb that was offered on that special night.

Moses speaks on behalf of God, just before the final plague on Egypt. The elders were to pass the instruction on to the whole people. The blood of the lamb on the doorposts would be the sign that God's judgment would pass over them.

Christians see in this an image of Christ, the Lamb of God, although the original text speaks of the deliverance of Israel.

Today we can learn to obey God with confidence, even when his instructions seem simple or strange. He takes care of those who trust his word. We can also serve as those elders did: faithfully passing on to our families what God says.
exp.35:36:
It says that Bezalel and his helpers made the curtain for the entrance of the tabernacle. They used threads of blue, purple, scarlet (a deep red), and twined linen, that is, fine linen tightly twisted and woven together. The phrase "of needlework" means the work was embroidered by hand, with colored designs. This curtain was different from the inner veil, since that one covered the inner doorway.

The book of Exodus is a narrative, and here the author, traditionally Moses, recounts how the tabernacle was built just as God had commanded it. The Israelites did it with obedience and care, following every detail. The entrance marked the passage into the place where God dwelt among his people.

For today: God cares about details and receives what we do with diligence. We can serve him with obedience and a good attitude, even in small or unseen tasks. Moreover, the entrance reminds us that God invites us to draw near to him with reverence and gratitude.
exp.28:3:
God tells Moses to bring Aaron and his sons to the entrance of the tent of meeting, where God met with his people, and there to wash them with water. "Tent of the testimony" was the sacred tent where the tablets of the law were kept. Here, "wash" means to cleanse the body with water before beginning their service.

God himself speaks to Moses, giving him instructions for setting apart the first priests of Israel. Before dressing them and presenting the offerings, the first step is the washing. Many see here a sign that whoever draws near to God needs to be cleansed, although the text only describes the rite.

For today: we do not come to God on the basis of our own merits. We can draw near with humility, asking him to cleanse our hearts, and trust that he receives us and prepares us to serve him.
exp.35:15:
It says that Bezalel and the craftsmen joined the eleven goat-hair curtains into two groups: five curtains together on one side, and six on the other. "By themselves" means "separately." "Apart" also refers to that second group. Afterward, the two groups would be joined with loops and clasps.

This is part of the account of how the tabernacle was made, just as God had commanded Moses. Here it is not a person giving a speech; it is the narrator describing the finished work. These curtains formed a covering, a "tent" over the tabernacle. The text insists on exact measurements to show careful obedience.

For today: God cares about the details of what we do for Him. Obeying Him in small things, with patience and order, is also worship. And separate pieces can form one whole when they are well joined together.
exp.34:25:
This verse says that the women who had skill, and whose heart moved them, spun goats' hair for the tabernacle. The phrase "whose heart stirred them up in wisdom" means that their inner desire moved them to use their skill. Goats' hair was used to make strong cloth, such as the coverings of the tent.

Moses has asked the people for offerings to build the sanctuary, and the account tells of it. Some people gave metals and wood; the women gave their work of spinning. It is emphasized that each person contributed according to what they knew how to do and with willingness. It does not say there was pressure, but a willing heart.

For today: God values what you do with your hands when you do it from the heart. Think of a simple skill you have, such as cooking, sewing, teaching, or fixing things, and offer it this week to help your church or someone in need.
exp.8:27:
Pharaoh asks Moses and Aaron to pray to the Lord so that the thunder and the hail will stop. In return, he promises to let the people of Israel go. The verse reads "Intreat the Lord," and "I will let you go, and ye shall stay no longer."

Pharaoh speaks in the middle of the seventh plague. The hail had destroyed crops and livestock, but it did not fall in Goshen, where Israel lived. Frightened, Pharaoh admits his sin and the righteousness of God. However, Moses replies that he knows Pharaoh still does not truly fear the Lord. He was right: afterward Pharaoh hardened his heart again.

For today: asking God for help in trouble is good, but He looks for a heart that changes. May our repentance not last only while the storm passes.
exp.17:9:
Jethro, Moses' father-in-law, praises God with these words: "Blessed be the Lord." He acknowledges that God rescued Israel from the power of the Egyptians and from Pharaoh. "Blessed" here means praised or worthy of thanks. "Delivered" means rescued, brought out of danger.

Jethro was a priest of Midian, and he had come to the desert to visit Moses. Moses had just told him everything God had done for Israel, and Jethro rejoiced greatly. Later he will say that he now knows the Lord is greater than all gods. We do not know exactly how far Jethro worshiped only the Lord before this, and scholars interpret this in different ways.

For today: when you hear how God helped another person, do not stay silent. Rejoice with them and give thanks to God out loud. Sharing testimonies encourages all of us to trust him more.
exp.17:25:
The explanation says that the judges appointed by Moses attended to the people at all times. The difficult cases they brought to Moses, and they settled the simple matters themselves.

The one who narrates is the author of the book, who tells how Moses obeyed the counsel of Jethro, his father-in-law. Jethro saw that Moses was wearing himself out judging the whole people alone from morning until evening, and he suggested spreading that burden among capable men. Moses listened and put the advice into practice.

For today: you do not have to carry everything by yourself. Sharing responsibilities with trustworthy people, in the family, the church, or the workplace, protects your health and serves others better. It is also wise to listen to good advice, even when it comes from someone who is not the leader.
exp.29:12:
God commands that every Israelite who is counted in the census gives half a piece of silver, called a half shekel, according to the measure used in the sanctuary. It is clarified that a shekel equals twenty gerahs (a small unit of weight). That half is an offering to the Lord.

God speaks to Moses when the people were about to be counted. This offering was called a ransom for their lives and was meant to prevent a plague during the counting. The verses that follow say that it was required of those twenty years old and above, and that the rich and the poor gave the same amount. Later it was used for the service of the tabernacle.

For today: before God we are all of equal worth, and no one can buy a special place with their money. We can give with gratitude and without comparing ourselves to others, remembering that God accepts us by his grace.
exp.34:0:
Moses gathers the whole congregation of Israel and tells them he is going to repeat to them what God commanded. "Congregation" means the entire community gathered together. "Said unto them" simply means "told them." "Lord" is the name of God, and "commanded" means these are instructions that He gave.

Moses speaks after the sin of the golden calf and the renewing of the covenant with God. Now he prepares the people to build the tabernacle, the place where God would dwell among them. The first thing he reminds them of, in the verses that follow, is the Sabbath. In this way he makes clear that work for God does not come before obeying Him and resting in Him.

Today we can learn that serving God begins by listening to what He says, not with our own ideas. Before beginning a project, a job, or a ministry, let us take time to pray and read His Word, and set aside time as well to rest in Him.
exp.29:22:
God tells Moses to take the finest spices to make a special oil. Moses is to take five hundred shekels of pure myrrh, two hundred and fifty of sweet cinnamon, and two hundred and fifty of sweet calamus. A shekel was a unit of weight, roughly eleven grams by common calculations, though the exact figure is debated.

The Lord speaks just after the instructions about the priests washing their hands and feet. He is giving directions for the oil of holy anointing, with which the tabernacle, its furnishings, and the priests would be set apart for God. Everything was to be done as God commanded.

For today: God deserves our best, not our leftovers. We might ask ourselves whether we give him our time, attention, and service with care and good will, and not only when we have something left over.
exp.16:14:
Moses built an altar and called its name JEHOVAH–nissi. The name is usually understood to mean "the LORD is my banner."

Israel had just been attacked by the Amalekites in the desert. Joshua fought, and while Moses held up his hand in prayer, Israel was winning. Moses is the one who acts here. With the altar he does not celebrate his own strength, but acknowledges that the victory came from God.

For today: when you overcome a difficulty, don't stop at relief alone. Pause and thank God in a concrete way, perhaps with a prayer or by writing down how he helped you. In this way you will remember that he was your banner and your support.
exp.26:3:
God asks Moses to make a grate of brass, woven like a net, for the altar. On this grate four brass rings are placed, one at each corner. "Brass" here refers to bronze (or copper); a "grate" is a kind of grill or mesh. The rings would serve to pass the poles with which the altar was carried.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai and gives him detailed instructions for building the tabernacle, his portable sanctuary. The altar for the sacrifices had to be movable while the people walked through the desert. Some details, such as the exact position of the grate, are understood in several ways among scholars.

For today: God cares about the details of what we offer him and of how we serve him. We can do with order and care what seems small, such as a daily prayer or a task in the church, knowing that God values faithfulness.
exp.36:17:
This verse describes how the lampstand of the tabernacle was made. Six branches came out of its central shaft, three on one side and three on the other, to form a lampstand with seven lamps in all. The word "candlestick" is what we would today call a lampstand or lamp holder.

It is part of the account where Bezaleel builds the holy objects, following the instructions God gave Moses (Exodus 25). The narrator repeats in detail what had already been commanded, showing that the work was done just as God had asked. The lampstand was made of pure gold, hammered into shape, and gave light inside the holy place. Christians often see in it a symbol of God's light, although the text here only describes its form.

For today: God cares about the details of what we do for Him. Do your work, your service, and your responsibilities with care and faithfulness, even when no one notices.
exp.21:24:
It says that if someone from God's people lends money to a poor person, they must not treat them like an abusive moneylender. A person who takes advantage of another's need to gain more than is fair is what the word "moneylender" describes here, and charging excessive interest is the problem being addressed.

God speaks through Moses, within the laws he gave Israel after leaving Egypt. Earlier, he had warned against mistreating widows, orphans, and foreigners, and that he hears the cry of those who suffer. Here the poor person is someone asking for help out of need, not for a business deal. The verses that follow connect this with God's compassion.

For today: if you help someone in difficulty, do it generously and without taking advantage of their need. Before lending or collecting, ask yourself whether your dealings reflect God's mercy.
exp.25:33:
This verse commands that the covering, also called the mercy seat, be placed over the ark of the testimony. The ark was the chest that held the tablets of the law, and it was to stand in the most holy place, the innermost room of the tabernacle, behind the veil.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai and gives him detailed instructions for building the tabernacle, a tent where He would dwell among Israel. The veil separated the holy place from the most holy place and showed that drawing near to God was a very serious matter. On that covering, according to Leviticus 16, atonement was made once a year.

For today: the covering over the law reminds us that God joins His justice with His mercy. Many Christians see in this a foreshadowing of Christ. We can approach God with reverence, but also with confidence, without carrying our guilt alone.
exp.22:29:
God promises Israel that he will drive out the peoples of Canaan "little by little," that is, gradually and not all at once. The purpose is that the people will grow ("until thou be increased") until they are numerous enough to fill the land and receive it as their own inheritance, that is, as their own possession passed down to them.

God himself speaks here, within the laws and promises he gives Israel through Moses at Sinai. Earlier he explains that he would not drive them out in a single year, so that the land would not be left empty and wild beasts would not multiply. His plan was gradual and careful, meant to protect his people.

For today: when God seems slow or moves at a gradual pace, it does not mean he has forgotten his promise. Often he is preparing us while we grow. Trust his timing and take the step that is yours to take today.
exp.29:33:
God gives Moses the recipe for the sacred incense. He asks for four fragrant ingredients: stacte, onycha, galbanum, and pure frankincense, all in equal amounts. Stacte and onycha are aromatic gums or substances, though it is not known for certain exactly what they were. Galbanum is a resin with a strong smell. "Pure" means clean, unmixed.

The Lord speaks and gives Moses instructions for worship in the tabernacle. Just before this, He explained the holy anointing oil, which was not to be used in an ordinary way. Here He does the same with the incense: it was to be set apart only for God, used before the testimony, where He would meet with Moses.

For today: God deserves the best and the pure, not what is left over. We can set apart a time each day, without haste or distractions, to pray and read His Word with reverence and sincerity.
exp.30:11:
This verse is an introductory phrase. It says that the Lord spoke again to Moses. The word "again" shows that God is adding something new to what He had already been saying. The word "saying" announces that an important message is about to follow.

God has just given Moses instructions for building the tabernacle, the garments of the priests, and the anointing oil. Now God changes the subject and speaks about the Sabbath. What follows is a command for the whole people: to rest one day as a sign of their relationship with God. The one speaking is God, and Moses is the messenger.

For today: God still speaks, and it is worth pausing to listen to Him. You could set aside a quiet moment each day to read His Word, without rushing, with your heart open to what He may want to tell you.
exp.17:7:
Moses tells his father-in-law Jethro everything that God did. He speaks of what the Lord did to Pharaoh and to the Egyptians for the sake of Israel, of the hardships they went through on the way, and of how God rescued them.

Moses has just welcomed Jethro, the priest of Midian, who arrives with Zipporah, Moses' wife, and their two sons. After greeting each other respectfully, they go into the tent, and Moses gives him an account of what happened. He does not boast about himself; he puts God forward as the author of the deliverance. This leads Jethro to rejoice and to bless the Lord.

When we talk with others about our lives, we can tell not only of our troubles but also of how God has helped us. Sharing simply what He has done can encourage others and lead them to give thanks to Him.
exp.21:20:
This verse commands that the stranger not be cheated or mistreated. To "cheat" someone is to take advantage of them through tricks or abuse, and to "oppress" someone is to press them down and make their life heavy. The reason is simple: the people of Israel were also strangers in Egypt.

God speaks to Israel through Moses, in the laws given after Sinai. Before this there are serious rules about faithfulness to the LORD; after it, the text speaks of the widow and the fatherless. In this way, God joins right worship with justice toward the most vulnerable. The Israelites knew what it was to live without rights, and God asks them not to repeat that pain with others.

Today we can treat immigrants, or anyone who arrives new to our neighborhood, job, or church, with respect and justice: paying them fairly, not mocking their accent, and reaching out a hand to them. Remembering our own difficulties makes us more compassionate.
exp.7:28:
Moses tells Pharaoh that as soon as he leaves his presence, he will ask the Lord that the flies may depart from him, from his servants, and from his people, tomorrow. But he warns him not to deal deceitfully again and not to keep the people from going to sacrifice to the Lord. The phrase "as soon as I go out" means "when I leave." The "swarms of flies" refers to the great numbers of flies that had come upon the land.

Moses speaks after Pharaoh, troubled by the plague, promised to let the people go if the flies were kept from going far away. Moses agrees to pray, but he reminds Pharaoh that his word must be kept. God responds and removes the flies, although Pharaoh afterward hardens his heart again.

For today: when God delivers us from a difficulty, feeling relief is not enough. We must do what we promised. Let us be people of our word, grateful and obedient.
exp.25:28:
God tells Moses that the boards that form the walls of the tabernacle must be overlaid with gold. They must also have rings of gold, through which the bars will pass that keep the boards firm and joined together. The bars are overlaid with gold too. "Overlay" means covering with a layer of gold, not making them out of solid gold.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai and gives him detailed instructions for building his movable sanctuary, where he would dwell in the midst of Israel. Shortly afterward he says that Moses must set it up according to the pattern that was shown to him. Nothing is left to human improvisation.

For today: God cares even for the details no one sees, like the rings and bars that hold the structure together. We can also offer him, with excellence, what is hidden: our steady work, our faithfulness in small things, and our character when no one is watching.
exp.36:21:
These knobs and branches were part of the same piece: the ornaments shaped like small balls or buttons, and the arms of the lampstand, were made together with it. Everything was "hammered" work, that is, beaten and shaped from one piece of pure gold, with no parts joined or attached on.

Here the narrator of the book describes how Bezaleel made the furnishings of the tabernacle, following the instructions God gave to Moses. The seven-branched lampstand gave light in the holy place. The text stresses that it was one unit, made with care and with the finest material.

For today: just as the lampstand was one piece, we are called to live united, without each going our own way. In the church, the family, or the workplace, let us seek unity and attention to detail, for God values what is done with dedication.
exp.7:1:
God warns Pharaoh that if he refuses to let his people go, He will send a plague of frogs over all his land. The words "terms" and "I will smite" mean "territory" and "I will punish." The expression "behold" is used to draw attention: what follows is serious.

The LORD speaks through Moses, who must present himself before Pharaoh. God had already asked that Israel be let go so that they might serve him. Upon the refusal, this warning comes. It is striking that God gives notice before acting, giving an opportunity to obey. Some scholars see here a challenge to the gods of Egypt, since the frog was connected with a deity of that people, though this is interpreted in different ways.

For today: God is patient and warns us before correcting us. When we sense his call to change something, let us not harden our hearts; let us obey in time and with humility.
exp.8:7:
God tells Moses and Aaron to take handfuls of ashes from a furnace. Then Moses is to throw them toward the sky, in plain view of Pharaoh.

The word "sprinkle" means "scatter" or "fling into the air." "Furnace" here refers to a place where something was burned, such as a brick kiln.

The Lord speaks. This comes after the death of the livestock, and Pharaoh was still stubborn. This sixth plague, the one with sores, is announced with a simple, public sign. Some think the ashes recall the hard labor of the Israelites with bricks, but the text does not say so, so this is only one possible interpretation.

Today we can learn that God can use small, ordinary things to accomplish his purpose. Our task is not to understand every detail but to obey with confidence, as Moses did. It also warns us: hardening the heart never leads to anything good.
exp.12:17:
God did not lead Israel by the shortest road, but made the people go around by way of the wilderness, toward the Red Sea. The verse says "led the people about," which means He took them on a roundabout path.

The verse says the children of Israel went up "harnessed" out of the land of Egypt. This can be understood as equipped for battle, or as arranged in ranks; scholars explain it in several ways.

The one telling the story is Moses. The people had just left Egypt. The nearer road passed through Philistine land, and God knew that war might frighten them and make them turn back to slavery. So He chose another route, longer but safer for their faith, which was still weak.

Today, when your path seems long or confusing, remember that God knows your limits and guides you with care. A detour is not always a delay; it can be His way of protecting and preparing you.
exp.22:21:
God says that if the people truly listen to the voice of the Angel who goes before them and obey everything He commands, He will be an enemy to their enemies. The word "afflict" means that God will act against those who oppress them. The words "hearken" and "do" are older forms of the same ideas: "if you listen" and "if you do."

God Himself speaks, through Moses, to the people of Israel after giving them the law at Sinai. He is preparing them to enter the promised land, where they will face hostile peoples. Their protection is tied to their faithfulness and obedience to the covenant. Some understand the Angel as a messenger sent by God; others see in Him a special divine presence, because God's name is in Him.

For today: trusting God is not only feeling protected, but listening to Him and obeying Him. Today you can choose one concrete action that you know God is asking of you and do it in faith, knowing that He cares for you.
exp.17:13:
Jethro, Moses' father-in-law, watches how Moses spends the whole day attending to the people, sitting as judge. He asks him two questions: "What is this thing that you are doing?" and "Why do you sit alone?" The word "father-in-law" refers to the father of one's wife, and the phrase "from morning until evening" means the people were waiting their turn to be attended to.

Israel had just left Egypt and was in the desert. Moses settled the people's disputes and taught them God's laws. Jethro, who came to visit, does not criticize him harshly. As an outsider, he sees clearly what Moses, caught up in the work, no longer noticed: this could not go on this way.

Even good work can become a burden that we should not carry alone. Listening to the sincere advice of someone we trust, and learning to share responsibilities, is also a form of wisdom.
exp.3:25:
It says that God stopped attacking Moses, or "let him go," after Zipporah circumcised her son. She repeated that Moses was a "bloody husband" because of the circumcision. "Then" means "at once," and "bloody husband" is an obscure expression.

Zipporah, Moses' wife, is the one speaking. Moses was on his way to Egypt to carry out his mission, but he had not circumcised his son, the sign of God's covenant with Abraham. God acted with severity, and she acted quickly. Scholars disagree about the exact meaning of her words and about who was in danger, Moses or his son. The text does not fully clarify this.

For today: God expects obedience, not just good intentions. If there is something He has already asked of us and we have put off, let us obey today with humility, especially before serving Him in something important.
exp.23:3:
Moses wrote down everything God had said. The next day he got up early and built an altar at the foot of Mount Sinai. He also set up twelve stone pillars, one for each tribe of Israel. The explanation of the name "Jehovah" and of the phrase "early in the morning" has been left out, since those words do not appear in the verse on your screen.

The people had just promised with one voice that they would obey everything God had said. Moses, as mediator, wrote down the words so they would not be forgotten. Then a ceremony followed, with sacrifices and blood, that sealed the covenant between God and Israel. The twelve pillars show that the whole people took part in that commitment.

For today: God wants his Word to be kept and taken seriously. We can write down what God shows us as we read the Bible, and decide early in the day on one concrete action to obey him that day.
exp.37:27:
It says that Moses used the 1,775 shekels of silver left over from the census to make the capitals, that is, the tops or decorative ornaments on the upper part of the pillars of the court. He also overlaid them (covered them with silver) and banded them, meaning he put silver rings or bands that joined them together. A shekel was a unit of weight.

This is part of the final account of the construction of the tabernacle. The narrator describes how the offerings of the people were used, and Bezaleel is named as the main craftsman. An exact record was kept of the silver. Some understand that these capitals were covered with silver, and others that they had bands; the Hebrew allows some room for discussion.

For today: God values faithfulness in the details and honesty with what is entrusted to us. We can handle with care, order, and transparency what is placed in our hands, whether money, time, or service in the church, knowing that even the smallest things are done to honor God.
exp.25:4:
It says that each set of curtains for the tabernacle was to have fifty loops (small fabric tabs or rings) along its edge. The loops on one curtain were to face the loops on the other, lined up directly opposite one another. In this way they could later be joined together with the gold clasps (hooks).

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai and gives him exact instructions for building a sanctuary where He would dwell among Israel. The curtains formed the tabernacle, the holy tent. The details show that God cares how His work is done and that the parts must fit together.

For today: just as those loops had to meet face to face in order to be joined, our life in community calls for attention to detail. Look today for a concrete way to line up with someone in your church or family, with patience and a willing heart, so that you can serve together.
exp.27:18:
This verse describes the third row of precious stones on the breastpiece of the high priest. It had three stones: a ligure, an agate, and an amethyst. The ancient names of the stones are uncertain, and translations vary in how they identify them. The stones set in gold are the settings that hold them fixed in gold.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai and gives him instructions for Aaron's garments. Each stone bore the name of one of the twelve tribes of Israel. Thus the priest carried the whole people upon his chest when he entered before God.

For today: God does not see his people as a faceless mass, but each one has a name and worth before him. You can pray with that confidence, and also remember to carry others in prayer, as the priest carried them close to his heart.
exp.37:21:
This verse says that Bezaleel, of the tribe of Judah, did everything that God had commanded Moses. His father and grandfather, Uri and Hur, are named to identify him clearly. The name of God appears in the source wording, and the verb for "commanded" means that God gave clear orders.

The narrator of the book of Exodus (tradition attributes it to Moses) ends here the account of the construction of the tabernacle, the tent where God would dwell among his people. Earlier, the accounts of the materials are mentioned, and afterward Aholiab is named as his helper. It stands out that Bezaleel invented nothing: he followed God's plan. The materials were offerings from the people.

For today: God values faithfulness in what he entrusts to us, even when the work is simple and hardly visible. We can ask ourselves what he has asked us to do and carry it out carefully, without changing it to suit our own taste.
exp.29:19:
It says that the priests had to wash with water each time they went into the tent of meeting or came near the altar to present a burnt offering to God. If they did not, they would "die," a very serious warning. The explanation of "minister" as serving, and of the phrase about offering the sacrifice by fire, is set aside here since those words do not appear in the verse you are reading.

God speaks to Moses while giving instructions about the tabernacle. Aaron and his sons would be the priests, and the bronze basin stood between the tent and the altar. God wanted them to approach Him with reverence, remembering that He is holy. The text does not explain every detail of its meaning, but it emphasizes cleanliness and obedience.

For today: when we pray or serve in the church, let us not do it in a hurried way or merely out of habit. We can pause, acknowledge our faults, and ask God for a clean heart. He receives us with grace, and yet He deserves our respect.
exp.32:4:
The Lord asks Moses to tell the people a serious message: they are "stiffnecked," that is, stubborn and rebellious, like an animal that will not let itself be led. If God were to walk among them, He could consume them in a moment. For this reason He orders them to put off their ornaments, that is, their decorations and jewelry, while He decides what to do with them.

This happens after Israel made the golden calf. God speaks to Moses, and the people respond with mourning. Taking off their ornaments was a sign of repentance. Some scholars think God was looking for a humble heart, not just an outward gesture.

For today: when God corrects us, it is not to destroy us, but to bring us back to Him. We can put off pride and whatever distracts us, and draw near with humility and sincerity.
exp.25:9:
This verse gives a building instruction: make fifty loops (small tabs or eyelets) along the edge of one curtain, at the place where it joins the other, and fifty more along the edge of the second curtain. The loops were small tie-like fastenings, probably of cloth, that would hook the two sections together. The place where two pieces come together is the joining point.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai and gives him the plan of the tabernacle, the tent where God would dwell among Israel. The curtains formed its inner covering. The verses that follow explain that they would be joined with metal clasps (hooks of metal) to form a single covering.

For today: God cares even about the small details of what we offer him. Caring carefully for everyday things, such as our work, our relationships, and our faith, can also be a way of honoring him.
exp.19:15:
This commandment says we should not lie about another person, especially when it comes to accusing them or making a statement about them. A "neighbour" is the person near us: a neighbour, a companion, an acquaintance. "Bear false witness" means saying something that is not true, such as when someone testifies in a court case or speaks about another person.

God speaks to Israel from Mount Sinai, after having brought them out of Egypt. These words are part of the Ten Commandments, which taught the people how to live righteously within the covenant with Him. In a community where cases were decided by witnesses, a lie could ruin someone's life. Afterward, the people trembled before the presence of God.

Today we can take care with our words: not making things up, not exaggerating, and not repeating gossip that damages the reputation of others. Before speaking about someone, ask yourself: is it true, and does it help?
exp.31:28:
Moses tells the Levites that on that day they have set themselves apart for the Lord. "Consecrate" means devoting oneself completely to God. They did so even at the cost of their own sons and brothers, and for this reason God grants them a blessing.

Moses speaks after the people made the golden calf and worshiped it. The Levites obeyed the command to punish the rebellion, and about three thousand died. The text does not explain every detail of that moment, but it shows how serious idolatry was. The Bible presents loyalty to God as more important than human ties.

For today: let us ask ourselves what things in our hearts occupy the place that belongs to God. Obeying Him can be costly, but we must never place anything above Him. Let us ask Him for help to be faithful, with love and humility.
exp.24:11:
God tells Moses to make four rings of cast gold for the ark. The rings go on the four corners, two on one side and two on the other. "Cast" means the gold is melted and poured into a mold. "Corners" here refers to the lower parts, where the ark would rest. Some scholars think these were the feet or the lower corners.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai while giving him the instructions for the tabernacle. The ark was the most sacred object, a symbol of God's presence with Israel. The rings were used to insert the poles and carry it, without touching it directly (vv. 13-14).

God cares about even the small details when it comes to approaching Him with respect. Today we might ask ourselves: do I treat with reverence and order what God has entrusted to me, even in the small things?
exp.18:23:
God tells Moses to go down from the mountain and then come back up, this time with his brother Aaron. But the priests and the people must not cross the boundary that was set around the mountain to approach God, because He could strike them down.

Israel is camped in front of Mount Sinai, and God is about to give them his law. Moses had said the people would not go up, but God insists on the warning. The boundaries show that God is holy and that drawing near to Him is not something to do carelessly. Aaron does go up, because God permits it.

Today we can draw near to God with reverence and gratitude, without taking Him lightly. He sets the way, and in Christ the door is opened to us, but we still come with humility and sincerity.
exp.25:3:
God gives instructions here for joining the curtains of the tabernacle. A loop is a small fastening of cloth, like an eye or a tab. The blue color is a dull violet-blue, and the joining point is where two pieces come together. Blue loops were to be made along the edge of the last curtain in each group of five, so that the two groups could be joined together.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai, after rescuing Israel from Egypt. He gives him the design of the tabernacle, the tent where God would dwell among his people. The verses that follow explain that gold clasps would join the loops, so that the curtains would form one single tabernacle.

For today: God cares about details and unity. Just as small loops joined separate pieces into one dwelling, we too can care for small attitudes, such as patience and forgiveness, that keep the family and the church united.
exp.32:11:
Moses speaks to God with candor. He reminds God that he was told to bring this people up from that place, but God has not told him who will go with him to help. Then he recalls God's own words: that God knows him by name, meaning in a personal and close way, and that he has found grace, or favor, in God's sight. Old words: "declared" means made known, and "to" is the word used for direction toward someone.

Moses speaks just after the sin of the golden calf. God had said that the people should go forward, but that He would not go up in their midst. Moses, as an intercessor, does not want to move ahead without God's presence. His closeness to the Lord, described as speaking with Him face to face, gives him confidence to pray this way.

For today: you can speak to God honestly, without pretending. If you feel that He is asking something great of you and you do not see the way forward, bring your doubt to Him and ask for His company. His presence is worth more than having all the answers.
exp.32:2:
God says that the people will indeed enter the good land, described as a place where "milk and honey" flow, meaning fertile and abundant. But God himself will not go up in the midst of them.

"Stiff neck" means a rigid neck, a way of speaking about stubborn people who refuse to bow down. The word "consume" means to destroy.

God speaks with Moses after the people made the golden calf (Exodus 32). God keeps his promise to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, but he announces that his close presence would be dangerous for a rebellious people. The people grieve, and Moses intercedes later on.

Today we can learn that God's gifts are not worth as much as God himself. Ask him for a humble heart that is willing to be corrected, because the most valuable thing is to walk in his presence.
exp.12:19:
The explanation says the Israelites left Succoth and camped at Etham, on the edge of the wilderness. The phrase "pitched camp" means they set up their camp to rest. The phrase "at the entrance" means at the edge, where the wilderness begins.

Here the narrator of the book, traditionally Moses, recounts the people's journey just after leaving Egypt. God was leading them by a longer road, not the shortest one. Succoth and Etham are places along the route; their exact location is not known with certainty. What matters is that God was already guiding them step by step, as seen in the cloud and the fire that go before them.

Today, sometimes God leads us along paths we do not understand, right at the edge of the unknown. We can move forward one step at a time, trusting that the one who guides us does not leave us alone in the wilderness.
exp.0:17:
The verse tells that the king of Egypt called for the Hebrew midwives. He asked them angrily: "Why have you done this? Why have you let the male children live?" In the wording of the verse, "called for" and "saved alive" are the phrases to note, meaning he summoned them and let the boys remain alive.

The one speaking is Pharaoh. Earlier he had ordered them to kill every newborn Hebrew boy, but they feared God and did not obey that unjust command. Pharaoh noticed that the boys kept being born and staying alive, and that is why he confronts them. He had the power, but they answered with cleverness and courage.

For today: when human authority asks us to do something that goes against life or justice, the fear of God gives us the firmness to say no. Doing so may cost us, but God sees the faithfulness of those who honor him, even when they seem small and insignificant.
exp.28:19:
It says that Moses must kill the second ram, the one for the ordination, and put some of its blood on three places of Aaron and of his sons: the lobe (the soft, fleshy part) of the right ear, the thumb of the right hand, and the big toe of the right foot. The rest of the blood is sprinkled around the altar.

God speaks to Moses and gives him instructions for setting apart Aaron and his sons as priests. The blood touched the ear, the hand, and the foot. Many understand that this pointed to their whole being being dedicated to God: hearing, acting, and walking. The text does not explain each detail, so that reading is a common interpretation.

For today: we can ask God that what we hear, what we do, and the places we go be dedicated to Him. Christians see in the blood a picture of Christ, who cleanses us and sets us apart to serve Him.
exp.38:10:
This verse describes the second row of precious stones on the breastpiece, the garment worn by the high priest. In that row there was an emerald, a sapphire, and a diamond. The exact Hebrew names of the stones are not entirely certain, and modern translations sometimes change them.

The account tells how the craftsmen made the holy garments just as God had commanded Moses. According to Exodus 28:21, each stone bore the name of one of the twelve tribes of Israel. In this way, the priest presented the people before God.

For today: God cares about details and does not see his people as a faceless crowd. Each stone had its place and its name. For Christians, Jesus is our high priest who carries us close to his heart. Today you can rest knowing that God knows you by name and values you.
exp.15:31:
Moses tells what God commanded: to fill an omer with manna and keep it for future generations. An omer was a small measure, roughly what one person would eat in a day. The purpose was that the descendants could see the bread with which God fed his people in the wilderness, after bringing them out of Egypt.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel, who had been weeks in the wilderness and depended on the manna each day. God wanted a visible reminder of his care to remain. Afterward, Aaron put the manna in a jar before the Testimony, as God had commanded. Scholars do not agree on details about where exactly it was kept, but the sense of the reminder is clear.

For today: do not let the memory of what God has done be lost. Tell your children, or others, how God has sustained you. Writing down those experiences can strengthen the faith of those who come after.
exp.6:17:
This verse announces what will happen when the water of the Nile turns to blood: the fish will die, the river will stink, and the Egyptians will be disgusted to drink from it. The word "stink" means it will smell very bad, and "disgusted" means it will make them feel sick.

God speaks through Moses, and commands him to tell Pharaoh to let the Hebrew people go to serve God in the wilderness. Pharaoh had not wanted to listen. This is the first of the plagues, a sign so that Pharaoh and Egypt would know that Jehovah is the Lord. The Nile was vital to Egypt, and many regarded it with great respect.

For today: God invites us to listen to Him in time. If there is something in which He calls us to change, let us not harden our hearts. And let us remember that nothing created, neither work nor money, should take the place of God.
exp.22:13:
This verse says that God asks Israel to hold three festivals each year in his honor. Later the verse names them: the festival of unleavened bread, the harvest festival of the first fruits, and the festival of ingathering at the end of the year.

God speaks, through Moses, within the laws he gave Israel after bringing them out of Egypt. Earlier he had commanded weekly rest and faithfulness to him alone. Now he orders a calendar that would remind them of his deliverance (the departure from Egypt) and his provision through the harvests. These festivals helped the people not to forget who had freed them and who sustained them.

For today: set aside fixed times to pause, give thanks to God, and remember what he has done for you. You might write from time to time a list of his care for you and share it with your family or your church.
exp.11:19:
God, through Moses, commands that during the Feast of Unleavened Bread nothing leavened may be eaten. Leavened bread is bread prepared with yeast, which makes it rise. The places where they lived, their houses and homes, are the dwellings mentioned in the verse. Everyone was to eat bread without yeast.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they leave Egypt. God gives them instructions for the Passover and for remembering their deliverance. According to the same account, unleavened bread is associated with the hurried departure from Egypt. The command also included the foreigner who lived among them. Some see in yeast a symbol of what spreads and corrupts, although here the text focuses on obedience and remembrance.

For today: take a moment to remember what God has done for you, and remove from your life some habit that keeps you from Him. Obeying in everyday matters, even in small things, can be a way of giving thanks.
exp.25:8:
This verse gives instructions for assembling the goat-hair covering. The eleven curtains were joined in two groups: five on one side and six on the other. The sixth curtain was folded over toward the front of the tabernacle. The phrase "before the face" means "at the front, at the entrance." It is not known for certain how that fold was arranged, and there are several interpretations.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai and gives him the design of the tabernacle, the tent where He would dwell in the midst of Israel. This goat-hair covering went over the fine linen curtains and protected the sanctuary. God cared about every detail of that place.

For today: if God took interest in such small details so that He could live among His people, He also takes interest in the everyday matters of your life. Do the small tasks He entrusts to you with care and faithfulness, as an act of worship.
exp.6:10:
After seeing Aaron's staff turned into a serpent, Pharaoh was not impressed. He called his wise men and sorcerers, and they did something similar with their enchantments. The sorcerers were men who practiced hidden arts or tricks. The wise men were advisers at the court.

Here the narrator tells us what happened. God had sent Moses and Aaron with a sign so that Pharaoh would let Israel go. Pharaoh answers with his own specialists. It is not known for certain how they did it: some think of tricks, others of deceptive spiritual power. The text only says that they did it, and then shows that Aaron's staff swallowed up the others.

For today: not everything that looks powerful comes from God. An impressive sign does not prove the truth. Always compare what you see or hear with God's Word, and trust Him even when others seem to match Him.
exp.37:7:
It says that Bezaleel and his helpers made the basin or laver of the tabernacle, together with its foot, and that they used metal, bronze or copper, from the mirrors of certain women. "The foot" is the base or stand. The women who assembled at the door are understood to have served or ministered at the entrance of the tent; it is not known precisely what their task was. "Testimony" refers to God's law.

Here the narrator of the book, traditionally Moses, speaks. He describes how the tabernacle was built as God had commanded it. The laver served so that the priests could wash before ministering. The mirrors were valuable personal possessions, and they were given for worship.

For today: God can use what we offer him sincerely, even when it seems small or personal. We can ask ourselves what "mirror" we have, a talent, time, or a resource, that we could place at the service of God and others.
exp.6:22:
He says that Pharaoh turned around and went back to his palace. The sentence about turning is rendered in the verse itself, so the explanation here is simply that he returned to his house. The phrase about not setting his heart on this even means that he did not take seriously or reflect on what had just happened, even though the water of the Nile had turned to blood.

This is not a character speaking; it is Moses' account of the first plague. God had sent Moses and Aaron to ask that Pharaoh let Israel go. The Egyptian magicians copied the sign, and Pharaoh held on to that to avoid changing his mind. His heart was already hardened.

For today: when God gets our attention, whether through his Word or through circumstances, let us not look for excuses or look the other way. Let us stop and reflect, and respond with humility.
exp.6:2:
God tells Moses that he himself will harden Pharaoh's heart, that is, make him stubborn and set in his decision. He also promises to fill Egypt with "signs and wonders," that is, mighty deeds that show who God is.

The Lord speaks, and explains to Moses what is coming. Moses already knows that Pharaoh will not obey easily. God wants Egypt and its people to know that he is the Lord. The text also says that Pharaoh hardened his own heart; for this reason many believers think that God confirmed a stubbornness that was already there. Others understand it in a different way.

For today: when obeying God seems to bring no results, remember that he keeps working with a purpose. Stay faithful, and do not let yourself be hardened against his voice.
exp.15:35:
This verse clarifies a unit of measure. It says that an omer equals one tenth of an ephah. The ephah was a measure for dry goods, such as grain or flour, and the omer was a much smaller portion. Although today it is usually calculated that the omer was about two liters, scholars do not fully agree on the exact amount.

The narrator, whom tradition identifies with Moses, closes here the story of the manna. God had commanded that each person gather one omer each day. This note helps readers understand how much that daily portion was, and it also makes clear God's care, since he fed his people for forty years.

God often gives us what we need for each day, not always more than enough. Today we can practice trust and gratitude: thanking him for what we have, avoiding the anxiety of accumulating, and asking him each morning to sustain us, knowing that he is faithful.
exp.6:1:
God tells Moses that he must say everything God commands him, and that his brother Aaron will be the one who speaks with Pharaoh. The goal is clear: that the king let the children of Israel go out of Egypt.

The explanation with the wording "á" being the old way of writing "a" is not included here, since that comment concerns the source text and does not apply to the verse your reader sees.

Jehovah speaks with Moses, who felt unable to speak well before Pharaoh (Exodus 6:30). God gives him Aaron as helper and spokesman. Moses receives God's message, and Aaron communicates it. God also announces that Pharaoh will resist, but that He Himself will act to free His people.

For today: God does not expect us to do everything alone. He gives us his word and also people who walk alongside us. Obey what God shows you, and accept the help of others without shame.
exp.24:38:
This verse says that the lampstand and all its utensils were to be made from a talent of pure gold. A talent was a very large unit of weight; it is usually estimated at between 30 and 35 kilograms, although the exact calculation is not certain. The word "vessels" here means utensils or instruments, such as the snuffers (tools for trimming the wick) and the trays (dishes for the waste).

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai. He gives him instructions for building the tabernacle, the place where Israel would worship and where God would be present among his people. The seven-lamp lampstand would give light in the holy place.

God deserves the best, not the leftovers. Pure, fine gold reminds us that we can serve him with excellence and devotion. Today it is not about giving valuable objects, but about offering him the best of our time, affection and effort, with a sincere heart.
exp.38:12:
This verse describes the fourth row of precious stones on the breastpiece of the high priest. It had a beryl, an onyx, and a jasper. The stones were set in their gold settings, each one surrounded and held firmly in place by a base of gold. The exact names of the stones are uncertain, and older and modern translations differ a little.

This passage is part of the account of how the craftsmen made Aaron's sacred garments, just as God had commanded Moses. The narrator tells us that every detail was carried out. The twelve stones represented the twelve tribes of Israel, with a name engraved on each one.

For today: God does not see his people as a faceless mass. Each name was engraved and held with care. You can rest in the knowledge that God knows you personally, and you can also value and care for each person in your church and in your family.
exp.24:0:
This verse says that God, called here "the LORD," spoke to Moses. The word "saying" is an old way of introducing a message that follows. It is only the introduction, but it shows that God takes the initiative to speak with his people.

The one speaking is God, and Moses is the one who receives the message to carry to Israel. This happens at Mount Sinai, shortly after the people left Egypt and received the commandments. Here a new section begins: the instructions for building the tabernacle, a place where God would be present among them. The first thing he asks for is an offering given willingly and from the heart.

For today: before asking anything of us, God speaks to us. We can set aside a moment to listen to his Word with attention, and then respond to him with sincere generosity, not out of obligation, but gladly and from the heart.
exp.33:8:
Moses asks God that, if he truly looks on him with favor, he would go in the midst of the people. He admits that Israel is "a stiffnecked people," that is, stubborn and hard to correct. Even so, he pleads: "pardon our iniquity and our sin, and take us for thine inheritance," meaning, stay with us as your people and your own possession.

Moses speaks after Israel made the golden calf. God had just proclaimed his name: merciful, forgiving, but also just. Moses bows down and takes the side of the people, saying "our sin," even though he did not make the calf. God responds by renewing his covenant.

For today: when you recognize your own stubbornness, do not run from God; come near humbly, ask him for forgiveness and for his presence. You can also intercede for others with compassion, instead of only pointing at them.
exp.3:6:
God tells Moses to put his hand back inside his clothing, at the height of his chest. The word "bosom" here means the fold of the robe over the chest. Moses obeys, and when he takes it out, the hand is no longer diseased: it has been made healthy again, "as his other flesh," that is, like the rest of his skin.

God speaks with Moses at the burning bush. Moses fears that the people of Israel will not believe him. For this reason God gives him signs to show that he is truly being sent. The hand that is diseased and then restored teaches that God has power over sickness and over life.

For today: Moses had to obey before he saw the result. When God asks you to take a simple step, take it with confidence, even though you do not understand everything. He is faithful to sustain you and to complete what he begins.
exp.14:5:
It says that God's power is great and that with that power he destroyed the enemy. The word "right hand" refers to the right hand, a symbol of strength and action. The phrase "glorious in power" means that his power was shown in a glorious way. "Dashed in pieces" means smashed or defeated. The words "thy right hand" are repeated to stress that the victory was the work of God.

Moses speaks together with the people of Israel, in the song they sang after crossing the Red Sea. They had just been delivered from the army of Pharaoh, who was pursuing them. They sing to give thanks and to acknowledge that God saved them when they had no way out.

When God helps you in a difficult moment, do not stay silent. Give him thanks out loud, tell what he did, and remember that help when the difficulty returns. In this way your trust in him grows.
exp.15:7:
Moses announces that God will give them meat in the evening and bread in the morning, enough to fill them completely. He says that God has heard their complaints, meaning their grumbling and quejas in the sense of grievances. He makes clear that although they were grumbling against Moses and Aaron, they were really grumbling against God.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel in the wilderness, shortly after leaving Egypt. They were hungry and said they would rather have stayed in Egypt as slaves with food. Moses reminds them that God had led them out and that He hears what they say, even when they think they are only criticizing their leaders.

For today: when you feel the urge to complain, pause and bring your need honestly before God. Asking Him for help with trust is better than grumbling, because He hears you and cares for you.
exp.1:14:
It says that Pharaoh heard about what Moses had done and wanted to kill him. So Moses fled far away from him and went to live in the land of Midian. There he sat down by a well.

The narrator is describing what happened after Moses killed an Egyptian who was mistreating a Hebrew. When a Hebrew confronted him, Moses was afraid, because the deed had come to light. His life changed suddenly: he went from the house of Pharaoh to being a fugitive. The well is the place where his new chapter begins, as the following verses show.

Sometimes our mistakes take us out of what we knew and leave us in places of waiting. Even there, God can keep working and preparing us. If you are in a season like this, do not lose heart: stay faithful in the small things.
exp.37:1:
It says that Bezalel made horns on the four corners of the altar of burnt offering. The horns were not pieces attached afterward, but came out of the same piece of wood. Then the whole altar was covered with bronze, which in other versions is translated as bronze or copper.

The narrator tells how the tabernacle was built, following the instructions God gave to Moses. This altar was the place where the sacrifices were offered. The horns are connected with the altar of atonement, and blood was sprinkled on them. Their exact meaning is interpreted in several ways, but they are usually associated with strength and forgiveness.

Today we can remember that drawing near to God requires a way that He Himself has provided. Christians see in Jesus that final sacrifice. We can approach with confidence, without trying to earn forgiveness through our works.
exp.34:3:
Moses gathers the whole people of Israel and tells them that what he is about to pass on is not his own idea but a command from the Lord, the name of God in this version. "Congregation" means the entire community gathered together. The phrase "this is the thing which the Lord commanded" introduces the instructions that follow.

Moses speaks after the sin of the golden calf and the renewal of the covenant. First he reminds them of the Sabbath, the day of rest, and then he asks for offerings to build the tabernacle, the place where God would dwell among his people. Before building, God reminds them that their rest comes before their work.

For today: before serving God with your resources or your effort, make space to rest and listen to him. Then give joyfully, not out of pressure, but out of love for him.
exp.18:18:
This verse tells that the sound of the trumpet grew stronger and stronger. Meanwhile, Moses was speaking with God, and God answered him with a voice that could be heard.

The people of Israel were at the foot of Mount Sinai, and Moses had brought them out of the camp to meet with God. The mountain was smoking and trembling. Moses acted as a go-between between God and the people, and God showed His holiness so that they would respect Him. It is not known with certainty where the sound of the trumpet came from.

God is not someone we can treat carelessly. Before praying or reading the Bible, take a moment to remember who God is and draw near with reverence. At the same time, He does answer those who speak to Him.
exp.28:8:
God tells Moses to put the sash (the belt) on Aaron and his sons, and to fasten the bonnets on them, which were simple caps or turbans for priests. In this way the priesthood will be theirs as a "perpetual statute," that is, as a lasting right and rule. "Fill their hands" is an old expression for consecrating or installing someone in office; its exact meaning is debated, but it refers to giving them priestly service.

God speaks to Moses at Sinai while giving instructions for consecrating the first priests of Israel. The garments, the oil, and the sacrifices that follow show that serving the Lord was not something each person took up on his own, but a calling that God himself established.

For today: serving God begins with being called and prepared by Him. Ask Him to clothe you with humility and willingness, and serve with reverence, not relying only on your own strength.
exp.17:1:
