This verse says that Jethro, Moses' father-in-law, took Zipporah, Moses' wife, to bring her along with him. This happened after Moses had sent her back. The word "sent" here means that he had her go home to her father's house.

The narrator of the book tells us that Jethro, priest of Midian, heard how God had freed Israel from Egypt. That is why he went out to meet Moses. The Bible does not explain why Moses had sent Zipporah away. Some believe it was to protect her during the conflict with Pharaoh, but this is not certain.

When we hear what God has done in the lives of others, it can encourage us to draw near, care for our family, and seek reconciliation.
exp.20:7:
It says that if a young woman was given over as a servant and her master had chosen her to be his wife, but afterward she no longer pleases him, he must allow someone from her family to redeem her, that is, to pay to set her free. He may not sell her to foreigners, because he has dealt deceitfully with her.

God speaks through Moses to Israel, shortly after the Ten Commandments. These laws regulated ancient customs, such as servitude because of debt, in order to limit abuse and protect the most vulnerable person. It does not mean that God approved of the whole system; the law put a check on harm within a society of that time.

For today: never use your position or power to take advantage of others. If you promise something, keep it honestly, and when you fail, seek to make things right with justice and compassion.
exp.5:17:
This verse lists the four sons of Kohath, who was a son of Levi: Amram, Izhar, Hebron, and Uzziel. It also says that Kohath lived one hundred and thirty-three years. The words "and" here only join the names together, just as we use "and" today.

Here the narrator of the book pauses in the middle of the story of Moses to show which family they come from. God has just promised to deliver Israel, and the list goes down to Amram, the father of Aaron and Moses. This shows that they belonged to the tribe of Levi. Some scholars think the list does not include every generation, but the text does not make this clear.

For today: God works through families and through real, specific people, even when no one remembers them. Your family history and your daily faithfulness matter to Him. Serve faithfully where you are, because God can use your life in ways you do not imagine today.
exp.32:18:
God replies to Moses that he will make all his goodness pass before him and will proclaim his name, the LORD, before him. He then adds that he will show mercy to whom he chooses to show mercy, and will be gracious to whom he chooses to be gracious. Being gracious means being kind and compassionate; to proclaim means to announce aloud.

God is speaking. Moses had just asked him, "Show me your glory," after the sin of the golden calf, when the people needed to know whether God would still be with them. God does not show his face, but he does reveal his character: goodness and mercy. Many understand that mercy is a free gift, not a payment earned by merit.

Today we can draw near to God without boasting about what we do, but trusting in his mercy. If you have failed, do not hide yourself: go to him with humility, because his goodness does not depend on you being perfect.
exp.38:8:
It says the breastplate, the piece the high priest wore over his chest, was square and doubled over. It measured a span in length and a span in width. The old name for this piece is "breastplate," which is the word used in the verse itself, so no separate explanation is needed here. A span was the measure of an open hand, about 22 to 23 centimeters, although the exact calculation is debated. Folding it double formed a kind of pouch.

Here the narrator tells how the craftsmen of Israel carried out what the LORD had commanded Moses for the tabernacle. This piece was to hold the precious stones with the names of the tribes, which are described in the verses that follow. Interpreters differ on the exact use of that pouch.

For today: God attends to the details and reminds us that his people are precious to him. You can do your work with care and obedience, and rest in the knowledge that God carries you in his heart.
exp.19:17:
This verse describes what the people of Israel saw and heard when God gave the Ten Commandments. The "voices" were thunder or loud sounds, and the "trumpet" was a horn that sounded very loudly. Mount Sinai was smoking and flaming with fire, and the people, frightened, stayed at a distance.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, telling what happened after God spoke the commandments. Shortly afterward, the people ask Moses to be the one who speaks with God. Moses explains to them that God came to test them, so that the reverence toward him would help them not to sin.

For today: to draw near to God with reverence, without losing trust. Before making decisions, we can pause to remember who God is, and that helps us live with more honesty and care.
exp.36:24:
This verse tells that Bezaleel made the incense altar from acacia wood (shittim). It was small and square: one cubit long and one cubit wide, and two cubits high. A cubit was roughly half a meter, though its exact measure is debated. The horns were projections at the four corners, made from the same piece as the altar.

Here the account describes how the tabernacle was built, following the instructions God gave to Moses. This altar was placed in front of the veil, inside the sanctuary. There aromatic incense was burned, and its smoke rose as a sign of prayer and worship to God.

For today: God cares about the details of worship, and He also wants us to seek Him consistently. Just as the incense rose every day, we can set aside fixed moments to pray with sincerity and gratitude.
exp.25:32:
God tells Moses to hang the veil under the clasps, that is, the hooks or fasteners that joined the curtains of the tabernacle. Behind the veil would go the ark of the testimony, the chest that held the tablets of the law. That veil would separate two spaces: the holy place and the most holy place.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai, giving him the plan of the tent where he would dwell in the midst of Israel. The veil showed that God is holy and that one does not come into his presence in just any way. Later, Leviticus 16 shows that only the high priest entered, once a year.

For today: Christians read in Hebrews 10:19-22 that, through Jesus, we can draw near to God with confidence. Come to Him in prayer with sincerity, gratitude, and reverence, without feeling that there is a closed door.
exp.39:8:
God tells Moses to take the special anointing oil and pour it over the tabernacle and everything inside it, including its furnishings. To "anoint" means to put oil on something to set it apart for God. To "consecrate" means to dedicate it solely to the service of God, and "furnishings" here refers to the tools or containers used in the worship.

God speaks with Moses at the end of the book of Exodus, when the people now have everything ready to raise the tabernacle, the tent where God would dwell among them. Before it was used, each object had to be formally set apart. This showed that the place and its contents belonged to God and were not for common use.

For today: we can ask ourselves which things in our lives (time, money, talents, home) we can consciously dedicate to God, offering them in prayer so that they serve his purpose.
exp.4:3:
The king of Egypt speaks to Moses and Aaron angrily. He asks why they are distracting the people from their work, and he orders them to go back to their burdens. Those words are the ones the King James gives as "burdens," which means their labors or workloads.

Moses and Aaron had just asked for permission to go three days into the wilderness to worship God. Pharaoh did not acknowledge the LORD, and he saw that request as an excuse to stop working. The Israelites were enslaved people who produced for Egypt, so he was thinking about his economy, not their worship. As the text goes on, his response was to make the work harder.

For today: sometimes the world sees faith as a waste of time or an obstacle. Even so, setting aside time for God is important. We can do it with patience and trust, even when we meet opposition.
exp.4:7:
Pharaoh orders the foremen to keep demanding the same quota of bricks as before, even though the workers will now have to gather their own straw. He says the Israelites are "idle," meaning they do not have enough work to keep them busy, and that is why they ask to go and sacrifice to their God. The foremen were the overseers who watched over the labor.

Pharaoh speaks after Moses and Aaron's first request to let the people go and worship. He answers with more pressure, so that the people will be so worn out they will not think about worshiping. He describes their desire for freedom as laziness, which was an unfair accusation.

For today: when someone tries to snuff out your faith by overloading you, remember that exhaustion does not cancel God's call. Guard your times of prayer and rest, and look for support in your community.
exp.6:7:
This verse says that God (Jehovah) spoke to Moses and to Aaron. It is an introductory phrase: the instructions come after it. The word "to" in the verse is the ordinary modern form, and "saying" means that the message follows right away.

The one speaking is God, and he does so just before the two brothers appear before Pharaoh. Moses was eighty years old and Aaron eighty-three. God tells them ahead of time what may happen: Pharaoh would ask them for a sign, and they had to know how to respond. In this way they would not go unprepared or alone.

For today: God still speaks before we face difficult things. We can seek him first in prayer and in his Word, and not depend only on our own strength. Age or experience is no obstacle when God guides the way.
exp.11:38:
This verse tells us that the Israelites made flat breads without yeast from the dough they had taken out of Egypt. The dough did not have time to rise because the Egyptians drove them out in a hurry, so they could not wait or prepare food for the journey.

The narrator is describing what happened after the last plague, when Pharaoh and the Egyptians pressed Israel to leave. This detail explains why the later festival of unleavened bread is celebrated, as a reminder of that sudden departure. God was bringing them out of slavery, and everything happened very quickly.

Today we can learn to remember with gratitude the times God has rescued us, even when it came unexpectedly. We can keep some simple reminder, such as a yearly prayer or a journal of gratitude, so that we do not forget his faithfulness.
exp.24:25:
God tells Moses to make four gold rings for the table of the tabernacle. The rings go at the four corners, where the legs are. Here the word for the table's "corners" refers to the table's edges, and the "legs" are its feet. These rings would hold the poles that were used to carry the table.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai. He gives detailed instructions for building the tabernacle, a place where Israel could worship him while they walked through the desert. The table held the bread of the presence. For that reason it had to be carried with care and respect, without anyone touching it directly.

For today: God cares about the details of what we do for him. We can serve him with order, care, and reverence, even in small tasks that no one sees, like a few simple rings. What is humble can also be holy when it is done for God.
exp.33:1:
He tells Moses to get ready that night and go up Mount Sinai early the next morning. There he is to wait for the Lord at the top of the mountain.

The Lord speaks. Moses had broken the first tablets of the law when the people made the golden calf. Now God gives him a second chance and renews the covenant. He asks Moses to cut new tablets and go up alone, showing that God is holy, but also merciful.

God invites us to meet with Him, and it is worth preparing ourselves. We can set aside an early time, in silence and with a willing heart, to listen to Him. And if we have failed, He gives us the chance to begin again.
exp.4:9:
It says that the taskmasters of the people and the Israelite officers went out and gave the people Pharaoh's order: there would no longer be straw for making bricks. The taskmasters who watched over the work were Egyptian overseers, and the officers were Israelites appointed to be in charge of the work crews. The straw was mixed with the clay to make the bricks.

Moses and Aaron had asked Pharaoh to let the people go to worship God. Pharaoh became angry and tried to crush that hope with more labor. He thought that if the people were tired, they would have no time to think about God. So he took away the straw and kept the same number of bricks required.

For today: sometimes, when we try to obey God, things become harder. That does not mean God has abandoned us. We can keep trusting Him and ask Him for strength while we wait for His answer.
exp.20:31:
It says that if an ox gores and kills a male or female servant, the owner of the ox must pay thirty pieces of silver to the master of that person, and the ox must be stoned to death. "Gore" means to wound with the horns. "Servant" here means a slave, and a "shekel" was a unit of silver weight used as money.

God speaks to Moses at Sinai, within the civil laws that follow the Ten Commandments. These rules governed the life of Israel and set limits on responsibility for damages. The verse before it deals with the owner of a dangerous ox who had already been warned. Here a fixed compensation is established, and the animal is also judged, which underlines that human life is serious before God. Scholars debate how to understand this law in its own time, and it is best not to assume more than the text says.

For today: if what I am responsible for can cause harm, I must take good care of it and answer honestly when someone is hurt by it.
exp.4:6:
This verse says that Pharaoh gives an order: the Israelites will no longer be given straw for making bricks, as they had been before. Now they themselves will have to go and gather it. Straw was mixed with the clay to make the bricks. The words addressed to the Egyptian overseers are the commands given to them.

Pharaoh speaks right after Moses and Aaron asked him to let the people go into the wilderness to worship God. Pharaoh becomes angry, accuses them of being idle, and decides to increase their burden so that they will not think about leaving. The overseers who watched over the work, and the Israelite officers in charge of the daily quota, are the ones who carried out these demands.

For today: sometimes, when we try to obey God, things become harder at first. That does not mean God has abandoned us. We can keep trusting in Him, praying, and asking for strength, remembering that He sees our affliction.
exp.15:34:
This verse says that the people of Israel ate manna for forty years while they traveled through the desert. They stopped eating it when they reached the inhabited land, that is, the border of Canaan. The word "border" means edge or limit. "Children of Israel" refers to the whole people.

Here the narrator of the book, traditionally understood to be Moses, is speaking, although some scholars think this final note was added later. Earlier in the account, God is said to have given the manna each day, and they kept an omer of it in a jar before the Testimony as a memorial for future generations. This verse sums up how long God's care lasted.

For today: God sustained his people day after day, without fail, for years. We can trust that he also provides what we need at every stage, and we can remember with gratitude how he has cared for us.
exp.1:4:
This verse tells that Pharaoh's daughter went down to the Nile to bathe. While her attendants walked along the riverbank, she saw a small basket among the reeds, a place of cane and rushes, and she sent one of her servants to bring it to her.

The narrator goes on with the story of the Hebrew boy whom his mother had hidden for three months, since Pharaoh had ordered the death of the Hebrew boys. When she could hide him no longer, she placed him in the river, and his sister watched from a distance. The text does not say whether the princess came there by chance or by habit; it only shows how the paths come together.

For today: even when we cannot see how God is working, we can do with faith what is ours to do, as this mother did, and trust Him with the rest.
exp.36:15:
This verse says that Bezalel made the items that went on the table of the tabernacle: the plates, the spoons (which were probably small cups for incense), the covers, and the bowls. The "covers" and "bowls" were pitchers and cups for pouring out drink offerings. To "pour out" means to pour out liquid as an offering to God. Everything was made of fine gold.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, recounting how the instructions God gave to Moses were carried out. The people were building the tabernacle, the place where God dwelt among them. Even the smallest item is mentioned to show exact obedience. Some scholars believe the table and the bread pointed to fellowship with God, though the text does not explain this directly.

For today: God cares about small details done with care and obedience. Do your everyday work with excellence, as an offering to Him.
exp.11:10:
God tells the Israelites how they were to eat the Passover meal. They were to be dressed and ready to travel: "with your loins girded" means having their clothing gathered up at the waist so they could walk quickly. Their shoes on their feet and the staff in their hand show that they were prepared to leave. And they were to eat in haste, because that meal was the Lord's Passover.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron, so they can pass it on to the people, on the night before the departure from Egypt. The Israelites were slaves, and God was going to judge Egypt and set them free. The blood of the lamb on the houses would be the sign for the judgment to pass over them.

For today: when God calls you to leave something that enslaves you, do not put it off for later. Trust in his provision and get ready today to obey promptly.
exp.23:13:
Moses tells the elders of Israel to stay and wait in that place until he and Joshua come back. He reminds them that Aaron and Hur remain with them. The words "Tarry ye" mean "wait for us," and "matters" here means issues or disputes. Anyone who has a problem to settle should go to Aaron and Hur.

Moses speaks before going up Mount Sinai, where God would give him the stone tablets and his law. He knew it would take time, so he left two leaders in charge of the people. The text does not say how long he expected to be gone. Later we see that the wait was long.

For today: when God asks us to wait, or when someone we trust is away, it is wise to have order and responsible people in place. And if we are the ones who must wait, let us do it with patience and faithfulness, without ceasing to seek God.
exp.23:8:
This verse tells that Moses went up the mountain together with Aaron, his sons Nadab and Abihu, and seventy of the elders of Israel. They were representatives of the people. The explanation of the wording in the source, which is not part of the verse your reader sees, has been removed here.

The narrator is Moses, who writes about what happened right after the people promised to obey God. The covenant was sealed with blood, and now God invites these leaders to come near. The verses that follow say they saw the God of Israel and ate and drank in his presence. It is a scene of fellowship with God after a solemn commitment.

For today: God invites us to draw near to Him, not only to obey Him from a distance. If you have said that you want to follow Him, seek His presence with humility and gratitude, knowing that fellowship with Him is a gift.
exp.35:32:
It says that Bezalel and his helpers placed a central wooden bar that ran through the boards of the tabernacle wall, from one end to the other. The "middle bar" is the bar that went in the center, and the word for "end" is the same as the verse's "one end to the other." These bars kept the boards joined together and firm.

It is part of the account of how the tabernacle was built, following the instructions God gave to Moses. The narrator describes each piece in detail, showing that the people did everything just as God had commanded. Some scholars see in the bars a symbol of unity, but the text does not say so directly.

God cares even for the details no one sees. Just as that bar held everything together from within, our faith is strengthened by simple, steady habits, such as praying and reading the Bible, even when they seem small.
exp.24:1:
God tells Moses to speak to the people of Israel so that they bring him an offering. But he makes clear how it should be given: freely, willingly, "with their heart." The words "take my offering" mean that they were to set something apart for God, and "that gives it willingly" means that no one was to be forced.

God speaks with Moses on Mount Sinai, shortly after freeing Israel from Egypt and giving them the law. He is about to ask for materials to build the tabernacle, a place of worship where his presence would be near the people. Before asking for anything, God looks at the attitude of the one who gives.

For today: God values the disposition of the heart more than the amount. Before giving your time, your money or your talents, ask yourself whether you are doing it with gratitude and freedom, not out of pressure or habit. A small gift given with joy pleases God.
exp.28:39:
The verse describes what was to accompany each lamb of the daily sacrifice: a tenth part of an ephah of fine flour mixed with a fourth part of a hin of beaten olive oil, and a fourth part of a hin of wine as a drink offering, that is, a liquid poured out as an offering. The ephah and the hin were ancient units of measure; their exact equivalents in liters are calculated in different ways.

God speaks to Moses as he gives instructions for consecrating the priests and organizing worship in the tabernacle. Every morning and every evening a lamb was offered, and so Israel maintained constant worship, for God wanted to dwell among his people and speak with them there.

For today: God values consistency. We can set aside a moment when we begin and another when we end the day to pray, give thanks, and offer to him what we are and what we have.
exp.2:5:
God presents himself to Moses as the God of his ancestors: Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Moses covers his face because he is afraid to look at God. The phrase "afraid" here expresses a deep reverence before something so holy, not just a sudden scare.

God speaks from the burning bush. He identifies himself this way so that Moses will understand that it is the same God who made promises to his family generations ago. Right after this, God says that he has seen the suffering of his people in Egypt and that he is going to deliver them. His holy presence and his care go together.

Today we can approach God with confidence, but also with reverence. Before asking him for something, we can pause for a moment to acknowledge who he is: holy, faithful to his promises, and attentive to the pain of his people.
exp.4:4:
Pharaoh says that the Hebrew people are already very numerous in the land, and he accuses Moses and Aaron of making them stop their work. The word "burdens" here refers to their labors or workloads, that is, the compulsory tasks they had to carry out.

Pharaoh, the king of Egypt, speaks in response to the request of Moses and Aaron to go three days into the wilderness to worship God. He does not acknowledge Jehovah and sees the request as an excuse to avoid work. He also mentions that they are many, perhaps because he worries about losing labor or about them organizing. His answer immediately leads to more oppression, as is seen afterward with the straw.

For today: sometimes those who hold power see worship and obedience to God as an obstacle. If your faith brings you opposition, do not lose heart right away; keep trusting God and act with respect and firmness.
exp.10:1:
God tells Moses to speak to the people of Israel so that each man and each woman will ask their Egyptian neighbor for objects of silver and gold. "Ask" here means request. "Articles" refers to valuable objects or items, not only cups.

The Lord speaks just before the tenth plague. Pharaoh would finally let the people go. Afterward, the text says that God gave them favor in the eyes of the Egyptians. Some understand this as a loan, and others as a gift or payment for years of labor. The text does not fully make this clear, but it shows that God was fulfilling what he had promised Abraham: that they would leave with great riches.

Today we can trust that God knows how to care for us and provide what we need, even when we come out of difficult situations. We can obey step by step, without anxiety about the future.
exp.15:4:
It says that on the sixth day, Friday, the people were to prepare what they had gathered, and that it would be twice as much as they gathered each day. The first quoted word means that they would get it ready, and the second word refers to keeping or putting away what was gathered for safekeeping. The word "gather" here means to collect.

God speaks to Moses after the people complained in the desert, longing for the food of Egypt. God promises to send bread from heaven, the manna, and uses it to test whether the people would trust him and follow his instructions. With this command, God is already preparing the rest of the seventh day, though here he does not yet explain it fully.

For today: God cares for us and asks us to trust and to be organized. We can plan wisely, set aside time to rest, and believe that he will provide what is needed.
exp.39:19:
This verse tells how Moses took "the testimony," that is, the two stone tablets with the Ten Commandments, and put them inside the ark. Then he set the poles, which were the carrying bars for the ark, and on top he put the "cover," the lid of the ark, also called the mercy seat.

Here the narrator of the book describes how Moses set up the tabernacle, the tent where God would dwell among his people. A year had already passed since the departure from Egypt. The phrase that is repeated, "as the LORD had commanded," shows that Moses obeyed every detail of what God had instructed him.

For today: God values simple and complete obedience, even in small details. We can ask ourselves what thing God has already shown us that we have left unfinished, and complete it with confidence in Him.
exp.0:3:
This verse closes the list of Jacob's sons who came to Egypt. Here appear Dan, Naphtali, Gad, and Asher. They are the sons born to Jacob's servants, Bilhah and Zilpah. The names are written in the older spelling of this translation, which is why "Naphtali" looks different from how we read it today.

The author, whom tradition identifies as Moses, begins the book of Exodus by recalling who the sons of Israel were. With this list he connects the story to Genesis and shows where the people come from who will later become slaves. He then says there were seventy persons in all, and that Joseph was already in Egypt.

For today: God knows each person by name, even those who seem less important in a list. You can trust that you too are seen and remembered by Him, and you can learn to value those whom others overlook.
exp.32:8:
What it says: When Moses went into the meeting tent, a pillar of cloud came down and stood at the entrance. There God spoke with Moses. The name of God is "the LORD," and "tent" here means a simple tent, not the large sanctuary that would be built later.

Context: This happens after the people made the golden calf. God had been angry, and Moses set up this tent outside the camp. It was a sign of distance, but also of hope: God was still willing to speak. The cloud showed his presence, and the people, when they saw it, would rise and worship.

For today: God does not withdraw completely when we fail; he still invites us to seek him. Set aside a quiet moment each day to pray and listen to his Word, with reverence and with confidence.
exp.23:4:
This verse tells how Moses sent some young men of Israel to present offerings to God. Some animals were burned up completely as whole burnt offerings, as a sign of total surrender. Others were peace offerings, offerings of fellowship, which expressed friendship with God. The animals were young bulls, that is, calves.

The people had just promised to obey everything God had said. Moses, who spoke as the mediator, built an altar and twelve pillars, one for each tribe. These sacrifices prepared the ceremony in which Israel would confirm its covenant with God. It is not known for certain who these young men were; the text does not say.

For today: when we say we want to follow God, our promise should be accompanied by sincere devotion. Today we can offer our lives to him each day, trusting that Christ made the final sacrifice.
exp.16:8:
Moses tells Joshua to choose men and go out to fight against Amalek. He himself will stand on the top of the hill the next day with the rod of God in his hand. A hill is what the source calls a rise or hill, so I'll describe the place simply as the top of the hill.

Moses, the leader of Israel, speaks at Rephidim, shortly after the people doubted God and asked whether he was among them or not. Amalek attacked them, and Moses organizes the defense. This is the first time Joshua appears in the Bible. The rod recalls the signs that God had done through Moses. Scholars do not fully agree on the exact meaning of the gesture with the rod, but the text shows that the victory depended on God.

For today: do your part responsibly, but do not forget to depend on God. Plan, work, and act, and also pray and seek his help. And you do not have to carry the struggles alone: God gives us people who support us.
exp.23:11:
God tells Moses to come up the mountain and to stay there. There he will give him tablets of stone with the law and the commandments that God himself wrote to teach the people. The word "á" is an older form of "a," and "espera allá" means to remain in that place until receiving what was promised.

The Lord speaks shortly after Israel agreed to the covenant, and after the leaders saw God's glory and ate in his presence. God calls Moses to give him in writing the foundations of the people's life with him. Moses goes up with Joshua, his helper, and leaves Aaron and Hur with the elders.

For today: God speaks so that we may know him, not to hide himself. Set aside a quiet time each day to read his Word and wait on him, unhurried, willing to obey whatever he shows you.
exp.39:3:
God tells Moses to bring the table into the tabernacle and set in order what belongs on it, that is, to arrange upon it what is appropriate, such as the bread of the presence. He is also to bring in the lampstand and light its lamps. The golden lampstand that gave light in the holy place is what is meant here.

God speaks, giving Moses instructions for the day the tabernacle would be set up, near the end of the book of Exodus. After so much work on the construction, God shows how everything was to be arranged so that He might dwell in the midst of His people. Nothing was done carelessly or according to each person's own taste.

For today: God cares about order and obedience in the simple things. We can give His Word and prayer a fixed place in our routine, doing it with care and consistency, not only when we happen to have time to spare.
exp.25:31:
God tells Moses that the veil of the tabernacle must be hung from four pillars made of acacia wood, overlaid with gold. The capitals, that is, the upper parts of the pillars, would also be of gold. Each pillar rested on a base of silver.

God himself speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai and gives him detailed instructions for building a place where he would dwell in the midst of Israel. This veil would separate the holy place from the most holy place, where the ark of the testimony would be. It was a sign that drawing near to God requires reverence.

For today: God cares about the details when it comes to his presence. We can draw near to him with respect and gratitude, without taking him lightly, remembering that he himself opened the way for us to be close to him.
exp.13:17:
The Egyptians will come to know that God is the Lord, that is, Jehovah. This will happen when God shows his glory, that is, his power and greatness, by defeating Pharaoh, his war chariots, and his horsemen.

God speaks to Moses beside the Red Sea. Israel had just left slavery, and the Egyptian army was pursuing them. God explains that he will open the sea for his people and that he will allow the Egyptians to follow them. In this way it will become clear, even to those who had denied it, that God rules over all human power.

For today: when you face a problem that seems bigger than you, remember that God is not limited by it. Trust that he can act in his own way and in his own time, and seek to give the glory to him, not to yourself.
exp.28:33:
If any of the meat from the ram of the ordination or of the bread was left until morning, it could not be kept or eaten. It had to be burned in the fire. The "ordination" refers to the ceremony in which the priests were set apart for God. The word "remain" means "be left over," and "holy" means set apart for God.

God speaks to Moses and gives him instructions to ordain Aaron and his sons as priests. That meal was part of the ceremony and had a sacred character. For that reason it was not to be treated as ordinary food or saved for later. Scholars explain the command in various ways, but all agree that it teaches respect for what belongs to God.

For today: treat with reverence what belongs to God, such as your time of prayer, your service, and your offering. Give Him your best and not what is left over.
exp.14:15:
He says that God will bring fear and dread upon the peoples who are in Israel's path. Before the power of his arm (a way of speaking about his strength), they will be as still as a stone. This will last until his people, the ones God redeemed, have finished crossing over.

Moses and the Israelites sing after crossing the Red Sea. They have just seen how God delivered them from Egypt. For that reason they look ahead with confidence: if God defeated the pharaoh, he can also lead them through lands of frightened peoples on the way to the promised land.

For today: when you face something that seems bigger than you, remember what God has already done for you. His past faithfulness can give you calm and courage for the next step.
exp.33:31:
After this, Aaron and the leaders came near to Moses, and then all the people of Israel also came near. Moses then passed on to them everything the Lord had spoken to him on Mount Sinai.

The account describes Moses coming down from the mountain with his face shining after being in God's presence. The people were afraid to come close, but he called them to himself calmly. First the leaders came, and then all the people. Moses was the messenger: he did not speak on his own authority, but passed on what God had told him. This takes place after the renewal of the covenant, following the sin of the golden calf.

For today: when we hear the Word of God, let us draw near with reverence and without fear, and seek to obey it as it was given, without changing it or cutting it short.
exp.21:18:
It says that whoever has sexual relations with an animal must die. The word "lieth" is an old way of saying sexual intercourse, and "beast" means an animal. It is a very firm prohibition against that practice.

God speaks to Moses and gives laws to the people of Israel shortly after bringing them out of Egypt. These rules were part of the covenant at Sinai and set out how a nation set apart for God was to live. The verse appears among laws about sorcery and idolatry, which suggests that the aim was to prevent practices of the neighboring peoples. Some scholars see a connection here with pagan rites, although the text does not explain this. The death penalty belonged to the civil law of ancient Israel.

Today it reminds us that God cares for the dignity and holiness of our sexuality. We can ask Him for help to live with purity, to flee from what degrades, and to treat with respect the life that He created.
exp.8:31:
It says the hail did not harm the wheat or the rye, because they had not yet grown up; they were late crops, sown later. The word "rye" in Hebrew is uncertain; some translate it as spelt or emmer, a grain similar to wheat. "Smitten" means struck down or destroyed.

The narrator explains the effect of the seventh plague in Egypt. Moses had said that Pharaoh still did not fear God. The flax and the barley were already grown and were lost; the wheat, still tender, was spared. So it is clear that the damage was real, but not total. Even so, Pharaoh hardened his heart.

For today: God's mercy often leaves something standing, and that should lead us to humility, not hardness. When God warns or corrects us, and we still have something left, let us respond with sincere repentance and not with pride.
exp.2:11:
God answers Moses: "Go, for I will be with you." The word "shall be" means "will be." God gives him a sign: when Moses brings the people out of Egypt, they will worship God on this very mountain. "You shall serve" means "you will serve" or "you will worship," and "to" is "to."

God speaks with Moses in front of the burning bush, on Mount Horeb. Moses has just asked, "Who am I?" God does not speak of Moses' abilities, but of his own presence. The sign would come only after obedience, so Moses had to trust first. Some understand the sign to be the bush; others, the future worship on the mountain.

When God calls you to something that feels too big for you, the key question is not "who am I?" but "who goes with me?" Take the step with confidence in his company.
exp.23:17:
It says that Moses went into the midst of the cloud, which represented the presence of God, and went up the mountain of Sinai. There he remained forty days and forty nights. The word "was" simply means that he stayed there. Forty is a number that appears often in the Bible in times of testing or preparation.

This verse is narration, not a speech. God had called Moses from the cloud, while the people saw his glory like an intense fire on the summit. Moses went up to receive God's instructions for Israel, among them the tablets of the law and the plan for the tabernacle, as told in the chapters that follow.

For today: drawing near to God takes time and attention. Moses set everything aside to listen to him. We can set apart a quiet moment each day, without hurry or distractions, to pray and read the Bible, trusting that God wants to speak to us.
exp.38:41:
This verse says that the Israelites did all the work of the tabernacle exactly as God had commanded Moses. The phrase about doing things according to instructions is rendered as "according to," and "work" refers to all the construction and the furnishings of the holy place.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, who is traditionally believed to be Moses. After many chapters of detailed instructions, the text summarizes that the people carried them out. Right after this, Moses inspects the work and blesses those who did it. The emphasis is on careful obedience, not just on finishing the project.

For today: obeying God in the details matters too. You can choose one specific thing God asks of you, such as forgiving, being honest, or serving, and do it completely, without leaving it half-done.
exp.27:29:
God tells Moses to place the Urim and the Thummim inside the breastplate of judgment, a piece that the high priest wore over his chest. In this way Aaron would carry them upon his heart whenever he went before God. The breastplate of judgment is the name used for that piece of clothing. No one knows for certain what the Urim and the Thummim were; the Bible suggests that they were used to seek God's will, but it does not explain how they worked.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai and gives him instructions for the priest's clothing. The breastplate bore the names of the tribes of Israel. Through this, God shows that the priest represented the whole people before Him and bore their decisions.

For today: whoever leads or cares for others can imitate this care, carrying them in their heart, praying for them with love, and seeking God's direction before making decisions.
exp.39:11:
God tells Moses to bring Aaron and his sons to the entrance of the tent of meeting and wash them with water. The explanation notes that the verse has the sense of "bring them near," and it describes the tabernacle as the place where the law tablets were kept inside.

God speaks to Moses at the end of the book, when the tabernacle was ready to be put into use. Before Aaron and his sons could serve as priests, God commanded that they be prepared: washed, clothed, and anointed. Many understand this washing as a symbol of cleansing so that they could come near to a holy God, although the text itself gives no further explanation.

For today: before serving God, we need to come near to Him with humility and let Him cleanse us. We can begin the day by asking Him for forgiveness and help, rather than serving only in our own strength.
exp.19:24:
God tells his people that if they build him an altar of stones, they must not shape the stones with tools. If they use that tool on the stones, God says, the altar is "profanado," meaning it stops being fit for its sacred use.

God speaks to Moses and the people shortly after giving the Ten Commandments at Sinai. He has just forbidden idols of silver and gold. Many understand that this command taught that worship should not rest on human cleverness or human artistry. Others also see a distance from pagan altars, though the text does not fully explain this.

For today: come near to God with simplicity, and do not decorate your faith to impress others. He looks for a sincere heart, not a perfect appearance.
exp.16:4:
God tells Moses to go ahead of the people and to take some of the elders of Israel with him. He also tells him to take the staff he struck the river with, meaning the Nile, and set out.

The Lord speaks. The people are thirsty in the desert, they complain against Moses, and he cries out to God, fearing they will stone him. God does not scold him; He gives him a specific instruction. The elders would be witnesses to what God was about to do, and the staff reminded them of how God had already delivered them in Egypt.

For today: when you feel pressured or afraid, do what Moses did: cry out to God sincerely. Then take the next step He shows you, even if you don't yet see the solution. God usually guides step by step, and remembering how He helped you before strengthens your trust.
exp.6:3:
The explanation says that the king of Egypt will not listen to Moses and Aaron. So God himself will act with his power against Egypt. "Lay my hand upon" means to intervene with force. He calls the Israelites his hosts, his people, and he will bring them out of Egypt through great judgments, that is, just and powerful punishments on that country.

God speaks to Moses, and also to Aaron, before the plagues. He warns them that there will be resistance, so that they will not lose heart when Pharaoh says no. Israel was living as an enslaved people, and God promises them deliverance. The text says that God would harden Pharaoh's heart, and interpreters explain this in different ways.

For today: when we obey God and things do not happen quickly, it does not mean that he has failed. We can remain faithful, trusting that he keeps his promises in his own time and in his own way.
exp.39:7:
God tells Moses that, in the end, he is to set up the court, that is, the open courtyard that surrounded the whole tabernacle, and hang up the curtain at the entrance. Without naming any old word, this sentence keeps the verse's own terms: "the court" and "the hanging at the court gate." The area around it is marked off as something separate from the rest of the camp.

God speaks to Moses when the people already have all the pieces ready, about a year after leaving Egypt. These are the final instructions for setting up the tabernacle, the place where God would dwell among Israel. Everything was to be done just as He commanded, step by step and in good order.

For today: drawing near to God is not something casual. Although Christ opened the way for us, we can set aside quiet times and places to pray and read the Bible, with reverence and gratitude.
exp.25:22:
Here God gives instructions for the back wall of the tabernacle, the one facing west. Six boards have already been mentioned, and now two more are added for the rear corners. The corners are what the text calls the angles, the places where two sides meet. So the back wall would have eight boards in all, and the corners would be firm and well joined.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai and explains how to build the tabernacle, the tent where He would dwell among Israel. Nothing is left to chance: even the corners have their place. Some scholars debate the exact detail of how those boards were joined, since the text is brief.

For today: God cares about the details, even the ones no one sees. We can serve Him with care in the small things, and trust that He also looks after the corners of our lives.
exp.30:4:
This verse says that God gave Bezalel the skill to cut and set precious stones, to work in wood, and to do every kind of skilled craft. The words quoted in the original explanation, meaning skilled art or craft and setting a stone into metal as in a ring, are not in the verse your reader sees, so I have left them out and described the work in the verse's own terms: cutting stones and carving timber.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai. He explains that he has chosen Bezalel, and then Aholiab, to build the tabernacle, the place of worship for Israel. God filled them with his Spirit so that the work would be done as he had commanded.

For today: our abilities, even practical and everyday ones, can be a gift from God. We can offer them with care and gratitude, serving others and honoring him in what we do.
exp.36:0:
It says that Bezaleel made the ark of the covenant from acacia wood, which the verse calls shittim wood, a tree of the desert. Its measurements were two and a half cubits in length, and a cubit and a half in width and in height. A cubit was the distance from the elbow to the tip of the fingers, roughly between 45 and 50 centimeters, so the ark measured about 1.10 meters in length and 70 centimeters in width and height.

Here the narrator of the book of Exodus is speaking. He tells us that the people obeyed the instructions God had given Moses on the mountain (chapters 25 through 31). Bezaleel was the craftsman whom God filled with skill to build the sanctuary. The ark would be the symbolic place of God's presence among Israel.

For today: God values obedience in the details and work done with care. We can serve Him faithfully in simple tasks, using our abilities as He has given them.
exp.34:26:
The explanation says that the leaders or rulers of the people brought onyx stones and other precious stones to be set, that is, to be mounted on the ephod and on the breastplate. The ephod was a special garment of the high priest, and the breastplate was a piece worn over the chest. The exact stones cannot be fully determined, since the meaning of some Hebrew names is uncertain.

Moses had passed on God's command to build the tabernacle, and the people responded with freewill offerings. Here the account shows the leaders giving after others had already given, and everyone contributing according to what they had.

For today: God values what we give with a willing heart, whether little or much. Those who hold responsibility among their people can set an example of generosity, without showing off, and serve with what God has entrusted to them.
exp.11:37:
This verse says that a great crowd of people from various backgrounds left Egypt together with the Israelites, along with a very large number of sheep, goats, and cattle. The phrase "diverse kinds of people" is rendered in the KJV as "a mixed multitude," and it means people of different sorts and origins. The verb used for the departure describes going up, as one would when leaving for higher ground.

Here the speaker is the narrator of the book, traditionally Moses. He describes how the departure from Egypt took place after the tenth plague. The text does not explain who these outsiders were. Some think they were Egyptians or slaves from other nations who had seen the power of God and wanted to leave with Israel. The text does not specify.

For today: God's family was never meant to be just a few. If someone comes to your church looking for hope, welcome them warmly and help them come to know the Lord.
exp.22:20:
It says the people must be careful about the Angel God sends. The phrase "Beware of him" means taking him seriously and showing him respect. One must listen to his voice and not rebel against him. The phrase "he will not pardon your transgressions" means that he will not overlook disobedience. The reason is that God's name is in him.

God speaks, through Moses, to Israel at Sinai, after giving them laws for their daily life. He promises an Angel who will guard them on the way to the promised land. Some think he is a special messenger with God's authority; others see in him a presence of God himself. The Bible does not make this completely clear.

For today: when you sense that God corrects you or guides you through his Word, do not ignore it. Listen with humility and obey, trusting that his direction seeks to care for you.
exp.29:35:
God tells Moses to take some of the special incense, grind it until it is a fine powder, and place it before the "testimony," that is, in front of the ark that held the tablets of the law, inside the tabernacle. There God would meet with Moses. He adds that this incense would be "most holy," set apart entirely for God.

The Lord is speaking to Moses while giving him instructions for worship in the tabernacle. This blend of fragrances was only for worshiping God, and for that reason it was not to be copied or used for anything else. Its perfume represented a worship reserved for Him alone.

For today: God deserves the best and most special of our time. We can set aside a moment each day, free from distractions, to pray and listen to Him with reverence, like a fragrance offered to Him alone.
exp.3:18:
God speaks to Moses while he is still in Midian. He tells him to go back to Egypt, because the men who wanted to kill him are already dead. The phrase "return" in the verse above is the same idea the source explains as "turn back," and the phrase about those who sought his life means "they were trying to kill you."

Years earlier, Moses fled from Egypt after killing an Egyptian, and Pharaoh wanted to punish him (Exodus 2:15). Now God calls him from the burning bush to free Israel. Moses had already asked his father-in-law Jethro for permission, and God adds this word to take away his fear. Some think it refers to the earlier pharaoh and others to those who were seeking him, but the text gives no further details.

When God calls us to a difficult step, He also cares for our fears. We can obey with confidence, knowing that He is already going before us and knows what we will face.
exp.36:4:
It says that Bezalel put the poles through the gold rings placed on the sides of the ark. In this way the ark could be carried without anyone touching it directly. The poles are long, firm wooden bars, and the rings are the loops where those poles fit. The wood is acacia.

Here the narrator of the book of Exodus speaks. He tells how what God had commanded Moses for the tabernacle, the meeting tent where God dwelt among his people, was carried out. The ark held the tablets of the law and represented God's presence. It had to be portable because Israel was walking through the desert.

For today: God cares about the details and wants to be treated with reverence. We can draw near to him with respect and obedience, even in small things. Moreover, his presence goes with us on the way, not only in one fixed place.
exp.38:3:
This verse says that the craftsmen made the shoulderpieces for the ephod, that is, two pieces that covered the shoulders. They were joined at their two edges, so that they formed one firm garment. The ephod was a special garment of the priest, and the shoulderpieces are the straps that go over the shoulders.

The narrator is Moses, who describes how the clothing of the high priest Aaron was made. The craftsmen followed the instructions God had given on the mountain to the letter. The shoulderpieces held up the ephod and, later on, would bear two stones with the names of the tribes of Israel.

For today: God cares about the small details and the parts no one sees. We can do our work with faithfulness and care, even when it seems unimportant, and remember that Christ, our High Priest, carries us on his shoulders.
exp.24:31:
This verse describes how the golden lampstand of the tabernacle was to be made. Six branches would come out of the central shaft, three on one side and three on the other, which together with the center would form seven lamps. What we would today call a lampstand or candelabrum is the object described here. The phrase about the branches coming out of the sides of it is simply the way the verse says three branches come from one side and three from the other.

God himself speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai. He gives detailed instructions for building the tabernacle, the place where God would dwell among Israel. The lampstand would give light inside the sanctuary, beside the table of the bread. Many see in its tree-like form a symbol of life, though the text does not explain this.

For today: God cares about order and care in what we offer him. We can serve him with devotion, even in small tasks, knowing that he gives light and purpose to what we do.
exp.14:8:
This verse shows what the pharaoh, the enemy of Israel, was thinking. He speaks with pride and confidence: he says he will pursue the Israelites, overtake them, and divide up what they have. He thinks his sword and his hand will be enough to destroy them.

Moses and Israel sing this song of praise after crossing the Red Sea. They recall the arrogant words of the Egyptian army and set them against what God did: the sea closed over them. In this way we see that the plans of the proud could not stand against the power of God.

For today: when something seems stronger than you, remember that no threat has the final word. Trust in God, and not in your own strength.
exp.27:10:
The explanation says that the two stones of the ephod were to be worked with great skill, as an engraver of seals does when he cuts fine letters into stone. The names of the twelve tribes of Israel would be engraved on them. The settings are the gold frames or mounts that hold and surround the stones. The word "ouches" in the verse refers to these same gold settings.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai and gives him instructions for the garments of the high priest Aaron. The stones were to rest on his shoulders, so that Aaron would symbolically bear the whole people before the LORD, as a reminder. The names were not written in any careless way: they were carefully engraved and surrounded with gold.

For today: God values his people and does not forget them. We can be confident that we are important to Him. In the same way, we can remember in prayer, with care and by name, the people whom God places in our path.
exp.3:5:
God asks Moses to put his hand inside his "bosom", that is, inside the front part of his clothing, pressed against the chest. When he takes it out, the hand is "leprous as snow", meaning it has a skin disease that leaves it white.

God speaks with Moses in front of the burning bush. Moses was afraid that the people of Israel would not believe him. So God gives him signs, such as the staff turned into a serpent and this diseased hand, to show that he had truly sent him. Afterward God healed the hand.

For today: when God asks you for something that seems impossible, remember that He can give power and support. Obey step by step, even when you have doubts, trusting that He sustains what He entrusts to you.
exp.38:17:
Here is described how the breastpiece (the high priest's chest ornament) was fastened to the ephod, a sacred garment. The two gold chains had their ends attached to two settings, or gold supports, placed on the shoulder pieces of the ephod, at the front. In this way the breastpiece stayed firm over the priest's chest.

The narrator tells how the craftsmen of Israel finished the priest's garments, following what God had commanded Moses. The breastpiece bore twelve stones with the names of the tribes, so the priest presented the people before God. The text insists that everything was done just as God had ordered it.

God cares even about the details of what we do for Him. Today we can serve Him with care and faithfulness in small things, without thinking that anything is unimportant. And let us remember that God carries us close to His heart, as the breastpiece carried the tribes.
exp.15:27:
God asks Moses how long the people will refuse to keep his commandments and his laws. It is a question that expresses sorrow and rebuke, not only anger. The word "Lord" is the name of God.

The people of Israel were traveling through the desert, and God gave them manna every day. He had told them to gather a double portion on the sixth day so they could rest on the seventh. Some went out anyway to look for manna on the seventh day and found nothing. God speaks to Moses because he was the leader who passed on God's word, and the question shows that doubting his provision was a repeated lack of trust.

Today we can ask ourselves in what area it is hard for us to trust that God will take care of us. Setting aside time to rest and pray, without worrying about everything, is a simple way to practice that trust.
exp.36:6:
This verse tells us that Bezalel made two cherubim of gold, hammered out of one piece, and placed them on the two ends of the cover of the ark. The cover of the ark is the lid, also called the mercy seat. "Hammered out of one piece" means the gold was beaten into shape, not melted down and poured into a mold.

The narrator recounts how the tabernacle was built, following the instructions God gave to Moses. The cherubim are spiritual beings connected with the presence of God. The Bible does not describe their appearance here, and people have imagined them in various ways. Above that cover, God promised to meet with his people.

For today: God cares about the details of how we draw near to him. Today we do so through Christ, so we can approach with reverence, but also with confidence, because he himself prepared the way.
exp.17:6:
This verse tells us that Moses went out to meet his father-in-law Jethro. He bowed down before him and kissed him, which was a respectful and affectionate way of greeting. Then they asked each other how they were, that is, they greeted one another and caught up. After that they went together into Moses' tent.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Israel had already left Egypt and was camped in the desert, near the mountain of God. Jethro arrived with Moses' wife and his two sons. After this greeting, Moses told him everything God had done for his people, and Jethro rejoiced.

For today: even as a very busy leader, Moses made time to receive his family with respect and affection. We can imitate him by valuing our relatives with a sincere greeting, time, and attention.
exp.17:3:
The second son of Moses was named Eliezer. That name means "my God is help." Moses chose it because God helped him and rescued him from the sword of Pharaoh. In the older wording, "knife" means sword, that is, the threat of death.

The narrator explains why Moses' sons have these names. Moses had fled from Egypt after killing an Egyptian, and Pharaoh wanted to kill him (Exodus 2:15). Now his father-in-law Jethro arrives at the camp with Moses' wife and sons. The text does not explain in detail when or how Moses was separated from his family, and there are different interpretations.

Today we can give names to our memories of God's faithfulness. Recording or telling how God helped us in difficult moments strengthens gratitude and confidence for what lies ahead.
exp.0:15:
The explanation says that the king of Egypt ordered the midwives that, when they helped women give birth among the Hebrews, they should look at the birth stools and kill the baby if it was a boy, but let the girls live. "You shall help in the birth" is the meaning of the verb in this verse. The birth stools most likely refers to the low seat or stones on which women gave birth; some scholars understand it this way, although the Hebrew term is not entirely clear.

The pharaoh, the king of Egypt, is the one speaking. The Hebrews had multiplied, and he oppressed them with hard labor. Seeing that they kept growing, he tried to restrain the people by eliminating the newborn boys, secretly using the midwives Shiphrah and Puah.

For today: the next verse shows that they feared God and did not obey this unjust command. When an authority asks us for something that goes against life or justice, let us ask God for courage and wisdom to obey Him first, with humility and firmness.
exp.5:21:
This verse names the three sons of Uzziel: Mishael, Elzaphan, and Zithri. Uzziel was the son of Kohath and therefore the uncle of Moses and Aaron. The names appear in the spelling of the older translation the explanation was written for; today they are usually written Uzziel, Mishael, Elzaphan, and Zithri.

Here the narrator presents a genealogy of the tribe of Levi, to show which family Moses and Aaron came from. God had already charged them to speak to Pharaoh. That is why the text pauses to say who they were. Later, Mishael and Elzaphan appear in Leviticus 10, when they carry away the bodies of Nadab and Abihu.

God works through people with names, families, and histories. Even if your role seems small or hardly visible, God knows you and can use you. Today you can thank him for your family, with its virtues and its failings, and ask him to help you serve faithfully where you are.
exp.11:40:
When the four hundred and thirty years were finished, on that very same day, the people of Israel went out of Egypt. They are called "the hosts of the Lord" because they went out in good order, as a great people, and not as aimless slaves. "The Lord" is the name of God. "Finished" means "completed."

Here the narrator of the book, traditionally credited to Moses, speaks. He has just described the hurried departure, when there was no time even to let the bread rise. With this phrase he stresses that God was exactly on time. Some scholars debate how to count those years, since other biblical passages give slightly different figures, but the emphasis here is God's faithfulness to his promise.

For today: God keeps what he promises, even when it takes far longer than we expect. If you are waiting for an answer, keep trusting and obeying. His timing is never late.
exp.13:30:
This verse says that the people of Israel saw the great work that God did against the Egyptians. Then the people revered the Lord, meaning they held Him in deep respect, and they believed in Him and in Moses, His servant.

The account is told by the narrator of the book, traditionally attributed to Moses. The Israelites had just crossed the sea on dry ground and had seen the Egyptians dead on the shore. After years of slavery, they saw that God had set them free. Their trust in Moses arose from seeing that God was acting through him.

For today: when you remember what God has done for you, let it strengthen your trust in Him. Write down the times He helped you, and return to them when doubt comes. Even so, Israel's faith was fragile, as the following chapters will show, so it is worth tending to it every day.
exp.35:37:
Bezalel and the craftsmen made five pillars for the entrance of the tabernacle, that is, the curtain at the door. They overlaid with gold the top part, called the capitals (the crowning piece of each pillar), and also their bands (the rods or strips that joined the pillars together). The bases on which they stood were of bronze, which almost certainly is what the word "brass" means here.

Exodus is a historical account, not a sermon. It tells how Israel built the tabernacle following the instructions God gave to Moses. Here the entrance is described, the way that led into the courtyard. The materials change as one moves closer to God: bronze outside, silver and gold inside. Many see in this a teaching about holiness, although the text does not explain it directly.

God cares about details and about doing things with care. Today, we can serve him with excellence and obedience in small tasks, even when no one notices them.
exp.7:18:
The magicians of Egypt, unable to copy the plague of gnats, say to Pharaoh: "This is the finger of God." But Pharaoh stayed stubborn and paid them no mind, just as the Lord had foretold. "Finger of God" means an obvious divine power. "His heart was hardened" means he became obstinate. The word "gnats" is the traditional rendering, though some think it could refer to mosquitoes or other small insects.

The speakers are Pharaoh's magicians, who until now had copied the signs of Moses and Aaron. This time they failed, and they recognized a power greater than their own. Even so, Pharaoh did not give in. The text says his heart was hardened, and in other passages it also says God hardened him; scholars explain this in different ways.

We can see the truth and still resist it out of pride. Today it is good to ask God for a humble heart, willing to obey when he speaks to us.
exp.18:0:
It says that three months after the people left Egypt, on that very day, they arrived at the wilderness of Sinai. The phrase "in the third month" means in the third month counted from the departure. The word "came" means that they arrived. It is a detail of time and place that marks a new stage of the journey.

The narrator of the book, traditionally Moses, tells how Israel reached the foot of the mountain after leaving Rephidim. There God would call Moses to offer the people a covenant. How long the journey lasted exactly and where precisely Mount Sinai was located are matters that are debated, but the text emphasizes that God brought them to that place.

For today: sometimes God leads us into a "wilderness" to prepare us and speak to us more clearly. When you are in a season of waiting or silence, do not take it as abandonment. Withdraw, listen, and trust that God is forming you.
exp.22:30:
God promises Israel that its borders will run from the Red Sea to the Mediterranean Sea, which is the sea of the Philistines, and from the desert to the river, which is usually understood to be the Euphrates. God says he will hand the people of the land over into Israel's hands, and that Israel will drive them out.

God speaks to Israel through Moses, after giving them laws at Sinai. He promises them the land, but says the conquest will come gradually, little by little. He then warns them not to make alliances with those peoples or with their gods, so that they do not fall into idolatry.

For today: God keeps his promises, but often at his own pace and not at ours. We can trust his slow timing and, in the meantime, make sure nothing draws us away from serving him alone.
exp.0:8:
This verse records the words of the new king of Egypt to his people. He says the Israelites are "more and mightier," meaning they are more numerous and more powerful than the Egyptians. The phrase "Behold" is an old way of saying "look" or "pay attention."

The speaker is a new king who did not know Joseph, that is, he did not value what Joseph had done for Egypt. His claim probably exaggerates the reality, and it was a way of stirring fear among his people. That fear led him to oppress Israel with hard labor. Some scholars discuss who this king was and when he reigned, so it is wise not to claim more than the text says.

For today: fear can make us see as a threat someone who is not one, and lead us to treat others badly. Before we react, let us ask God for calm and a just heart.
exp.33:29:
He says that when Aaron and the people saw Moses, his face shone with a strong light. It frightened them so much that they did not dare to come near him. "Skin of the face" is the meaning of the word for the face's surface, and "to come near him" means to approach him. Hmm.

Moses had just spent forty days with God on Mount Sinai, receiving the ten words of the covenant written on tablets. He did not know that his face was shining. The account tells it this way; Moses is not the one speaking. The brightness showed that he had been in the presence of God. Afterward, Moses called to them, and they came close to hear what God commanded.

Spending time with God changes us, even when we do not notice it. Seek a daily time of prayer and Bible reading, and let others see the change, with humility.
exp.11:13:
God says that the day he passed over Egypt must remain as a memorial for his people. They are to celebrate it as a feast kept to the Lord, from generation to generation. The phrase "a fixed rule for all time" means an ordinance that is kept forever. A "solemn" feast means a celebration that is serious and holy.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron, and through them to Israel, just before the tenth plague. That night, the blood on the doorposts would be the sign that let the judgment pass over. God wants his people never to forget how he rescued them from slavery.

For today: Remembering is part of faith. We can set aside regular moments, such as prayer or the Lord's Supper, to tell others, especially the younger ones, how God has cared for and saved us.
exp.22:11:
This verse commands six days of work and a seventh day of rest. "You shall do your work" means you shall do your tasks and your labor. "You shall rest" means you shall stop and rest. "Refreshment" means relief or renewal of strength. The rest was for working animals, for the son of the female servant (the servant of the household), and for the foreigner.

God speaks to Israel through Moses, in the laws that follow the Ten Commandments. Just before this, He commands that the land be left to rest every seventh year so that the poor may eat. In this way, the weekly rest shows God's care for the most vulnerable, including those who were neither family nor members of the people.

For today: let us set aside a regular time of rest, trusting that God sustains our life. And let us think of those who work for us or with us; let us make sure they too can rest and recover their strength.
exp.28:12:
God tells Moses that, after the bull has been killed, he is to take all the fat that covers the inner organs, the fatty membrane that lies over the liver, and both kidneys with their fat, and burn it all on the altar.

God speaks to Moses in the rite for setting apart Aaron and his sons as priests. In that time the fat was considered the best part of the animal, and for that reason it was offered whole to God. The meat and the hide were burned separately, outside the camp. Scholars explain the meaning of each gesture in several different ways.

For today: let us give God the best, not the leftovers. We can ask ourselves what is first and most valuable in our lives, such as our time, our attention and our affection, and offer it to him with gratitude.
exp.9:13:
The locusts spread out and covered all of Egypt, settling over the whole land. They were very heavy and destructive: there had never been a plague of locusts like that before, and there would never be one like it after.

The narrator describes the eighth plague. God, through Moses, sent it because Pharaoh kept refusing to let the people of Israel go. The locusts ate whatever little the hail had left in the fields. Then Pharaoh quickly called for Moses and Aaron and admitted his wrongdoing, though the account shows that his heart changed very little.

Today: saying "I have sinned" is not enough when trouble arrives. God looks for a sincere and lasting repentance. Let us ask him to give us the humility to obey him before the consequences force us to admit it.
exp.18:21:
This verse says that the priests, who already drew near to God, also had to sanctify themselves, that is, prepare and set themselves apart for Him. If they did not, God could break out against them, that is, cause them harm or destruction. The phrase about coming near means that they approach God.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai, just before giving the Ten Commandments. He had set limits around the mountain so that the people would not go up. Even the priests, who had a special role, had to take God's holiness seriously. There are different views about who these priests were, because the priesthood had not yet been formally established.

For today: drawing near to God is not something to take lightly. Before praying, worshiping, or serving, it is good to pause, acknowledge who God is, and ask Him to cleanse our hearts.
exp.6:18:
God commands Moses to tell Aaron to stretch out his staff over all the waters of Egypt: rivers, streams, ponds, and reservoirs. All of them would turn into blood, including the water stored in vessels of wood and of stone.

The Lord speaks in the midst of the confrontation with Pharaoh, who did not want to let the people of Israel go. This is the first plague. God wanted Pharaoh and the Egyptians to know that He is the Lord. Some scholars think it also challenged the Egyptian reverence for the Nile, although the text does not say so in those words.

For today: God is greater than anything in which we place our security. Today we can ask ourselves what we trust more than God, and hand it over to Him with humility.
exp.24:39:
It says that Moses must pay close attention and make everything according to the pattern that God showed him on the mountain. The word "look" is a command: pay attention. "According to" means "in agreement with." "Pattern" is the design or model that must be copied exactly.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai while giving him instructions for building the tabernacle, the tent where the people of Israel would worship. This verse closes the description of the golden lampstand. Hebrews 8:5 quotes this verse and connects it to heavenly realities. It is not known with certainty what that "pattern" was: whether it was a vision, a drawing, or something else.

For today: God is concerned with how we serve him, not only with whether we do it. We can ask ourselves what his Word says and follow it carefully and obediently, without replacing it with our comforts or ideas.
exp.31:29:
Moses tells the people, the next day, that they have committed a great sin. He announces that he will go up again to the mountain, where the Lord is, in the hope of obtaining forgiveness for them. The verse's wording "peradventure" shows that Moses gives no guarantee; he only intercedes.

Moses speaks after the people made a golden calf and after about three thousand men fell that day. He does not minimize the sin, but neither does he abandon the people. He places himself between God and the people as an intercessor, and in the following verse he pleads for them with great devotion.

For today: we can speak honestly about sin, without excuses, and still pray with love for those who have failed, even when we do not know how God will respond. This also reminds us of Christ, who intercedes for us.
exp.22:27:
God promises to send hornets ahead of the people of Israel to drive out the Hivites, Canaanites, and Hittites from the land. "Drive out" means to force out, and "before you" means as Israel moves forward. These names are the peoples who lived in Canaan.

God speaks to Israel through Moses, after giving them laws at Sinai. He promises help as they enter the promised land. It is not certain whether the hornets are a real insect or an image of the fear and confusion that God would send; interpreters understand it in both ways. What follows makes clear that the conquest would be gradual.

For today: God often helps us step by step, not all at once. Trust that he goes ahead of you, and do not be discouraged if progress is slow; he knows the pace that suits you best.
exp.32:3:
It says that when the people heard the harsh news from God, they grieved and put on clothes of mourning. A phrase here means a painful word, one that hurts the heart. Mourning is the sign of deep sadness. The ornaments were the decorations and jewelry, and no one put them on.

God, through Moses, had just told them that He would keep His promise to give them the land, but that He would not go up in their midst. This came after they worshiped the golden calf. That is why their response of sorrow seems to show repentance. God had asked them to take off their ornaments, and the text does not explain in detail everything He intended to do.

For today: when God shows us something wrong in ourselves, we should not defend ourselves or act strong. We can stop, feel sincere sorrow, and return to Him with humility, trusting that He seeks to restore us.
exp.25:19:
It says the north side of the tabernacle was also to have twenty boards, just like the south side. The word "north" is the one used here, so the two long sides matched, with the same measurements and the same number of boards.

God himself spoke to Moses on Mount Sinai and gave him precise instructions for building the tabernacle. Israel had just left Egypt, and God wanted to live in the midst of his people. That is why every detail, even the smallest, was commanded with care. The text repeats the measurements because each side had to stand firm on its silver bases.

For today: God cares about the small and the ordinary. We can serve him faithfully in simple, repetitive tasks, trusting that nothing done for him is without value.
exp.20:2:
He says that if a Hebrew servant came to serve single, then when his time was complete he would go out free and single. But if he was already married when he came in, he would go out free together with his wife. "Servant" here refers to someone who worked for another person, often to pay off a debt. Going free means no longer bound to serve, and "for nothing" means without paying anything.

God speaks to Moses, shortly after giving the Ten Commandments, and gives him laws for the daily life of the people of Israel. These rules set a limit of six years on a Hebrew's service and protected the most vulnerable. The next verse deals with the case of a wife given by the master, a difficult situation that is interpreted with care.

For today: God cares about the dignity and the family of those who have less power. We can treat with justice and respect those who work for us or depend on our decisions.
exp.4:0:
Moses and Aaron come before Pharaoh, the king of Egypt. They bring him a message from God: "Let my people go." The phrase about holding a feast means a celebration of worship to God. The name "Jehovah" is the name of God used in this older version.

Moses and Aaron speak as messengers sent by God. The Israelites were living as slaves in Egypt. God called them "my people" and wanted them to worship him freely in the wilderness.
