Pharaoh will answer with contempt, saying that he does not know the Lord. This is the first step in a long confrontation.

For today: sometimes obeying God means speaking with courage, even when the one listening does not want to hear it. We can be faithful in what God asks of us and trust that he takes care of the outcome.
exp.28:38:
God tells Moses that every day one lamb is to be offered in the morning and another at evening, that is, at nightfall. These are the two one-year-old lambs mentioned before, and they were offered every day, without interruption, so that not a single day was missed.

God speaks to Moses while giving him instructions for consecrating Aaron and his sons as priests and for preparing the altar. This daily offering set the rhythm of Israel's worship. The verses that follow say it was a pleasing aroma to the LORD, an expression describing an offering that He receives with delight.

For today: God wanted His people to begin and end the day with Him. We can do the same with a brief prayer on waking and another at bedtime, thanking Him and placing the day in His hands.
exp.7:31:
He says that Pharaoh hardened his heart again, that is, he became stubborn once more. The verb "hardened" in the verse above shows that he made his own heart harder, and even after he saw that God had taken away the flies, he did not let the people of Israel go.

This is part of the account of the plagues of Egypt. Moses had prayed, and God removed the plague of flies, just as Pharaoh had asked. Pharaoh had promised to let the people go, but when the relief passed, he did not keep his word. The text presents this as his own decision, and in other passages it also says that God hardened his heart; scholars explain this in different ways.

For today: when God gives us relief in a difficulty, let us not forget what we promised. Let us be grateful and obedient, without waiting for the hardship to return before we humble ourselves.
exp.13:24:
What it says: God caused the wheels of the Egyptian chariots to come loose or get stuck, and the soldiers could not move forward. The phrase that describes this means that God threw them into confusion and disorder. Then the Egyptians understood that they were not fighting only against Israel, but against the Lord, and they said, "Let us flee from the face of Israel."

Context: The narrator tells what happened at the Red Sea, when Israel had just left Egypt. Pharaoh regretted letting them go and pursued them. The Israelites were trapped between the army and the sea, but God protected them from the pillar of cloud and fire. The final words belong to the Egyptians themselves, who recognize the hand of God.

For today: When you feel cornered and without a way out, remember that God can act in ways you do not expect. Trust in Him and take the next step of faith, knowing that He cares for His people.
exp.1:6:
Here the child's sister, who until now had been watching from a distance, comes up to Pharaoh's daughter and asks a very simple question: whether she would like her to go and find a Hebrew woman who can nurse and raise the baby. A nurse is a woman who feeds a child at her breast and takes care of it.

The child's sister speaks (the text of this passage does not give her name; later she is called Miriam). The baby was crying, the princess felt compassion, and she recognized that he was a Hebrew. The young woman takes that moment with prudence, and so the child's own mother ends up caring for her son.

Today we can learn to be attentive and to act with wisdom and courage when a door opens. God often works through small gestures and ordinary people who speak the right word at the right time.
exp.0:13:
The verse says that the Egyptians made the lives of the Israelites very bitter. They forced them to work hard making mortar and bricks, and also in the labor of the field. "Hard bondage" means forced labor, and "rigour" means cruel treatment without pity. They demanded everything from them with severity.

Here the narrator of the book of Exodus speaks, a book traditionally attributed to Moses. The Israelites were becoming more and more numerous in Egypt, and this troubled the Egyptians. For that reason they oppressed them even more. But, as the previous text says, the more they were oppressed, the more they grew. Later the king will go on to order something even more cruel.

For today: if you are going through a heavy burden or an injustice, remember that God sees the suffering and does not ignore it. Pray with confidence, seek support from other believers and, if you can, help someone who today is being treated harshly.
exp.18:12:
The explanation says that no one was to touch the person who stepped onto Mount Sinai. If anyone or anything touched it, it would be put to death from a distance, by stones or by arrows. ("Shot through" in the verse above matches this idea of being struck from afar.) This applied to people and to animals alike. Only when the trumpet, or horn, sounded a long blast could the people go up the mountain.

God speaks to Moses before he goes down to meet Israel. The mountain was set apart as a holy place because God was going to come down there. The boundary protected the people and taught them to respect God's holiness. Some scholars think the horn signaled when the restriction ended, although the text does not fully explain this.

For today: draw near to God with reverence and gratitude. He is loving, but He is also holy. Before you pray or read His Word, take a moment in silence to remember who He is.
exp.31:18:
Moses came down from Mount Sinai, and when he drew near to the camp, he saw the golden calf with his own eyes, and the people dancing. His anger burned hot, and he threw down the stone tablets he was carrying and broke them at the foot of the mountain. The sentence about anger burning hot means that his anger was kindled with great force. The dancing refers to the celebrations around the idol.

Moses had spent forty days with God receiving the law. Meanwhile, the impatient people asked Aaron for a visible god, and he made the calf. Joshua heard the noise and thought of war, but Moses already knew, because God had told him, that it was an idolatrous feast. The broken tablets show that the covenant had been violated.

We can examine what things take the place of God when waiting becomes long for us. We can also learn that anger at sin should lead us to seek restoration, as Moses did, who afterward interceded for the people.
exp.9:14:
The explanation says that the plague of locusts was so great that it covered the entire surface of the earth, and the ground grew dark because of so many insects. They ate all the grass and all the fruit of the trees that the hail (the previous plague) had not destroyed. The word "face" in the verse means the surface, and the darkening refers to the land becoming dark. Nothing green remained in all of Egypt.

Here the narrator of the book of Exodus speaks. He recounts the eighth plague, which came after Pharaoh refused again and again to let the people of Israel go. God used an east wind to bring the locusts. Soon Pharaoh admitted his sin, although his repentance did not last long.

For today: acknowledging our faults only when the consequences arrive is not enough. God looks for a humble and sincere heart, one that turns back to Him before pressure forces us to.
exp.2:13:
God answers Moses with his name: "I AM THAT I AM." Then he tells Moses to say to Israel that "I AM" has sent him. The words "á" and "vosotros" are old forms of "a" and "ustedes." The Hebrew can also be understood as "I will be what I will be," and so it is explained in several ways.

Moses is standing before the burning bush, and God speaks to him. Moses fears that the people, enslaved in Egypt, will ask him who sent him. God presents himself as the eternal and faithful God, the same God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. His name and his promise to be with Moses go together.

For today: when you feel small or unsure before a difficult task, remember that God does not change and does not depend on your strength. He is the one who is present and faithful with you. Trust in his company and take the next step.
exp.5:0:
God tells Moses that he will soon see what He is going to do to Pharaoh. By a strong hand, that is, by a power greater than the king's, Pharaoh will let the people of Israel go and will even drive them out of his land. In this old version of the text, the name of God is written in a form the reader will not see in the verse above, and the explanation is only about the meaning of the verse itself.

God is the one speaking. Moses had complained because, when he asked Pharaoh to let the people leave, Pharaoh increased the work of the Israelites and things got worse (Exodus 5). God answers to encourage him: the process will be hard, but He Himself will fulfill what He promised. Some understand that the strong hand also refers to Pharaoh being forced by God.

When things get worse after you obey God, it does not mean that He has failed. You can keep trusting that He keeps His promises in His own time and in His own way, even when you do not yet see the result.
exp.7:21:
On the day of the plague of flies, God promises to make a separation: the land of Goshen, where the Israelites lived, will have no swarms of flies at all. "Sever" means to separate or set apart. "Swarms of flies" refers to a kind or swarm of flies. "The Lord" is the name of God. The purpose is that Pharaoh would know that God is present and acting in the midst of the land.

God speaks, giving Moses instructions to warn Pharaoh. This is the fourth plague, and Pharaoh was refusing to let the Hebrew people go to worship God. This distinction between Egypt and Goshen shows that God protects his people and that his power is not the same as that of the Egyptian gods.

For today: even when there are problems around us, we can trust that God cares for his own and works with purpose. Today you can ask him to help you rest in his care and to recognize his presence in your daily life.
exp.11:16:
It says that the people were to keep the feast of unleavened bread, because on that very day God brought the tribes of Israel out of Egypt, whom it calls "armies," meaning organized multitudes. This feast was to be repeated always, from generation to generation. Its lasting observance means it is a fixed, permanent rule.

God speaks through Moses, just before the departure from Egypt. He wants the people to remember their deliverance with a concrete act: eating bread without yeast for seven days. Some see in yeast an image of what must be left behind; the text, in any case, stresses above all remembrance and obedience.

For today: take a moment to remember how God has helped you and give him thanks. You can build a simple habit, such as writing those memories down, so that you do not forget his faithfulness.
exp.5:20:
This verse lists the three sons of Izhar: Korah, Nepheg, and Zichri. Izhar was a son of Kohath and a grandson of Levi, so these three belong to the same branch of the family as Moses and Aaron.

Here the narrator, who according to tradition is Moses, pauses the account of the deliverance to give a genealogy. He wants to show which family Moses and Aaron came from, the leaders whom God chose. Among these names is Korah, who would later rebel against Moses (Numbers 16). The Bible does not hide the fact that within one family there were both faithful people and rebellious ones.

For today: God knows each person by name and by family history. Your origin does not decide your course. What matters is how you respond to God, with humility and faithfulness.
exp.13:8:
The Egyptian army, with its horses, chariots and soldiers, caught up with the Israelites. They were camped by the sea, near Pihahiroth and facing Baalzephon. The places named are uncertain, and scholars debate their exact location. The verse says the horses and chariots of Pharaoh, his horsemen and his army pursued them, and overtook them there.

It is part of the story in the book of Exodus. Pharaoh had let Israel go, but changed his mind and went after them. The text says God hardened his heart. The Israelites found themselves trapped between the army and the sea, which is why their fear and complaints appear in the verses that follow.

There are moments when it seems there is no way out. This passage encourages us not to let fear take over, but to cry out to God, even with doubts, trusting that he can act where we see no path.
exp.3:2:
God tells Moses to throw the staff he is holding onto the ground. Moses obeys, and the staff becomes a snake, that is, a serpent. Moses is frightened and runs away from it.

Here the Lord speaks with Moses at the burning bush. Moses is afraid that the people of Israel will not believe him when he says that God appeared to him. God responds with a sign: he uses something ordinary, a simple shepherd's staff, to show that his power is with Moses. Some see in the serpent a symbol of the power of Egypt, but the text does not state this clearly.

God often uses what we already have in our hands, even when it seems like very little. When we give him our abilities and resources, he can work beyond what we imagine. Even when we feel fear, we can obey step by step.
exp.19:12:
This commandment forbids taking another person's life. The Hebrew word used (ratsaj) refers above all to murder, that is, killing unjustly or out of hatred. Many scholars point out that the same law allowed criminal justice and war in certain cases, although Christians debate how this applies today.

God speaks to Israel at Mount Sinai, shortly after rescuing them from Egypt. This commandment is among the Ten Commandments, between honoring one's parents and the prohibitions against adultery and theft. All of them protect life and relationships within the community. Jesus, in Matthew 5:21-22, deepened this command: hatred and contempt also harm the heart.

Today we can obey it by taking care with our words and attitudes. If you hold a grudge against someone, ask God to heal your heart, and seek reconciliation when it is possible. Valuing every life as sacred begins with how we treat those around us.
exp.8:22:
Moses raised his rod toward heaven, and God sent thunder and hail. Lightning also fell and ran along the ground. The phrase "sent thunder" means that he caused thunder to roar, and "fire" here is understood as lightning or bolts. God made hail rain down over all of Egypt.

This is the seventh plague. Through Moses, God was demanding that Pharaoh let the people of Israel go free. Before the storm, God had warned what was coming, and some Egyptians, believing him, sheltered their servants and animals. Others paid no attention and suffered the consequences.

When God speaks, it is wise to listen in time. Today it is not always easy to obey, but his warnings are meant to protect us. Ask yourself: is there something God has already shown you in his Word that you have been putting off? Today you can take one simple step of obedience.
exp.37:6:
Bezalel and his helpers put the poles through the rings on the sides of the altar of burnt offering, so that it could be carried when the people moved. It also explains that the altar was hollow, made of boards (of acacia wood, covered with bronze).

This is part of the account of how the tabernacle was built, following the instructions God gave Moses on the mountain. The narrator describes in detail that everything was made as it had been commanded. The altar had to be portable, because Israel was still traveling through the wilderness and God was walking with his people.

For today: God cares even for the small details of our service to him. We can obey him faithfully in simple things, and remember that he accompanies us at every stage of the journey, even when our life changes place.
exp.29:15:
God tells Moses to collect the money from the atonement payments the people will give and to use it for the work of the tabernacle. "To atone" means to cover or make right a wrong so as to be at peace with God. "For a memorial" means "as a reminder." That money would serve to remind God that the people belonged to him and had been redeemed.

God speaks with Moses while the worship in the wilderness is being organized. Every Israelite aged twenty and up, rich or poor, gave the same amount: half a shekel. In this way it was shown that everyone needed forgiveness equally and that no one was worth more before God. Scholars understand in different ways how that money made atonement, but the text ties it to the service of God.

Today we can remember that before God we all stand on the same level of need. Giving gratefully and simply for the service of his work is a way of recognizing that he sustains us.
exp.34:19:
All the people of Israel withdrew from Moses' presence. They had heard what Moses explained to them, and now they were leaving, but not to forget it: they went away to think and to prepare what each one would give.

Moses had just passed on what God asked for building the tabernacle, the tent where God would dwell among them. He included cloth, posts, cords, and sacred garments for the priests. After this, the people went away, and the verses that follow show that they came back with offerings given willingly.

For today: after hearing God's Word, there is a moment of decision. Leaving the gathering is simple, but what matters is what we will do afterward. We can ask God how to respond with a willing heart, giving time, talents, or resources.
exp.30:5:
God tells Moses that, in addition to Bezalel, he has also appointed Aholiab, of the tribe of Dan, as his helper. He also says that he has given skill to everyone who is wise of heart, that is, to people with ability and good judgment, so that they may make everything he has commanded. The phrase "wise of heart" in the verse refers to the inner life of the person, and "that they may make all that I have commanded" points to the purpose of that wisdom.

God is speaking on Mount Sinai while giving instructions for building the tabernacle, the place of worship for the people. Many objects had to be made from gold, silver, wood, and stones. God does not only give the plan; he also chooses and equips the people who will carry it out.

For today: your abilities, whether great or simple, can be a gift from God for serving others. Offer them with humility and work as a team, as Bezalel and Aholiab did.
exp.26:9:
It says the south side of the tabernacle courtyard would have twenty pillars, each set on a base of bronze. In the older Reina-Valera, the word translated here as "bronze" is the one meaning the bronze. The top parts are the pieces at the top of the pillars, and the connecting pieces were probably rods or rings that joined the pillars together; only those parts were silver.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai and gives him exact instructions for building his portable sanctuary. The courtyard was the outer open area, enclosed by linen curtains hung from these pillars. It marked a set-apart space where the people came near to God with their offerings.

For today: God cares about details and about doing things with order and reverence. We can ask ourselves whether we are giving God our best effort, even in small and unremarkable tasks, like a base that quietly holds things up.
exp.18:11:
God tells Moses to set a boundary around Mount Sinai. The people must not go up the mountain or touch its edge, because whoever touches it will die.

God speaks with Moses before he gives the law to the people. Israel was preparing to meet with God: they washed their clothes and consecrated themselves. The boundary taught that God is holy and that drawing near to Him is not to be done lightly. According to the text that follows, the penalty was carried out without anyone laying a hand on the person.

For today: God deserves reverence. Today we can draw near to Him with confidence through Christ, but without losing our respect for Him. Before praying or reading the Bible, pause and place your heart before Him with humility and gratitude.
exp.27:5:
It says that the ephod, a special garment of the priest, was to be made with threads of gold, blue, purple, and scarlet, together with fine twined linen. The word for the deep blue-violet and the word for the bright red are each explained in the sense of a deep blue or violet and a vivid red, and the phrase about the work of an embroiderer means that it was to be a piece made with great artistry and care.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai. He gives instructions for clothing Aaron and his sons as priests. These garments were for their service in the tabernacle. Scholars understand the meaning of each color in several ways, but the text itself does not explain it; it does show that God wanted beauty and order in his worship.

For today: if God cared for every detail of this service, we too can serve him with diligence and reverence. Let us do with excellence, and with a sincere heart, even the small tasks he entrusts to us.
exp.4:1:
Pharaoh responds with pride. He asks who the Lord is that he should have to obey him, and he says he does not know the Lord. For that reason he refuses to let Israel go. The phrase about hearing his voice means obeying his word, and the phrase about letting Israel go means letting them leave free.

Moses and Aaron have just come before Pharaoh with God's message: let the people go into the wilderness to hold a festival for him. Pharaoh was the king of Egypt, and in his culture he was seen as a divine figure. For that reason he does not acknowledge a God of Hebrew slaves. His answer opens the conflict that will lead to the plagues.

For today: when God's voice makes us uncomfortable, it is easy to say "I do not know him" so that we do not obey. Let us pray for a humble heart that listens first, before making excuses.
exp.8:1:
This verse is part of a warning. God says that if Pharaoh keeps refusing to let the people go and continues holding them back, there will be consequences. The word "refuse" in the verse means holding them back by force, that is, continuing to keep them from leaving.

God speaks, and Moses must carry the message to Pharaoh. This is the fifth time God asks for Israel's freedom, so that they may serve Him. Before sending the plague on the animals, God gives a warning. In this way He gives Pharaoh another chance to change his attitude.

For today: God often speaks to us patiently before correcting us. If we feel that He is asking something of us, such as forgiving or leaving a bad habit, let us not harden our hearts. Responding quickly with humility is better than waiting until consequences force us to act.
exp.16:2:
This verse tells how the people of Israel felt great thirst in the desert and complained against Moses. They held him responsible for bringing them out of Egypt, since they thought they and their children and their livestock were going to die of thirst.

The people speak here, already free from slavery and camped at Refidim, where there was no water. Moses had told them that by arguing this way they were putting God to the test. Their need was real, but the complaint forgot what God had already done for them. Moses, distressed, cried out to God, and God answered him.

When we face a need, we can do what Moses did: bring it to God in prayer, instead of letting fear make us forget his faithfulness in the past.
exp.22:17:
It says that when an offering was made to God, its blood was not to be offered together with leavened bread, that is, bread made with yeast. It also says that the fat of the animal offered (the "fat" of the animal) was not to remain from night until morning; it had to be used promptly.

The animal presented in the sacrifice is what is meant here.

God speaks, giving laws to Israel through Moses, after the Ten Commandments. These rules sit alongside the annual feasts. Many believe the unleavened bread recalls the departure from Egypt, and that the fat had to be burned without delay out of respect for what was set apart. The text does not explain all the reasons.

For today: let us give God our best and not put it off. Let us avoid mixing our worship with things that harm it, and let us respond quickly when He calls us.
exp.38:16:
This verse tells how the craftsmen put the two small chains of braided gold into the two rings at the upper corners of the breastpiece. The breastpiece was a cloth piece set with precious stones, which the high priest wore over his chest. The chains are braided strands of gold, and the corners are the ends or edges where the rings were attached.

Here no person is speaking; it is Moses' account describing how the craftsmen carried out, exactly as God had commanded, the work on the priest's garments. The breastpiece bore the names of the twelve tribes of Israel, and the chains held it firmly to the ephod.

For today: God cares even for the small details of what is done for Him. We can serve Him with faithfulness and care in the ordinary things, and remember that He holds his people firmly, just as these chains held the names upon the priest's chest.
exp.2:10:
Moses answers God with a question full of doubt: "Who am I?" He feels far too small to stand before Pharaoh and bring the whole people of Israel out of Egypt. The word "to" in that question is simply an older way of writing it.

God has just spoken to him from the burning bush. He told him that he had heard the cry of his oppressed people and that he was sending him to Pharaoh. Moses, who had fled from Egypt years earlier and was now a shepherd, responds with humility and also with fear. God does not argue with his weakness, but promises him: "I will be with you."

Today, we often feel unable to do what God asks of us. The key is not how strong we are, but that God goes with us. Take the step you can, trusting in his presence.
exp.11:48:
This verse says that Israel was to have one standard for everyone: the one born among the people and the foreigner who lived among them. The first word refers to the native, the one born in that land or community. The second means living as an outsider, as a temporary visitor or as a resident. The requirement was the same for both.

God speaks through Moses just as he gives instructions about the Passover, the celebration that remembered the deliverance from Egypt. A foreigner could take part if he accepted circumcision, the sign of the covenant with God, and then he was treated as one more member of the people. Afterward, the text says that Israel obeyed.

For today: God shows no partiality in his household. We can welcome with respect and without favoritism someone who is new to the church or to our community, treating them as part of the family.
exp.27:32:
God tells Moses that on the lower hem of the priest's robe there are to be ornaments shaped like pomegranates, made of blue, purple, and deep red (scarlet) yarn. Between the pomegranates, golden bells are to be placed all the way around the hem. "Hyacinth" here refers to a shade of blue.

God speaks to Moses at Sinai, giving him instructions for the clothing of the high priest Aaron. The verses that follow explain that the bells would ring when Aaron went in and out of the sanctuary. Some believe the sound showed that he was still alive and was serving with reverence, though the text does not give more detail. The meaning of the pomegranates is interpreted in several ways.

God cares about service done with reverence and care. Today I can draw near to Him with respect and gratitude, remembering that Jesus is our high priest and opens the way for us with confidence.
exp.29:25:
This verse says that Moses was to use the holy oil to anoint, that is, to pour or spread oil on the tabernacle and on the ark of the testimony. The testimony refers to the tablets of the Ten Commandments, which were kept inside the ark. The tabernacle was the sacred tent where God made his presence felt among his people.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai and gives him instructions for worship. Earlier he described the recipe for the oil, made of spices and olive oil. To anoint the objects meant setting them apart for God, separating them from all common use. Afterward the text mentions the other furnishings that would also be anointed.

For today: God values what is dedicated to him with intention. We can set apart a time, a talent, or a space in our home to pray and serve him, remembering that our whole life belongs to him.
exp.21:2:
If the sun had already risen when someone killed the thief who had broken into the house, the one who killed him is guilty of murder. Also, the thief had to return everything he had stolen; "make full restitution" means paying back in full. If he had nothing to pay with, "he shall be sold for his theft": that is, he would be put to work as a servant to cover the debt.

God speaks through Moses to the people of Israel, within the laws given after Sinai. The verse before permits defending oneself at night, when the danger is greater and nothing can be seen clearly. In daylight the situation is different: the thief can be identified and justice can be sought without taking his life. The law protects property, but it values human life more.

For today: even when someone harms us, let us seek justice with moderation, without revenge. If we have harmed another, let us make right what we did.
exp.30:7:
This verse continues the list of what God commanded to be made for the tabernacle: the table with its utensils, the lampstand of pure gold with all its accessories, and the altar of incense, where incense was burned. The word "pure" here refers to gold of the finest quality. Utensils, or containers of various kinds, is the general sense of the word the verse uses for the table's furnishings.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai. He had already chosen Bezalel and Aholiab and given them skill for the work. Nothing was left to chance: God wanted his place of meeting with the people made exactly as he had directed.

For today: God cares about the details and also about the abilities of each person. Think of a talent you have, however simple it may seem, and offer it this week to serve your church or others, trusting that God values it.
exp.30:16:
It says that the Sabbath is a lasting sign between God and the people of Israel. The reason is that God made the heavens and the earth in six days, and on the seventh He "ceased, and rested," that is, He stopped working and rested. "Lord" is the name of God. "For ever" speaks of a sign that was meant to last through all generations.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai, right after giving him instructions for building the tabernacle. He wants to remind Israel that the Sabbath was part of His covenant with them. It was a mark that set them apart as God's people. Christians understand in different ways how the Sabbath applies today.

For today: set aside a regular time to rest and remember that God is the Creator. Your worth does not depend on what you produce, and resting can be a way of trusting Him.
exp.17:12:
On the next day Moses sat to judge the people, that is, to settle their problems and disputes. The people stood around him from morning until evening, that is, the whole day.

The narrator describes what happened after the visit of Jethro, Moses' father-in-law, who had come to the camp and celebrated with the leaders. Moses was the only one who attended to everyone, and the people came to him to learn the will of God. This picture sets up the advice that Jethro is about to give him.

For today: serving with devotion is good, but no one should carry everything alone. If you are exhausted from taking on all the responsibilities, consider asking for help and sharing the load with trusted people.
exp.7:17:
This verse tells how the magicians of Egypt, the enchanters at Pharaoh's court, tried to copy the plague of lice with their spells (rituals or secret arts), but they could not do it. The lice covered both people and animals. Some translate the word for these pests as gnats or sand flies; it is not known for certain which exact insect it was.

God had told Moses and Aaron to strike the dust with the staff. Until now the magicians had been able to copy some of the signs, but here they reach their limit. Afterward they acknowledge: "This is the finger of God." Even so, Pharaoh would not listen.

For today: We can see that the power of God has no rival. Also, seeing the truth is not enough; the heart must be opened. Today we can ask ourselves whether we are resisting something that God has already shown us clearly.
exp.19:19:
Moses tells the people not to be afraid. But he also explains that God came to test them, so that the fear of God, that is, a deep respect for Him, would stay with them and help them not to sin. The word "test" here means to examine or try someone. A "trumpet" is a horn-shaped instrument.

Moses is the speaker. The Israelites had just heard the voice of God giving the Ten Commandments amid thunder, fire and smoke on Mount Sinai. They trembled and stepped back, asking that Moses speak with God on their behalf. Moses comforts them, but he does not take away their awe. That fear had a good purpose. Some understand the "test" as seeing whether they would obey.

For today: do not confuse the fear of God with living in terror. It means taking Him seriously and loving Him, remembering that He is present. Before deciding something difficult, ask yourself: "How do I want to honor God in this?"
exp.12:11:
This verse says that the people were to set apart for God every firstborn male child and every firstborn male of their animals. The phrase "make pass over to the Lord" means giving it, dedicating it to God. "Open the womb" refers to the first birth. The "firstling" is the one born first.

God speaks to Moses, and Moses passes this on to the people, right after the departure from Egypt. This practice would remind them that God had set them free, and that the firstborn of Israel were spared when the firstborn of Egypt died. The verses that follow explain that the firstborn human child was to be bought back, that is, redeemed by a payment, and that the children would ask what it meant.

For today: the first and best of what we have, such as our time, money, or energy, we can dedicate to God with gratitude, remembering that He rescued us and that everything comes from His hand.
exp.29:11:
It says that when Moses counted the Israelites, each person was to give the LORD a "ransom" for their life. A "ransom" is a payment that protects or redeems. This would keep a plague from falling on the people because they were counted. The old words in the verse that match "take the sum" and "number" are the ones being explained here.

The LORD speaks to Moses just after the instructions about the incense altar and the yearly atonement. The verses that follow explain that the ransom was half a shekel for every man twenty years old or older. The explanation does not go into detail about why counting the people was dangerous; interpreters understand it as a reminder that life belongs to God.

For today: our life is not our own property or our own merit; it belongs to God. We can live thankfully, without boasting of our achievements, remembering that Christ paid the ransom for us (Mark 10:45).
exp.27:16:
The explanation says the high priest's breastpiece was to hold four rows of precious stones set in settings. In the first row there were three stones: a sardius (probably a red stone, like carnelian), a topaz, and a carbuncle (a bright stone, perhaps red or green; experts are not sure of its exact identity). The breastpiece is the one used for making decisions and representing the people.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai and gives him instructions for the tabernacle and the garments of Aaron. According to Exodus 28:21, the twelve stones represented the twelve tribes of Israel, each with its name engraved on it. In this way, the priest carried the people near his heart when he entered before God.

For today: God does not see his people as a faceless mass, but as precious stones with their own names. You can pray with confidence, knowing that God knows you personally, and you can also pray for others by name, carrying them in your heart.
exp.5:12:
God speaks again to Moses and Aaron and gives them a clear command: they are to go to the Israelites and to Pharaoh, king of Egypt, to bring the Israelites out of that land.

Moses had just said that not even his own people listened to him, so he doubted that Pharaoh would. He described himself as having uncircumcised lips, an expression that probably refers to his difficulty in speaking. God does not argue with him. He repeats the assignment and adds Aaron to it. Then comes a list of families, which shows where these leaders came from.

God keeps calling people who feel unsure of themselves. If God gives you a task and you doubt your abilities, do not wait until you feel ready. Take the next step in obedience, lean on others who walk with you, and trust that the mission belongs to God, not to you.
exp.16:11:
It says that Moses' arms grew tired while he held them up. So they put a stone under him so that he could sit, and Aaron and Hur held up his hands, one on each side. In this way his hands stayed steady until sunset. The word that reads "held up" in the verse means held up, and "steady" means stable.

Israel was fighting against Amalek at Rephidim, and Joshua led the soldiers. While Moses raised his hand, Israel won; when he lowered it, Amalek won. The text does not explain the gesture in detail; many see it as a sign of dependence on God, and others as a prayer. In any case, the victory came from God, and the narrator shows that Moses needed help.

No one can carry the whole burden alone. If you are tired, allow others to support you, and if you see someone worn out, help them with prayer, time, or words of encouragement.
exp.34:24:
It says that all the women with skill and a willing heart spun with their own hands and brought what they had spun for the sanctuary. They were colored fabrics: the first color is a dark blue or violet (other versions say "blue"), purple and scarlet are reddish and purple tones, and the fine linen is a delicate cloth made of flax.

Moses had just asked the people for freewill offerings to build the tabernacle, the tent where God would dwell among Israel. The men brought metals, woods and skins; the women contributed their work and their talent. The text highlights that they were "wise-hearted," that is, willing and skillful people.

For today: God does not ask for what you do not have, but for what you know how to do. Offer your skill joyfully, whether it is cooking, teaching, repairing or accompanying others, in service to them.
exp.33:0:
God tells Moses to prepare two tables of stone, like the first ones. God himself will write on them the same words that were on the earlier tables, the ones Moses broke. The Hebrew phrase is best rendered as "hew" the stone, meaning to cut and shape it. The name of God is the LORD.

God speaks, addressing Moses on Mount Sinai. Shortly before this, the people had made a golden calf, and Moses, filled with grief, broke the first tablets (Exodus 32). After Moses interceded for Israel, God gives them another chance and renews his covenant with them.

For today: when we fail, God does not discard us. He offers to begin again. We can come to him with sincerity, ask for forgiveness, and receive his grace to move forward, without being trapped by the past.
exp.33:23:
It says that God himself will drive out the nations who lived in the promised land and will enlarge the territory of Israel. It also promises that no one will try to take their lands while the men travel to appear before God three times a year. "Borders" means the territory or the edges of the land. To "desire" something means to long for what belongs to someone else. "To appear before the Lord" means to present oneself before him in worship.

God is speaking, and he gives Moses the instructions of the renewed covenant after the golden calf. Israel was going to leave their homes and fields to go to the feasts, and that could seem risky. God answers with a promise of protection. How that promise was fulfilled is something the Bible tells, with ups and downs, in the history of Israel.

For today: when obeying God, for example by setting aside time to worship him, seems to leave something exposed, we can trust that he cares for what we leave in his hands.
exp.27:41:
God tells Moses to make linen undergarments for the priests. The garments are underwear, and the phrase used for the private parts of the body is a gentle way of referring to them. They were to cover the body from the waist to the thighs.

God himself speaks to Moses on the mountain, giving him instructions for the tabernacle and its service. Aaron and his sons were to be set apart as priests, and their clothing was meant to give them honor and beauty. The following verse explains that they were to wear this garment when approaching the altar, so that they would not incur guilt and die. This shows that God required reverence and propriety in his presence.

For today: when we pray or serve God, let us do so with respect and simplicity of heart. He is as concerned with the details of our conduct as he is with our worship.
exp.6:16:
God tells Moses what he is to say to Pharaoh: "Thus says the Lord." The purpose is that Pharaoh may come to know who God is. Moses will strike the water of the river (the Nile) with the rod he holds in his hand, and the water will turn to blood. The phrase "I will smite" means I will strike.

God speaks. Moses is to meet Pharaoh in the morning, at the edge of the river. Earlier, God had asked that he let the Hebrew people go to worship him in the wilderness, but Pharaoh would not listen. This is the first plague. Some scholars see here a challenge to the gods of Egypt, though the text does not say so in those words.

For today: God acts so that we may truly know him. Today we can ask him to give us a heart willing to listen to him in time, without hardening ourselves, and to obey him when he speaks.
exp.36:1:
It says that Bezalel, the craftsman, overlaid the ark with pure gold, both inside and outside. He also put around it a gold molding, that is, a decorative edge or border running along the top.

The one telling the story here is Moses, who writes how the instructions God gave him for the tabernacle were carried out. The ark would hold the tablets of the law and would be the place where God met with his people. That is why it was made with such care and with valuable materials. Many see in the gold a sign of purity and holiness, although the text itself does not explain it that way.

For today: God cares about the details, including the ones nobody sees. Just as the ark was beautiful inside and out, we can ask him to help us live with sincerity, so that what we are in private matches what we show to others.
exp.4:18:
This verse says that the Israelite foremen, the men set to supervise their own people, were distressed. The phrase "in evil case" means that they realized they were in serious trouble. They had been ordered that not even one brick could be taken off the daily quota, even though they would no longer receive straw.

Pharaoh had just answered the request of Moses and Aaron to let the people go to worship God. He called them lazy and increased the burden. The foremen, caught between Pharaoh and the workers, left his presence and came face to face with Moses and Aaron.

When we do what is right, sometimes things get worse before they get better. That does not always mean we have made a mistake. We can bring our distress honestly to God, as they did, and keep trusting while we wait for his answer.
exp.7:4:
God tells Moses to instruct Aaron to stretch out his hand with the staff over the streams, the rivers, and the pools of Egypt, so that frogs would come up over the whole land.

The Lord speaks. This is the second plague. Pharaoh was refusing to let the people of Israel go, and God had warned him of what would come. The frogs would reach into the houses, the beds, and the ovens. The Nile River was very important to Egypt, and many regarded it as a source of life. The magicians also produced frogs, but they did not remove them.

For today: God has authority over everything we consider safe, even what gives us life. We can ask ourselves what we trust more than Him, and surrender it to Him with humility.
exp.30:2:
God says that he filled Bezalel with his Spirit. "Filled" here means filled completely. God gave him wisdom, understanding, knowledge, and skill in every kind of craftwork.

Here the LORD speaks to Moses, right after giving him the instructions for the tabernacle, the tent where God would dwell among his people. God himself chooses Bezalel, from the tribe of Judah, to lead the work in gold, silver, bronze, stone, and wood. His talent comes as a gift from God for serving his people.

For today: your abilities, whether manual, creative, technical, or organizational, can be a gift from God. Offer them with excellence and humility to serve others and honor him, without thinking that only "spiritual" work pleases him.
exp.9:11:
God tells Moses to stretch out his hand over Egypt so that a plague of locusts will come. They would rise up across the whole country and eat what the hail had not destroyed. Here "locust" refers to flying insects that devour plants. "Consume" means to bring everything to an end.

God speaks to Moses after Pharaoh had driven Moses and Aaron out of his presence. Pharaoh was willing to let only the men go, not the families, and Moses did not accept that half-hearted obedience. Then came the eighth plague, which took away what was left of the crops.

For today: God does not settle for partial obedience. Pharaoh wanted to bargain and keep control. We can ask ourselves in which area of life we are giving God only a part, and hand over everything to him with trust.
exp.21:23:
It says that God will be angry with whoever mistreats widows and orphans. The verse uses a very strong word for anger, and the phrase "with the sword" means that those who harm them would be killed by the sword. The punishment would be that the offenders die, their wives become widows, and their children become orphans, meaning they would suffer the same thing they caused.

God speaks, giving laws to Israel through Moses, shortly after freeing them from Egypt. Widows and orphans had no one to defend them or provide for them, and that is why God declares himself their protector. When they cry out, he listens. The verses that follow add care for the poor, such as not charging abusive interest.

For today: God pays attention to the most vulnerable. We can ask ourselves who near us is alone or in need, and help them with time, a visit, or support, without taking advantage of their situation.
exp.29:36:
God tells Moses that the sacred incense of the tabernacle had a special formula. No one was to copy it for their own use. The word "composition" in the verse refers to the recipe, and the mixture was "holy for the Lord," that is, set apart only for him.

God speaks to Moses while giving him instructions for worship in the tabernacle. The incense was burned in the place of God's presence and represented the worship reserved for him. The prohibition, which the following verse reinforces with a serious penalty, protected the distance between the common and the holy.

For today: let us take care that our worship does not become something casual or for show. We can set aside times of sincere and reverent prayer, dedicated only to God, without using them to impress others.
exp.21:10:
If someone looks after a neighbour's animal and the animal dies, is injured, or is carried off without anyone seeing it, the keeper must take an oath before God. He swears that he did not take for himself what belonged to another (to "lay a hand" on something means to appropriate it). If he swears, the owner must accept his word, and the keeper does not have to pay.

God speaks to Moses and gives Israel laws for everyday life together in community. In a time without cameras or paperwork, there were often no witnesses. This command protected the one who cared for another's property, and it also called both parties to trust, placing God as the witness to the truth.

For today: when someone entrusts something to you, look after it as if it were your own, and always speak the truth, because God sees what no one else sees. And if someone gives you his honest word, learn to trust generously.
exp.24:37:
This verse says that the lampstand of the tabernacle also had to have snuffers and trays, all of pure gold. The snuffers were like tongs or pincers used to trim and remove the burnt part of the wicks of the lamps. The trays were small dishes where those burnt parts or the remains were placed.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai and gives him detailed instructions for building the tabernacle, the place where God would dwell among his people. Here he describes the equipment of the lampstand with seven lamps. Everything had to be made according to the pattern God showed him.

For today: if God cared for even the small details of his service, we too can serve him with care in simple things. Removing what gets in the way of the light, such as pride or bad habits, helps us shine better.
exp.24:33:
This verse describes the central shaft of the lampstand: it had four cups shaped like almond blossoms, and each one carried its knop and its flower. The word for the knop here is not the fruit; it refers to a round ornament, like a knob or button. The lampstand is the stand that held the lamps.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai and gives him detailed instructions for building the tabernacle. The lampstand would be placed in the holy place, and its light would illuminate that space. Every detail of beauty was intended for that service. Some see in the almonds an image of life and renewal, but the text does not explain this, so it is an interpretation.

For today: God cares about what we offer him, even in the small details. Let us do our work and service with care and affection, as for him.
exp.36:2:
It says that Bezalel, the craftsman in charge, made four rings of cast gold for the ark of the covenant. He placed them at the four corners, two on each side.

The passage is narrative. Moses received God's instructions on the mountain (Exodus 25), and here the text tells how they were carried out. The rings held the poles with which the Levites would carry the ark. In this way no one had to touch it, and it could be moved when God guided the people.

For today: God cares even for small details, and the rings, almost hidden, made it possible for the ark to advance with the people. In the same way, our simple and little-seen service also has value when it is done with faithfulness and obedience.
exp.7:13:
This verse says that the Egyptians gathered the dead frogs and piled them up, and because of that the whole land stank terribly. The verse's wording is "stank," which means it gave off a horrible smell.

Here the narrator of the book of Exodus is speaking. Moses had prayed to the LORD about the plague of frogs, and God took it away just as Pharaoh had asked. But the relief left a mark: the heaps of dead frogs reminded everyone of what had happened. Right after this, the text tells us that Pharaoh, once he felt relief, hardened his heart again.

For today: when God delivers us from a problem, let us not forget what we learned. The consequences sometimes remain visible, and they serve to remind us that we should respond to God with gratitude and obedience, not with a hard heart.
exp.7:22:
God says he will make a clear difference between his people, Israel, and the people of Pharaoh. The word "redemption" here can be understood as rescue or separation: God will free his own from the plague of flies. He announces that this sign will happen "tomorrow," that is, the next day.

God speaks, through Moses, to a Pharaoh who refused to let the Israelites leave their slavery. This is the fourth plague, and for the first time God separates the land of Goshen, where his people lived. In this way Pharaoh would see that the Lord rules over the whole earth and cares for his own.

For today: God knows those who belong to him and cares for them, even in the middle of troubles that affect everyone. We can trust that he does not lose sight of us, and live with that assurance.
exp.19:20:
This verse says that the people stayed far from the mountain, while Moses drew near to the thick darkness, that is, to the dense cloud where God made himself known. The phrase in the text is rendered as the thick darkness of the King James Version. Moses drew near to God in that cloud.

The people had just heard the Ten Commandments amid thunder, lightning and the sound of a trumpet, and they were afraid. They asked that Moses speak with God on their behalf. Moses explained to them that God wanted them to revere him and not sin. While the people preferred to keep their distance, Moses approached as mediator.

For today: we can draw near to God with reverence, but without running away from him. If we feel fear or unworthiness, let us remember that God invites us to know him. As Christians, we believe that Jesus is our mediator and opens the way for us to the Father.
exp.5:7:
God promises to bring Israel into the land that he swore to give to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. The phrase "raised my hand" is an old way of saying that he made a solemn oath. An "inheritance" is a property that is received as a gift and passed down from generation to generation. The passage ends with "I am the Lord," the name by which God presents himself as faithful to his word.

God speaks, through Moses, to a people enslaved in Egypt. Moses had already spoken with Pharaoh and things had grown worse. That is why God renews his promises. Even so, the people did not listen, because they were worn out by harsh slavery and anguish.

For today: when you are tired or discouraged and find it hard to believe, remember that God's promise does not depend on your mood, but on his faithfulness. You can rest in the fact that he keeps what he says, even when it takes time, and ask him for strength to keep trusting.
exp.19:3:
God forbids making images or figures of anything in order to worship them: neither of what is in heaven, nor on the earth, nor in the sea. The word "likeness" means a resemblance or a representation. The next verse makes clear that the problem is bowing down to them and honoring them.

God himself speaks, the one who has just brought Israel out of slavery in Egypt. He says this to his people at Mount Sinai, alongside the Ten Commandments. The neighboring peoples worshiped idols, but God wants Israel to know him as the living God, who cannot be contained in a figure made by human hands. Christians interpret in different ways how to apply this commandment to religious art, but all agree that God must not be replaced.

Today we can ask ourselves: what thing occupies in my heart the place that belongs to God? Surrender that to him in prayer and trust in him.
exp.19:18:
The explanation says that the people, frightened, asked Moses to be their go-between. They would listen to God through him, but they did not want to hear God's voice directly, out of fear of dying. Some old words: the word "á" is "to", and "but" means "however", and the phrase "lest we die" means "so that we would not die."

The people of Israel, newly freed from Egypt, speak at the foot of Mount Sinai. They had just seen thunder, fire, smoke, and heard the sound of the trumpet, right after receiving the Ten Commandments. They felt the holiness of God and were filled with awe. Moses immediately explains to them that God did not want to destroy them, but wanted them to revere Him and not sin.

For today: Reverencing God is healthy, but there is no need to run away from Him. Today we can draw near with respect and confidence, reading His Word and praying, knowing that God wants to speak to us to care for and guide us.
exp.39:0:
This verse says that God spoke to Moses to give him a new instruction. "Jehovah" is the proper name of God in the Old Testament. The word "spoke" and the phrase "saying" signal that an important message is coming right after.

The one speaking is God, and Moses is the one who listens. At this point, the people of Israel had already made all the parts of the tabernacle, the tent where God was going to dwell among them. What remained was to assemble it and put it into use, and God gives Moses the exact orders to do so.

For today: God is accustomed to guiding his children with clarity. Before acting, it is worth pausing to listen to his voice in the Bible and in prayer. Obeying step by step what he indicates, even in small things, prepares the place for his presence in our lives.
exp.36:23:
This verse says that the lampstand of the tabernacle, together with all its utensils, was made from a talent of pure gold. A talent was a large unit of weight; it is estimated at about 30 to 35 kilograms, although the exact value is debated. "Vessels" here means the utensils or fittings of the lampstand, such as the snuffers (scissors for trimming the wick) and the trays.

The passage is part of the account of how Bezalel, the craftsman whom God filled with skill, built the furnishings of the tabernacle according to the instructions God gave to Moses. The narrator recounts in detail that what was commanded was carried out, without changing anything.

For today: God cares about the details and deserves our best. We can serve Him with excellence and obedience, even in small tasks that no one sees, because we do them for Him.
exp.16:6:
This verse says that Moses gave the place the names Massah and Meribah. "Massah" is connected with testing or trying, and "Meribah" with quarreling or disputing. The people's complaint and their doubt are described in the verse itself, and the question they asked was whether the Lord was among them or not.

The one telling the story is Moses. Israel was thirsty in the desert and complained against him and against God. Although God had already rescued them from Egypt, they doubted his care. Then God gave them water from the rock at Horeb, and the place remained as a reminder of that distrust.

For today: when we go through a need, we can bring our distress honestly to God, but without demanding proof that he loves us. Remembering how he has helped us before helps us trust that he is still with us.
exp.37:28:
This verse says that the bronze the people gave as an offering came to seventy talents and two thousand four hundred shekels. The talent and the shekel were units of weight. Their exact modern equivalents are not known for certain; the talent is usually estimated at about 30 kilograms and the shekel at about 11 grams, though these figures are approximate.

Moses commands that the amount be recorded, and the text gives the account of what was received for building the tabernacle. It then details how this bronce was used: the bases of the gate, the altar, its grating, the utensils, and the pegs of the courtyard.

For today: what is given to God and to his work deserves order, honesty, and transparency. If you handle money in a church or ministry, give a clear account of it, and if you give, do so with confidence that God values every gift.
exp.33:28:
This verse tells that Moses came down from Mount Sinai carrying the two stone tablets of the law in his hands. His face was shining because he had spoken with God, but he did not realize it. The phrase "the skin of his face" refers to the surface of his face, and the "tables of testimony" are the Ten Commandments, which bore witness to God's covenant with his people.

The narrator describes what happened after Moses spent forty days and forty nights with God, writing down the words of the covenant. This takes place after the sin of the golden calf, when God renewed his covenant with Israel. Afterward, the people were afraid to come near him.

Spending time with God transforms us, even when we do not notice it. Moses did not work at shining; he simply stayed with God. If we seek God sincerely in prayer and in his Word, others may see his work in us, without our having to boast about it.
exp.15:11:
God tells Moses that he has heard the complaints of the people. He promises them meat at evening, and bread in the morning until they are filled, that is, fully satisfied. Then they will know that the Lord is their God.

God speaks to Moses after the people complained about the hunger in the desert. Aaron had gathered the congregation, and the glory of God appeared in the cloud. God does not respond with anger, but with provision. Then the quail and the manna came, as the following passage tells.

God hears our complaints and continues to care for us. When you feel need or weariness, bring it to Him honestly, and notice how He has provided for you day after day. Trust in Him grows when we remember His faithfulness.
exp.21:13:
If someone borrows an animal from their neighbor, and the animal is injured or dies while the owner is not present, the one who borrowed it must pay for it.

God speaks to Moses, and Moses to the people of Israel, within the laws that follow the Ten Commandments. These were rules for the daily life of a farming community. The underlying reason is to protect the owner and to promote justice. If the owner was present, the responsibility changed, because he himself could look after his animal.

For today: when you borrow something, whether a car, a tool, or money, treat it with more care than you would your own, and if it gets damaged, take responsibility without excuses. In this way you honor your neighbor and show integrity.
exp.27:20:
This verse says that the twelve stones of the high priest's breastpiece would bear the names of the sons of Israel, one name on each stone. The phrase "like the engravings of a signet" means that the letters were cut with great care, like the marks of a seal used to stamp documents. The breastpiece itself is the one the verse calls "the breastpiece of judgment." Each stone represented one of the twelve tribes.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai and gives him instructions for Aaron's garments. The high priest would serve before God on behalf of the people. By bearing the names upon his chest, he symbolically carried all of them before the Lord.

For today: God does not see his people as a faceless crowd, but knows each one by name. You can pray with confidence, knowing that he cares for you personally. We can also imitate that care, bringing before God in prayer, by name, the people he has placed near us.
exp.26:18:
This verse says that all the furnishings of the tabernacle, that is, the objects used in its service, were to be made of bronze. The pins or stakes that held the tent and the courtyard in place were also to be bronze. The word "brass" here is bronze, though some translate it as copper. The courtyard that surrounded the tabernacle is the court. The vessels are the utensils in general.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai and gives him detailed instructions to build a place where He would dwell among his people. These details show that God cares about order and that nothing in his service is improvised. Even the smallest pieces, which almost no one would see, had their purpose.

For today: nothing we do for God is insignificant. Even small and hidden tasks, done faithfully, are valuable to Him.
exp.3:7:
God tells Moses that if the people do not believe him or heed the first sign (the staff that turns into a serpent), they will still believe the second sign: the hand that becomes leprous and then is made clean again.

The Lord speaks with Moses beside the burning bush. Moses fears that Israel will not believe that God sent him. So the Lord gives him signs to confirm his message. The Bible does not explain in detail why the second sign would persuade more; it only shows that God provides what is needed.

When God asks you something that seems hard, do not look only at your fears. He knows the doubts of others and your own too, and he knows how to give you what you need to move forward. Obey with confidence, one step at a time.
exp.18:24:
This verse says that Moses came down from Mount Sinai to where the people were and spoke to them. It is a short and simple phrase. The text does not make clear the exact words he said to them, but it is understood that he repeated the warnings God had just given him.

Moses is the one acting here. God had called him up the mountain, but also told him to go back down to remind the people not to cross the boundary that had been set. God is holy, and approaching without reverence could bring harm. Moses serves as a bridge between God and the people, faithfully carrying God's message.

For today: God speaks to us so that we will obey, not only so that we will know. Moses did not keep to himself what he heard on the mountaintop; he shared it with others. We can ask ourselves what God has been teaching us lately, and to whom that message needs to reach with humility and clarity.
exp.28:45:
This verse says that the people of Israel will come to know, or recognize through experience, that the Lord is their God. The reason is that He brought them out of Egypt with a purpose: to live among them. "Dwell" means to remain, to live with someone. God repeats "I am the Lord their God" to give firmness to His promise.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai while giving him instructions to consecrate Aaron and his sons as priests and to make the tabernacle holy. The deliverance from Egypt was not only an escape from slavery, but also an entry into a close relationship with God, who makes His presence known among His people.

For today: God does not only rescue us from what binds us, but He desires to be near us. You can set aside a moment each day to speak with Him, remembering that His desire is to be with you.
exp.7:16:
Moses and Aaron did what God had commanded them. Aaron stretched out his staff and struck the dust of the ground, and all that dust became gnats, meaning tiny insects that troubled both people and animals. The word for the insects is not used here; it is simply described. The staff is the rod Aaron carried. It is not certain whether the Hebrew term refers to lice, mosquitoes, or biting midges; this is still debated.

This is the third plague on Egypt. Pharaoh had asked for relief from the previous plague, but afterward he hardened his heart and did not keep his word. God then sent this plague, and even the magicians of Egypt, who could not reproduce it, acknowledged: "This is the finger of God."

For today: when God shows us something and we ignore it, the heart grows harder little by little. Today we can respond with humility and obey in time, without waiting for the situation to get worse.
exp.30:8:
He says that God also commanded that the altar of burnt offering be made, where the burnt sacrifices were offered, with all its utensils. In addition, the basin, which was a large bronze vessel for washing, and its base, that is, the stand on which it rested. Here "furniture" means utensils or containers.

God is speaking to Moses on Mount Sinai. He has just named Bezalel and Oholiab as craftsmen filled with his Spirit. This verse continues the list of what they were to build for the tabernacle, the place where God would dwell among his people Israel.

For today: God cares about details and about work done with dedication. We can offer him our skills, even if they seem simple, and do carefully what is ours to do, knowing that God uses ordinary people for his purposes.
exp.34:22:
It says that every person who had cloth or skins for the sanctuary brought them. "Blue, purple" refers to wool dyed blue or violet; "scarlet" is a deep red; "fine linen" is delicate cloth. The "red-dyed ram skins" are skins that had been dyed red. The "badger skins" are a disputed translation: some believe they were skins of sea animals, such as dolphins or dugongs, but this is not certain.

Moses had just asked the people for materials to build the tabernacle, the tent where God would dwell among them. The text emphasizes that each person gave willingly, according to what they had. No one was forced; their hearts moved them.

Today, God does not need everyone to give the same thing, but for each person to offer with joy what they have: time, money, skills, or help. Ask yourself what you have in your hand, and give it generously to God and to others.
exp.38:37:
This verse is part of the list of the tabernacle items that were presented to Moses. It mentions the golden altar, where the incense was burned; the anointing oil, used to set apart the priests and the objects for God; the sweet incense, that is, the fragrant perfume; and the hanging, which was the curtain that covered the entrance to the holy place.

The narrator reports that the Israelites finished the work just as God had commanded Moses. This list of pieces shows that everything was complete and made according to the instructions. Afterward Moses will inspect the work and bless it.

For today: God values obedience in the details, not only in the great things. We can ask ourselves what simple task He has asked of us and do it with care, trusting that nothing we do faithfully goes unnoticed by Him.
exp.36:27:
He says that Bezalel made the poles, or long bars, of acacia wood and covered them with gold. These poles were inserted into the rings of the incense altar so that it could be carried without anyone touching it. The word "overlaid" here simply means that the wood was covered with gold.

This is part of the description of how the tabernacle was built, the tent where God dwelt among Israel. The speaker is not a character but the narrator, who tells us that Israel followed the instructions given to Moses. Here the incense altar is completed, and right afterward the holy anointing oil and the fragrant incense are mentioned.

For today: God cares about small details, even simple poles. We can serve Him with excellence and faithfulness in ordinary and hidden things, knowing that nothing done for Him is insignificant.
exp.28:16:
This verse describes how to prepare the ram for the sacrifice. It was to be cut into pieces, the inner parts and the legs were to be washed carefully, and then they were to be placed with the pieces and the head. In this way the whole animal was ready to be burned completely on the altar.

God speaks to Moses and gives him instructions to set apart Aaron and his sons as priests. This ram was a burnt offering, an offering burned whole for the LORD. Before this, the priests laid their hands on the animal's head, which many understand as a sign of identifying themselves with the offering.

For today: the careful washing reminds us that God values sincerity and inner purity. We can ask ourselves which hidden areas of our lives we need to surrender to him honestly, trusting in his forgiveness.
exp.26:20:
This verse says that Aaron and his sons were responsible for the lamps of the tabernacle. They would prepare them and keep them burning from evening until morning, in the holy place, outside the veil that covered the ark of the testimony. The phrase "shall order it" means that they would tend and arrange the lamps. The words "a statute for ever" mean a law forever, one that would be passed down from generation to generation.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai while giving him instructions for building the tabernacle. After asking for pure oil of olives for the light, God names who would be responsible for caring for it. The priests served God on behalf of the people. Interpreters see in the light a symbol of God's presence, although the text does not explain this in detail.

For today: just as the priests tended the light each night, we can set aside a steady moment to pray and read the Bible, so that our relationship with God does not go out.
exp.7:12:
This verse tells us that God did what Moses had asked: the frogs died in the houses, in the villages (the farmhouses and courtyards of the countryside), and in the fields. The plague ended, not because the frogs left, but because they died.

Moses had prayed for Pharaoh after Pharaoh asked him for help to be rid of the plague. God answered clearly, showing that He has power over creation. However, the account that follows shows that Pharaoh, once he felt relief, hardened his heart again.

For today: sometimes we ask God for help in a difficult situation, but we forget to obey Him once everything calms down. We can learn to thank Him for His help and keep a willing heart, not only in the crisis but also in the calm.
exp.29:14:
It says that, when they bring the offering to the Lord, everyone would pay the same: half a shekel. The rich would not give more, nor the poor give less. "Atonement" means covering or buying back the guilt; "souls" refers to their lives. "Give more" means "give over and above."

God speaks to Moses when the census of the people is taken. Every man twenty years old and up gave this offering, and that money supported the service of the tabernacle. The equal amount showed that before God everyone needs the same ransom. Interpreters explain in various ways how the atonement worked exactly here, but the emphasis on equality is clear.

Today we can remember that no one is worth more or less before God because of their money or position. Practice this by treating everyone in your church with the same respect, without favoring the one who has more.
exp.8:4:
God did not act suddenly or in secret. He set a clear date. The word "tomorrow" is what the passage uses, and the phrase translated as "appointed a set time" means that he fixed an exact time, a specific day, for sending the plague on Egypt's livestock.

Moses speaks on God's behalf to Pharaoh. This is the fifth plague, and God announces it beforehand so that Egypt will know it comes from him. He also gives notice that there will be a separation: Israel's livestock would not die. Even so, Pharaoh saw that the livestock of the Israelites was well, and still he hardened his heart.

For today: God is patient and gives chances to recognize him and turn back. When we sense that God speaks to us through the Bible, through our conscience, or through wise counsel, it is not wise to harden our hearts or put the matter off. It is better to respond today with humility.
exp.22:10:
Every seventh year the land was to rest. The phrase "let it rest and lie still" means that it was not to be planted, and "let it lie still" means that whatever the land produced on its own would be left free. That growth on its own was for the poor of the people, and whatever was left over the beasts of the field would eat. The same applied to the vineyard and the olive grove.

God speaks to Israel through Moses, in the laws given after the Ten Commandments. It comes right after the command not to mistreat the foreigner, reminding Israel that they too were foreigners in Egypt. The year of rest is tied to the Sabbath day: both protect the poor, the worker, and the land. They show that God is the true owner of everything.

For today: we can learn not to cling to everything we produce. Sharing part of what we have, generously and without boasting, is a way of trusting that God provides.
exp.15:29:
This verse says that the people of Israel rested on the seventh day, that is, the Sabbath. The word "rested" means that they stopped working and gathering food, and stayed quietly in their places.

God had just given manna in the desert. Some Israelites had gone out to look for it on the seventh day and did not find it, so God, through Moses, corrected them. He reminded them that the day before he had already given them bread for two days. The text shows that God provided enough and wanted to teach them to trust him.

For today: setting aside regular time to rest is an act of trust that God cares for us. We can practice that rest by putting work and worries aside for a while to pray, be with family, and give thanks.
exp.11:29:
It says that the same night Pharaoh got up, along with his servants and all the Egyptians, and there was a very great outcry throughout the land, because in every house there was someone dead. "Outcry" is a loud cry of grief. "Servants" are his attendants or officials.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. This is the tenth plague, the last one. God had warned Pharaoh many times, but he hardened his heart. That night, the death of the firstborn led him to let Israel go. Some scholars understand "there was not a house where there was not one dead" literally, and others as a very strong expression to point to widespread grief. The text gives no further detail.

For today: this passage reminds us that ignoring the voice of God has serious consequences. Today we can respond with humility when He corrects us, before pride leads us into a greater sorrow.
exp.33:5:
The explanation says that God passed by before Moses and proclaimed his own name and character. He is described as mighty, compassionate toward those who suffer, and full of grace. He is slow to anger, meaning patient, and abundant in goodness that stands firm and in faithfulness.

Moses had just broken the first tablets of the law, after the people made the golden calf. Now God gives him new tablets and reveals himself to him. The one speaking is the Lord himself, and he does so to show what he is like before renewing his covenant with a people who had failed.

Today we can come before God honestly after we fail. He is not impatient or indifferent: he is just, but also compassionate and faithful. His character invites us to return, not to hide ourselves.
exp.34:15:
This verse lists some of the items that were to be made for the tabernacle: the altar where the sacrifices were burned, its grate of bronze, the poles for carrying it, all its utensils, and the basin of water with its stand. An offering that was burned up completely on the altar is what the explanation calls a whole burnt offering. A stand or support is what the base means. The word "vessels" here refers to utensils.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel after the sin of the golden calf. He explains what God commanded in order to build a place where God would dwell among them. He asks them to take part with their gifts and their labor. This list repeats what God had already indicated before.

For today: God cares about the details and values the participation of his people. There is room for small, unremarkable tasks. We can serve faithfully in simple things, knowing that God takes them into account.
exp.36:5:
It says that Bezalel made the mercy seat of pure gold. This cover is the lid, also called the mercy seat. It measured two and a half cubits in length and a cubit and a half in width, or about 110 by 70 centimeters, although the exact length of a cubit is calculated in several ways. It was the same size as the ark.

It is part of the account of the building of the tabernacle. The narrator tells how the instructions that God gave to Moses were carried out. Earlier the ark and the poles for carrying it were described; afterward come the golden cherubim. This lid was the place where God met with his people and where atonement was made.

For today: God attends to every detail in order to draw near to us. We can approach Him with confidence, knowing that He Himself provides forgiveness, and do faithfully what He asks of us.
exp.38:5:
The explanation says that the craftsmen worked stones, and it names them as onyx, probably, though some scholars doubt the exact type of stone.
