They surrounded the stones with settings of gold, which are the bases where a precious stone is set. Then they engraved on them the names of the children of Israel, as one does with a seal, carving the stone with great detail.

Here the narrator describes how the clothing of the high priest Aaron was made, following what God had commanded Moses. These stones were placed on the shoulder pieces of the ephod, and the verses that follow describe them as stones of remembrance: the priest carried the people on his shoulders before God.

For today: God does not forget his people, and every name matters. Jesus, our great high priest, presents us before the Father with care. We can pray for others with the same attitude, bearing their names and their burdens with love and perseverance.
exp.19:10:
This verse gives the reason for the command to keep the Sabbath day: God made the heavens, the earth, the sea, and everything in them in six days, and rested on the seventh day. For that reason he blessed the Sabbath day and set it apart for himself. To set something apart means to dedicate it for a special purpose. To rest means that he stopped working, not that he was tired.

God speaks to Israel from Mount Sinai, shortly after bringing them out of Egypt. He gives them the Ten Commandments. This day of rest was for everyone: family, servants, animals, and foreigners. Christians do not agree on how the Sabbath applies today, but almost all recognize the value of rest.

For today: set aside time each week to rest without guilt, to pray, and to give thanks to God. Trust that he sustains your life, even when you stop working.
exp.38:19:
This verse describes another piece of the high priest's clothing. Two rings of gold were made and placed on the lower part of the shoulder straps of the ephod (a priestly garment), at the front, near the joining, just above the sash, which was the embroidered band of the same ephod. Their purpose was to secure the breastpiece (called the "breastplate" in this version).

It is part of the account of how Israel built the tabernacle and the priestly garments. The narrator repeats that everything was done as the LORD had commanded Moses. Here the emphasis is on careful obedience, down to the small details.

For today: God cares about what seems small. We can obey him faithfully in simple tasks without looking down on them. Also, the breastpiece bore the names of the tribes and was held securely; so we are reminded that God firmly holds his people.
exp.32:17:
Moses makes a request to God: "I beseech thee, shew me thy glory." The word "beseech" is an older way of saying "ask earnestly" or "beg." "Glory" refers to God's greatness and his presence, as he truly is.

Moses speaks. God has just promised him that he will keep accompanying Israel after the sin of the golden calf, and tells him that he knows him by name. Moses, encouraged by that closeness, wants more: to know God better. God answers that he will make all his goodness pass before Moses and will proclaim his name, but not his full face. Some understand this as the human limits before divine holiness.

Today we can desire to know God more, not only to receive his blessings. Ask him humbly to show you who he is through prayer and the reading of his Word, trusting that his goodness and mercy are enough for you.
exp.25:14:
God tells Moses to make boards of acacia wood for the tabernacle, standing upright, that is, set in an upright position. The acacia is a desert tree with strong, durable wood. These boards would form the walls or the framework of the sanctuary.

God speaks with Moses on Mount Sinai and gives him detailed instructions to build a place where He would dwell among Israel. Earlier He spoke of the curtains and the coverings; now He moves on to the framework that would hold everything together. The verses that follow give exact measurements, which shows that God cares about the details.

For today: God values what is firm and well made. Ask yourself what framework holds up your life of faith, such as prayer, the Word, and community, and take care to keep it straight and strong, so that God may be the center of everything.
exp.9:19:
After God removed the plague of locusts, this verse says, Pharaoh again refused to let the people go.

The narrator of the book speaks here. Moses had prayed, God responded by removing the locusts, and yet Pharaoh did not yield. In Exodus, it is sometimes said that Pharaoh hardened his own heart and at other times that God hardened it. Scholars explain this in several ways, but both ideas appear in the text.

For today: when God delivers us from a problem, let us not harden our hearts. Let us respond with gratitude and obedience, rather than returning to the same stubbornness as before.
exp.11:34:
The verse tells that the Israelites did what Moses had instructed them: they asked their Egyptian neighbors for articles of silver, articles of gold, and clothing. The word "asked" here means requesting, not demanding by force.

The people were leaving Egypt after the last plague. The Egyptians were afraid and wanted them to leave quickly. Earlier, God had told Moses that Israel would leave with goods (Exodus 3:21-22). The texts say that God gave them favor in the eyes of the Egyptians. Some understand the word as a loan, and others as a gift; the Hebrew word allows several translations.

For today: God keeps His promises, even when they seem impossible. We can obey step by step and trust that He provides what is needed for each stage of the journey.
exp.19:0:
God spoke and gave "all these words," that is, the Ten Commandments that come next. The name "Jehovah" is the traditional form of God's name as revealed to his people. The phrase "saying" signals that what follows is a direct message to be heard and obeyed.

Here God speaks to the people of Israel, who were camped near Mount Sinai shortly after leaving Egypt. Before giving the instructions, God presents himself as the one who rescued them from slavery. In this way, the commandments grow out of a relationship: God first sets free, and then teaches how to live in freedom.

For today: before you see the Bible as a list of rules, remember who is speaking. It is a God who rescues and cares. This week, read a passage with that attitude: listen with confidence, not fear.
exp.14:3:
It says that God cast Pharaoh's chariots and his army into the sea. The finest Egyptian officers, whom the text calls "chosen captains," sank in the Red Sea, which is the ancient name of the Red Sea. Some scholars debate the exact place of the crossing, but the text clearly says that God acted.

Moses speaks together with the people of Israel. They sing after crossing the sea, when God delivered them from slavery in Egypt and from an army that was pursuing them. It is a song of gratitude and praise, in which they acknowledge the LORD as their strength, their salvation, and their defender.

For today: when you face something that seems stronger than you, remember what God has done before for his people. Give thanks for the times he helped you and trust that he can sustain you again. Praising him out loud strengthens faith.
exp.26:10:
This verse describes the north side of the tabernacle courtyard. The word "north" is what this side is called here. Just like the south side, it would have hangings one hundred cubits long (about 45 meters, although the cubit is measured in several different ways), twenty pillars and twenty bases, that is, metal bases. The capitals (the tops of the pillars) and the fillets (the rings or rods that joined them together) were made of silver.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai and gives him instructions to build a place where he can dwell in the midst of Israel. The courtyard was the open area surrounding the tabernacle, and it marked the boundary between the camp and the sacred space.

For today: God cares about details and order as we draw near to him. We can prepare our hearts with respect and without haste, remembering that he invites us to come close, but with reverence and gratitude.
exp.38:7:
This verse tells how the craftsmen made the "racional," a special piece of the high priest's clothing. Today it is usually called the breastpiece or chest piece. It was made with the same fine workmanship as the ephod, another priestly garment, using threads of gold, blue (hyacinth), purple, scarlet, and linen twined together, that is, spun tightly.

It is part of the account of how the tabernacle was built and Aaron's clothing was made. The narrator repeats that everything was made just as God had commanded Moses. What follows explains that the breastpiece held twelve stones, which represented the tribes of Israel.

For today: God cares about details and values work done with care and obedience. We can offer our daily work, even when it seems small, with dedication and honesty, as something done for God and for the good of others.
exp.29:4:
God tells Moses to make the poles, that is, the long bars used to carry the altar of incense. They are to be made of shittim wood (today it is usually understood to be acacia) and overlaid with gold. They were put through the rings that had already been described.

God speaks, giving Moses the instructions for the tabernacle, the tent where Israel worshiped in the wilderness. This altar stood before the veil, near the ark, and there Aaron burned incense every morning. The poles made it possible to carry it without touching it, since it was a holy object and the people were always on the move.

Even small details matter to God when it comes to approaching him with respect. Today we can take care of our daily prayer: setting aside a moment each morning, with reverence and without rush, to speak with God.
exp.7:25:
Moses rejects the Pharaoh's offer to sacrifice within Egypt. The word "meet" in the verse means "fitting" or "wise." "Abomination of the Egyptians" refers to what the Egyptians regarded as detestable, probably the animals the Israelites would offer. Moses asks whether the Egyptians, seeing it, would not stone them.

Moses speaks to Pharaoh in the middle of the plague of flies. Pharaoh offers a half-way arrangement: worship God, but without leaving Egypt. Moses explains that their sacrifices would offend the Egyptians and bring violence. Scholars disagree about which animals are meant (perhaps sheep or oxen, tied to their religion), but the text does not make it clear. Moses insists on obeying as God commands.

For today: sometimes we are offered a faith that is "convenient," practiced without stepping outside what the world accepts. We can be wise and peaceable, but without bargaining away obedience to God for convenience.
exp.13:13:
It says that God himself will fight the battle for his people, and that they only need to stay calm. The word "fight" here is the same idea as "will fight," and "you" refers to the people being addressed. The phrase about staying still means to keep calm, without giving way to despair or acting out of fear.

Moses is the one speaking. The people of Israel had just left Egypt, but Pharaoh's army caught up with them by the sea. Frightened, they began to complain and even said it would be better to go back to being slaves. Moses asks them to trust. Note that "hold your peace" does not mean God asks nothing of them afterward, because right away he tells them to move forward.

For today: when you feel fear before a problem you cannot solve, do not let panic take over. Pray, trust God, and calm your heart. Then take the step he shows you, without doubting that he is with you.
exp.20:13:
This verse speaks of someone who kills another person on purpose, with pride, planning it and acting through deception. The phrase "come presumptuously" describes a person who becomes arrogant and bold in wrongdoing, and "with guile" means killing by treachery, with calculated malice. The law says that even the altar will not protect him: he is to be taken from there so that he may die.

God speaks to Moses and the people of Israel shortly after giving them the Ten Commandments. Earlier, a place of refuge was mentioned for the one who kills without intending to. Here the difference is made clear: the accident receives protection, but deliberate murder does not. The altar was a sacred place, and the law makes it plain that no one may use what is holy to hide his wickedness.

Today we can remember that God looks at the heart and the intentions. We must not use religion, or a good reputation, to cover what we do wrong. If there is pride or resentment in us, it is best to acknowledge it before God and set it right soon.
exp.21:26:
This verse explains why the poor man's cloak must be returned to him before nightfall. It was the only thing he had to cover himself and keep warm while he slept. The words "covering" and "raiment" speak of that garment, and "skin" refers to the body. God says that if the poor man cries out to him, he will hear him, because he is merciful.

God himself speaks to Israel through Moses, within the laws that shaped the people after they left Egypt. Earlier, the people were commanded not to charge the poor abusive interest. If someone took a poor man's cloak as security for a loan, he had to return it by evening. In this way the law protected the weakest.

For today: if you have power over someone in need, such as a debtor, an employee, or a neighbor, do not take away what is basic for living with dignity. Be just and compassionate, because God hears the cry of the needy.
exp.28:27:
This verse says that the breast and the thigh of the ram of consecration will be the fixed portion for Aaron and his sons, forever. It is called a "heave offering" because it was first lifted up or waved before God, and then it was given to the priests. A "statute for ever" means a law that remains in force permanently. The "peace offerings" were offerings of fellowship and thanksgiving.

God speaks to Moses at Sinai while explaining how to consecrate Aaron and his sons as priests. This portion was a way of providing for those who served in the tabernacle, and the people gave it as an offering to the Lord.

For today: God cares for those who serve his people, and we can do so with gratitude. Supporting your church, your teachers, and those who serve you spiritually with generosity is a way of honoring God.
exp.23:1:
It says that only Moses could come near to the Lord. The others, that is Aaron, his sons, the elders and the people, were to remain at a distance. "Shall come near" means "shall draw close," and "shall not come nigh" means "shall not draw close."

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai, just after giving him the laws of the covenant. Before the people answered with their commitment, God set out degrees of nearness: some went up to a certain point, and only Moses went closer, as mediator. This shows the holiness of God and the need for someone to represent the people before Him.

For today: draw near to God with reverence and gratitude. For Christians, Christ is the mediator who opens the way (Hebrews 4:16), so we can pray with confidence without losing reverence.
exp.32:13:
God answers Moses: "My presence shall go with you, and I will give you rest." The "presence" of God means his very presence, his personal nearness. And "rest" means giving him calm, peace, and relief in the midst of the task. It is a promise: God will not send him alone.

Here God is speaking, answering Moses. After the sin of the golden calf, Moses fears leading the people without God's company. He asks to know God's way and reminds God that Israel is God's people. This promise calms his concern, although Moses later insists that he does not want to move forward without God's presence.

For today: when you feel the weight of a responsibility or a difficult decision, do not look only for solutions. Ask God for his company and trust that he walks with you. His presence gives rest to the heart, even before everything is resolved.
exp.4:20:
The Israelite foremen say to Moses and Aaron that God should look upon them and judge them. They blame them for having made their smell "stink," that is, for having made them hateful in the eyes of Pharaoh and his servants. It is as if they had put a sword in Pharaoh's hand to kill them.

These were Hebrew foremen, who were responsible for making sure their people met the quota of bricks. After Moses asked Pharaoh to free the people, Pharaoh increased the burden, and the foremen suffered the consequences. They are frightened and hurt, and they vent their frustration on Moses. He, in turn, will bring their complaint to God.

When things get worse after we obey God, it is easy to blame others. Instead, we can do as Moses did: bring our honest complaint to God and wait on Him.
exp.34:13:
This verse lists part of the furnishings of the tabernacle: the lampstand that gave light, its equipment, its small lamps, and the oil that kept them burning. The word rendered "lamps" refers to the light itself, and the "vessels" are the tools or fittings that belong to the lampstand.

Moses speaks to all of Israel after coming down from Sinai. He repeats what God commanded for building the sanctuary and invites the people to take part with their gifts and skills. The list includes the ark, the table, and the altars, so that the people would know what was to be made. Some scholars see in the lampstand a symbol of God's guiding presence; the text, however, presents only its practical function.

For today: God cares even for small details, such as the oil in a lamp. Serve God faithfully in the ordinary things, and keep your life of prayer and faith burning.
exp.11:33:
They took their dough before it had risen with yeast. They wrapped it in their blankets or bedclothes (the "sheets" of that time were large pieces of cloth) and carried it on their shoulders. They left in such a hurry that there was no time to let the bread rise.

The narrator tells what happened after the tenth plague, the death of the firstborn. Pharaoh had let the people go, and the Egyptians were urging them to leave, out of fear of dying. That is why Israel departed in great haste. Later on, the Feast of Unleavened Bread would commemorate this moment.

For today: when God opens a door, it is wise to respond with confidence and obedience, without delay. Leaving what enslaves us may call for quick decisions, taking what is essential and trusting that God will look after the way ahead.
exp.23:16:
This verse says that the glory of God looked like a consuming fire on the top of Mount Sinai. All the people of Israel could see it. The word "appearance" is used here for how it looked, and "devouring" means that it burns and consumes. "Lord" is the name of God.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, telling what happened after God gave the law and the people promised to obey. Moses went up to receive further instructions. A cloud covered the mountain, and God showed his presence in a visible, powerful way, full of holiness. Afterward Moses entered the cloud and stayed there forty days.

For today: God is loving, but he is also holy, and he deserves respect. Today we can draw near to him with reverence and confidence, setting aside a moment each day to listen to him with humility.
exp.24:7:
It says that God asks Israel to build him a sanctuary, that is, a holy and set-apart place. The promise is that God himself will dwell "among them," not merely near them or far away. The word "dwell" means that God wants to be present in the midst of his people.

God speaks and gives these instructions to Moses on Mount Sinai. The Israelites had just left Egypt, and God was giving them directions for the tabernacle, a kind of holy tent. The materials mentioned earlier, such as the oil and the stones, would be part of that place and of the priest's clothing.

For today: God still desires closeness with his people. We can set aside a moment each day to pray and read the Bible, remembering that God wants to be present in our life and in our community, not only in a building.
exp.0:9:
The explanation says that the king of Egypt proposes to act with "wisdom," that is, with cunning, against the Israelites. He fears that they will keep growing in number and that, if a war breaks out, they will join Egypt's enemies, fight against them, and leave the country.

The phrase "if it come to pass that there fall out any war" means "if it should happen that a war comes."

The speaker is the new pharaoh, who "knew not Joseph," meaning he did not value what Joseph had done for Egypt. He is addressing his people. His motive is fear of losing power and security. Scholars do not agree on which pharaoh this was, so we cannot point to a name with certainty.

For today: fear, when it is not surrendered to God, can lead us to mistreat others. Before reacting against someone out of fear, stop, pray, and ask whether you are acting with justice and compassion.
exp.17:0:
This verse says that Jethro, Moses' father-in-law, heard about everything God had done for Moses and for the people of Israel. He learned that the Lord had brought Israel out of Egypt. The word "heard" here means that the news reached him. Jethro was a priest of Midian, the land where Moses lived before he returned to Egypt.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. He presents Jethro as someone who receives the report of Israel's deliverance. What follows shows that he travels to visit Moses, bringing with him Zipporah, Moses' wife, and their two sons. The text does not say everything Jethro was thinking when he heard this, but his visit shows interest.

For today: when we hear what God has done in the lives of others, let us not receive it with indifference. Let those testimonies encourage us to trust God and to draw near to Him.
exp.25:16:
It says that each board of the tabernacle was to have two tenons, that is, two pegs or projections at the bottom. These fit into the silver bases. The boards were to be set in order, fitted one against another. This was done for all the boards.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai and gives him detailed instructions for building a place where he would dwell among Israel. The boards formed the walls of that holy tent. The details about how to join them show that the work was to be firm and orderly, just as God directed.

For today: God cares about details and about unity. Just as the boards were held together, we strengthen the life of the church when we stay firm, well connected to one another, and faithfully doing our part, even when it seems small.
exp.39:32:
This verse describes the final step in building the tabernacle. Moses set up the court, that is, the enclosure with fabric walls that surrounded the sacred tent and the altar. He also hung the curtain at the entrance of the court. The words "round about" are used in the verse, and "finished" means that he completed the work.

Here the narrator of the book, traditionally understood to be Moses himself, speaks. The people of Israel had received detailed instructions from God for building a place where He would dwell among them. Each piece was made just as the Lord had commanded. Once the work was finished, God fills the tabernacle with His glory.

For today: Moses obeyed to the last detail, leaving nothing unfinished. We can ask God to help us faithfully complete what He entrusts to us, even the small and less visible tasks, trusting that He is the one who gives the fruit.
exp.27:1:
God tells Moses to make special clothing for his brother Aaron, the priest. The words "honor and beauty" mean that these garments were to show respect and loveliness, because Aaron would serve in something holy. "Holy" means set apart for God.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai while giving him instructions about the tabernacle. He has just chosen Aaron and his sons as priests. He then specifies that skilled craftsmen, gifted by God, would make the clothing. Scholars understand the symbolism of each garment in different ways, but the text emphasizes that they served to consecrate the priests.

For today: to approach God with reverence and care, without carelessness. Today what matters most is a sincere, humble, and grateful heart, and we can also honor him with the best of our work and our time.
exp.27:35:
God tells Moses to make a plate of pure gold for the high priest. On it was to be engraved, the way a seal is cut, the words "HOLINESS TO THE LORD." The phrase about the engraving refers to a fine carving, like the carving on a ring used to seal a document. "Holiness" means being set apart for God.

God speaks with Moses on the mountain and gives him instructions about the clothing of Aaron, the first high priest. This plate was worn on the turban, on the forehead, where everyone could see it. According to the verses that follow, Aaron bore the guilt of Israel's offerings, so that the people would be accepted before God.

God wants what we are and what we do to belong to him. Today we can ask ourselves: do my work, my words, and my thoughts show that I live for God? Ask him for help to live that way today.
exp.6:13:
The explanation says God speaks to Moses and explains how Pharaoh is on the inside. "Hardened" is an old word meaning heavy, hard, stubborn. Pharaoh has a closed heart, and that is why he does not want to let the people of Israel leave Egypt.

The Lord speaks, and he speaks to Moses after Aaron's staff swallowed the staffs of the Egyptian magicians. Even seeing that sign, Pharaoh did not yield. God tells Moses what is coming and prepares him to present himself again before Pharaoh with a new message, the beginning of the plagues.

For today: when someone resists change, and also when we do, it is good to ask God for a humble heart. A person can see many signs and still not yield because of pride. Today we can listen to God with simplicity.
exp.24:5:
It says the people were to bring oil for the lamps of the sanctuary, and spices for preparing the anointing oil and the fragrant incense. The word "lamps" refers to the lampstand, the light that gave light. The word "incense" is the sweet smoke burned to give a pleasant fragrance.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai. He had just freed Israel from Egypt, and he asked for a freewill offering to build a sanctuary. This list of materials shows that the whole people could take part. The purpose, according to verse 8, was that God would dwell among them.

For today: God values what we give from the heart, even what is small and everyday, like oil or spices. Think about what resource, time, or skill you can offer joyfully to serve your community of faith.
exp.20:29:
This verse says that if the owner of a dangerous ox is asked for a ransom for the life of the person who died, he must pay whatever is laid upon him. A ransom is a payment to save his life. The phrase "his own person" means his own life. So the careless owner would not die if the payment was accepted.

God gives these laws to Israel through Moses, after the Ten Commandments. It deals with the case of an ox that had already gored before, and its owner was warned and did not keep it under control. That carelessness was serious. The law shows that human life is very valuable. Scholars do not agree on who set the ransom; the text does not make it clear.

For today: if what I have or do can harm others, I must take care of it with responsibility. When someone warns me of a danger, I must act in time and not ignore it.
exp.22:32:
This verse says that the peoples of Canaan were not to remain living in the land of Israel. The reason was that they could cause Israel to sin, leading them to serve their gods.

God speaks to Israel through Moses, after giving them the laws at Sinai. He promises them the land and warns them not to make alliances with those peoples or with their gods. His concern was that Israel remain faithful to Him. How and when this was fulfilled is a matter of debate, since history shows that Israel lived alongside some of those peoples.

For today: this is not about rejecting people, but about guarding against what can pull us away from God. Think about which influences, habits, or friendships weaken your faith, and set wise limits with God's help.
exp.35:16:
The explanation says that Bezalel and the craftsmen made fifty loops, that is, small eyelets or fasteners, along the edge of the last curtain in each set. One set had five curtains joined together and the other had six. The loops on one side faced the loops on the other, at the seam, the place where the two sets came together. Afterward, clasps, which were hooks, would be used to join them.

This is part of the account of building the tabernacle, the tent of meeting. The narrator, traditionally Moses, tells how the people obeyed in every detail what God had commanded on the mountain. This section repeats the instructions of Exodus 26, but now they have become reality.

For today: God values faithfulness in small things. Hardly anyone saw those loops, but they were necessary so that everything would be one. Let us do with care and honesty the simple tasks entrusted to us, even when no one notices.
exp.7:29:
Moses left the presence of the king of Egypt and began to pray to God. Few of the words here are old: the phrase "went out from Pharaoh" simply means leaving Pharaoh where he stood, and the name of God is the Lord.

Pharaoh had just asked Moses to pray that God would take away the plague of flies, and he promised to let the people go. Moses agreed to pray, but he warned Pharaoh not to deceive him again. After Moses prayed, God removed the flies, but Pharaoh hardened his heart once more and did not keep his word.

For today: Moses prayed for someone who had mistreated him and who had already broken his word before. We can learn to pray even for those who are not sincere with us, trusting that God sees each person's heart and knows what to do.
exp.35:35:
This verse describes the four pillars that held up the veil of the tabernacle. They were made of acacia wood, covered in gold. Their tops, that is, the upper parts, were also gold. They rested on four bases, or sockets, of cast silver.

The passage is a narrative, not a speech. It tells how Bezalel and the craftsmen built the tabernacle by following the instructions God gave to Moses. That veil separated the holy place from the most holy place, where the ark was kept. The passage stresses that everything was made according to the pattern God showed.

For today: God cares about the details and values faithful obedience, even in tasks that seem small or hidden. We can serve Him with care in everyday life, trusting that what we do for Him has value.
exp.37:24:
This verse says that the silver collected from the men counted in the census of the people was one hundred talents and one thousand seven hundred and seventy-five shekels, measured by the shekel of the sanctuary, which was the official standard weight. The phrase "that were numbered" means those who were registered in Israel's census.

Moses and the people in charge of the work are giving an account of the materials used to build the tabernacle. This silver came from the half-shekel ransom that each man twenty years old and above paid. According to the verses that follow, it was used to make the bases of the sanctuary and of the veil. The text pays close attention to the details.

For today: God values honesty and order in handling what is offered for his work. If you take part in your church or in some ministry, try to be open about money and thankful for each person's offering, since everyone contributes.
exp.3:27:
Moses tells his brother Aaron all that God had said to him and had commanded him to do. He also shows him the miraculous signs that God had given him. "The Lord" is the name of God, and the "signs" are the miracles Moses would perform as proof.

God had sent Aaron to meet Moses in the wilderness. They meet at the mountain of God, probably Sinai or Horeb. Moses was nervous about speaking, and God had said that Aaron would be his spokesman. That is why Moses explains everything to him, so that the two of them would go together before Israel and the people would believe.

When God gives us a task, he often also places other people beside us. Today we can honestly share with a trusted person of faith what God has shown us, and accept their help in serving together.
exp.19:16:
It says we should not covet anything that belongs to our neighbor: his house, his wife, his workers, his animals, or anything else. "Covet" means to desire strongly and with envy what belongs to someone else. The people who worked in the home were the men and women servants. The "ass" is the donkey.

God himself speaks to Israel on Mount Sinai, after bringing them out of Egypt. This is the last of the ten commandments. Unlike the earlier ones, it reaches the heart, not only the actions. Afterward, the people tremble before the smoke, the fire, and the sound of the trumpet, and they ask Moses to speak for them.

For today: when you feel envy for what another person has, thank God for something specific he has given you, and bless that person with a sincere prayer.
exp.35:1:
It says that Moses called Bezaleel, Aholiab, and all the skilled men to whom God had given wisdom. He also called those whose hearts stirred them to come forward and help with the work. The phrase "wise hearted" means a person with practical skill and a willing spirit. The phrase "come unto the work" means to come forward to take part in it.

The narrator describes how the construction of the tabernacle, the tent where Israel would worship God, began. Moses organizes the workers, and the text shows that their abilities came from God. Both those who had talent and those who felt the urge to contribute took part. Afterward, the people continue bringing freewill offerings.

Today we can see that our abilities are a gift from God. If you feel the desire to serve in your church or community, do not ignore it. Offer what you know how to do with humility and joy.
exp.34:18:
These are the special garments that Aaron and his sons would wear when they served as priests in the sanctuary. They are part of a list of things the people were to make for the tabernacle.

Moses speaks to the whole congregation of Israel and repeats what God had commanded him. He wants every person to know what is needed to build the place where God would dwell among them. The verses that follow show that the people responded with generosity, bringing offerings given willingly.

Today we can learn that God cares about the details of our service, but above all about a willing heart. Everyone can contribute something, great or small, joyfully: time, talents, or resources. Serve God with what you have, and do it from the heart.
exp.25:35:
God tells Moses to make a curtain for the entrance of the tabernacle. It was to be made of blue, purple, scarlet (a deep red), and fine twined linen (strong, fine thread), with embroidery, that is, with figures or designs worked by hand.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai, giving him instructions for building a place where He would dwell with Israel. This curtain was the entrance to the tabernacle, separate from the inner veil that divided the Most Holy Place. Many see in it a sign that drawing near to God has an order and a way. Others interpret its colors in symbolic ways, but the text does not explain them.

Today, God still cares about how we draw near to Him. For Christians, Jesus is that way. We can approach with gratitude and reverence, knowing that the door is open.
exp.25:30:
God tells Moses to make a special curtain for the tabernacle. It was to be made of blue thread, purple, and bright red, together with fine twined linen. It would be made with skilled craftsmanship, meaning very fine and carefully done work, with cherubim embroidered on it, which are heavenly beings.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai as He gives the design of His dwelling among the people. This veil was to separate the holy place from the most holy place, where the ark would be. It showed that God is holy and that approaching Him had an order. Christians often see here a sign pointing to Christ, since the veil of the temple was torn when Jesus died (Matthew 27:51).

Today we can draw near to God with reverence and confidence, grateful that Jesus opened the way.
exp.29:5:
God tells Moses where to place the altar of incense: in front of the curtain (the veil) that separated the Holy Place from the Most Holy Place, near the ark of the testimony. The sentence explaining the lid of the ark, called the mercy seat, is set aside here because that term is not in the verse above. The phrase about testifying of me means that God would make himself known there.

God speaks to Moses at Sinai, giving him instructions for the tabernacle. The altar of incense stood very close to where God revealed his presence. The text then explains that Aaron would burn incense every morning and every evening. Many understand the incense as a picture of prayer, although the text does not say this directly here.

For today: God wants to meet with us, and daily prayer is a good place for that meeting. You might set aside a moment each morning and each night to speak with God and to listen to him, with simplicity and steadiness.
exp.17:15:
Moses explains that when people have a conflict or an unresolved matter, they come to him. He decides between the two parties and teaches them what God commands. Here "matters" means issues or disputes, not business. "Ordinances" are God's commands, and "laws" are his instructions.

Moses is speaking in answer to Jethro, his father-in-law. Jethro saw him handling the people alone, from morning until evening, and asked him why he did it. Moses believes he is serving the people and God, but Jethro will warn him that this pace will wear him out, and the people too.

For today: serving with good intentions does not mean carrying everything alone. If you are carrying too much, ask for help and share responsibilities. That cares for your health and also for those you serve.
exp.25:34:
God tells Moses where to place the furniture of the tabernacle. The table and the lampstand go in the holy place, outside the veil that hides the ark. The lampstand is on the south side, opposite the table, and the table is on the north side.

God speaks to Moses at Sinai, giving him instructions to build a place where he can dwell among Israel. The veil separated the holy place from the most holy place, where the ark was. Every detail showed that drawing near to God called for order and reverence.

For today: God cares about what is orderly and what is everyday. We can give a fixed place to prayer and to the Bible in our week, so that our time with him is not left to chance.
exp.5:29:
Moses tells God that he is "uncircumcised in lips." This was an old way of saying that he did not speak well or that he felt clumsy in expressing himself. That is why he asks how Pharaoh will hear him, since he does not even feel able to speak to him. "Hearken" means to listen, and "the Lord" is the name of God.

Moses speaks with God after Pharaoh rejected the first request to free the people. God had just commanded him to repeat before the king everything that God would tell him. Moses had already voiced this same doubt before, in Exodus 6:12. Here he repeats it, and the Bible does not explain in detail what his difficulty was.

For today: when God calls you to something and you feel little capable, bring Him your fears with sincerity, as Moses did. God does not expect you to be perfect, but to obey Him and trust that He sustains you.
exp.29:16:
This verse is a transition phrase. It says that the Lord spoke again to Moses. The words "spake more" mean "kept speaking" or "spoke again." After giving instructions about the money of atonement, God is about to give a new instruction.

Here God is speaking, and Moses is the one who receives the message for the people. We are in the instructions for the tabernacle, the tent where God dwelt among Israel. What comes next is the bronze laver, where the priests Aaron and his sons would wash their hands and feet before serving. This is understood to point to the importance of approaching God with respect and cleanliness.

For today: God still speaks and cares about the details of how we come near to Him. We can take a moment before prayer or Bible reading to pause, ask forgiveness, and prepare our hearts to listen.
exp.17:8:
Jethro was filled with joy as he heard about all the good things God had done for Israel. The verse says he rejoiced over the goodness the Lord had shown to Israel, the people He had rescued from the hand of the Egyptians.

The narrator tells us that Jethro, Moses' father-in-law and a priest of Midian, came to Israel's camp in the wilderness. Moses welcomed him with respect and told him how God had brought them out of Egypt and cared for them along the way. Jethro responds with gladness, and soon he blesses God and acknowledges that He is greater than all the gods.

When someone tells us about the good that God has done, we can truly rejoice, even if it did not happen to us. Today we can simply tell what God has done in our lives, and also celebrate from the heart what He is doing in the lives of others.
exp.6:14:
God tells Moses to go early to meet Pharaoh. He says that Pharaoh goes out "to the waters," that is, toward the Nile River. Moses is to wait for him on the riverbank and take in his hand the staff that had turned into a snake.

The LORD speaks to Moses. Pharaoh had already hardened his heart and did not want to let the people of Israel go. So God sends Moses again, this time with a warning: the water of the river would be turned into blood. Many believe that Pharaoh went out to the Nile for some religious reason or out of routine, but the text does not make this clear.

God does not lose heart in the face of a hardened heart. He invites us to obey faithfully, even when others do not listen. Our task is to go and speak the truth; the results are in God's hands.
exp.27:27:
This verse explains how the breastplate, a kind of pouch or chest piece set with twelve stones, was to be fastened to the ephod, the special garment worn by the high priest. The gold rings of each were tied together with a cord of blue, so that the breastplate would stay firmly above the ephod's belt and would not come loose.

God speaks to Moses at Sinai and gives instructions for Aaron's garments. What follows makes the purpose clear: Aaron would carry the names of the tribes of Israel over his heart when he entered before God. The detail that it must not come loose shows that this act of representing the people was to be constant and secure.

For today: God does not forget his people, and Christians see in Jesus the priest who carries us with love and firmness. We can pray with confidence, and we can also carry others in our hearts when we pray for them.
exp.29:24:
God tells Moses to mix spices and olive oil to make a special oil. It will be holy, meaning set apart only for God. The mixture is a blend made with fragrant ingredients, and it must be prepared with the skill of an expert in perfumes.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai while giving him instructions for the tabernacle. This oil would be used to anoint, or set apart, the tent, its furnishings, and later the priests. It showed that these objects and people belonged to God and were not for ordinary use.

For today: God values what is dedicated to Him with care and reverence. We can ask ourselves what part of our time, work, or talents we can set apart on purpose to serve Him, rather than giving Him only what is left over.
exp.25:11:
This verse says that the curtains of the tent were longer than needed to cover the tabernacle. The half curtain that was left over was to hang over the back part. "Tabernacle" is the structure of boards and curtains, and "over the back" refers to the rear side, on the west.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai and gives him exact instructions for building a place to dwell among Israel. The curtains of the tent were joined with loops and clasps to form a single covering. The details about the leftover part are best understood by seeing that they covered the tabernacle completely. Some think it also had a symbolic meaning, but the text does not explain this.

For today: God cares about details and does not do things halfway. We can serve him with order and care, even in small tasks that no one sees, trusting that he values them.
exp.29:37:
It says that no one was to make a perfume like the sacred incense in order to enjoy its scent. Making a mixture like it means preparing the same blend. Enjoying its smell means taking pleasure in its fragrance. "Shall even be cut off from his people" means he would be separated from the community of Israel; scholars debate whether that meant death, banishment, or exclusion by God himself.

God speaks to Moses while giving him instructions for the tabernacle. That special incense, with its exact recipe, was reserved for worship of the LORD. Copying it for personal use was treating what is holy as something common, and that is why it was forbidden.

For today: let us learn not to use for our own pleasure or display what belongs to God, such as prayer, praise, or the gifts he gives us. We can examine whether, when we serve, we seek to honor him or only to feel good ourselves.
exp.29:34:
It says that Moses was to prepare a special incense, made the way an expert perfumer would make it. "Aromatic confection" is a mixture of perfumes. "Well mixed" means that the ingredients were very well combined. "Pure and holy" indicates that it had no improper mixtures and that it was set apart for God.

God speaks to Moses as He gives him instructions for the tabernacle. This incense was burned in the place of worship, and God asked that it not be used for common purposes or copied for personal use. This taught Israel that God is holy and that He must be approached with respect.

For today: when we pray or worship, let us do so with sincerity and reverence, without treating God as something common. We can set aside a moment of the day to be with Him with a clean and attentive heart.
exp.33:11:
The explanation says that Israel had to be careful not to make agreements with the peoples who lived in the land they were about to enter. A covenant is a pact or friendly deal. A snare is something that makes a person fall, like a stone on the road. Being in the midst of them means that this danger would be very close to them.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai, when he renews his covenant with Israel after the sin of the golden calf. He promises them his mighty help and orders them not to make deals with those peoples. The verses that follow explain the reason: those nations had altars to other gods, and God wanted his people to be faithful to him alone.

For today: be careful with friendships, partners, and habits that slowly pull you away from God. This is not about looking down on people, but about being wise and not giving in on what matters most for your faith.
exp.23:7:
Moses takes the blood of the sacrificed animals, sprinkles it on the people, and declares that this blood seals the covenant that God made with them. A covenant means a formal promise between two parties. To sprinkle means to splash or scatter the blood over them.

Moses speaks after reading the book of the covenant, that is, the laws God had given. The people answered that they would do everything and obey. With the blood, the agreement is confirmed in a solemn way. Scholars explain the exact meaning of the rite in several ways, but all agree that it showed the seriousness of the commitment. Then the leaders go up and see God.

For today: God invites us into a relationship, not only into rules. Christians see in Jesus the blood of a new covenant. Today you can respond to him with gratitude, taking seriously your promises to follow and obey him.
exp.31:2:
It says that all the people took off the gold earrings that were in their ears and brought them to Aaron. Earrings are the rings worn in the ears. Everyone went along with Aaron's request.

Moses had been on Mount Sinai with God for a long time, and the people grew impatient. They asked Aaron for a visible god who would lead them. Aaron himself asked them for the gold, and with it the calf was made. There are different opinions about whether he did it out of fear or weakness, but the text shows that the people did take part eagerly.

When God seems slow, it is easy to look for quick solutions and to give to other things what belongs to Him. Today we can ask ourselves where we place our time, money and effort, and ask God for patience to wait for Him.
exp.5:14:
This verse lists the sons of Simeon, the second son of Jacob: Jemuel, Jamin, Ohad, Jachin, Zohar, and Shaul. It notes that Shaul was the son of a Canaanite woman, that is, a woman from the people who lived in Canaan before Israel. Each name stands for a family within the tribe of Simeon.

The one telling the story is the author of the book, traditionally understood to be Moses. After God gives Moses and Aaron the task of bringing the people out of Egypt, the account pauses to present their family origins. In this way it shows what lineage the leaders and the people God was going to rescue came from. Reuben is mentioned first, then Simeon, and then Levi, the family of Moses.

For today: God does not forget anyone, not even those who have a different or unusual background. He knows your name and your story, and he includes you in his plan.
exp.38:24:
They made bells of pure gold and placed them on the lower edge of the priest's robe, alternating them with the cloth pomegranates they had already made. The robe is the blue tunic the high priest wore beneath the ephod.

This is part of the account of how Aaron's garments, the garments of the high priest, were made. The text says that everything was done just as the LORD commanded Moses. Moses does not invent the design; Israel obeys it. Exodus 28:35 says the sound of the bells was heard when Aaron went in and out of the holy place. Some think this showed that he was still alive and serving, but the text does not fully explain it.

For today: God cares about the details of our service. Let us do even the small and little-seen things faithfully and carefully, since they are done for Him.
exp.30:15:
God tells the children of Israel that they must keep the sabbath, that is, rest and set that day apart for Him. They must do this from generation to generation, as a perpetual covenant, meaning a commitment that lasts forever. Here the word "generations" is the meaning of the old term used in the text.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai, after giving him instructions for building the tabernacle. He reminds the Israelites that the sabbath is a sign of His covenant with them, and He ties it to God's own rest after creating the world. Shortly afterward He gives Moses the two tablets of stone.

For today: Christians understand in different ways how the sabbath applies to them. Whatever your position, you can practice the principle of setting aside regular time to rest, trusting that God sustains your life, and devoting time to Him, without living enslaved to work.
exp.2:15:
God commands Moses to gather the leaders of the people, the elders of Israel. He is to tell them that the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob appeared to him. The word "visited" here does not mean a simple visit: it means God draws near to act. And the phrase "seen that which is done to you" means that He has seen the mistreatment they suffer in Egypt.

God speaks from the burning bush. Israel had been enslaved for a long time, and Moses had to earn the trust of his people. That is why God asks him to begin with the elders and to remind them that He is the same God of their ancestors, faithful to His promises.

Today we can remember that God sees what we suffer, even when He seems silent. You can pray with confidence, telling Him what weighs on you, and expect that He will act in His own time.
exp.6:5:
This verse says that Moses and Aaron obeyed God in everything he commanded them. [Rewritten for a verse word: the verse itself says "so did they," which is the same idea, and the explanation's point is that they did exactly as told.]

The context is that God had just told them that Pharaoh would not listen to them. Moses and Aaron knew it would be difficult, but they obeyed. The text adds that they were eighty and eighty-three years old, which means they were already elderly when they began this task.

For today: sometimes obeying God does not seem to bring immediate results, or people do not pay attention to us. Even so, we can take the next step with confidence, because the outcome belongs to God, and our part is to be faithful.
exp.21:8:
This verse describes cases of fraud or dispute over ownership: an animal, a garment, or anything lost, when two people each say "this is mine." Both parties were to come before the judges. The one the judges found guilty had to pay back twice as much to his neighbor.

God gave these laws to Israel through Moses, shortly after the Ten Commandments. They were rules for the daily life of a people newly freed. They aimed to protect property and secure justice, so that no one settled conflicts on their own. Some of the exact legal details are interpreted in different ways.

For today: when there is a conflict over money or goods, let us seek the truth honestly and turn to a fair way of resolving it. And if we have taken something that is not ours, the right thing is to acknowledge it and make amends for the harm.
exp.5:24:
Eleazar, the son of Aaron, married one of the daughters of Putiel, and she bore him a son named Phinehas. The text then sums up that these are the leaders of the families of the Levites, according to their clans.

The one telling the story is the author of the book, who pauses the account of Moses before Pharaoh to present a family record. This shows which Levite family Moses and Aaron came from, and why they would be leaders. Phinehas will appear later as a priest, but this verse only mentions his birth.

For today: God cares for people by name and by family, and works through generations. Today you can thank those who taught you to trust God, and ask yourself how you can pass that faith on to those who come after you.
exp.5:28:
This verse says that God spoke to Moses and introduced himself by his name: "I am the Lord." Then he gave him a clear command: to tell Pharaoh, king of Egypt, all that God would tell him.

God is the one speaking. Moses and Aaron had already gone before Pharaoh, but he rejected them and made the work of the Israelites harder. So God repeats his name and his charge, to remind Moses who is sending him. In the next verse, Moses feels unsure and says that he has uncircumcised lips, an expression usually understood to mean clumsiness or difficulty in speaking.

For today: when you feel small or afraid to speak about what God has placed on your heart, remember that your confidence is not in your abilities but in the One who sends you. Be faithful and pass on what God says, without adding or taking away.
exp.39:25:
This verse tells us that Moses placed the golden altar inside the tent of meeting, right in front of the curtain. The words "tent of meeting" refer to the sacred tent where the tablets of the law were kept. The curtain was the thick cloth that separated the holy place from the most holy place, where the ark was.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, and describes how Moses, when the work was finished, put each piece of furniture in its place. It is repeated that he did this "as the LORD had commanded." Incense was burned on this altar, a special fragrance that rose before God. Many see it as a picture of prayer.

For today: God values obedience in small and orderly things. You can set aside a fixed moment each day to pray, like that incense that rose continually before Him.
exp.33:25:
It says that the Israelites were to bring to the house of God the first and best of each year's harvest. It also forbids boiling a young goat in its mother's milk. "Firstfruits" means the first things the land yields, and "young goat" refers to a kid of the goat.

God speaks with Moses on Mount Sinai, when he renews his covenant with Israel after the sin of the golden calf. These are rules for the feasts and for worship. The prohibition against the kid is interpreted in several ways: some think it opposed a pagan rite, others that it teaches compassion and respect for life. It is not known with certainty.

For today: before you spend or give away what you receive, set aside something first for God, whether time, money, or service. Do it with gratitude, recognizing that everything comes from Him.
exp.28:6:
This verse says that Moses was to take the special anointing oil and pour it on Aaron's head to set him apart as a priest. "Anoint" means to put oil on someone as a sign that God sets them apart for sacred service.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai and gives him instructions for consecrating Aaron and his sons. First they dressed him in the priestly garments, and then came the anointing. The oil showed that the priest had not chosen himself, but that God was calling him. Many Christians see here a shadow of Christ, whose title means "the Anointed One," although the text does not say this directly.

For today: God calls and equips those who serve. Before asking whether we are enough, we can ask him to use us and depend on his help.
exp.37:26:
It says that of the silver that was gathered, one hundred talents were used to cast the sockets, that is, the bases or pedestals on which the boards of the sanctuary and the pillars of the veil rested. There were one hundred sockets, and each one weighed a talent. A talent was a very large unit of weight; its exact equivalent in kilograms is debated, but it was a great deal of weight. The word "cast" means metal melted down and poured into a mold.

Here the narrator of the book, going through the details of how the offerings were used to build the tabernacle, is speaking. That silver came from the half-shekel that each man counted, from twenty years old and upward, contributed. In this way everyone took part equally, rich and poor alike, in what upheld the house of God.

For today: God values what holds things up, even when it is not seen. The sockets stood low, nearly hidden, yet everything depended on them. Serve faithfully in what is small and hidden; in the kingdom of God, that too is foundational.
exp.2:21:
It says that every Israelite woman will ask her Egyptian neighbor, and the foreign woman who lives in her house, for objects of silver and gold and clothing. With these they will dress their sons and daughters. The word "ask" here means to request, "guest" refers to a woman who lives temporarily in the house, and "plunder" is understood here as carrying off the wealth of Egypt.

God speaks to Moses from the burning bush. He announces that he will free Israel from slavery. After years of forced labor without pay, God promises that they will not leave empty-handed. He will make the Egyptians look on them with goodwill. Some understand this as compensation for their labor; others emphasize God's action in changing hearts.

For today: God cares for us even in the details. We can trust that he provides, and receive with gratitude, without pride or abuse.
exp.14:2:
The explanation says that the Lord is "a man of war," meaning a warrior who fights and wins. It does not mean that God is violent by nature, but that he acts with power against the evil that oppresses his people. It then adds "the Lord is his name," which reminds us that this God has a distinct identity, is faithful, and is not like false gods.

Moses speaks together with the Israelites, who sing after crossing the sea. The Egyptians, who were coming after them, were covered by the waters. The Israelites see that they did not win by their own strength, but because God fought for them. Their song is praise and gratitude for their deliverance.

For today: when you face something that is bigger than you, do not trust only in your own strength. Bring it to God in prayer, and when he helps you, do not stay silent: give him thanks and tell what he has done.
exp.5:2:
God tells Moses that he appeared to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob as "God Almighty," but that he did not make himself known to them by the name "Jehovah." The words "I appeared" mean "I showed myself," and "I did not make myself known" means "I did not reveal myself."

God speaks in the middle of Israel's slavery in Egypt. Moses is discouraged, and God reminds him who he is and that he will keep his promise. Scholars debate the exact meaning: some think it refers to a deeper revelation of the meaning of the name, since the name already appears in Genesis.

Today we can learn that God reveals himself little by little and is always faithful to his word. When your situation seems to have no way out, remember his promises and trust that he knows your cry and remembers you.
exp.27:6:
The explanation says that the ephod, the special garment of the high priest, would have two shoulderpieces, that is, two straps that covered the shoulders. These pieces were joined at their two edges, that is, at the front and at the back, so that the garment would be firm and form a single piece. The phrase quoted above means that they were joined at the ends.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai and gives instructions for the clothing of Aaron and his sons, who would serve as priests. On the shoulderpieces two stones would later be placed with the names of the tribes of Israel, so the priest would symbolically carry the people on his shoulders.

Today we can learn that God cares about unity and about bearing one another's burdens. Ask yourself whom you can lift up in prayer or help this week.
exp.25:6:
God tells Moses to make eleven curtains of goats' hair to form a covering over the tabernacle. The tabernacle here refers to the sacred tent, with its fine linen curtains that had already been described. These goats' hair curtains were to go on top, as a second, protective layer.

God speaks to Moses at Mount Sinai, shortly after rescuing Israel from Egypt. He gives detailed instructions for building a place where his presence would dwell among the people. The goats' hair curtains were a simple and durable material. Some scholars think they protected the more delicate curtains beneath, although the text does not explain this in detail.

For today: God values the beautiful and the simple and durable alike. There are unglamorous tasks, such as caring for, protecting, and serving quietly, that hold up what others see. Today you can do a humble task with care, knowing that God appreciates it.
exp.10:4:
It says that God will bring death to every firstborn son in Egypt, from the firstborn of the king, who rules seated on his throne, down to the firstborn of the maidservant who is behind the mill. It also says that the firstborn males of the animals will die.

Moses speaks here, repeating what the LORD told him, before Pharaoh. This is the announcement of the tenth plague. Pharaoh had hardened his heart again and again and refused to let Israel go, though they lived as slaves. The text presents this as God's judgment on Egypt, and also as the final step toward the people's freedom.

For today: God takes seriously the injustice and suffering of the oppressed. When He asks something of us, it is wise not to harden our hearts. We can trust that God hears the cry of those who suffer.
exp.8:2:
This verse announces that God will send a very serious disease upon the animals of Egypt that are in the field: horses, donkeys, camels, cattle and sheep. "The hand of the Lord" is a way of speaking of God's power acting. "Pestilence" means a deadly plague or epidemic, and it is what the verse calls the disease itself.

God speaks to Moses and tells him to warn Pharaoh. This is the fifth plague. Pharaoh refused to let the Israelites go, though they lived as slaves. Before punishing, God gives a warning and another chance. Afterward it is made clear that the animals of Israel would not die, and God sets the exact day.

For today: God is patient and gives us chances to correct our course. If you sense that God is speaking to you through his Word or your conscience, do not harden your heart or put it off for later. Respond with humility today.
exp.1:11:
Moses looks around, and seeing that there is no one there, he kills the Egyptian who is beating a Hebrew and hides him in the sand. The phrase "no one in sight" means that no one could be seen. "Adopted" means that she took him in as her own son.

This is the narrator's account. Moses, raised in Pharaoh's house, goes out to see his enslaved people and witnesses the mistreatment. He acts in secret, and the fear he feels afterward shows that he knew something was wrong. The Bible does not clearly approve or condemn here, and interpreters see it in different ways: some as an act of justice carried out badly, others as an impulsive outburst.

For today: the desire to defend the mistreated is good, but doing so with violence and in secret brings consequences. Let us seek justice with wisdom, in the light, and asking for God's guidance.
exp.30:13:
God tells Moses that the people must keep the Sabbath because it is a holy day, that is, set apart for God. The word "defile" in the verse above means treating as common what is sacred. Whoever worked on that day would be punished with death, and being "cut off from among his people" means being separated from the community of Israel. Some scholars believe this refers to execution and others to expulsion; the text leaves it with great seriousness.

The Lord speaks to Moses right after giving him the instructions for building the tabernacle. The Sabbath was the sign of the covenant between God and the Israelites, so that they would remember that He makes them holy, that is, sets them apart as His own.

For today: set aside a regular time to rest and to remember that your life is in God's hands, not only in your work. Put down anxious striving, give thanks, and trust that He sustains your needs.
exp.21:22:
This verse says that if someone mistreats a widow or an orphan, and they cry out to God for help, God will surely hear them. The word "afflict" in the verse means to mistreat, oppress, or cause pain. The phrase "cry at all" means to call out or plead for help with urgency.

Here God speaks, giving laws to Israel through Moses, after they have left Egypt. He reminds them that they themselves were foreigners and were oppressed. For this reason they must care for those who have no one to defend them. The following verse shows that God takes this very seriously.

For today: look at the vulnerable people around you, such as a widow, a fatherless child, or an immigrant. Ask yourself how you can help them, and never take advantage of their weakness. God hears them.
exp.9:12:
It says that Moses raised his staff over Egypt, and God caused an east wind to blow for one full day and night. By morning, that wind brought the plague of locusts. The "staff" was the rod Moses used as a sign of God's authority.

Pharaoh had just driven Moses and Aaron out of his presence, because he refused to let the whole people go, only the men. God had commanded Moses to stretch out his hand so that the locusts would devour what the hail had left behind. The writer emphasizes that God directs even the wind.

Today we can remember that no force escapes God's control. When someone hardens their heart and refuses to obey, the consequences come. But we can also trust: the God who moves the winds can care for those who serve him.
exp.37:23:
This verse tells us how much gold was used to build the sanctuary, the place of worship for Israel. It was "offering gold," that is, gifts that the people gave of their own free will. It is given as about twenty-nine talents and seven hundred thirty shekels. The talent and the shekel were units of weight. Today we do not know their exact equivalent in kilograms; scholars give approximate figures.

The one who records this is the author of the book, traditionally Moses. After telling that Bezalel and Aholiab did the work just as God commanded, the text presents an accounting report. In this way it shows that what was given was used with order and honesty.

For today: God values generosity given with joy, and also transparency. If we manage resources of the church or of others, let us do so with clarity and faithfulness, so that God is honored.
exp.18:20:
He says that God orders Moses to go down from the mountain to warn the people once more. They must not cross the boundary set for them in order to look at the LORD, because many of them would die. Here, "warn" and "charge" carry the sense of insisting firmly on the warning, and the boundary is the line they must not pass.

God speaks amid thunder and the trumpet, while Israel is at the foot of Sinai. God has just called Moses up to the summit, but He insists on the warning. The boundary was not cruelty; it showed that God is holy and that drawing near to Him calls for respect and reverence. Interpreters see it as a protection for the people.

For today: draw near to God with confidence, but also with humility and respect. He is not someone we treat lightly. Today Christians believe that Christ opened the way for us to draw near (Hebrews 4:16), and even so, that closeness is lived out with gratitude and reverence.
exp.1:18:
The daughters of Reuel tell their father what happened at the well. They say that an Egyptian man defended them from the shepherds who were driving them off, and also drew water for them and watered the flock.

The ones speaking are the seven daughters of the priest of Midian. Their father is surprised that they have returned early, and they explain the reason. Moses had fled from Egypt, and because of his clothing or his way of speaking, they took him to be an Egyptian (the text does not make this clear).

His selfless help opened the door to lodging and to a new home.

For today: Moses helped some strangers without expecting anything in return. A simple act of justice and service can open paths we never imagined. Today we can defend or help someone close to us, trusting that God sees the small things.
exp.27:21:
God tells Moses to make small chains of pure gold, twisted like little cords. The breastpiece is a cloth piece holding twelve precious stones that the high priest wore over his chest. These chains would be used to fasten that piece in place.

God himself speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai and gives him detailed instructions for the clothing of Aaron, the high priest. Each stone bore the name of one of the tribes of Israel, so the priest was symbolically carrying the whole people over his heart when he approached God. Scholars explain the meaning of each detail in several ways, but the whole shows care and closeness.

For today: if God attended even to the detail of small chains to hold up the names of his people, he also holds you with care. Today you can pray for someone, carrying them in your heart with the same affection.
exp.28:0:
God tells Moses what he must do to set apart Aaron and his sons as priests. First he asks for one young bullock (a young bull) and two rams (male sheep) without blemish, that is, without any physical defect.

God speaks to Moses at Sinai, after giving him the instructions for the tabernacle. Before the priests could serve, they had to be prepared. The text shows that no one draws near to God on their own merit, but by the way He Himself establishes. Animals without defect indicate that the best is offered to God, not what is left over.

For today: God still seeks people dedicated to Him, not people who are perfect in themselves. We can ask ourselves what part of our time, talent, and affection we give to God: the best or the leftovers? Today we can offer Him something concrete, with gratitude, trusting that Christ makes us acceptable before Him.
exp.21:25:
It says that if someone borrows from his neighbor and leaves as security his clothing or cloak, the lender must return it before the sun goes down. "Pledge" is an object left as security for a debt.

God speaks to Israel through Moses, in the laws given after the Ten Commandments. These rules protect the poor. The following verse gives the reason: that cloak was the only thing the poor person had to keep warm at night, and God says he hears the cry of the one who suffers, because he is merciful.

For today: when you have power over someone in a debt or in a deal, do not seek your advantage at the cost of their dignity. Make sure that what is basic for living with decency is not lacking to them, and treat the needy with the compassion with which God treats you.
exp.27:17:
This verse describes the second row of precious stones on the breastpiece of the high priest. According to the King James Version, that row held an emerald, a sapphire, and a diamond. The Hebrew names of the stones cannot be identified with full certainty, which is why translations vary quite a bit.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai and gives him instructions for making Aaron's garments. The breastpiece had twelve stones, one for each tribe of Israel (Exodus 28:21). In this way, the priest carried the whole people over his heart when he came before God.

For today: God does not see his people as a faceless crowd, but values each one by name. You can rest in the fact that God knows you personally, and you can also imitate him by praying for others by name, as one who carries them in the heart.
exp.26:19:
God tells Moses to ask the people for pure olive oil, beaten, for the light. "Beaten" means pounded or pressed by hand, so as to get clean oil. With this oil the lamps were to burn continually. The "light" is the light of the lampstand of the tabernacle.

God speaks to Moses while giving him instructions for building the tabernacle, his tent of meeting with Israel. The verses that follow explain that Aaron and his sons would tend the lamps each evening and morning. The whole people took part by bringing the oil, and the priests were responsible for keeping the light burning.

For today: serving God requires steadiness and care, not just enthusiasm for a single day. We can set aside a fixed time each day to pray or read the Bible, and so keep our faith alive. In addition, each person can contribute something to the church, as Israel did with the oil.
exp.2:12:
Moses says to God that he will go to the Israelites and tell them that the God of their ancestors has sent him. But imagine that they ask him, "What is his name?" Moses wants to know what to answer.

Moses speaks with God in front of the burning bush, on the mountain. God calls him to bring Israel out of slavery in Egypt. Moses feels unsure, and God has just promised him: "I will be with you." At that time, a name said a great deal about the character and authority of the one who bore it. That is why the question is so important to the people.

When God calls us to something difficult, it is good to bring our doubts to him honestly. Moses does not pretend to be confident; he asks. And God responds by giving him more of himself, not just instructions. Today we can trust more in who God is than in how capable we feel.
exp.28:34:
God tells Moses to do with Aaron and his sons everything he has already explained, to set them apart as priests. That ceremony was to last seven days. The word "consecrate" means to set someone apart for God's service.

Here God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai while giving him instructions about the tabernacle and the priesthood. Before Aaron and his sons could serve, they needed to be prepared with sacrifices, special clothing, and oil. The seven days show that this setting apart was not something quick or casual, but serious and complete.

For today: serving God deserves preparation and reverence. Before serving in the church or in the family, we can set aside time to pray, ask for forgiveness, and offer God our hearts.
exp.39:26:
He burned fragrant incense on the golden altar, inside the tabernacle. The explanation says that "burned" here means to burn or to make the incense smoke. The special incense that God had specified is what is meant by the sweet incense. And it is repeated that he did it just as the Lord commanded.

This is part of the end of the book of Exodus. The narrator tells how Moses raised and set up the tabernacle, a year after leaving Egypt. Each piece is placed according to the instructions God had already given. The altar of incense stood before the veil, near the most holy place. Many see it as a picture of prayer rising to God, though the text does not explain this here.

God values obedience in what is simple and steady. We can pray and serve not out of cold obligation, but trusting what He has said, even in small tasks that no one sees.
exp.9:27:
Pharaoh tells Moses to leave and not come before him again. He warns that if Moses sees him again, he will die. The archaic-word glosses are dropped, since they belong to the original wording and do not appear in the verse your reader has.

Pharaoh speaks in anger, after nine plagues. Moses had just said that all the animals must leave Egypt to worship God. Pharaoh refused to give way and ended the conversation with a threat. The text says that God hardened his heart, and this is understood to have confirmed the stubbornness Pharaoh already showed. Moses accepts that he will not see him again.

For today: when God asks us to obey him fully, it is not wise to negotiate halfway or to harden our hearts. It is better to respond with humility before resistance closes doors on us.
exp.14:1:
This verse says that the Lord gives strength to the one who sings, that he is the reason for their joy, and that he saved them. By saying "God of my father," it shows that this faith comes from earlier generations.

Moses speaks together with the people of Israel. They have just crossed the Red Sea, and the Egyptian army that was chasing them was destroyed in the waters. This song is born out of gratitude for a deliverance they could not achieve by their own strength.

For today: when God helps you through a difficulty, do not let it pass in silence. Take a moment to thank him with a prayer, a song, or by telling someone about it. Remembering what God has done strengthens your faith for the hard days.
exp.33:33:
Moses, whenever he went in to speak with God, would take the veil off his face. He stayed without the veil until he came out. When he came out, he would tell the people what God had commanded him.

The explanation notes that Moses's face was shining because he had spoken with God on Mount Sinai. The account was written to show how close Moses was to God. Some think the veil kept the people from being frightened; Exodus gives no further explanation. In 2 Corinthians 3, Paul also mentions this, and commentators understand it in several different ways.

For today: Moses first came before God with nothing covering him, and only then spoke to others. We can seek sincere times of prayer, without masks, and let that closeness with God shape what we say and do afterward.
exp.11:31:
Pharaoh tells Moses and Aaron to take all their livestock, just as they had asked, and to go. At the end he adds: "bless me also." Some older wording needs a note: the phrase "and be gone" means "and go away," and "me" is the word "me" in "bless me."

Pharaoh speaks at night, after the death of the firstborn of Egypt. Earlier he had refused to let the people go, and now he gives in completely, overcome by grief and fear.
