His request for a blessing can be understood as a sincere plea for mercy or as an attempt to calm God's judgment. The text does not make clear what was in his heart.

For today: let us not wait until disaster comes to submit to God. Obeying him in time and with humility spares us much pain.
exp.30:12:
God tells Moses to instruct the people to keep his sabbaths. He calls them a sign between himself and the Israelites, to last for all their generations. The purpose is that they may know that the Lord is the one who makes them holy, that is, the one who sets them apart as his people.

The Lord speaks to Moses at the close of the instructions for building the sanctuary. Perhaps the sabbath is mentioned here so that, even in such sacred work, the people would not forget to rest. It was a sign belonging to the covenant with Israel.

For today: although Christians understand the sabbath in different ways, we can all learn to set aside time to rest and worship. Slow down for a while, trust that God sustains your life, and remember that he is the one who makes you his own.
exp.37:5:
It says that Bezalel made the poles to carry the altar. They were of acacia wood, called shittim, a sturdy wood of the desert. Then he overlaid them with metal, which in other versions appears as bronze or copper. The phrase about covering them is simply the verse's own wording, "overlaid them with brass."

Here the text tells how the altar of burnt offering for the tabernacle was built, following what God had commanded Moses. A character does not speak; this is the writer's account, describing the finished work in detail. The poles served to move the altar without touching it, when the people moved through the desert.

For today: God cares about small details and faithful service, even in what almost no one sees. We can do the simple tasks entrusted to us with care and obedience, knowing that God values them.
exp.14:19:
This verse tells that Miriam, the sister of Aaron, took a timbrel in her hand, and all the women followed her with timbrels and dances. A timbrel is an instrument similar to a tambourine. Here Miriam is called a prophetess, that is, someone who spoke on behalf of God. "Went out after her" means that they went out behind her, following her.

The narrator is describing what happened just after God opened the sea and saved Israel from Pharaoh's army. Moses and the people had just sung. Now Miriam leads the women in a celebration and answers them with a song of praise. The Bible does not say here what the dancing was like, so it is best not to imagine further details.

When God helps you, do not keep your gratitude silent. Be encouraged to give thanks out loud, and if you can, do it together with other people, so that the joy and faith of everyone may grow together.
exp.29:6:
Aaron, the high priest, was to burn fragrant incense on the altar every morning. He did this at the same time he tended the lamps in the holy place. The word for the incense burnt here is simply "incense," and "to tend" means to trim and prepare the lamps so they were ready for the day.

God speaks to Moses and gives him instructions about the tabernacle. This altar of incense stood in front of the veil, near the place where God would meet with his people. The incense rose as a picture of prayer and worship. Later, the Bible uses that image to speak of prayers (Psalm 141:2; Revelation 5:8).

For today: God values faithfulness. We can begin the day with a moment of prayer, even a brief one, to put ourselves in his presence before rushing into our tasks.
exp.14:17:
It says that Jehovah, that is, the Lord, the God of Israel, will be King forever. "Will reign" means that he governs with authority and power. The phrase "for ever and ever" is a way of saying "eternally," without end. It is a short and firm statement about the eternal rule of God.

The speaker is Moses together with the people of Israel, in a song of praise. They have just crossed the Red Sea and seen the armies of Pharaoh defeated. After being slaves in Egypt, they celebrate that God rescued them. This verse closes the song: God, and not Pharaoh, is the true King. Then Miriam and the women join in with tambourines and dancing.

For today: when you feel that circumstances or powerful people have the last word, remember that God reigns and does not change. Take a moment to thank him for something he has already done in your life, and entrust to him what worries you today.
exp.27:11:
This verse says that Moses was to place the two engraved stones on the shoulder pieces of the ephod, which was a sacred garment of the priest. Those stones were for a memorial, that is, a reminder. The names of the twelve tribes of Israel were engraved on them, and Aaron would carry them on his shoulders before the Lord, who is God's name in this version.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai and gives him instructions for the clothing of the high priest. Shoulders speak of bearing weight. In this way, Aaron represented the people before God, symbolically carrying them on himself when he entered to serve in his presence.

For today: God does not forget his people, and he invites us not to forget one another. This week, choose a person who is going through a difficult burden, pray for them by name and, if you can, help them with something concrete.
exp.31:9:
God tells Moses to stop interceding, because his anger burns against the people and he intends to destroy them. The phrase "let me alone" sounds like a request, and "consume" means to finish off or destroy. Furthermore, God promises to make a great nation of Moses. "To thee" means "to you," and "great nation" is the same as "great nation."

God is speaking on Mount Sinai. While Moses was receiving the law, the people made a golden calf, worshiped it, and broke their covenant with God. God calls the people "stiffnecked," that is, stubborn. What follows shows that Moses intercedes, and many understand that when God says "let me alone," he reveals the value of that prayer. Christians interpret this passage in different ways.

For today: when you see sin or failure around you, do not limit yourself to criticizing. Pray sincerely for those people, as Moses did, trusting in God's mercy.
exp.20:4:
This verse speaks of a Hebrew servant who, after six years of service, could go free. But if he declared that he loved his master, his wife, and his children, and that he did not want to go out free, he could stay. A "servant" here is someone who worked for another, often because of debts.

God speaks to Moses and gives laws to the people who had just come out of Egypt. This law protected the servant: his service had a limit, and the decision to stay had to be voluntary and public, before the judges. Some see here also a difficult situation, because the wife and children belonged to the master, and the servant had to choose between his freedom and his family.

For today: true love shows itself in free commitments, not forced ones. Ask yourself to whom or to what you have committed yourself out of love, and whether you keep that commitment faithfully and with a good heart.
exp.19:13:
It says that adultery should not be committed, that is, that a married person must not have sexual relations with someone who is not their spouse. The phrase about the verb form is an old way of saying the same thing, so I'll simply render it as: the command means "thou shalt not commit adultery." In the Bible, adultery is understood as breaking the marriage promise of faithfulness.

God himself speaks to Israel, shortly after bringing them out of Egypt, at Mount Sinai. This command is among the Ten Commandments, alongside the commands not to murder, not to steal, and not to lie. All of them protect the life of the community and the most important relationships, such as the family. God presents these laws as part of his covenant with his people.

For today: guard your faithfulness through simple words and decisions. Avoid conversations, relationships, or habits that weaken your commitment, and if you are married, spend time strengthening your marriage with honesty, respect, and affection.
exp.12:2:
Moses asks the people not to forget the day they came out of Egypt, the place of bondage, meaning the place of slavery. He says that God brought them out by a strong hand, that is, with great power. For this reason they must not eat bread with yeast in it.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel just after the exodus from Egypt. God had just set them free, and He gives them instructions to remember this event every year. The bread without yeast is connected with the hasty departure, and the text ties it to the feast that would follow in the month of Abib. God also reminds them that they belong to Him.

For today: take time to recall the times God has delivered or sustained you. You can write them in a notebook and give thanks for them. Remembering with gratitude strengthens faith when difficult times come.
exp.24:13:
The explanation says that the wooden staves covered in gold were to be passed through the rings on the sides of the ark. In this way, those in charge could carry it without touching it.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai and gives him instructions for building the tabernacle, the place of worship for the people in the desert. The ark would hold the testimony, the tablets of the law, and it represented God's presence with Israel. Since the people were on the move, the ark had to be able to be transported in an orderly and reverent way. The following text says that the staves were not to be removed.

For today: God wants us to carry him with us everywhere, not only in one place or on one day. We can ask ourselves how ready we are to follow him with reverence in everyday life: at work, at home, and through the changes of life.
exp.39:14:
He says that Moses must anoint the sons of Aaron in the same way he anointed their father. In this way they will be set apart as priests of God. "Anoint" means pouring oil on someone as a sign that God sets them apart for a task. "Everlasting" means it lasts forever, or for a very long time. "Throughout their generations" means it would pass from fathers to sons.

God speaks to Moses at the end of the book of Exodus, when the setting up of the tabernacle, the tent where God dwelt among his people, is completed. God wants there to be priests who serve there and represent the people before him. Moses obeys, as the next verse says.

For today: God calls and sets apart people to serve him, and he does it with order and care. You might ask yourself how to serve with seriousness and gratitude in what God has entrusted to you, whether in your family, your work, or your church.
exp.12:21:
It says that the pillar of cloud never departed from the people during the day, nor the pillar of fire during the night. The sign of God's presence went with them constantly, at all hours.

The one who tells the story is the author of the book, traditionally Moses. The Israelites had just left Egypt, where they had been slaves, and were entering the wilderness without knowing the way. The text presents the cloud and the fire as signs that the LORD himself was guiding and caring for them. It does not explain what they were physically like; the account simply says they were there.

For today: even when we do not see a visible sign, we can trust that God does not abandon his own. When you do not know which path to take, pray, seek his direction in the Bible, and take the next step calmly, remembering that he accompanies us both in the bright days and in the dark nights.
exp.13:12:
Moses tells the people not to be afraid and to stay calm, standing firm in their place. He asks them to see the Lord's salvation, that is, his rescue or deliverance, which God will bring about that very day. The Egyptians they see now, they will never see again.

Moses speaks to the Israelites, who had just left Egypt. They had the Red Sea in front of them and the army of the pharaoh behind them. Frightened, they complained to Moses and even said they would rather go on serving as slaves. Moses does not answer with anger, but points to God as the one who will rescue them.

Today, when fear pushes us toward despair or toward looking back with longing, we can stop, pray, and trust that God is at work. Standing still is not doing nothing, but resting in him, and then taking the step he indicates, as happens in the next verse.
exp.37:11:
This verse describes the west side of the tabernacle courtyard. There were hangings there of fifty cubits in length (a cubit is roughly half a meter, so about 25 meters). They were held up by ten pillars, each with its own socket. The sockets are the bases into which the pillars were set. The "capitals" were the pieces at the top of the pillars, and the "fillets" were the bands or rods that joined the hangings to the pillars. Those pieces were made of silver.

This is part of the account in which Moses records how the tabernacle was built, following the instructions God gave him on the mountain. The text repeats measurements side by side because the courtyard surrounded the whole holy place and marked off a separate space for worship.

For today: God cares about even the small details when it comes to drawing near to Him. We can serve Him with order and care in everyday life, knowing that nothing done for Him is insignificant.
exp.0:12:
This verse says that the Egyptians forced the Israelites to work for them in a cruel way. "Made to serve" means they enslaved them, and "with rigour" means with harsh treatment, without compassion. This is the point where the oppression becomes heavier.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, describing how the people of Israel went from being welcomed in Egypt to living under a pharaoh who feared them because they had grown so numerous. Since he could not hold them back, he increased the pressure on them. This suffering sets the stage for God to hear the cry of his people and deliver them.

For today: if you are going through a hard and unjust time, remember that God sees what you suffer, even when you do not feel him close. And if you have any power over others, treat them with respect and justice, never with harshness.
exp.14:18:
This verse sums up what happened at the sea: Pharaoh went in with his chariots and his horsemen, and God caused the waters to come back over them. The people of Israel, on the other hand, passed through the middle of the sea on dry ground, that is, on firm land.

Here Moses speaks together with the people, within a song of praise. They have just been rescued from the Egyptian army that was pursuing them. The verse works as a summary of the miracle, and after it comes Miriam's celebration with tambourines and dancing. The song also looks forward, to the land that God would give them.

For today: when you remember how God helped you in difficult moments, do not keep it to yourself. Give thanks out loud, tell others about it, and let that memory strengthen your trust for what lies ahead.
exp.26:13:
This verse gives the measurements for the courtyard of the tabernacle. On the side of the entrance, on each side of the gate, there would be hangings fifteen cubits long, supported by three pillars, each with its base. A cubit was about half a meter, so these would be about seven and a half meters. The bases were the supports on which the pillars rested.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai and gives him detailed instructions for building a portable place of worship. The courtyard surrounded the tabernacle and marked off a set-apart space, where Israel approached God with order and reverence. The gate stood in the middle, between these two sides of hangings.

For today: God cares about even the small details, and reminds us that drawing near to Him is something both serious and beautiful. We can give our time of prayer a quiet space, without rush, setting aside distractions so that we can come before Him calmly.
exp.0:20:
It says God rewarded the midwives because they reverenced and obeyed him. "Feared God" does not mean being afraid, but honoring him and taking him seriously. "Made them houses" is an old expression that probably means giving them family and descendants, or also well-being and stability. Scholars understand it in several ways.

The narrator of the book tells this after Pharaoh ordered the Hebrew boys to be killed. The midwives, Shiphrah and Puah, did not obey that order. They gave Pharaoh an excuse, and the text stresses that what God saw was their reverence for him. Meanwhile, the people kept growing, even though Pharaoh's pressure increased.

For today: when a human order clashes with what God teaches us about caring for life and doing good, let us ask him for courage and wisdom to obey him, trusting that God sees what we do in silence.
exp.33:3:
What it says: Moses prepared two new stone tablets, like the first ones. "Hewed" means he cut them and smoothed them. He rose early, went up Mount Sinai just as God had commanded him, and took the two stone tablets in his hand. "Jehovah" is the name of God.

Context: Shortly before, Moses had broken the first tablets when the people made the golden calf. Now God gives him a second chance and calls him alone to the mountaintop. What follows shows the purpose: God reveals himself as merciful, slow to anger, and abounding in goodness and truth.

For today: Moses obeyed promptly and with his hands full, without staying behind to mourn his past failure. When we fail, God invites us to return. We can respond with simple, timely obedience, trusting that his mercy is waiting for us.
exp.21:14:
If the owner was present when the animal was hurt or died, the one who had borrowed it does not have to pay. Nor does he pay more if the animal was rented: the rental price already covers the loss. The owner already receives what was agreed.

God speaks to Moses at Sinai, within the civil laws given to Israel after the Ten Commandments. These rules aimed at justice in specific cases of loans and damages. The idea is that whoever looks after something belonging to someone else is responsible for it when the owner is not there to watch over it. Some scholars discuss details of the wording, but the general meaning is clear.

For today: when you look after something that is not yours, treat it with care and be honest. And if the owner was present or has already been compensated, there is no need to demand more.
exp.11:9:
God commands that nothing of the Passover lamb be left over until the next day. If anything remained by morning, it had to be burned in the fire. The words "you shall let" and "you shall burn it" mean "they shall not leave" and "they must burn it."

God speaks to Moses and Aaron in Egypt, just before the last plague. Each Israelite family was to eat the lamb that night, ready to leave in a hurry. That nothing was to be kept shows that they were to trust God to take care of them the next day. Some think that respect for what was holy was also being protected; the text does not fully explain this.

Today we can practice trust: doing what God asks us today, without clinging to keep everything "just in case," and believing that He will care for tomorrow.
exp.7:23:
This verse tells us that God did what he had announced: a plague of very troublesome flies filled the house of Pharaoh, the houses of his servants, and all of Egypt. The land was ruined and spoiled by the swarm. The original text does not specify what kind of insect it was, and some scholars think of horseflies or other biting flies.

The narrator recounts what God had said earlier through Moses. Pharaoh still refused to let the people of Israel go. God set apart the land of Goshen, where the Israelites lived, to show that he is the Lord and that he cares for his people.

For today: God keeps his word, and his warnings and promises are serious. We can trust that he cares for his own, and we should listen to him before hardening our hearts.
exp.9:2:
Moses and Aaron go again before Pharaoh with a message from God. They ask him: "How long will you refuse to humble yourself before me?" Humbling yourself here means acknowledging that God is greater and submitting to Him. Then comes the command: "Let my people go, that they may serve me," that is, so that they may worship Him.

God speaks through Moses and Aaron. Several plagues have already fallen, and Pharaoh keeps refusing. Before this passage, the text says that God hardened Pharaoh's heart in order to show His signs, so that future generations would know who the Lord is. Scholars explain that phrase in different ways.

For today: when we feel that God is correcting us, it is not wise to harden ourselves out of pride. Today you can recognize in prayer something in which you have resisted God, and decide to obey Him with humility.
exp.29:21:
This verse is a transition phrase. It says that the Lord spoke again to Moses. With this, a new instruction begins, distinct from the one before.

God is the one who speaks, and Moses is the one who receives his directions for worship in the tabernacle. Just before, God had commanded that the priests wash their hands and feet before serving. Now he begins to explain how to prepare the anointing oil, with aromatic spices, which would be used to set apart the tabernacle and the priests for God.

God continues to speak and guide his people step by step. Today we can set aside a quiet moment to read his Word, with a willingness to listen and not only to speak. God still wants to be attended to with respect and sincere attention.
exp.0:16:
This verse tells how the Hebrew midwives honored God and did not carry out the Egyptian king's order to kill the baby boys. Instead, they let them live. "Feared God" means they held God in deep reverence and wanted to please Him. "Saved the men children alive" means they kept the babies alive and protected their lives.

Pharaoh feared that the Hebrew people would grow too large and become a threat. So he ordered Shiphrah and Puah, the midwives of the Hebrew women, to kill the newborn boys. The narrator, traditionally understood to be Moses, emphasizes that they put God above the king. Interpreters debate the extent of their later answer to Pharaoh, but the text highlights their fear of God.

For today: when an authority or pressure asks you to do something clearly unjust, ask God for the courage to obey Him first and to protect the vulnerable, even when it costs you.
exp.12:1:
God asks Moses to set apart for Him every firstborn of Israel, that is, the first male child and the first young of the animals. The verse's word "sanctify" is explained by the words "set apart, dedicate to me." "Openeth the womb" refers to a mother's first birth. God says: "it is mine."

The same God speaks here, right after freeing Israel from Egypt. According to the account in Exodus, in the last plague the firstborn of the Egyptians died, but the Israelites were protected. For this reason God claims the firstborn as a reminder that He saved them and that they belong to Him.

For today: everything we have comes from God, and He deserves the first and the best, not the leftovers. We can give God our time, our money, and our decisions with gratitude, remembering that He rescued us.
exp.34:16:
This verse is part of a list of things the people were to make for the tabernacle. Here the curtains that surrounded the court are named, the posts that held them up, the bases where those posts rested, and the curtain at the entrance of the court.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel, now in the wilderness. He repeats to them what God had commanded, so that everyone could take part with their gifts and their labor. The court marked a boundary: to come near to God there was one entrance and an appointed way.

For today: God pays attention even to the details that almost no one sees. No service done in faith is small. Today you can offer God whatever simple things you have, such as helping, putting things in order, or listening, knowing that he values your contribution to his work.
exp.13:1:
God tells Moses to tell the people to turn around, that is, to change direction, and to camp near the sea, in front of Pi-hahiroth, between Migdol and the sea, facing Baal-zephon. The instruction to "set up their camp" means that they should pitch the camp. The exact locations are uncertain, and there is debate about where they were.

The LORD speaks. Israel had just left Egypt, and God guides them with an order that seems strange: to camp in a place that leaves them hemmed in. The verses that follow explain that God had a purpose: to show his power before Pharaoh and the Egyptians.

For today: sometimes God leads us along paths that do not seem logical, and we feel there is no way out. Trust that his guidance has a purpose, even when you do not yet understand it. Obey step by step, and remember that he can open a way where we see only a limit.
exp.18:6:
This verse tells how Moses came down from the mountain, called together the elders of the people, that is, the leaders and representatives of the families, and laid before them clearly everything the Lord had told him. Here "laid before" means that he set it in front of them, without changing anything.

God had just offered Israel a special relationship: if they obeyed him and kept his covenant, they would be his treasured possession, a kingdom of priests and a holy nation. Moses acts as the messenger. First he speaks with the leaders, and then the whole people answer that they will do everything the Lord has said.

For today: when God speaks to us in his Word, it is good to pass it on faithfully and humbly, without taking away from it or adding to it. And before saying "we will do everything," it is good to listen carefully and to depend on his help.
exp.8:16:
It says that Pharaoh still raises himself up in pride against God's people. The word "exaltest" means setting oneself above others, and here it refers to resisting with arrogance. God asks him whether he will still keep that attitude and not let the Israelites go.

God speaks, through Moses, during the plagues of Egypt. Israel was enslaved, and Pharaoh had hardened his heart again and again. This question is almost a final call to reconsider. Immediately God announces the hail, but He also gives a warning so that the people can protect their livestock and their lives.

For today: pride shuts our ears to God. If He corrects us or warns us about something, we can yield quickly and with humility, instead of becoming hardened. His warning is often a sign of patience and mercy.
exp.13:28:
This verse says that the people of Israel crossed the sea walking on dry land. "Dry land" means there was no mud or water under their feet. "Right hand" means the right side, and "left hand" means the left side. The waters were standing up on both sides like a wall that protected them.

The account is told by a narrator, whom tradition identifies as Moses. The people of Israel had just left Egypt, and Pharaoh's army was chasing them. This verse recalls how God saved them. While they passed safely, the Egyptians were covered by the waters. Seeing this, the people feared the LORD and believed in Him.

For today: when you see no way out, remember that God can open a path where it seemed impossible. Trust Him and take the next step in faith, even though you do not yet understand everything. He cares for His own.
exp.8:6:
Pharaoh sent men to check, and he found that not a single animal belonging to Israel had died. Even so, his heart "se agravó," that is, it became hard and stubborn, and he did not let the people go.

This happens during the fifth plague, the one that fell on the livestock of Egypt. God had given warning the day before, and he carried it out. The account shows that God distinguished between Egypt and Israel. Moses records the event to show who holds the power and how Pharaoh rejected the evidence.

For today: sometimes we see clear signs that God is at work, and yet we resist out of pride. Let us ask him for a humble heart, one that recognizes the truth and obeys when God speaks, without waiting for more proof.
exp.13:21:
This verse tells that the people of Israel crossed the sea walking on dry ground. The waters stood still like a wall on both sides. "Sea" here refers to the Red Sea, or according to some, a sea of reeds; the exact location is not known with certainty.

It is part of the account of the exodus. The narrator tells how God rescued Israel from Egypt. Pharaoh was pursuing them, and God placed a cloud between the two camps. Then, through Moses and a strong east wind, he opened a path through the sea.

For today: when you feel cornered, remember that God can open a way where you see no way out. Take the next step of obedience, trusting that He sustains you, even when you do not understand everything.
exp.18:3:
You remember what the people had already lived through: they saw how God judged the Egyptians. He says that he carried them "on eagles' wings," an image of careful and powerful rescue, like an eagle that lifts and shields its young. And the phrase "and brought you unto myself" means that the purpose of the deliverance was not only to leave Egypt, but to come near to God.

The Lord speaks from Mount Sinai, and Moses carries the message to Israel. They have just arrived in the wilderness after leaving Egypt. Before giving the law, God reminds them of his faithfulness, so that their obedience will grow out of gratitude and trust, not fear.

For today: before worrying about what God asks of you, remember how he has cared for you up to this point. That gratitude strengthens trust and encourages you to draw near to him.
exp.39:12:
God commands Moses to dress Aaron in the holy garments, to anoint him with oil, and to sanctify him, that is, to set him apart for God. The purpose is for Aaron to serve as God's priest. Anointing means pouring oil on someone as a sign that they are set apart for a special service.

God speaks to Moses near the end of the book, as the tabernacle is being prepared to begin its work. Before the service can start, everything must be dedicated: the furnishings, the basin, and also the priests. First they are washed with water, then they are clothed and anointed. This shows that serving God does not depend on one's own merits, but on his calling and his preparation.

For today: before serving God in any task, ask him to cleanse and prepare you. What matters is not feeling capable, but answering the call with humility and dependence on him.
exp.24:9:
God commands that an ark, that is, a chest, be made of shittim wood, which today is usually called acacia. It measures two and a half cubits in length, and a cubit and a half in width and in height. A cubit was the distance from the elbow to the tip of the fingers, about 45 centimeters, although its exact length is not known. Thus the ark measured roughly 110 by 70 by 70 centimeters.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai. He has just freed Israel from Egypt and wants a sanctuary to dwell among his people. The ark is the first object he describes, and it would hold the tablets of the law. God gives the measurements with care, and Moses must follow the pattern that He shows him.

For today: God desires to be close to us, and He invites us to obey Him attentively, including in small things. Today we can ask ourselves what instruction from His Word we have left unfinished.
exp.38:29:
It says that the craftsmen made a plate of pure gold, called "the holy crown." On it they engraved, the way a seal is engraved, the words "HOLINESS TO THE LORD." A "plate" is a flat sheet of metal, and an "inscription" is a written mark carved into a surface. The "turban" was the headdress of the high priest.

The narrator tells how the Israelites finished the garments of Aaron, the high priest, in the wilderness. Everything was done "just as the LORD had commanded Moses," and the text repeats this to show obedience. The plate was to sit on the forehead, fastened with a blue cord, and it reminded everyone that the priest and his service belonged to God.

Today we can ask ourselves what we keep in plain sight in our daily lives. Even if we do not wear a plate, we can ask God that our work, our words, and our decisions show that we belong to Him.
exp.12:13:
This verse says that when a child asks in the future, "What is this?", the father should answer that the Lord brought Israel out of Egypt by a strong hand, that is, with great power. The phrase "house of bondage" refers to the place of slavery, the land where they were held as servants.

Moses speaks to the people before they leave Egypt and gives them instructions for when they enter the promised land. He asks them to dedicate the firstborn to God and to redeem the sons, as a reminder of the night the Egyptian firstborn died. In this way, the child's question opens the door to telling what God did.

For today: do not assume that your children or the younger ones will come to know the faith on their own. When they ask, tell them simply how God has rescued and cared for you.
exp.8:9:
What it says: Moses and Aaron took ashes from a furnace and stood before Pharaoh. Moses threw them toward the sky, and there appeared a sore or infection on the skin, with blisters full of pus, which affected both people and animals. The blains here are painful eruptions, and the boils are filled with pus.

Context: This is the sixth plague on Egypt. God had commanded this action, and the account presents it as the fulfillment of his word. Pharaoh kept refusing to let Israel leave. The Egyptian magicians, who had earlier imitated some signs, now cannot even stand before Moses. Some see in this a judgment against Egypt's reliance on its own powers and gods.

For today: We can trust that God's word is fulfilled, even when we do not see it right away. It is also a call not to harden our hearts when God speaks to us.
exp.12:12:
The first male offspring of a donkey could not be given to God as a sacrifice, because the donkey was an unclean animal. So it had to be redeemed, that is, bought back by paying a lamb in its place. If the owner did not buy it back, he had to put it to death by breaking its neck.

The firstborn sons of people were also redeemed; they were not sacrificed.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter Canaan. He explains how they were to remember that God delivered them from Egypt, when the firstborn of the Egyptians died and the firstborn of Israel were saved. This law served to teach the children that story.

For today: everything we have comes from God and belongs to him. We can dedicate to him, with gratitude, the first and best of our time, money, and affection, and tell our children how God has redeemed us.
exp.25:12:
This verse says that the curtains of the tent were longer than the tabernacle. Each curtain measured 30 cubits, and one extra cubit was left over on each side. That extra cubit hung down over the sides and covered the boards. A cubit was an ancient measure, roughly the length of the forearm. The phrase "hang over" means the cloth hung down.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai and gives him detailed instructions for building the tabernacle, a portable sanctuary where He would dwell in the midst of Israel. Here it is explained how the curtains of goat's hair would cover the structure. Other coverings of skins are added afterward.

For today: God cares for even the small details, such as one extra cubit left over to provide protection. We can trust that He also cares for what seems minor in our lives. And we can do with care and faithfulness the small part that is ours to do.
exp.14:13:
The verse says that the nations around them will hear what God did at the sea and will be filled with fear. The word "shall hear" is what the phrase refers to. The text says the pain will take hold of them, meaning the anguish will overcome them. The "inhabitants of Palestina" are the people who lived along the Philistine coast, to the southwest of Canaan.

Moses and the Israelites sing this hymn after crossing the Red Sea and seeing the Egyptian army fall. They celebrate God's salvation and look ahead: news of this victory would spread among the peoples they would meet on the way to the promised land.

For today: what God has done before gives us confidence for what lies ahead. When you face an uncertain road, remember how God has sustained you before, and walk with the assurance that the same God goes with you.
exp.11:45:
It says the Passover lamb had to be eaten inside one single house. Nothing could be carried out of the house in the form of meat, and none of its bones were to be broken. The word "break" in the verse means "shatter" or "smash"; the verse uses "break" as the word for what must not happen to the bones.

God is speaking to Moses and Aaron just before Israel leaves Egypt. He wanted each family to celebrate the Passover together, in one place, as a people who had been rescued. The verses nearby explain who could take part: those who belonged to the covenant. The New Testament, in John 19:36, connects the rule about the bones with Jesus, the Lamb of God.

For today: value being united with your family of faith. Take part in the life of your church, and trust that Christ, our Lamb, protects us and gathers us together as one people.
exp.38:21:
It says that Bezalel and the craftsmen made the robe worn beneath the ephod, the sacred vest of the high priest. It was "work of a weaver," that is, woven by hand, and entirely of "blue," which is not a flower but a cloth of a violet-blue color. The "ephod" was a special garment, and the "robe" was a long tunic worn underneath.

It is part of the account of how Aaron's clothing, the high priest's, was made. The narrator repeats that everything was done "as the LORD had commanded Moses." It stresses the people's obedience in building the tabernacle.

For today: God cares about the details of what we do for Him. We can serve Him with diligence and obedience in small things, whether at work, at home, or in church, without looking for shortcuts.
exp.16:3:
Moses speaks to God aloud and in distress. He asks what he should do with the people, because he feels that they are about to stone him. He cried out to God, which means he asked for help with great urgency. "They be almost ready to stone me" means they are very close to killing him by throwing rocks at him.

The people of Israel, now out of Egypt, had no water in the desert. Thirsty and afraid, they complained against Moses and even blamed him for bringing them out of Egypt. Moses does not answer them in anger before God, but brings his pressure directly to the Lord. God answers him with clear instructions and provides water.

When you feel pressured or criticized, do not carry everything alone. You can speak to God honestly, tell him what you feel, and ask him for direction. He can hear you and show you the next step.
exp.13:14:
Here God speaks to Moses and asks him, "Why do you cry out to me?" Then God orders him to tell the people of Israel to move on, to go forward.

The word "cry out" in the verse above is the one that means asking for help with great urgency. The sea is the Red Sea, and the name of God is the LORD.

The people were trapped between the sea and the Egyptian army that was coming up behind them. Moses had told them to stand still and trust. But now God shows that it is time to move. Scholars explain God's question in several ways: some see it as a gentle correction, others as an invitation to move from prayer to obedient action. The text does not fully make this clear.

For today: prayer is good and necessary, but sometimes God shows us the next step and asks us to trust and take that step, even when we do not yet see how everything will be resolved.
exp.6:0:
It says that God speaks to Moses and gives him a special position before Pharaoh: he is made "a god" to him, and Aaron, his brother, will be his prophet, that is, the one who speaks on his behalf. Here "a god" does not mean that Moses is divine, but that he will represent God's authority before Pharaoh.

God speaks with Moses, who felt unable to speak well (Exodus 6:30). That is why God gives him Aaron as a spokesman. Moses receives God's message and Aaron delivers it. This prepares the confrontation with Pharaoh and the signs that will come upon Egypt.

For today: when God entrusts you with something and you feel little capable, remember that his authority and his help are greater than your weakness. Accept the support of other people, and trust that God can use you just as you are.
exp.14:20:
This verse says that Miriam encouraged the women to sing to the Lord, because He had shown Himself great and glorious. The reason was that He had thrown the horse and its rider into the sea. The word "answered" in the verse and the word "sing" both point to her leading the others in praise, and "triumphed gloriously" means that God showed His greatness in an enormous way.

Miriam speaks here, called a prophetess and the sister of Aaron. She had just seen how Israel crossed the sea on dry ground and how Pharaoh's army was covered by the waters. She takes the timbrel and leads the women in praise, repeating the theme of Moses' song. Soon after, the people become thirsty and find bitter waters, which shows that praise and trial can come very close to one another.

For today: when God helps you, do not let it pass in silence. Thank Him out loud and tell what He has done, so that others may also trust in Him.
exp.33:24:
It says that when the people brought the blood of the sacrifice, it was not to be offered with bread made with leaven, that is, bread containing yeast. It also says that the meat of the Passover sacrifice was not to be kept until the next morning. The order God had given was to be respected.

God is speaking within the renewal of the covenant with Moses on Mount Sinai, after the sin of the golden calf. Before these rules, God promises to protect the land of Israel while the men go up to the three yearly feasts. Leaven is usually understood as a symbol of what corrupts, although scholars explain its exact meaning here in several ways. What is certain is that God asked for orderly worship, without mixture.

Today we can learn to come near to God with sincerity, without mixing his Word with our customs, and without putting off what he asks of us today.
exp.25:25:
God commands Moses to make five bars of acacia wood to hold together the boards on one side of the tabernacle. The tabernacle is the sacred tent, and the bars were crossbars that kept the boards firm and in line.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai, after rescuing Israel from Egypt. He gives him precise instructions for building a place where his presence would dwell among the people. The bars were part of the structure that held everything together while they traveled through the desert.

For today: God cares even for the details no one sees, like hidden bars that hold everything up. In the same way, our humble and steady service in the family or in the church also matters to God, even when no one notices. We can support others faithfully and without seeking applause.
exp.38:4:
It says that the curious girdle of the ephod, that is, the sash that fastened this sacred garment, was made of the same material and with the same workmanship as the rest: gold, blue thread (the one called "hyacinth"), purple, scarlet, and fine twined linen. Everything was done just as the Lord had commanded Moses. The ephod was a special garment of the high priest.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, recounting how the craftsmen of Israel carried out the instructions given earlier on Mount Sinai. The tabernacle and Aaron's garments are being finished. That is why the phrase "just as the Lord had commanded" is repeated so often: the emphasis is on careful obedience.

For today: God values faithful obedience, even in the small details that no one notices. Today we can serve him with that same care in everyday life: at work, in the family, and in the church, doing things with excellence and with a heart ready to obey him.
exp.20:25:
God speaks to Moses and gives laws to Israel after they leave Egypt. The text says that if a master strikes his male or female servant in the eye and it is destroyed, he must let that servant go free as compensation. The explanation notes that the sense of the word rendered "destroyed" is to harm or disable the eye. The servant here refers to a slave or worker under the control of a master.

At that time slavery existed among all peoples, and these laws set limits on the power of masters. A servant was not merely property: his or her body had value and their suffering mattered. The verse before shows the principle of proportionate justice. Some scholars see here a check on violence, though it is not God's final ideal.

For today: God cares for those who have less power. If you have authority as a boss, parent, or leader, use it to care for others and not to harm them. Treat with dignity those who depend on you.
exp.39:31:
This verse says that Moses, Aaron and his sons washed every time they entered the tent of meeting or approached the altar. They did this because God had commanded Moses to do it. The tent of meeting was the sacred tent where God met with his people.

The one telling the story is the author of the book, traditionally understood to be Moses. He recounts that everything was done just as God had ordered. The priests had to wash before serving, which showed that God is holy and that drawing near to him required cleanness and reverence. Right after this, the glory of the Lord filled the tabernacle.

For today: before praying or serving God, take a moment to ask him to cleanse your heart. Confess what weighs on you and come near with reverence, knowing that he receives you with mercy.
exp.37:16:
This verse describes how the pillars that held up the curtains of the court of the tabernacle were made.

Here the narrator of the book of Exodus speaks, recording how the tabernacle was built according to the instructions God gave to Moses. It is part of a detailed report of the work and of the materials the people offered. Some exact details of these pieces are understood in several ways.

For today: God cares about the details, and nothing done for Him is small. We can serve Him with faithfulness and care in simple things, even when no one notices.
exp.29:28:
God tells Moses that the anointing oil will be used to set apart the tabernacle and all its furnishings. To "sanctify" means to dedicate something solely to God. The most holy things are objects of great importance, reserved for his service. The phrase "whatsoever toucheth them shall be holy" is understood in several ways: some think that whatever came into contact with them was set apart for God; others, that only those who had the right to touch them could do so.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai. He gives him instructions for the tabernacle, the tent where God would dwell among his people. He wants everything used in his worship to be treated with respect and kept distinct from the ordinary. Next he calls for Aaron and his sons to be anointed as priests.

For today: God deserves our first and best, not what is left over. We can deliberately dedicate our time, our work, and our decisions to him, and treat with reverence whatever has to do with him.
exp.13:6:
This verse says that Pharaoh gathered a large army to pursue Israel. He took six hundred chosen chariots of war, that is, the best and strongest ones, along with all the other chariots of Egypt. Over them he placed captains, who were the officers who commanded them.

The text is narrated by Moses. Pharaoh had let the Israelites go after the plagues, but he changed his mind when he saw that he was losing his workers. So he set out with all his military power. Even so, the account makes clear that God was in control, and that the Israelites went out with a mighty hand. Interpreters explain in different ways how Pharaoh's hardening of heart relates to his own decision.

For today: sometimes problems look enormous, like an army with six hundred chariots. But God is greater than any threat. When you feel fear, remember that He was already at work before the problem arrived, and trust that He will take care of you.
exp.23:15:
This verse says that the glory of God rested on Mount Sinai, and a cloud covered it for six days. The word "abode" means that it stayed there and settled in place. On the seventh day, God called to Moses from within the cloud. The name of God is "the Lord," and the old-fashioned spelling of the word "to" appears in the verse as well.

Here the narrator tells what happened after Moses went up the mountain. Before he climbed, he left the elders with Aaron and Hur to handle the affairs of the people. Israel had left Egypt and had just accepted the covenant with God. Moses was about to receive his instructions.

For today: Moses waited six days in silence before God spoke. We can learn to wait on God without rushing, knowing that he speaks in his own time.
exp.22:5:
This verse commands that justice not be twisted against the poor when they have a legal dispute. The word "poor" here refers to the person in need, without resources or power. "Twist" is to turn justice aside, to judge unfairly, and "cause" is a legal case or dispute.

God speaks to Israel through Moses, in the laws given after Sinai. Just before, he asks that one help even an enemy, and just after, that one reject lies and bribes. This shows that God's justice does not depend on sympathy, money, or convenience.

For today: if you are asked to give an opinion, make a decision, or give testimony in a conflict, do not lean toward the stronger party or the one who suits you. Strive to be fair, especially toward those who have less voice and less defense.
exp.38:32:
The explanation says that the Israelites brought the tabernacle to Moses, now finished, along with all its parts. It names the taches (the hooks or clasps that joined the curtains), the boards (the wooden frames that formed the walls), the bars (which held them together), the pillars (the posts), and the sockets (the bases on which they rested).

This is part of a account of how the work was completed. Moses is the one who receives and inspects the work. The text insists that everything was done "as the LORD had commanded." Afterward it goes on with a detailed list of the remaining pieces, which Moses will go on to inspect.

For today: God is concerned with the great things as much as with the small details. We can serve him faithfully in what seems minor, like a hook or a base, trusting that every task done with obedience and care has value before him.
exp.36:12:
He says that Bezalel made four rings of gold, cast in a mold, and set them at the four corners of the table, right where its four feet were.

The narrator of the book of Exodus is describing how the table of the tabernacle was built, following the instructions God gave to Moses. The rings were there to hold the poles, so the table could be carried. This was necessary because the tabernacle was a tent that moved with the people through the wilderness.

For today: God cares about even the small details, such as a few rings. We can serve him faithfully in what is simple and practical, trusting that nothing we do with a sincere heart goes unnoticed by him.
exp.29:7:
This verse says that Aaron, the priest, was to burn incense every evening, when he lit the lamps of the tabernacle. Incense is a fragrant mixture that is burned so that it rises as perfumed smoke. Together with the morning service, this made up a daily offering, a constant offering that was to continue throughout your generations.

God speaks to Moses as He gives the instructions for the tabernacle. The altar of incense stood before the veil, near the place where God met with His people. The incense marked the day with worship. Many see it as a picture of prayer, as in Psalm 141:2, although here the text speaks only of the ritual.

For today: set aside a moment at dawn and another at dusk to pray, even if briefly. A life of constant prayer reminds us that God deserves our whole day.
exp.2:14:
God tells Moses what he should say to the people: that the God of their fathers Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob has sent him. The name "Jehovah" is the way this translation writes the divine name, which in Hebrew is connected to "I AM." "Memorial" means remembrance: it is the name by which God wants to be remembered by all generations. "Unto" is the preposition "to," written in an older style.

Moses stands before the burning bush and fears that the Israelites, who are enslaved in Egypt, will not believe him. He asks what God's name is. God answers that he is the same faithful God of their fathers, the one who made promises and has not forgotten them. In this way Moses will be able to speak with authority.

For today: God is not a stranger, and he does not change. The same God who cared for past generations cares for you. When you doubt, remember his faithfulness in history and in your own life, and trust that he continues to keep what he promises.
exp.11:24:
It says that when the people of Israel enter the land God promised them, they must keep on observing this rite, that is, the ceremony of the Passover.

Moses speaks to the people, passing on what God commanded him, just before the last plague and the departure from Egypt. God wanted them to remember their deliverance. The rite was not only for that moment, but for future generations, and their children would ask what it meant.

For today: God keeps what he promises, and we can deliberately remember his works. Tell your children, or others close to you, how God has helped you, and look for simple habits, such as praying with thankfulness or reading his Word, that keep that memory alive.
exp.34:20:
The explanation says the people responded to Moses' call. Every person whose heart moved them and whose spirit made them willing came and brought an offering to the Lord. That offering was for building the tabernacle (the tent where God dwelt among his people), for all its service, and for the holy garments of the priests. "Stirred up" means prompted or encouraged; "making" means construction.

Moses had just asked the congregation for materials for the sanctuary. This happens after the sin of the golden calf, when God renewed his covenant with Israel. The people left his presence and returned with voluntary offerings, no one forced to give.

God takes more delight in giving that springs from the heart than in giving done under pressure or out of habit. Today you might ask yourself: what is God moving me to give, whether time, talent, or money? Do it gladly and without comparisons.
exp.33:34:
This verse says that the people of Israel saw that the skin of Moses' face shone. After speaking with them, Moses would put the veil over his face again, and he kept it there until he went back in to speak with God.

The skin of the face is the word the verse uses for "face," and the old spelling of the word "a" is no longer needed here, so that comment is removed.

Moses had just been with the LORD on Mount Sinai and was bringing the commandments to the people. His face shone because he had been in God's presence. The text does not explain in detail why he used the veil. Later, Paul comments on this passage in 2 Corinthians 3, and readers have understood it in different ways.

For today: spending time with God changes us inwardly, even if we do not shine outwardly. Try to set aside time each day to pray and read the Bible, and let that closeness shape the way you treat others.
exp.3:28:
This verse says that Moses and Aaron went together to Egypt and gathered all the elders of Israel. "Elders" refers to the respected leaders and heads of the families and tribes of the people. "Gathered together" means they called them and brought them together in one place.

After meeting on God's mountain, Moses told Aaron everything God had said to him and the signs God had given him. Now they begin the mission: first they speak with the leaders, who represented the people. God had prepared Aaron to be Moses' spokesman, since Moses felt unsure about speaking.

For today: God often carries out his plans through people who work as a team. Accepting the help of others, and beginning by sharing the message with those who guide the community, can open the way with order and confidence.
exp.37:2:
This verse tells that Bezalel made all the utensils of the altar of burnt offering. The pots were used to collect the ashes, the tongs and the hooks were for handling the meat and the fire, the bowls were for catching the blood, and the shovels were for cleaning the altar. All of them were made of bronze, the metal that is usually understood here, though some versions say copper.

This is part of the account where the narrator describes how the tabernacle was built, following the instructions God gave to Moses. Here God is not speaking; the author reports that everything was made as it had been commanded. The altar was the place where sacrifices for sin were offered.

For today: God cares even about the small details of our service. What seems simple or hidden, like cleaning or preparing something, matters when it is done with faithfulness and for Him.
exp.13:19:
It says that the pillar of cloud stood between the Egyptian army and the people of Israel. For the Egyptians the cloud was darkness, and for the Israelites it gave light during the night. Because of this, the two camps did not come near each other all that night. The phrase "gave light to Israel" means the cloud gave light to Israel. The phrase "one to another" means "one another."

The people of Israel had just left Egypt, but Pharaoh was pursuing them, and they were standing in front of the sea. The account is not a person speaking; Moses is the one who tells it. God himself protects his people and gives them time before he opens the sea. How exactly the cloud worked is not explained in detail.

For today: when you feel cornered, remember that God can take care of you even before you see the way out. Trust that he is between you and the danger, and take the next step he shows you.
exp.28:22:
This verse describes three loaves taken from a basket that held unleavened bread: one loaf of bread, one flat cake made with oil, and one thin, flat wafer. These loaves were presented to the Lord together with the parts of the ram.

God speaks to Moses and gives him instructions for consecrating Aaron and his sons as priests. These loaves were placed with the meat in the hands of Aaron and his sons and were waved before the Lord. Scholars understand this gesture as one of surrender and offering. Bread without yeast suggests simplicity and purity.

God values our offering of the everyday, even our daily bread. Today we can offer Him, with simplicity, our work, our time, and our hands, so that He may use them for His service.
exp.23:2:
Moses comes down and repeats to the people everything God had said, both his words and his judgments, meaning his rules and laws for living righteously. Everyone answers together, with one voice, that is, in full agreement, saying that they will do everything the Lord has spoken.

This takes place at Mount Sinai, shortly after the Ten Commandments. God is making a covenant with Israel, and Moses is the mediator who carries the message. The people accept the conditions before the covenant is sealed with the altar and the sacrifices. Later history shows that they struggled to keep this promise.

For today: before promising something to God, listen carefully to what He says in His Word. And when you commit yourself, do it with humility, asking Him for His help to keep it.
exp.29:18:
This verse says that Aaron and his sons, who were the priests, were to wash their hands and their feet with water from the bronze basin.

God speaks to Moses while giving him instructions for the tabernacle, the tent where God dwelt among his people. The basin stood between the tent and the altar. The priests had to wash before they served, and the text that follows says it was a matter of life or death, to teach that God is holy and must be approached with reverence.

Today we can draw near to God with sincerity, asking him to cleanse our hearts and our actions. Before we pray or serve others, we can pause for a moment and say: "Lord, cleanse me and guide me."
exp.9:18:
This verse tells us that God changed the direction of the wind. A very strong west wind lifted up the plague of locusts and drove them into the Red Sea, which is often called the Sea of Reeds today. Not one locust was left in all of Egypt.

Pharaoh had just confessed his sin and asked Moses to pray that this plague of death would be taken away, meaning the destruction the plague had caused. Moses prayed, and God answered. The same God who had brought the east wind with the locusts now sends another wind to remove them. Even so, the text goes on to say that Pharaoh's heart became hard again.

For today: when God rescues us from a difficult situation, we should not treat it as a mere pause. Let us give thanks and respond with a real change, not only with words spoken in the middle of our distress.
exp.27:33:
This verse describes the lower edge of the priest's robe: a golden bell, then a pomegranate, and so they alternate all around. The "robe" is the blue garment worn beneath the ephod. The "pomegranates" were ornaments shaped like that fruit, made of colored threads, and the "hems" are the lower edges.

God gives Moses instructions about the clothing of Aaron, the high priest. According to the verses that follow, the sound of the bells would be heard when Aaron went in and out of the sanctuary, so that he would not die. The text does not explain all the symbolism of the pomegranates and bells; some see in them a sign of respect and reverence, and others see fruit and witness.

For today: draw near to God with reverence, knowing that his presence is holy. Let your life combine the fruit of good character with words and deeds that bear witness to him.
exp.20:5:
This verse says that if a Hebrew servant decides to stay with his master out of love for him and his household, the master will bring him before the judges. Then he will place him by the door or the doorpost, and pierce his ear with an awl, which is a pointed tool similar to a punch. In this way the servant would remain in his master's service "forever," an expression that many understand to mean for life.

God speaks through Moses as he gives laws to Israel shortly after leaving Egypt. These rules regulated servitude so that Hebrew servants would be treated justly and released in the seventh year. Staying was a voluntary decision, and it was made before witnesses. Scholars do not fully agree on the exact meaning of the pierced ear, but it was clearly a public sign of that commitment.

Today we can learn that true service springs from love and not from obligation. Ask yourself whom you serve and why, and seek to make your commitments free, honest, and full of love.

sum.12: In Exodus 13, God asks that every firstborn be set apart for him, and the people are to remember each year their deliverance from Egypt through the Feast of Unleavened Bread, teaching it to their children. Then God leads Israel through the wilderness, by day in a pillar of cloud and by night in a pillar of fire. Moses also takes the bones of Joseph with him.
sum.2: Moses is tending the sheep when he sees a bush that is on fire but is not burned up. There God calls to him, tells him that he has seen the suffering of his people in Egypt, and sends him to bring them out of there. Moses hesitates, but God promises to be with him and reveals his name: "I am who I am."
sum.21: God gives laws for living justly: paying back for theft and damage, taking care of what belongs to others, and protecting widows, orphans, foreigners, and the poor. He also commands worship of Jehovah alone, respect for those in authority, and living as a holy people, dedicating the first of the harvest and of the animals to him.
sum.16: At Rephidim the people had no water, and they complained against Moses and tested God, but God caused water to flow from the rock. Then Amalek attacked, and Israel won while Moses kept his hand raised, supported by Aaron and Hur. Moses built an altar, acknowledging that God is the one who gives the victory.
sum.35: The skilled craftsmen, whom God had given ability, received the offerings from the people. There were so many gifts that Moses had to order them to stop bringing them. With these materials they built the tabernacle: the curtains, the coverings, the frames, the bars, and the veils, just as the LORD had commanded. We see a generous people and workers who used their gifts to serve God.
sum.19: God speaks to Israel from the mountain and gives them the Ten Commandments: to love only Him, not to make idols, to respect His name, to rest on the seventh day, to honor their parents, and to protect life, marriage, property, truth, and the heart. The people tremble in fear, and Moses draws near to God. Then God gives simple instructions for how to worship Him.
sum.36: Bezalel built the sacred furnishings of the tabernacle: the ark with its cover and two golden cherubim, the table with its utensils, the pure gold lampstand with seven lamps, and the altar of incense. He also prepared the holy anointing oil and the fragrant incense. Everything was made with precious materials and with great care, for the worship of God.
sum.34: Moses gathers the people and reminds them to keep the Sabbath as a holy day of rest. He then asks them for a freely given offering to build the tabernacle. Men and women bring gold, fabric, and other materials gladly, and God fills Bezalel and Oholiab with wisdom to lead the work.
sum.33: God tells Moses to cut new stone tablets and go back up Mount Sinai, where God reveals himself as merciful and gracious, slow to anger and abounding in love, though he does not leave wrongdoing unpunished. God renews the covenant with Israel, warns them against idolatry, and reminds them of their festivals and the Sabbath day of rest. Moses comes down with his face shining.
sum.20: God gave Israel laws for living together in community. Hebrew servants were to be set free in the seventh year, and the rights of women were protected. The chapter also sets out punishments for murder, assault, and carelessness, and calls for fair compensation for damages, with the "eye for an eye" rule serving as a limit on revenge.
sum.17: Jethro, Moses' father-in-law, visits the camp along with Moses' wife and sons, and he praises God for rescuing Israel from Egypt. Seeing Moses worn out from judging the people alone, he advises him to choose capable, trustworthy men who fear God to help him. Moses listens, does as he suggests, and shares the burden with others.
sum.18: In the third month, Israel arrives in the Sinai desert. God reminds the people how he rescued them and offers them to be his special treasure, a kingdom of priests and a holy people, if they keep his covenant. The people promise to obey, they prepare themselves, and God comes down on the mountain with fire, smoke and thunder, showing his holiness.
sum.7: God tells Moses and Aaron to ask Pharaoh to let his people go, and He sends frogs, gnats, and flies over Egypt. The magicians copy the frogs but cannot produce the gnats, and they say, "This is the finger of God." Goshen is free of flies, and although Pharaoh promises to release the people once relief comes, he always hardens his heart.
sum.6: God tells Moses and Aaron to go and speak to Pharaoh, and warns that the king's heart will become hard. Aaron's staff turns into a snake and swallows the staffs of the magicians, but Pharaoh does not listen. Then the Nile River turns into blood, and even so Pharaoh refuses to let the people go.
sum.10: God tells Moses that He will bring one more plague, and that after it Pharaoh will let the people go. Moses announces that at midnight every firstborn in Egypt will die, but that Israel will be protected, so that it will be seen that God distinguishes between His own people and the Egyptians. Even so, Pharaoh remains hardened and does not let them leave.
sum.28: God explains to Moses how to set apart Aaron and his sons as priests: they are washed, dressed in their garments, anointed with oil, and sacrifices with blood are offered. He also commands that two lambs be offered every day. God promises to dwell among the Israelites and to be their God, the one who brought them out of Egypt.
sum.9: God sends a plague of locusts, which devours everything green that the hail had left behind. Then comes three days of thick darkness in Egypt, while the Israelites have light. Pharaoh admits his sin and asks for forgiveness, but he hardens his heart and does not let the people go. In the end he drives Moses away and forbids him to ever see him again.
sum.3: Moses fears that no one will believe him and that he is not a good speaker, but God gives him signs with the staff, the hand, and the water, and sends his brother Aaron to help him. Moses returns to Egypt with his family, and the people believe and worship when they hear that God has seen their suffering.
sum.30: God calls Bezalel, from the tribe of Judah, and Oholiab, from the tribe of Dan, and fills them with wisdom and skill to build the tabernacle and everything that would be used in it. Then God commands Israel to keep the Sabbath as a sign of the covenant between Him and His people, reminding them that He rested on the seventh day. When this is finished, He gives Moses the two stone tablets.
sum.13: God leads Israel to the sea, and Pharaoh pursues them with his army. The people are frightened, but Moses tells them that God will fight for them. God opens the sea so they can cross on dry ground, and then closes the waters over the Egyptians. The people believe in God and in Moses.
sum.1: A Hebrew mother hides her baby and places him in a basket in the river. Pharaoh's daughter finds him, rescues him, and raises him as her own son, naming him Moses. As an adult, Moses kills an Egyptian, flees to Midian, and there starts a family. Meanwhile, Israel cries out from its slavery, and God hears them and remembers his covenant.
sum.4: Moses and Aaron ask Pharaoh to let the people go to worship God, but he refuses and makes their work much harder by taking away the straw they used to make bricks. The Israelite foremen blame Moses, and Moses complains to God about why the people are suffering more and still have not been set free.
sum.37: In Exodus 38, Bezalel and Oholiab finish the bronze altar for burnt offerings, the bronze basin, and the courtyard with its linen curtains and pillars, just as the LORD had commanded. Then the people's gold, silver, and bronze offerings are accounted for. The chapter teaches that worship of God is built on devotion, order, and offerings given from the heart.
sum.38: The craftsmen made the sacred garments for Aaron and his sons: the ephod, the breastpiece with twelve stones bearing the names of the tribes, the robe with its bells, and the plate that read "Holy to the LORD." Everything was made just as the LORD had commanded, and when Moses saw the finished work, he blessed the people.
sum.15: The people of Israel complained of hunger in the desert, and God responded by sending quail in the evening and manna every morning. Each family was to gather only what it needed, and on the sixth day twice as much, so they could rest on the Sabbath. The chapter teaches trust in God's daily care and obedience to him.
sum.25: God gives Moses instructions for building the tabernacle: fine linen curtains with cherubim woven into them, coverings made of goat hair and of skins, frames of acacia wood overlaid with gold, and bases of silver. He also commands a veil that separates the Holy Place from the Most Holy Place, where the ark of the testimony will be placed. Everything was to be made according to the pattern shown on the mountain.
sum.8: In Exodus 9, God sends three plagues on Egypt: the death of the livestock, boils, and hail mixed with fire, while He protects Israel and the land of Goshen. Pharaoh acknowledges his sin, but when the punishment stops, he hardens his heart again. The chapter shows God's power and the danger of ignoring His word.
sum.5: God promises Moses that he will free Israel with a mighty hand, and he reveals his name, Jehovah, reminding Moses of his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. The Israelites do not listen because of their distress, and Moses doubts that Pharaoh will pay attention to him. The chapter also includes the genealogy of Levi, the tribe from which Moses and Aaron come.
sum.29: God tells Moses to make an altar for burning incense, and explains that Aaron will use it every morning and every evening. He also requires a ransom of half a shekel from each person counted in the census, a bronze basin for washing before ministering, and a holy anointing oil and a holy incense, reserved exclusively for God.
sum.22: In Exodus 23, God commands justice and impartiality: do not lie, do not accept bribes, help even your enemy, and care for the foreigner. He also orders rest every seventh day and every seventh year, and the celebration of three festivals each year. He promises to send his Angel to guide and protect Israel, and warns them not to serve other gods.
sum.0: In Exodus 1, the descendants of Jacob grow greatly in Egypt, and a new pharaoh, fearing their strength, oppresses them with hard labor. Two midwives, Shiphrah and Puah, fear God and do not kill the Hebrew boys, and God blesses them. Even so, the pharaoh orders that every boy be thrown into the river.
sum.32: God tells Israel that they may go to the promised land, but that he will not go up in the midst of them because of their stubbornness. Moses intercedes, asking that God's presence go with them and that God show him his glory. God agrees and promises to pass before him, protecting him in the cleft of the rock.
sum.24: God tells Moses to ask the people to bring offerings, given willingly from the heart, so that they can build a sanctuary where He may dwell among them. He gives Moses detailed instructions for making the ark of the testimony with its cover and two cherubim, the table for the bread, and the gold lampstand, all according to the pattern He showed him on the mountain.
sum.23: God calls Moses, Aaron, and the elders to come near, and the people promise to obey everything He has said. Moses seals the covenant with an altar, sacrifices, and blood, and the leaders see God and eat in His presence. Then Moses goes up the mountain, into the cloud and the glory of God, and stays there for forty days.
sum.31: While Moses was taking a long time to come down from the mountain, the people asked Aaron to make them gods. He made a golden calf, and they worshiped it. Moses pleaded for them, broke the tablets, and about three thousand people died. God showed that sin brings consequences, but also that he listens to the one who prays for his people.
sum.14:
Moses and Israel sang to God because he had saved them from Pharaoh's army at the sea, and Miriam led the women with tambourines and dancing.

Then, in the desert, the people complained about the bitter water at Marah. God made the water sweet and taught them to obey him, and they came to Elim, where there was water and palm trees.
sum.39: God told Moses to set up the tabernacle, put each piece of furniture in its place, and anoint Aaron and his sons with oil to serve as priests. Moses did everything exactly as he was commanded. When the work was finished, the cloud and the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle. From then on, Israel would travel or rest depending on whether the cloud lifted or stayed in place.
sum.26: In Exodus 27, God gives Moses instructions for building the altar of acacia wood overlaid with bronze, with horns at its corners and rings for carrying it. It also describes the courtyard of the tabernacle, with linen curtains and pillars. At the end, God commands that pure olive oil be brought so that Aaron and his sons can keep the lamps burning every night.
sum.27: God tells Moses to set apart Aaron and his sons to serve as priests, and to have skilled craftsmen make sacred garments for them, using gold, fine fabrics, and precious stones. The names of the twelve tribes of Israel would be placed on their shoulders and over their hearts, and a plate on their forehead would read "Holiness to the LORD." In this way it is shown that serving God calls for reverence.
sum.11: In Exodus 12, God commands Israel to sacrifice a lamb without blemish and put its blood on the doorposts and the top of the door, so that the judgment would pass over them. That night every firstborn in Egypt dies, and Pharaoh lets the people go. God establishes the Passover as a lasting reminder of his deliverance.
